c.d: An untargeted, bulk-sent phishing email — sent to many unrelated recipients with no individual tailoring — whose delivery mechanism or payload type has not yet been determined.
An untargeted, bulk-sent phishing email carrying a malicious attachment (macro-enabled document, malicious archive, disguised executable, etc.) intended to compromise the recipient's device on open.
An untargeted, bulk-sent phishing email containing a link to a fake login page designed to capture usernames and passwords directly, without a real-time relay to the legitimate service.

An untargeted, bulk-sent phishing campaign using a reverse-proxy phishing kit (e.g. Evilginx-style) that transparently relays the victim's real credentials and MFA approval to the legitimate service while capturing the resulting session cookie for account takeover.

An untargeted, bulk-sent phishing email or flyer containing a QR code that, when scanned (typically with a personal/unmanaged mobile device), directs the victim to a credential-harvesting or malware-delivery page.

An untargeted, bulk-sent phishing email that impersonates a recognizable brand or online service — using its logo, tone, and typical notification format — to induce the recipient to click through, regardless of the specific payload mechanism used.

An untargeted phishing email or web pop-up impersonating a software vendor or browser update notification, inducing the victim to download and run a malicious installer disguised as a legitimate update.

A phishing or malware-delivery page reached when an employee clicks a malicious search-engine ad or a poisoned organic search result — commonly for common software downloads — rather than through an emailed lure.

c.n: Unclassified / General Targeted Spear Phishing Campaign
c.d: A phishing email crafted and sent to a specific, identifiable individual or small group — using personal or organizational detail to increase credibility — whose delivery mechanism has not yet been confirmed.
A phishing email sent to a specific individual, carrying a malicious attachment whose filename or content is tailored to reference that individual's role, project, or context.

A phishing email sent to a specific individual, containing a link to a fake login page tailored to the target's organization (e.g., a spoofed internal SSO portal), without real-time session-token relay.

A phishing attack against a specific individual using a reverse-proxy AiTM kit that relays the real login flow and steals the resulting session token, bypassing standard MFA for that targeted account.

A targeted phishing email sent from an already-compromised legitimate email account belonging to a trusted colleague, partner, or vendor, leveraging that account's real trust relationship to reach a further target.
A targeted phishing email that impersonates a trusted sender's identity through display-name spoofing or a lookalike sending domain, without the sender's actual mailbox having been compromised.

A targeted phishing attack conducted across multiple messages over time — an initial benign or rapport-building message followed by a later message carrying the actual malicious link or attachment — designed to lower the target's guard before the payload arrives.

A targeted phishing email inducing a specific individual to grant a malicious third-party application OAuth consent (e.g., mailbox read access) via a legitimate identity-provider consent prompt, rather than harvesting a password directly.

A phishing message or physical lure sent to a specific individual containing a QR code — tailored with the target's context (e.g., referencing a real meeting or delivery) — that directs a scan to a credential-harvesting or malware page.

A phishing message that closely replicates a real, previously seen legitimate email — reusing its formatting, branding, and often its actual prior content — with a malicious link or attachment substituted in, whose exact cloning mechanism is not yet known.

A phishing attack in which an attacker who has gained access to a mailbox (or a downstream copy of a thread) sends a malicious reply into a genuinely ongoing email conversation, relying on the thread's real history to appear legitimate to other participants.

A phishing attack in which a genuinely legitimate email is intercepted before reaching its intended recipient — via a compromised mail server, relay, or malicious forwarding/transport rule — and then resent to the recipient with a malicious link or attachment substituted in.

A phishing email that closely replicates a legitimate, publicly observable communication template — such as a standard vendor newsletter or system notification format — without any actual interception of a specific real message or mailbox compromise.

A phishing email cloned from a real prior message in which the original legitimate attachment has been replaced with a malicious file, while the rest of the message content is preserved to maintain credibility.

A phishing email cloned from a real prior message in which the original legitimate hyperlink has been replaced with a malicious link, while the rest of the message content is preserved to maintain credibility.

A phishing attack whose defining characteristic is a landing site that is a near-exact functional and visual replica of the legitimate destination it impersonates — including working secondary pages, correct branding, and realistic error handling — regardless of how the victim was directed to it.
A phishing attack that clones a real prior message or thread to deliver a link into an AiTM reverse-proxy kit, which relays the real login flow and steals the resulting session token.

A phishing message cloned from a real prior communication and sent to a broad distribution list or group alias — via a compromised list-management account or spoofed list address — rather than to a single hijacked thread's participants.

A phishing attack specifically directed at a senior executive, board member, or other high-value individual, whose specific technique (attachment, link, AiTM, personal-channel targeting, etc.) has not yet been confirmed.

A phishing attack directed not at the executive directly but at their executive assistant or another delegate who holds proxy access to the executive's communications, calendar, or approval authority, exploiting that access as a softer entry point.

A phishing attack directed at senior executives or board members using a lure themed as board governance, investor relations, or M&A-related communication, exploiting the sensitivity and urgency typical of that content.

A phishing attack directed at a senior executive's personal email address, personal phone/messaging app, or personal device, deliberately bypassing corporate email security controls that would apply to their work account.

A phishing attack against a senior executive timed to coincide with their known travel itinerary or a public event appearance, using publicly gathered (OSINT) detail about the trip or event to increase the lure's credibility and urgency.
A phishing email sent to a senior executive carrying a malicious attachment tailored to reference their role, organization, or a plausible business document they would expect to receive.

A phishing email sent to a senior executive containing a link to a fake login page tailored to the organization, designed to capture the executive's credentials directly without real-time session-token relay.
A phishing attack against a senior executive using a reverse-proxy AiTM kit that relays the real login flow and steals the resulting session token, bypassing standard MFA for the executive's account.

A phishing email sent from an already-compromised legitimate email account, directed at a senior executive and leveraging that account's real trust relationship with the executive to increase credibility.
A phishing-style email sent as part of a verified, organizationally sanctioned security-awareness testing program, logged here before the specific outcome (passed, failed, sponsor type) is recorded.

A phishing-style email that claims or implies it is part of a sanctioned internal security test, but which does not match any registered campaign in the security awareness program and cannot be verified as legitimate — handled as a suspected genuine attack pending verification.

A logged outcome of a sanctioned phishing simulation in which the targeted employee interacted with the simulated lure — clicking a link, opening an attachment, or submitting credentials into a simulated capture form.

A logged outcome of a sanctioned phishing simulation in which the targeted employee correctly identified the email as suspicious and reported it through the proper channel (report-phishing button or mailbox) without clicking or submitting information.

A tracked pattern in which a specific employee fails (per ITID-11153) multiple sanctioned phishing simulations within a defined program window, indicating elevated individual phishing susceptibility requiring targeted intervention.

A sanctioned phishing simulation campaign executed through a third-party security-awareness vendor's platform (e.g., a commercial phishing-simulation-as-a-service provider) under a verified contract with the organization.

A sanctioned phishing simulation campaign designed and executed by the organization's internal red team, intended as a population-wide security-awareness test rather than a stealth, narrowly-scoped intrusion exercise.

A sanctioned phishing simulation campaign that was misconfigured or technically flawed in its execution — for example, sent to the wrong distribution list, using an inappropriate or overly realistic template, or with broken click/reporting telemetry — requiring operational correction.

An unsolicited phone call in which the caller falsely claims to represent a specific trusted identity (institution, colleague, or individual) in order to manipulate the recipient, whose specific impersonated identity has not yet been confirmed.

A phone call in which the caller falsely claims to represent the recipient's bank or another financial institution, typically citing suspicious account activity, in order to extract account credentials, card details, or authorization for a transaction.

c.n: Law Enforcement / Government Agency Impersonation Call
c.d: A phone call in which the caller falsely claims to represent a law enforcement agency, tax authority, or other government body, typically threatening legal consequence, arrest, or fines to compel the recipient to disclose information or make a payment.

A phone call in which the caller falsely claims to represent a known vendor or supplier, using the existing business relationship to request updated payment details, sensitive account information, or system access.

A phone call in which the caller falsely claims to be a specific, known internal colleague — often a superior or someone in another department — to induce the recipient to disclose information or take an action they would not for an unknown caller.

c.n: AI Voice Clone / Deepfake Impersonation Call
c.d: A phone call in which the caller uses AI-generated synthetic audio that closely mimics the voice of a specific real, known individual (an executive, colleague, or family member), in order to impersonate them convincingly enough to defeat voice recognition as a trust signal.

A phone call in which the caller falsely claims to be a family member of the recipient, typically claiming to be in an emergency (arrested, injured, in trouble) requiring an urgent, often untraceable payment.

A phone call in which the caller, posing as a trusted party (bank, IT support, etc.), induces the victim to read aloud a one-time passcode they just received, or to approve a live MFA push notification, so the attacker can complete an authentication in real time.

A phone call in which the caller falsely claims to be from the organization's own internal security, IT, or fraud team, asserting that the recipient's account or device has already been compromised in a prior incident, in order to induce urgent compliance with a request (password reset, remote access, information disclosure).

An unsolicited phone call whose primary apparent goal is to induce the recipient to make a payment, disclose financial account detail, or authorize a financial transaction, whose specific mechanism (live-transfer, robocall funnel, threat-based coercion, etc.) has not yet been confirmed.

A financial fraud phone call in which the victim is transferred, mid-call, between multiple colluding fraudulent personas (e.g., a 'bank representative' who transfers to a 'fraud investigator' who transfers to 'law enforcement'), each reinforcing the pretext and increasing pressure to comply.

A financial fraud phone call in which a single caller, maintaining one persona, creates urgency around a time-limited window to induce the victim to make an immediate payment before the call ends, without resorting to legal or personal threats.

A financial fraud phone call that begins as a pre-recorded automated robocall (often via an IVR-style menu) and, upon victim engagement (e.g., pressing a key to 'speak to a representative'), connects the victim to a live fraudulent agent to complete the scam.

A financial fraud attack initiated by a voicemail message — often citing an urgent account or legal matter — that prompts the recipient to call back a provided number, at which point the victim is connected to a live fraudulent agent who initiates the scam.

c.n: Multi-Channel Financial Fraud Call (Call + Email/Text Corroboration)
c.d: A financial fraud phone call that is deliberately corroborated by a supporting email or SMS message — sent shortly before, during, or after the call — designed to lend the call additional credibility by appearing to independently confirm its claims.

c.n: Spoofed Internal Extension Financial Fraud Call
c.d: A financial fraud phone call in which the caller spoofs the caller ID to display a specific known internal extension or phone number belonging to the organization, using that technical spoofing (rather than a claimed name alone) as the primary trust signal.

A financial fraud phone call in which the caller explicitly threatens a specific negative consequence — arrest, service disconnection, legal action, or harm — if the victim does not make an immediate payment.

A financial fraud phone call that incorporates specific, accurate detail about the target, their organization, or an executive's activity (schedule, travel, org structure) gathered through prior reconnaissance, used to substantially increase the call's credibility.

c.n: Unclassified / General SMS Credential Harvesting Link
c.d: An SMS or SMS-like text message containing a link to a fake login/credential-capture page, logged before the specific lure theme (delivery, banking, carrier, toll, etc.) has been confirmed or where the lure does not clearly match a more specific sibling leaf.

A smishing message impersonating a shipping carrier or retailer (USPS, FedEx, UPS, DHL, Amazon, etc.), claiming a delivery problem, redelivery fee, or customs charge, with a link to a fake login or payment-and-account page.
A smishing message impersonating a bank or financial institution, claiming fraud, a locked card, or suspicious activity, with a link to a fake bank login page.

c.n: Toll Road / Parking Violation Payment Smishing
c.d: A smishing message claiming an unpaid toll or parking fine, threatening late fees or legal action, with a link to a fake payment portal that captures card details and/or account credentials.
A smishing message impersonating the target's mobile carrier, warning of an account suspension or billing issue, with a link to a fake carrier-account login page.

c.n: Fake Login Verification Code Link Smishing
c.d: A smishing message stating a verification code was sent or is needed, but whose link leads to a fake login page capturing username and password — no OTP/code is actually requested back from the victim.

A smishing message using a shortened URL, homoglyph/lookalike domain, or open-redirect chain to disguise the true destination of a credential-harvesting link, logged when the obfuscation technique — used to evade carrier or URL filtering — is the primary point of interest, independent of or spanning multiple lure themes.

A credential-harvesting smishing message delivered through iMessage or RCS (Rich Communication Services), leveraging rich link previews, images, or interactive buttons — a delivery channel that often bypasses carrier-level plain-SMS filtering.

A spear-smishing message crafted using organization-specific reconnaissance (the target's real name, internal tool branding, department context) impersonating the organization's own SSO or VPN login, aimed at harvesting corporate credentials for enterprise entry.

An SMS or SMS-like text message containing a link intended to install malware on the recipient's mobile device, logged before the specific delivery mechanism (fake update, malicious profile, drive-by exploit, etc.) is confirmed.

c.n: Fake App Update / Sideload APK Smishing
c.d: A smishing message claiming an app or OS update is required, linking to a malicious APK for the target to sideload outside the official app store.

A smishing message linking to a malicious iOS configuration profile (or MDM enrollment profile) which, once installed, grants the attacker device-management-level control, certificate trust, or traffic-interception capability — an iOS-specific vector with no direct Android equivalent.

c.n: Fake Voicemail / Media Player App Smishing
c.d: A smishing message claiming the target has a new voicemail or needs a media/codec player to view content, linking to a malicious app install rather than a system-update or security pretext.

A smishing link that, upon being opened in the mobile browser, exploits a browser or OS vulnerability to compromise the device directly, without the victim needing to download, sideload, or install anything.
A smishing message claiming the target's device is infected or at risk, urging installation of a 'security' or 'antivirus' app that is in fact a malware trojan.

A smishing message delivering a malware-install link, sent immediately after or as part of a completed/attempted SIM swap, exploiting the hijacked number's inherited trust or the confusion window during the swap to push malware onto the victim or a related contact.

A QR code (on a physical flyer, poster, or compromised screen) that, when scanned, opens or pre-fills an SMS conversation which then delivers a malware-installation link — classified here because the payload delivery occurs via the SMS channel, even though the initial lure is a QR code.

A smishing message targeting an employee's corporate-owned or BYOD device, spoofing an internal MDM enrollment or device-compliance notification, to get the employee to enroll into an attacker-controlled MDM profile or install an attacker-controlled management agent.

c.n: Unclassified / General SMS OTP/MFA Fatigue Attempt
c.d: An SMS-based attempt to obtain, relay, or exploit a one-time-passcode or MFA-related code, logged before the specific tactic (fake code flood, real trigger+relay ask, spoofed sender, volume barrage, etc.) is confirmed.

A flood of SMS messages that look like OTP codes but are not tied to any real, backend-triggered authentication event; sent purely to desensitize, confuse, or bait the target into replying with information (or simply to erode trust in legitimate OTP messages).

c.n: Real OTP Trigger + Relay Request Smishing
c.d: An attacker-initiated real login or password-reset attempt that causes a genuine OTP SMS to be sent to the victim, followed by a separate text message asking the victim to reply with or forward that code.

A text message posing as a security alert asking the target to confirm or deny a login attempt by replying (e.g., 'Reply YES to approve' or 'Tap to confirm'), exploiting alert fatigue and the routine nature of such confirmations rather than soliciting an explicit numeric code.

c.n: Spoofed OTP Short Code Impersonation Smishing
c.d: A fake OTP/MFA-related text sent using a spoofed sender ID or short code matching a legitimate service's real OTP sender, causing the fraudulent message to appear in the same conversation thread as the victim's genuine past OTP messages, substantially increasing perceived legitimacy.

A high-frequency barrage of genuine, backend-triggered OTP SMS messages against a single account within a short time window, intended to fatigue or confuse the victim into forwarding or approving one out of frustration.

A text message warning that the target's account will be locked unless they act immediately, driving urgency without necessarily including an OTP code — the call to action is to reply, call back, or click a link 'to prevent lockout.'

An OTP/MFA fatigue trigger or barrage deliberately timed to late night, early morning, or other off-hours periods, exploiting reduced alertness and slower verification behavior to increase the odds of an erroneous approval or code relay.

An OTP/MFA fatigue attack that triggers authentication attempts across multiple different accounts or services belonging to the same target (e.g., corporate SSO, personal email, and banking simultaneously), overwhelming the victim and increasing the odds that at least one approval or code relay slips through.

An interaction (email, chat, ticket, in-person, or other non-voice-call channel) in which an attacker poses as a representative of a known or plausible vendor to make a request of staff, logged before the specific request type is confirmed.
An attacker posing as a known vendor's representative, contacting staff to request a password reset, credential handoff, or disclosure of a shared vendor-portal account's login details.
An attacker posing as a vendor technician, delivery contractor, or maintenance representative, requesting or attempting physical access to a facility under a fabricated service pretext.

An attacker posing as a vendor's representative, asking staff to install a piece of software, a monitoring/support agent, or an 'update' on organization systems — a potential malware-delivery vector achieved through social pretext rather than a malicious link.
An attacker posing as a vendor's representative, requesting sensitive internal data, reports, or exports under a plausible business pretext (e.g., 'we need this for our audit/integration').

c.n: Fake Vendor Banking/Payment Detail Change Request
c.d: An attacker posing as a known vendor's representative, contacting accounts-payable/finance staff to request a change to the vendor's banking or payment details, in order to redirect future payments to an attacker-controlled account.

An attacker posing as a vendor's representative, attempting to manipulate the procurement or contracting process — for example, requesting an approval bypass, an expedited purchase order, or altered contract terms — rather than directly requesting credentials, data, or a payment-detail change.

c.n: Fake Vendor Support Ticket/Portal Access Request
c.d: An attacker posing as a vendor's support representative, requesting elevated access to the organization's internal ticketing system or portal, or asking staff to grant the vendor account elevated permissions, under a support-related pretext.

A fake vendor request — of any type (access, data, payment, software) — where the attacker's primary lever is manufactured urgency or crisis framing (e.g., 'critical outage, we need this now') intended to short-circuit the target's normal verification process.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fake IT Support Request
c.d: An interaction in which an attacker poses as the organization's own internal IT/help-desk staff to make a request of an employee, logged before the specific request type is confirmed.

An attacker posing as internal IT/help-desk staff, contacting an employee to request they reveal their current password or perform a password reset in a way that discloses or resets credentials to attacker control.

c.n: Fake IT Remote Access Tool Installation Request
c.d: An attacker posing as internal IT staff, instructing an employee to install a remote access/remote support tool (e.g., AnyDesk, TeamViewer, or similar) on their device — granting the attacker direct remote control once installed.

An attacker posing as internal IT/help-desk staff via chat, ticket, email, or an in-person/ambiguous-channel interaction, requesting the employee approve an MFA push notification or read out an OTP/security code.

An attacker posing as internal IT, notifying an employee that their device has been flagged as non-compliant and instructing them to take a remediation action (install an agent, change a setting, provide device access) that in fact compromises the device.

An attacker posing as internal IT handling a (fabricated) new-hire onboarding or employee-offboarding action, requesting account creation, credential handoff, or an access transfer under that process pretext.

c.n: Fake IT Software License/Update Compliance Request
c.d: An attacker posing as internal IT, contacting an employee to enforce (fabricated) software-license or update-compliance requirements, pushing a malicious 'compliance' download or requesting license-key/account information.

c.n: Fake IT Help Desk Callback Verification Request
c.d: An attacker posing as internal IT/help-desk, instructing the employee to call back a given number 'to verify their identity' or resolve an issue — where the number is attacker-controlled, exploiting the general trust placed in callback-based verification.
An attacker posing as internal IT running a (fabricated) data backup or system migration project, requesting the employee provide access, credentials, or a data export under that project pretext.

c.n: Unclassified / General Executive Fraud Support Request
c.d: A channel-agnostic, interactive impersonation of an organization's executive (phone, text, chat, or in-person) directed at a subordinate or staff member to manipulate them into an action, logged before the specific request type is confirmed.

c.n: Fake Executive Gift Card Purchase Request
c.d: An attacker posing as an executive, contacting an employee via an interactive channel (text, chat, in-person) to urgently request the purchase of gift cards on the executive's behalf, with the gift card codes to be sent back to the attacker.

c.n: Fake Executive Urgent Task/Personal Favor Request
c.d: An attacker posing as an executive, requesting an employee handle an urgent personal errand or favor (beyond a specific gift card, document, or approval request) as a way to establish rapport and authority pressure before a further ask.
An attacker posing as an executive, requesting an employee urgently and confidentially send sensitive internal documents, financial reports, or data.

An attacker posing as an executive or their assistant, manipulating calendar entries or meeting arrangements — inserting a fake call, redirecting a real one, or altering meeting details — to create an opportunity for a further social-engineering or fraud attempt.

An attacker posing as an executive, giving a fraudulent approval or sign-off — for a transaction, an access grant, a policy exception, or a document — to unblock a process that legitimately requires that executive's authorization, where the approval is not specifically a wire-transfer authorization.

An attacker posing as an executive who is (supposedly) traveling and hard to reach, requesting an employee make or change travel arrangements — or use that framing to justify other unusual, hard-to-verify requests made 'while I'm away'.

An attacker posing as an executive, whose primary tactic is an explicit insistence on confidentiality or secrecy ('don't tell anyone', 'don't call me, I'll call you', 'keep this between us') used specifically to suppress the target's normal instinct to verify the request through another channel.

An attacker posing as an executive, claiming to be locked out or without access, asking an employee to share their own account credentials, badge access, or perform an action on the executive's behalf using the employee's own access.

An unsolicited offer of a reward, prize, gift, or benefit used as a pretext to get the target to click a link, share information, pay a fee, or take an action, without enough detail captured to classify it under a more specific incentive type.

A message notifying the target that they have won a prize, lottery, or sweepstakes they never entered, requiring them to pay a fee, provide personal/financial details, or click a link to 'claim' the winnings.

A message offering a reward (cash, gift card, points) in exchange for completing a survey, where the survey itself is a pretext to harvest personal/financial data or redirect the target to a malicious site.
An unsolicited offer of a free product, gift, or sample requiring the target to pay a small shipping fee or provide personal/payment details to receive it.

A message impersonating an internal HR/rewards program, notifying an employee of a recognition award or bonus and directing them to a fake portal to 'claim' it, harvesting credentials or banking details.
A message claiming the target's loyalty program points are expiring or can be redeemed for a discount, directing them to a fake login/redemption page that harvests account credentials or card data.

A message claiming an employer, vendor, or public figure will 'match' the target's charitable donation, directing them to donate through a fraudulent portal that pockets the funds instead of forwarding them.
A message claiming the target is owed a referral bonus for a job candidate they referred, directing them to a fake HR portal to 'confirm' banking or identity details to receive payment.

An offer of a free trial for a software product or online service that requires payment-card registration and either bills the target without proper disclosure or delivers a malicious installer/app instead of the advertised product.

An attacker posing as legitimate technical support convinces the target their device has a problem requiring paid assistance, remote access, or software installation, without enough detail captured to classify the initiation vector.

A full-screen browser pop-up or scareware alert falsely claims the device is infected or locked and instructs the target to call a phone number for 'support', leading into a paid remediation or remote-access scam.

An attacker cold-calls the target claiming to be from a well-known technology vendor, alleging a detected problem with the target's device and pressuring them into a paid remediation or remote-access session.

c.n: Fake Remote Desktop Session Tech Support Scam
c.d: As part of a tech support scam, the target installs a remote-access tool and grants the attacker a live remote desktop session, during which the attacker may install malware, harvest data, or manipulate the target into authorizing a payment.

An attacker claims to owe the target a refund for prior tech support services, deliberately 'overpays' (often via a fabricated bank transfer receipt or manipulated on-screen balance), and pressures the target to return the difference via gift cards or wire transfer.

During a tech support scam, the target is directed to download and run a fake diagnostic or 'PC health check' tool that displays fabricated errors, malware detections, or performance warnings to justify a paid remediation service.

c.n: Fake Corporate Help Desk Vendor Callback Scam
c.d: An attacker impersonates a legitimate third-party vendor's technical support representative, calling an organization's IT/help desk staff to offer unsolicited 'assistance' with a supposed vendor-side issue, aiming to gain remote access to corporate systems.

An attacker poses as printer or peripheral-device support (often via a fake support number found through a poisoned search result), convincing the target to grant remote access or pay for a service to resolve a fabricated printer/peripheral issue.

A fake renewal or upgrade notice for security/antivirus software (often referencing a real vendor the target already uses) prompts a call to a fraudulent support number, leading into a paid remediation or remote-access scam.

An adversary leaves a removable USB device somewhere a target is likely to find and plug it in out of curiosity or good intent, without enough detail captured to classify the specific drop location or lure mechanism.
A USB device is deliberately left in a parking lot, sidewalk, smoking area, or other external grounds area near a facility, relying on a passerby's curiosity to pick it up and plug it into a device.

A USB device bearing a curiosity-provoking label or branding (e.g., 'Confidential', 'Salaries', 'Executive Bonuses') is left where a target will find it, exploiting curiosity to drive a higher plug-in rate than an unlabeled device.

A USB device is mailed or couriered to a target — often accompanied by a letter impersonating a known brand, government agency, or internal department — to lend it legitimacy and increase the likelihood it is plugged in.

A USB device is distributed as apparent promotional swag at a conference, trade show, or networking event — either from a fraudulent booth/vendor or by tampering with a legitimate sponsor's giveaway stock — exploiting the trust attendees place in event-branded items.

A USB device is deliberately left inside a secured internal facility area (desk, break room, printer station) rather than an external or public location, indicating the attacker gained some level of physical facility access to place it.

An adversary leaves or gifts a USB charging cable, adapter, or other small accessory that has been modified to act as a keystroke-injection or data-exfiltration device, exploiting the fact that a cable is far less likely to be treated with suspicion than a flash drive.

A USB device bearing the branding of a trusted vendor or business partner is left or delivered to the target, exploiting the existing trust relationship rather than curiosity, to increase the likelihood it is plugged in without suspicion.

A USB device is deliberately placed to appear as though someone innocently lost it (e.g., near a lost-and-found desk, in a common area with an apparent personal item attached), exploiting the target's good-faith intent to identify the owner by plugging it in.

A target is lured into downloading a file advertised as one thing (software, media, a document) that is actually malicious, without enough detail captured to classify the specific content lure category.

A target downloads what is advertised as a cracked/pirated version of paid commercial software (e.g., a keygen or crack tool) from an untrusted site, which is actually malware or bundled with malware.
A target downloads what is advertised as a video game cheat, mod, or trainer from an untrusted site or forum, which is actually malware or bundled with malware.

A target downloads what is advertised as a media file (movie, TV episode, or music album) via a torrent or direct-download site, which is actually malware disguised with a media file extension or bundled codec/player installer.

A target downloads what is advertised as a free productivity tool or system utility (PDF converter, file compressor, cleanup tool) from search results or an ad, which is actually malware or a potentially unwanted program bundled with malware.

An attacker applies for an open position or otherwise reaches a recruiter/hiring manager, attaching or linking to a 'resume' or 'portfolio' file that is actually malware, exploiting the recipient's expectation of routine document review.

A target is prompted (via a fake pop-up, spoofed email, or search result) to download what is presented as an official update or installer from a specific known software vendor, which is actually malware.
A target downloads what is advertised as an AI tool, model weights, or AI content-generation application (capitalizing on current AI trend interest) from an untrusted site, which is actually malware.

A developer is lured — via a forum post, fake GitHub repository, or search result — into manually cloning or downloading a package/repository presented as a legitimate open-source project, which actually contains malicious code.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fake Social Media Profile
c.d: A fabricated social media profile created to deceive, without enough detail captured to classify the specific persona type it impersonates.

A social media profile impersonating a recruiter or talent-acquisition professional, used to establish contact with job-seeking targets as a pretext for a later scam (fake job offer, data harvesting, or malware delivery).

A social media profile impersonating a specific named executive or colleague from the target's own organization, used to build false trust for a subsequent request (financial, informational, or credential-related) directed at other employees.

A social media profile impersonating a known vendor's or brand's official corporate account (rather than a specific named individual), used to deceive customers, partners, or the public — often for phishing, fraud, or reputational harm.
A fabricated social media/dating profile used to build a long-term romantic relationship with a target, ultimately leveraging that emotional trust to solicit money, gifts, or sensitive information.

c.n: Sock Puppet Network (Coordinated Fake Profile Cluster)
c.d: A coordinated cluster of multiple fake ('sock puppet') social media profiles, operated by the same actor or group, working together to amplify a message, manufacture apparent consensus, or reinforce a single scam narrative across many apparent independent voices.

A fabricated profile claiming membership in a group the target belongs to or values (a school alumni network, professional association, industry group, veteran's organization) to establish false in-group trust before pursuing a scam or data-harvesting objective.

c.n: Fake Profile Using Stolen Real Identity
c.d: A fake social media profile constructed using an actual real person's stolen name, photos, and biographical details — distinct from a wholly invented persona — used to deceive that real person's actual contacts or to commit fraud in their name.

A fake social media profile using AI-generated (deepfake/synthetic) photos and often AI-generated biographical text, constructed as an entirely fabricated persona with no direct real-world individual whose identity was stolen.
A scam conducted via a social media platform's direct messaging feature, without enough detail captured to classify the specific scam type or account status (fake vs. compromised).
An attacker who has compromised a real person's social media account uses it to send scam direct messages to that account's real contacts, exploiting the target's existing trust in the account owner.
A direct message offering a fake cryptocurrency or investment giveaway, requiring the target to send funds (often crypto) first with the promise of a larger amount returned, which is never paid back.

A direct message offering the target an unsolicited job opportunity — often with unrealistically high pay for minimal work — used to harvest personal/banking data under the guise of onboarding, or to extract an upfront fee for 'equipment' or 'training'.

An attacker monitors public complaints or mentions of a brand and sends a DM posing as that brand's official customer support, directing the target to a phishing link or requesting account/payment details to 'resolve' the issue.

An attacker joins a group chat, forum, or online community (often one with an established shared interest or trust, such as an investment or hobbyist group) as a new member, building credibility within the group before targeting individual members with a scam via direct message.

An attacker, via direct message, obtains or fabricates compromising images/video of the target (or claims to) and threatens to release them to the target's contacts or publicly unless a payment is made.

A direct message falsely claims the target's account is at risk of suspension, has been flagged, or requires urgent 'verification'/'recovery' action, directing them to a phishing page that harvests their login credentials.

c.n: QR Code/Link-in-DM Malware or Credential Scam
c.d: An attacker sends a QR code image or a shortened URL directly within a platform's direct messaging feature, leading the target to a credential-harvesting page or a malicious download, entirely within the messaging interaction.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Media Credential Harvesting Campaign
c.d: A campaign designed to harvest social media account credentials from targets, without enough detail captured to classify the specific pretext or mechanism used.
A phishing page precisely mimicking a social media platform's real login page, designed to capture the username and password entered by a target who was directed there via any pretext.

A target is lured (via a quiz, game, or utility app) into authorizing a malicious third-party application through the platform's legitimate OAuth consent flow, granting the attacker persistent API-level access to the target's account without ever capturing a password.

c.n: Fake Account Flagged/Under Review Credential Harvest
c.d: A message falsely claiming the target's account has been flagged for a violation and is under review or pending suspension, directing them to a fake login page to 'appeal' or 'verify' their identity, harvesting their credentials.

A message offering the target a free or discounted official verification badge (checkmark) for their social media account, directing them to a fake login/application page that harvests their credentials or payment card data.
A message falsely claiming the target has posted content violating copyright or community guidelines, directing them to a fake 'dispute' or 'appeal' login page to harvest their credentials.

A message offering the target a lucrative brand partnership or sponsorship deal, directing them to a fake login/application portal (often requiring re-authentication to 'confirm eligibility') that harvests their credentials.

c.n: Fake Platform Security Alert Credential Harvest
c.d: A message impersonating the social media platform's own security team, falsely claiming unusual login activity or a security issue with the target's account, directing them to a fake login page to 'secure' their account.

A message directed at the administrator of a social media group or business page, falsely claiming an admin-transfer or ownership-verification action is required, directing them to a fake login page that, once compromised, grants the attacker control of the group/page and its full audience.
An unauthorized person following an authorized person through a secured entry point without a specific pretext technique yet identified.
An unauthorized person gains entry by an authorized employee courteously holding a secured door open for them, exploiting social norms around politeness rather than any disguise or story.
An unauthorized person gains entry by appearing to have their hands full — carrying boxes, bags, or equipment — prompting an authorized employee to open or hold the door for them.
An unauthorized person gains entry by wearing a uniform, vest, or branded clothing/equipment associated with a trusted role (delivery, utility, contractor) to tailgate through a secured door.
An unauthorized person enters a secured facility by blending into a crowd or group (shift change, event, evacuation re-entry) where individual badge verification is not practically enforced.
An unauthorized person gains entry through a smoking-area door, loading dock, or other secondary entrance that employees prop open or use casually, bypassing the main reception/badge point entirely.

An individual follows an authorized employee out through a secured exit-only or badge-out door without their own exit being logged, typically used to leave undetected after gaining entry by other means or to probe exit-side control gaps.
An unauthorized vehicle follows an authorized vehicle through a gate, barrier arm, or car-park access point before it closes, bypassing vehicle-level credential checks.
An unauthorized person tailgates into a facility during after-hours, overnight, or low-staff periods when fewer employees are present to notice or challenge an unfamiliar face.
An adversary searching a facility's discarded waste for useful information or materials, with the specific waste stream (paper, electronics, badges, recycling) not yet identified.
An adversary retrieves discarded paper documents (memos, org charts, printed emails, phone lists) from waste receptacles to gather intelligence for a later social-engineering attack.
An adversary retrieves discarded electronic media (USB drives, external disks, backup tapes, optical media) from waste receptacles that may still hold recoverable data.
An adversary retrieves discarded IT equipment from waste or e-waste areas that may retain recoverable data or reusable components.
An adversary retrieves a discarded, deactivated, or improperly destroyed access badge or credential from waste to attempt reuse or cloning.
An adversary searches unsecured recycling bins — often positioned separately from general waste with lower physical security — for discarded sensitive materials.
An adversary conducts reconnaissance at a third-party waste hauler, landfill, or recycling facility handling the organization's waste, beyond the organization's direct physical controls.

An adversary searches waste generated at a company event or conference (badges, handouts, printed presentations, sign-in sheets) discarded in venue receptacles outside normal office disposal controls.

An adversary searches waste generated by an on-site vendor, contractor, or managed-service crew (e.g., a maintenance or IT contractor's discarded work notes, device packaging, or access documentation) rather than the organization's own employee waste stream.

An adversary physically presenting as someone they are not to gain facility access or cooperation, with the specific persona (delivery, maintenance, IT, cleaning, new-hire, auditor, interview candidate, emergency responder) not yet identified.
An adversary presents as delivery or courier personnel — using a branded uniform, packages, or handheld scanner props — to gain entry to a facility or reach a specific individual/area.
An adversary presents as a maintenance/facilities technician — carrying tools, a work order, or branded coveralls — to gain access to utility rooms, server closets, or restricted back-of-house areas.
An adversary presents as cleaning/janitorial staff — often after hours — to gain broad, low-scrutiny access to offices, desks, and unattended workstations.
An adversary presents as IT support or a telecom technician — citing a fabricated ticket or outage — to gain access to network infrastructure, server rooms, or an employee's workstation.

An adversary presents as a new hire or newly onboarded contractor — claiming their badge/credentials are still being processed — to be escorted or granted temporary access by staff unfamiliar with the actual onboarding roster.
An adversary presents as an external auditor, compliance inspector, or regulatory official — invoking implied authority to compel cooperation and gain access to records or restricted areas.
An adversary presents as a scheduled interview candidate to gain a plausible, escorted entry into the facility, potentially deviating from the escort to reach unauthorized areas.
An adversary presents as a firefighter, paramedic, utility crew member, or other emergency responder — leveraging the urgency of the persona to be waved through access controls without verification.
A phishing campaign deliberately coordinated across two or more communication channels against the same target, without enough detail captured to classify which specific channels were combined.

An attacker sends a phishing email and a coordinated SMS text to the same target — often referencing each other or reinforcing the same pretext — to increase credibility and give the target a second path to the malicious link.

An attacker sends a phishing email and follows up (or precedes it) with a live phone call to the same target, using the call to build urgency, walk the target through the email, or verbally provide credentials/codes the email link requests.

An attacker initiates contact via a social media platform (a connection request, DM, or comment) and follows up with a phishing email to the same target, using the social media contact to establish apparent legitimacy before the email lure.

An attacker embeds a QR code in one channel (a printed flyer, a screen during a video call, a physical notice) specifically to move the target from that channel onto their mobile device, where the actual phishing page or app-install prompt is delivered — with the channel bridge itself, not the destination content, being the differentiating feature.

An attacker leaves a voicemail (often via a spoofed number, sometimes AI-generated) referencing an urgent matter and directing the target to check an email that follows, using the voicemail to prime the target to trust and act on the email.

An attacker contacts the same target through more than one social media platform (e.g., a LinkedIn message and an Instagram DM referencing each other, or a coordinated cross-platform impersonation), reinforcing the same pretext across platforms without involving email, SMS, or voice.

An attacker begins contact on one channel and, upon detecting resistance, filtering, or suspicion, deliberately switches to a different channel to continue the same pretext — the escalation/evasion behavior itself, rather than a fixed channel pairing, is the defining feature.

An attacker builds and maintains a consistent fake identity or persona (name, title, photo, backstory) across multiple channels (email signature, LinkedIn profile, voicemail greeting) so that a target who cross-checks the story across channels finds it corroborated, reinforcing trust rather than raising suspicion.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cyber-Physical Social Engineering Attack
c.d: An attack deliberately combining a digital social-engineering component with a physical-world component against the same target or facility, without enough detail captured to classify the specific combination or sequencing.

An attacker uses digital means — social media reconnaissance, phishing for a badge photo or org chart, or a fake digital communication establishing a pretext — specifically to gather information or credentials used to carry out a later physical intrusion into a facility.

An attacker gains physical access to a facility (via tailgating, a fabricated visitor pretext, or an unlocked area) specifically in order to carry out a digital compromise — plugging into a network jack, accessing an unlocked workstation, or installing a rogue device — that would be harder to achieve remotely.

c.n: Fake Physical Mail/Package Bridging to Digital Lure
c.d: A fabricated physical letter or package is delivered to the target, directing them to a digital destination (a website, QR code, or phone number) to 'claim', 'verify', or 'track' something, using the physical delivery to lend credibility to the subsequent digital lure.

c.n: Digital Impersonation Confirmed via Physical Presence
c.d: An attacker who has established a digital impersonation (fake executive, vendor, or colleague identity) reinforces the pretext by physically showing up in person — at a facility, a meeting, or an event — matching the fabricated identity, to overcome any residual digital-verification skepticism.

c.n: Video Call Deepfake Combined with Physical Follow-up
c.d: An attacker uses AI-generated deepfake video and/or audio to impersonate a known individual on a live video call, and follows up with a real-world physical action (a package delivery, an in-person meeting, a physical document) to reinforce the pretext established during the deepfake call.

An attacker socially engineers access to or control of a smart building system or IoT device (smart locks, badge readers, HVAC, cameras) — via a fake vendor support call, a phished management-portal credential, or a fake maintenance request — to produce a physical-world effect such as unlocking a door or disabling a camera.

c.n: Fake Physical Signage/Notice Bridging to Digital Credential Harvest
c.d: A fabricated physical sign or notice (e.g., a fake 'Wi-Fi password reset' or 'password expiring, click here' notice posted in a common area) directs employees or visitors to a digital credential-harvesting page or QR code, exploiting the apparent legitimacy of an on-site physical posting.

An external attacker actively coordinates with a complicit or coerced insider, combining the insider's legitimate physical facility access with the external attacker's digital capabilities (credentials, malware, exfiltration infrastructure) to achieve a compromise neither could accomplish alone.

c.n: Phishing with Credential Harvest and Confirmed Submission
c.d: A phishing incident in which the victim was presented with a credential-harvesting page or form and is confirmed (via form-submission telemetry, attacker infrastructure logs, victim self-report, or observed anomalous login activity) to have entered valid credentials.

A phishing incident involving credential theft where the specific target system (SSO, VPN, cloud admin, email, SaaS, personal, or financial) has not yet been determined or does not fit a more specific sibling leaf.

A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for the organization's primary single sign-on or identity provider account (e.g. Okta, Azure AD/Entra ID, Ping, Google Workspace primary identity).
A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for a VPN client, remote desktop gateway, or other remote-access portal.

A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for a cloud administrative console or infrastructure-management account (e.g. AWS/Azure/GCP root or admin console, on-prem hypervisor/domain admin portal).
A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for a corporate or personal email/webmail account.

A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for a standalone SaaS or third-party application account (e.g. a project-management tool, CRM, or vendor portal) not tied to the corporate identity provider.

A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for a personal account (e.g. personal email, social media, personal cloud storage) but has confirmed or plausible corporate impact, typically via password reuse or stored corporate access on the same device.
A phishing incident in which the credential harvested was for a corporate banking portal, payment platform, or financial services account.

An incident involving suspected or confirmed keystroke-capture software or hardware where the specific mechanism (software, hardware, browser-based, kernel-level, RAT-embedded, mobile, cloud-session, or insider-installed) has not yet been identified.
A software keylogger installed on an endpoint via a malicious file, email attachment, or drive-by download, running in user-mode to capture keystrokes.
A physical device inserted inline between a keyboard and computer, or embedded within a keyboard/peripheral, that records keystrokes for later retrieval or wireless exfiltration.
A browser-based keylogger that captures keystrokes typed into web form fields via injected or malicious JavaScript running within the browser's rendering context.
A keylogger implemented as a kernel-mode driver or rootkit component that hooks keyboard input at a privilege level below standard EDR visibility.

c.n: Remote Access Trojan (RAT) with Keylogging Capability
c.d: A Remote Access Trojan installed on an endpoint that includes a keylogging module alongside broader remote-control capabilities (screen capture, file access, remote shell).
A malicious mobile application or exploit that captures keyboard input (including on-screen keyboard taps) on a smartphone or tablet.
A malicious or over-permissioned browser extension that captures keystrokes and/or session data specifically during interaction with cloud/SaaS applications.
A keylogger (hardware or software) installed by an individual with authorized access to the affected system or environment, for the purpose of surveilling another user's credentials or activity.

c.n: Unclassified / General Credential Harvesting Malware Incident
c.d: An incident involving malware confirmed or suspected of extracting stored credentials from an endpoint, where the specific target (browser passwords, memory, password manager vault, cached tokens, email client, Wi-Fi credentials, or commodity infostealer family) has not yet been identified.
Malware that reads and decrypts browser-stored credentials from the local password store (e.g. Chrome's Login Data SQLite database and associated DPAPI-protected encryption keys).
Malware or tooling that dumps and parses credential material directly from process memory (e.g. LSASS memory on Windows holding cached logon credentials/hashes).

Malware that locates and attempts to decrypt or exfiltrate a dedicated password manager application's local vault (e.g. a local encrypted vault file, unlocked in-memory vault contents, or clipboard capture during vault access).

Malware running on an infected endpoint that locates and exfiltrates cached browser session cookies, OAuth/SSO tokens, or other locally-stored authentication artifacts, typically to enable session replay without needing the original password.

c.n: Email Client Stored Credential Extraction Malware
c.d: Malware that reads stored email account credentials from a desktop email client's configuration files, registry entries, or credential cache.
Malware that reads stored Wi-Fi network profile credentials or other cached network authentication material (e.g. saved VPN pre-shared keys) from an endpoint's operating system configuration.

Infection by a widely available, commercially or freely distributed commodity infostealer malware family with built-in multi-target credential harvesting capability (browsers, wallets, FTP clients, etc.), delivered via a human-targeted vector (phishing, malicious ad, cracked software).

c.n: Credential Harvesting Malware via Trojanized Software
c.d: Credential harvesting malware bundled within a trojanized copy of otherwise legitimate or expected software (a cracked application, a fake update, or a supply-chain-compromised installer) that the victim knowingly installs believing it to be genuine.

Automated login attempts using previously breached username/password pairs against an organization's authentication endpoint, where the specific source (combolist, botnet, low-and-slow, API/mobile, SSO, SaaS, CAPTCHA-bypass) has not yet been identified.
Credential stuffing where the username/password pairs used are traceable to a specific, identified prior data breach combolist circulating on breach forums or dark-web marketplaces.
Credential stuffing where login attempts originate from a large number of distinct IP addresses consistent with a distributed botnet, used to evade IP-based rate limiting and blocklisting.

Credential stuffing conducted at a deliberately slow rate (e.g. one or a few attempts per account per hour/day, spread across a long campaign window) specifically to stay under automated detection thresholds.

Credential stuffing conducted directly against a backend API or mobile application authentication endpoint, often bypassing web-layer bot-management controls that only cover the browser-based login form.
Credential stuffing attempts made directly against the corporate SSO/identity provider login page.

c.n: Credential Stuffing Against a Specific SaaS Portal
c.d: Credential stuffing attempts made against a specific, individually-authenticated SaaS or third-party application login page.

Credential stuffing where the automated tooling successfully solves or bypasses CAPTCHA/bot-verification challenges, typically via a CAPTCHA-solving service, browser automation mimicking human behavior, or a CAPTCHA-farm.

c.n: Successful Credential Stuffing with Confirmed Account Takeover
c.d: A credential stuffing incident in which at least one login attempt succeeded and account takeover is confirmed via subsequent unauthorized activity, session establishment, or account-setting changes.

Login attempts using a small number of common passwords against many usernames, staying under per-account lockout thresholds, where the specific pattern (seasonal, botnet, low-and-slow, SSO, legacy protocol, org wordlist, VPN) has not yet been identified.
Password spraying using a set of passwords derived from predictable seasonal/date-based patterns commonly adopted by users under mandatory password rotation policies.
Password spraying where login attempts originate from a large number of distinct IP addresses consistent with a distributed botnet.
Password spraying conducted at a deliberately slow rate (e.g. one attempt per account per lockout-observation-window) specifically to remain under automated lockout and alerting thresholds.
Password spraying attempts made directly against the corporate SSO/identity provider login page.

c.n: Password Spraying Against Legacy/Non-MFA Protocol Endpoint
c.d: Password spraying attempts made against a legacy protocol endpoint that lacks modern authentication/MFA support, such that any successful password guess grants immediate account access with no secondary factor to stop it.
Password spraying using a custom wordlist built from organization-specific or industry-specific terminology, indicating attacker reconnaissance beyond generic common-password lists.
Password spraying attempts made against a VPN client or remote-access gateway login.

c.n: Successful Password Spraying with Confirmed Account Takeover
c.d: A password spraying incident in which at least one login attempt succeeded and account takeover is confirmed via subsequent unauthorized activity, session establishment, or account-setting changes.

Unauthorized or inappropriate use of a legitimately-shared or reused credential where the specific context (shared team account, vendor account, departed employee, cross-system reuse, service account, family device, documented password, or M&A legacy account) has not yet been identified.

Exploitation of a credential legitimately shared among multiple members of a team or department (e.g. a shared support mailbox login, a shared operations dashboard account) beyond its authorized use, by an authorized team member acting improperly or by an external party who obtained the shared credential.

Exploitation of a credential provided to a vendor or contractor organization and shared among multiple individuals at that vendor beyond the organization's authorization, or compromised at the vendor and reused against the organization.
Authentication or access using a credential belonging to an individual whose employment or engagement has ended, indicating an offboarding process failure.
Unauthorized access to a system achieved by reusing a password/credential obtained from a different system where the same individual had set an identical or closely similar password.

Unauthorized use of a non-human service/automation account credential that is shared across multiple applications, scripts, or integration points, typically discovered hardcoded or broadly distributed.

A corporate credential shared with a family member (e.g. for convenience, or by a minor using a parent's device) or otherwise exposed via use on a shared, multi-user personal/family device without adequate profile separation.
Unauthorized access achieved by discovering a credential that was written down or stored in plaintext in an easily accessible location, such as a sticky note, notebook, or unencrypted document.

Unauthorized use of a credential belonging to a legacy system or account structure inherited from a merged or acquired entity, where post-merger identity consolidation and access review was incomplete or delayed.

Systematic, exhaustive automated attempts to guess a password (as opposed to dictionary/wordlist or rainbow-table-based methods) where the specific method (offline hash, online interactive, GPU cluster, mask-based, SSH/admin protocol, API, PIN) has not yet been identified.

Exhaustive password guessing performed offline against a stolen password hash using local computing resources, with no interaction with the target system and therefore no lockout or rate-limiting exposure during the cracking process itself.

Exhaustive password guessing performed directly against a live login endpoint, one interactive authentication attempt at a time, subject to whatever lockout or rate-limiting controls the endpoint enforces.

Offline password cracking performed using GPU-accelerated hardware or a distributed compute cluster, dramatically increasing the feasible keyspace and hash strength that can be attacked within a practical timeframe.

Offline or online brute forcing constrained to a specific character-mask pattern (e.g. known minimum length, required character classes, or a known prefix/suffix convention) derived from knowledge of the organization's password policy, dramatically narrowing the effective keyspace versus a fully exhaustive attack.
Exhaustive or automated password-guessing attempts against an SSH server or comparable remote-administration protocol endpoint (e.g. Telnet, WinRM).
Exhaustive or automated password/API-key guessing attempts made directly against a backend API authentication endpoint.
Exhaustive guessing of a short numeric PIN code, exploiting the dramatically smaller keyspace compared to an alphanumeric password.

c.n: Successful Brute Force with Confirmed Access
c.d: A brute force incident (any of ITID-12312 through ITID-12318) in which the guessing attack succeeded and access to the target account or system is confirmed.

Password-guessing attempts using a curated wordlist of likely candidate passwords (as opposed to exhaustive brute forcing or precomputed rainbow tables), where the specific wordlist type (common list, org-specific, rule-based mutation, language-specific, hybrid, leaked list, trivial pattern) has not yet been identified.
Password-guessing attempts using a generic, publicly available list of the most common passwords, with no organization-specific or leaked-data targeting.
Password-guessing attempts using a custom wordlist built from organization-specific or industry-specific terminology (company name, products, jargon), indicating prior reconnaissance.

Password-guessing attempts using a wordlist processed through mutation/mangling rules (e.g. hashcat-style rule sets) that systematically apply common substitutions and appendages to base dictionary words to match typical complexity-policy patterns.

Password-guessing attempts using a dictionary wordlist derived from a specific non-primary language, indicating either targeting of a specific regional user population or an attacker of a particular linguistic background.

Password-guessing attempts that combine a curated dictionary word/phrase base with an exhaustively brute-forced suffix or prefix (e.g. dictionary word plus an exhaustively tried 2-4 digit number), blending both technique families.
Password-guessing attempts using a wordlist compiled from an actual, identifiable leaked or breached password dataset (as opposed to a generic synthetic common-password compilation).
Password-guessing attempts using extremely common, trivially guessable patterns that require minimal or no reconnaissance and succeed purely due to weak password hygiene.

c.n: Successful Dictionary Attack with Confirmed Access
c.d: A dictionary attack incident (any of ITID-12322 through ITID-12328) in which the guessing attack succeeded and access to the target account or system is confirmed.

Use of a precomputed hash-to-plaintext lookup table to recover a password from a stolen hash without live per-guess computation, where the specific method (unsalted hash, legacy algorithm, custom table, cloud lookup service, LM hash downgrade, exfiltrated database, unpatched legacy system) has not yet been identified.
Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen unsalted hash database using a precomputed rainbow table, exploiting the absence of a per-password salt.

c.n: Legacy/Weak Hash Algorithm Rainbow Table Attack
c.d: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen hash database using a precomputed rainbow table, exploiting the use of a legacy or cryptographically weak hashing algorithm for which comprehensive public rainbow tables already exist.

Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen hash database using a precomputed table custom-built by the attacker for a specific character-set, length, or policy-constrained keyspace not covered by publicly available generic rainbow tables.

c.n: Cloud-Based Rainbow Table Lookup Service Attack
c.d: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a stolen hash by submitting the hash to a commercial or criminal cloud-based rainbow table lookup service rather than performing the lookup with locally-held infrastructure.

c.n: Windows LM Hash Downgrade Rainbow Table Attack
c.d: Recovery of plaintext passwords from a Windows environment by exploiting the presence of the legacy LAN Manager (LM) hash format, either because it remains stored alongside NTLM or because an attacker forced a downgrade to generate it, and then using a precomputed table against its structurally weak design.

c.n: Exfiltrated Database Hash Rainbow Table Attack
c.d: Recovery of plaintext passwords via precomputed table lookup against a hash dataset confirmed to have been exfiltrated from a specific, identified compromised database or application breach.

c.n: Rainbow Table Attack Against Unpatched Legacy System
c.d: Recovery of plaintext passwords via precomputed table lookup against a hash exfiltrated from an unpatched, end-of-life, or otherwise unsupported legacy system that inherently uses a weak/legacy hashing scheme and cannot be readily upgraded.

c.n: Successful Rainbow Table Attack with Confirmed Recovery
c.d: A rainbow table attack incident (any of ITID-12332 through ITID-12338) in which plaintext password recovery is confirmed and subsequent unauthorized use of that recovered credential is observed.
An incident involving use of an administrative credential in a manner inconsistent with its authorized purpose, not yet matched to a more specific misuse pattern.

c.n: External Attacker Using Compromised Admin Credential
c.d: Use of a valid administrative credential by an external threat actor who obtained it through compromise (phishing, credential stuffing, malware, purchase), distinguishing attacker-driven misuse from insider misuse of the same credential class.

c.n: Admin Credential Used Outside Approved Change Window
c.d: Use of an administrative credential to make changes to a system or environment outside the time boundaries of an approved change ticket, whether by an insider or by an attacker exploiting the change process's blind spot.

c.n: Admin Credential Used for Unauthorized Data Access
c.d: Use of an administrative credential's elevated data-access rights to view, export, or exfiltrate data not required for the holder's legitimate duties.

c.n: Admin Credential Used to Disable Security Controls
c.d: Use of administrative access rights to disable, tamper with, or degrade a security control (EDR, logging, firewall rule, MFA enforcement) rather than to access data or make routine changes.
Misuse of an administrative account that is shared among multiple individuals or systems, where the lack of individual attribution is itself a contributing factor to the incident.

Misuse of administrative access that an individual retains due to accumulated, un-reviewed privilege grants (role changes, project assignments) rather than a fresh or deliberate grant, where the excess privilege itself is the root cause of the exposure.
Unauthorized or unjustified use of a break-glass/emergency administrative account outside a declared emergency, or failure to follow required post-use review of a legitimate break-glass activation.

c.n: Admin Credential Used for Lateral Movement
c.d: Use of administrative credentials and access rights to pivot from an initially accessed system to additional systems within the environment, as a distinct technique from single-system data access or control tampering.
An incident involving abuse of a non-human service account, not yet matched to a more specific exploitation pattern.

c.n: Service Account with Excessive Permissions Exploited
c.d: Compromise or misuse of a service account where the scope of resulting impact is enabled specifically by excessive/over-provisioned permissions relative to the account's functional need.

c.n: Service Account with Never-Rotated Credential Exploited
c.d: Compromise or misuse of a service account where a long-lived, never-rotated static credential (password, API key, certificate) is the contributing factor enabling the exploitation.

A service account, which by design should authenticate only programmatically/non-interactively, observed performing an interactive human logon (console, RDP, SSH shell) — a strong indicator of compromise or of a control gap enabling misuse.

c.n: Service Account Used Outside Its Expected Source System
c.d: A service account observed authenticating from, or acting on behalf of, a host/system other than its documented, expected source system — indicating either credential theft or unauthorized reuse.

Compromise or misuse of a service account used by a continuous integration/continuous deployment pipeline (build agent, deployment automation, artifact registry) to gain unauthorized access to source code, secrets, or production deployment capability.

Compromise or misuse of a cloud platform's native identity construct (AWS IAM role, Azure managed identity, GCP service account) rather than an application-layer service account, to gain unauthorized access to cloud resources.
Compromise or misuse of a service account/API credential used to connect a third-party or vendor integration (SaaS app, monitoring tool, OAuth-connected app) to internal systems.

Compromise or misuse of a service account that has become orphaned — its original owning application, team, or business justification no longer exists or is untracked — leaving it unmonitored and typically over-privileged relative to any current need.
An incident involving misuse of an account that should have been deprovisioned or disabled but remained active, not yet matched to a more specific abandonment pattern.

Use of a former employee's still-active credential, following a failure of the offboarding process to disable or delete the account, by the former employee or by another party who obtained the credential.

c.n: Contractor/Temporary Account Left Active Past Engagement
c.d: Use of a contractor, vendor staff, or other temporary worker's still-active credential after their contract or engagement end date.
Use of an account originally created for testing or development purposes, which was never removed when the associated system moved to production, typically carrying weak or default credentials.
Use of an account originating from an acquired, merged, or divested entity's identity environment that was never migrated, disabled, or reconciled into the current organization's IAM process.
Use of a vendor-provided default or built-in account (e.g. default admin, factory-set service account) that was never disabled, renamed, or had its default credential changed after deployment.

An attacker reactivating, re-enabling, or restoring access to an account that had gone dormant/inactive (but was not necessarily a failure of the offboarding process), as a persistence or initial-access technique.

An abandoned account whose retained access rights are themselves elevated or legacy in nature (former admin rights, deprecated system access), amplifying the impact of its exploitation beyond a standard abandoned standard-user account.

Exploitation of an identity/credential bound to a physical or virtual device/endpoint (machine account, IoT device certificate, decommissioned laptop's cached credential) that was never deprovisioned when the device left service.
An incident involving a credential discovered exposed to the public internet, not yet matched to a more specific exposure channel.

c.n: Hardcoded Credential in Public Code Repository
c.d: A credential (API key, password, token, private key) embedded directly in application source code that has been pushed to a publicly accessible repository (GitHub, GitLab, npm/PyPI package, etc.).

c.n: Credential Exposed via Misconfigured Cloud Storage
c.d: A credential file, backup, or configuration containing secrets discovered in a cloud storage bucket (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) that was misconfigured for public/anonymous read access.

c.n: Credential Exposed in Public Paste Site/Forum Post
c.d: A credential discovered posted on a public text-paste service (Pastebin and similar) or a public technical forum (Stack Overflow, Reddit, vendor support forum), typically pasted incidentally alongside troubleshooting content.

c.n: Credential Exposed via Search Engine Indexing
c.d: A credential discoverable via a standard web search engine (Google, Bing) because a page containing it — a misconfigured directory listing, an unindexed-by-intent but crawlable admin page, a cached document — was indexed.

c.n: Credential Exposed in Public API Response/Debug Output
c.d: A credential or secret exposed because a production or public-facing API returns it in a response body, error message, or verbose debug/stack-trace output.

c.n: Credential Exposed in Public Configuration File
c.d: A credential embedded in a static configuration file (.env, web.config, config.json, .git/config) that is directly web-accessible due to a deployment or web-server misconfiguration.
A credential included, typically as an oversight during authoring, in publicly published documentation such as a knowledge base article, API reference, README, or public wiki page.

c.n: Credential Exposed via Third-Party Vendor's Own Public Leak
c.d: Organizational credentials (typically for a shared platform or integration) exposed because a third-party vendor suffered its own breach or public exposure incident, unrelated to any control failure within the organization itself.

c.n: Unclassified / General Dark Web Credential Listing
c.d: An incident involving discovery of organizational credentials listed for criminal use on a dark web or underground channel, not yet matched to a more specific listing type.

Listing of organizational credentials or an authenticated foothold packaged and sold as "access-as-a-service" on a criminal marketplace, typically by an Initial Access Broker offering a specific, verified entry point rather than a raw credential list.

c.n: Breach Forum Bulk Credential Dump Listing
c.d: Discovery of organizational credentials as part of a large-scale, typically third-party-origin bulk credential dump posted to a breach/hacking forum, distinct from a curated, targeted listing.

c.n: Ransomware Group Leak Site Credential Exposure
c.d: Discovery of organizational credentials within data published (or threatened for publication) on a ransomware group's dedicated leak site, typically as part of double-extortion following a ransomware incident.
