Discovery of organizational credentials posted, sold, or shared within a Telegram channel/group or other encrypted-messaging-based criminal marketplace, a channel increasingly favored over traditional forums.

Discovery of organizational credentials indexed on a purpose-built combolist aggregator platform that compiles and makes searchable credentials from many prior breaches, distinct from a single dump posting.

Threat-intelligence-confirmed interest, reconnaissance, or general marketplace reputation activity by a known Initial Access Broker (IAB) actor concerning the organization, without yet a discrete access-for-sale listing.

c.n: Credential Listed with Verified/Confirmed Working Status
c.d: A dark web credential listing where the seller, a threat-intelligence provider, or internal verification has confirmed the credential is currently valid and functional against the target system, as opposed to a stale or already-rotated credential.

A dark web listing specifically curated and packaged around the organization's own employees/domain — a targeted credential bundle assembled and marketed as being about this specific organization, rather than the organization's credentials appearing incidentally within a larger, unrelated dataset.
An incident involving unintentional, non-malicious disclosure of a credential by an internal party, not yet matched to a more specific disclosure channel.
A credential (password, API key, temporary access token) transmitted via email without encryption or adequate protection, exposing it to interception or later inbox compromise.
A credential visible in a screen-sharing session (video call, remote presentation) or captured in a screenshot that was subsequently shared, recorded, or published.

A credential typed or pasted into the text content of a document or spreadsheet (e.g. a password tracking sheet, a runbook) that is then shared more broadly than intended, via a collaboration platform.

c.n: Credential Disclosed in Support/Help Desk Ticket
c.d: A credential included, typically by an end user seeking assistance, in the free-text description or attachment of an IT support/help-desk ticket, exposing it to the ticket's broader audience (support staff, ticket history, integrated tools).

A credential disclosed because the communication carrying it (email, chat message, file share) was sent to the wrong recipient — due to autocomplete error, similarly named contact, or manual mistake — as distinct from a credential sent correctly but over an insecure channel.

A real, valid production credential accidentally included in a training, demo, or sandbox environment that has broader or less-controlled access than production (e.g. shared with trainees, contractors, or a wider internal audience).

c.n: Credential Exposed via Improper Offboarding Handoff
c.d: A credential disclosed as an unintended side effect of the offboarding handoff process itself — e.g. shared passwords communicated to a successor insecurely, or account contents (including saved credentials) transferred without proper review.

c.n: Credential Exposed via Third-Party Support Session
c.d: A credential disclosed to, or visible to, a third-party support technician during a live remote-assistance session (screen sharing, remote desktop control) — whether shared verbally/typed for the technician to use, or incidentally visible on-screen.
An incident of MFA token phishing not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type, logged before enough detail is available to reclassify.

An adversary lures a victim to a fake login page that captures the victim's password and time-based one-time passcode (TOTP) in real time and relays both to the legitimate service before the code expires.
An adversary uses a phishing lure (email, chat, or fake portal) to convince a victim to approve a single push-notification MFA request triggered by the adversary's own sign-in attempt.
An adversary phishes a victim for the numeric code displayed on, or the challenge-response generated by, a hardware OTP token, then relays it to the legitimate service before expiry.
An adversary phishes a victim into revealing one or more single-use MFA backup/recovery codes, then uses a code to authenticate without needing the primary MFA factor.
An adversary social-engineers a victim into completing a biometric confirmation step on the victim's own device to approve an authentication request the adversary initiated.

An adversary presents a victim with a QR code (in person, via phishing email, or via a compromised display) that, when scanned during an MFA enrollment flow, registers an attacker-controlled device or authenticator as a valid second factor on the victim's account.

An adversary uses an AiTM reverse-proxy phishing kit to sit between the victim and the legitimate identity provider, transparently relaying credentials and whichever MFA factor the victim completes, then capturing the resulting authenticated session token/cookie.

c.n: Successful MFA Token Phishing with Confirmed Bypass
c.d: A confirmed instance of MFA token phishing (any factor) in which the captured code, approval, or session token was successfully used by the adversary to authenticate to the target account.
An incident of repeated MFA push prompting intended to fatigue a user into approval, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
An adversary with a valid password repeatedly triggers MFA push prompts in rapid succession, relying on the sheer volume to wear down the victim into approving one.
An adversary sends repeated MFA push prompts during off-hours, exploiting reduced user alertness to increase the odds of an accidental approval.

c.n: Push Bombing Combined with Live Call
c.d: An adversary triggers MFA push prompts and simultaneously places a live phone call impersonating IT support or security, instructing the victim to approve the prompt to 'resolve an issue.'
An adversary directs repeated MFA push prompts at an account holding elevated/administrative privileges to fatigue that specific user into approval.
An adversary uses automated scripts or tooling to generate MFA push prompts at machine-consistent intervals, often as part of a broader credential-stuffing or account-takeover toolkit.

c.n: Push Bombing Across Multiple Linked Accounts/Devices
c.d: An adversary triggers MFA push prompts across several accounts or MFA-enrolled devices linked to the same identity, increasing the chance one is approved.

c.n: Push Bombing Against Shared/Break-Glass Account MFA
c.d: An adversary triggers MFA push prompts against a shared or break-glass account, where approval may reach any of several monitoring personnel or an on-call rotation rather than one dedicated user.

c.n: Successful Push Bombing with Confirmed Approval
c.d: A confirmed instance of push-bombing MFA fatigue in which the target ultimately approved a fraudulent prompt, granting the adversary an authenticated session.
An incident of an adversary presenting a device as trusted/compliant when it is not, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.

An adversary manipulates browser/device fingerprinting signals (User-Agent, screen metrics, installed fonts, etc.) to make an untrusted device appear to a service as a device the victim has previously used.

An adversary exfiltrates a device's enrollment certificate or hardware-bound authentication token and replays it from adversary-controlled infrastructure to be recognized as the legitimate trusted device.

An adversary or malware on a rooted/jailbroken device uses root-cloaking tooling to defeat compliance attestation, causing the device to be granted trust it does not qualify for under device-compliance policy.
An adversary runs an emulator or virtual device instance configured with spoofed hardware identifiers to be accepted by device-trust checks as a genuine physical device.
An adversary programs adversary-controlled hardware with the cloned hardware identifiers of a victim's legitimate enrolled device, so that identifier-based trust checks cannot distinguish the two.

An adversary steals a persistent 'trusted device' cookie or token (issued after a prior successful MFA challenge) and replays it to skip MFA on subsequent logins as if from the original trusted device.

Malware resident in the victim's browser on their own trusted device intercepts and manipulates the authentication flow in real time (injecting requests, altering responses) to extend or abuse the device's existing trust without the device itself being spoofed.

c.n: Successful Device Impersonation with Confirmed Bypass
c.d: A confirmed instance of device impersonation (any technique) in which the adversary successfully bypassed device-trust/compliance checks and authenticated as the impersonated device.
An incident of an adversary hijacking a victim's phone number to intercept SMS/voice-based MFA, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
An adversary contacts the victim's mobile carrier, impersonating the victim using gathered PII, and convinces a support representative to port the victim's number onto a SIM the adversary controls.
An adversary pays or coerces a carrier employee to directly execute an unauthorized SIM swap on the victim's number, bypassing normal identity-verification procedures entirely.

An adversary logs into the victim's carrier self-service account (using stolen credentials or a weak account-recovery flow) and initiates a SIM swap or eSIM transfer directly through the automated portal.

An adversary requests or triggers activation of a new eSIM profile for the victim's number, causing the carrier to deactivate the victim's existing SIM/eSIM and route service to the adversary's device.

An adversary submits a fraudulent number-port request to move the victim's phone number to a new carrier and a device under the adversary's control, severing the number from the original carrier entirely.
An adversary obtains physical possession of, or clones the identifiers from, the victim's physical SIM card to receive SMS/voice-based MFA intended for the victim.

c.n: SIM Swap Enabled by Prior Credential/PII Leak
c.d: An adversary uses PII or credentials obtained from an earlier, unrelated data breach to satisfy the identity-verification questions required to execute a SIM swap.

c.n: Successful SIM Swap with Confirmed Downstream Account Takeover
c.d: A confirmed instance of SIM swapping (any mechanism) in which the adversary successfully used control of the victim's phone number to complete SMS/voice-based MFA and take over one or more downstream accounts.
An incident of forged Kerberos ticket-granting-ticket (TGT) use based on a compromised krbtgt account hash, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.

c.n: Golden Ticket via DCSync-Obtained krbtgt Hash
c.d: An adversary with directory-replication rights (or rights obtained through privilege escalation) issues a DCSync request to a domain controller to extract the krbtgt account's password hash, then uses it to forge golden tickets.

c.n: Golden Ticket via Direct Domain Controller Extraction
c.d: An adversary with direct administrative or physical access to a domain controller extracts the krbtgt password hash from LSASS memory or the NTDS.dit database, then uses it to forge golden tickets.

An adversary forges a golden ticket with an extended or effectively unlimited lifetime value, bypassing the default Kerberos ticket-renewal window to maintain long-term domain access without needing to re-forge tickets.

c.n: Golden Ticket with Forged Group Membership
c.d: An adversary forges a golden ticket embedding privileged group SIDs (such as Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins) into the ticket's PAC, granting privileges the referenced account was never actually assigned.

c.n: Golden Ticket Used for Cross-Domain/Forest Trust Abuse
c.d: An adversary uses a golden ticket forged in one domain, together with inter-realm trust material, to obtain access in a trusting domain or forest, extending the compromise across a trust boundary.

c.n: Golden Ticket Detected via Anomalous Ticket Lifetime
c.d: An incident where golden ticket use was identified specifically through automated detection of a Kerberos ticket whose lifetime, renewal pattern, or encryption type deviates from domain policy baselines.

c.n: Golden Ticket Used After Single krbtgt Password Reset
c.d: An adversary continues to use a previously-forged golden ticket successfully after the organization has reset the krbtgt password only once, exploiting the fact that a single reset does not immediately invalidate tickets encrypted with the prior password's second-to-last hash history entry under some configurations.

c.n: Successful Golden Ticket Attack with Confirmed Domain-Wide Access
c.d: A confirmed instance of golden ticket use (any mechanism) in which the adversary is verified to have accessed resources domain-wide consistent with the forged privileges in the ticket.
An incident of NTLM hash reuse to authenticate without cracking the underlying password, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.
An adversary dumps NTLM password hashes from the LSASS process memory of a compromised endpoint, then replays a hash to authenticate to other systems without knowing the plaintext password.
An adversary extracts NTLM hashes from a system's local SAM database (offline or via registry hive dump), then replays a hash to authenticate as a local account elsewhere on the network.

An adversary replays a hash obtained from one workstation to authenticate to other workstations as a local administrator, moving laterally across the endpoint fleet without touching servers or domain controllers.
An adversary replays a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate directly to a domain controller, typically as a step toward broader domain compromise (e.g. enabling DCSync or golden ticket forgery).

An adversary captures NTLM/NTLMv2 challenge-response traffic over the network (e.g. via LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay positioning) and uses the captured material to authenticate as the victim account.

c.n: Pass-the-Hash Using a Shared Local Administrator Hash
c.d: An adversary leverages the fact that a local administrator account's password (and therefore NTLM hash) is identical across many hosts in the environment, allowing one captured hash to authenticate broadly.

c.n: Pass-the-Hash Detected via Anomalous Logon Type
c.d: An incident where pass-the-hash activity was identified specifically through detection of an anomalous logon type (e.g. NTLM Type 3 network logon where Kerberos is expected, or a logon pattern inconsistent with the account's normal behavior).

c.n: Successful Pass-the-Hash Attack with Confirmed Lateral Movement
c.d: A confirmed instance of pass-the-hash (any extraction source or target) in which the adversary is verified to have successfully authenticated to and acted on one or more additional systems using the replayed hash.
An incident of exported/stolen Kerberos ticket reuse, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.

An adversary exports a victim's legitimately-issued TGT from the source host's memory and imports it into a session on adversary-controlled infrastructure to request service tickets as the victim without knowing their password.
An adversary exports a victim's legitimately-issued service ticket (TGS) for a specific resource and reuses it to access that single resource without needing the victim's TGT or password.

c.n: Pass-the-Ticket via LSASS Ticket Cache Extraction
c.d: An adversary uses credential-dumping tooling to extract cached Kerberos tickets directly from LSASS process memory, then replays one or more of them on adversary-controlled infrastructure.

An adversary reuses a Kerberos ticket in a session context different from where it was originally issued (e.g. via shared credential caches, remote session artifacts, or ticket copy between sessions), extending its validity beyond its intended session boundary.

An adversary presents a stolen ticket at a point where the application/service required re-authentication (e.g. a step-up MFA prompt or session-timeout re-login), and the ticket satisfies the check without triggering the intended re-authentication challenge.

An adversary uses a stolen NTLM hash to request a legitimate TGT from the KDC (overpass-the-hash / 'pass-the-key'), converting hash-based access into a genuine Kerberos ticket, then passes that ticket to another session.

c.n: Pass-the-Ticket Detected via Ticket Renewal Anomaly
c.d: An incident where pass-the-ticket activity was identified specifically through detection of an anomalous ticket-renewal pattern (e.g. a renewal request from a host inconsistent with original issuance, or renewal beyond expected policy).

c.n: Successful Pass-the-Ticket Attack with Confirmed Access
c.d: A confirmed instance of pass-the-ticket (any ticket type or mechanism) in which the adversary is verified to have successfully authenticated to and accessed resources using the replayed ticket.
An incident of an adversary stealing or duplicating a Windows access token to act with another user/process's privileges, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under this Type.

c.n: Token Impersonation via Named Pipe Impersonation
c.d: An adversary creates a named pipe and induces a higher-privileged process (often SYSTEM) to connect to it, then calls ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to assume that process's security token.

An adversary injects malicious code into a running higher-privileged process and calls token-manipulation APIs (e.g. OpenProcessToken, DuplicateToken) from within that process's context to steal and reuse its token.

c.n: Token Impersonation for SYSTEM-Level Privilege Escalation
c.d: An adversary uses any token-impersonation technique to elevate their session from a standard/service-account privilege level to full SYSTEM privilege on the local host.

c.n: Token Impersonation for Remote Lateral Movement
c.d: An adversary uses a stolen/impersonated token to authenticate to and act on a remote host, extending token-impersonation privilege escalation into network lateral movement.

c.n: Token Impersonation via Rogue Service Creation
c.d: An adversary with sufficient privilege creates a new Windows service configured to run as SYSTEM (or another privileged account), starts it, and captures the resulting privileged token from the spawned service process.

An adversary exploits an account holding SeImpersonatePrivilege (commonly granted to IIS/SQL/service accounts by default) using a known local privilege-escalation exploit chain to obtain a SYSTEM-level token.

c.n: Token Impersonation Detected via Anomalous Process Token Lineage
c.d: An incident where token impersonation was identified specifically through detection of anomalous parent-child process token lineage (e.g. a low-privilege process's descendant unexpectedly running with a higher-privilege token).

c.n: Successful Token Impersonation with Confirmed Privilege Escalation
c.d: A confirmed instance of token impersonation (any mechanism) in which the adversary is verified to have successfully escalated privilege and acted with the impersonated token's authority.
An incident involving an attempt to determine which usernames/accounts exist in a system, not yet matched to a more specific enumeration technique.

Enumeration of valid usernames/accounts by exploiting a login form that returns different error messages for "account not found" versus "incorrect password", allowing an attacker to distinguish valid from invalid accounts without ever guessing a password.

Enumeration of valid usernames/accounts by measuring statistically significant differences in server response latency between requests for valid vs. invalid accounts (e.g. because a valid-account lookup triggers an extra password-hash comparison).

Enumeration of valid usernames/accounts by exploiting a password reset flow that reveals, through message, timing, or behavioral difference, whether a submitted identifier corresponds to an existing account.
Enumeration of already-registered accounts by exploiting a sign-up flow that reveals whether a submitted email/username is already in use (e.g. "this email is already registered" messaging).

Enumeration of valid accounts by exploiting an API endpoint (rather than a rendered web form) that returns a different HTTP status code, response schema, or field set depending on whether the queried identifier corresponds to an existing account.

An enumeration campaign characterized primarily by its scale and automation (bulk/scripted requests against an authentication-adjacent endpoint), where the volume and automated tooling itself is the notable characteristic, potentially combining multiple techniques.

c.n: Enumeration via Third-Party Login/SSO Provider Response
c.d: Enumeration of valid accounts by exploiting differential behavior in a third-party identity provider or SSO flow (e.g. "redirecting to your organization's login" only for known domains, or a federated provider revealing account existence during the handoff).

c.n: Enumeration Feeding a Downstream Targeted Attack
c.d: Confirmed correlation between a prior account enumeration event and a subsequent targeted attack (credential stuffing, password spraying, phishing) specifically directed at the accounts confirmed to exist through that enumeration.
An incident involving exploitation of an account lockout mechanism, not yet matched to a more specific exploitation pattern.

An attacker intentionally submitting repeated failed login attempts against a target account specifically to trigger the lockout policy and deny the legitimate user access, rather than as a byproduct of a credential-guessing attempt.

An attacker deliberately submitting a controlled, small number of failed attempts against one or more accounts to determine the exact number of attempts, time window, or reset behavior of the lockout policy, as reconnaissance for a subsequent attack designed to stay just under the threshold.

A deliberate account-lockout denial-of-service attack (per ITID-12822's general pattern) where the target is specifically a privileged, administrative, or otherwise business-critical account, elevating the business impact and threat intent.

An attacker triggering or falsely claiming an account lockout, then contacting the help desk/support channel posing as the legitimate user to obtain an unauthorized unlock or password reset, exploiting the help desk's identity-verification gap.

c.n: Lockout Bypass via Distributed Source IPs
c.d: A credential attack (brute force, password spraying, credential stuffing) designed to stay under the lockout threshold by distributing failed attempts across a large number of distinct source IPs, such that no single IP or short time window triggers detection or lockout.

Successful credential attack enabled by an actual defect or inconsistency in how the lockout policy is implemented — such as a policy that applies to one authentication endpoint but not another for the same account, or a counter that does not reset/apply correctly — as distinct from evading a correctly functioning policy via distributed sources.

Exploitation of an automated, self-service account unlock/reset portal (e.g. security-question-based unlock, SMS/email-based unlock) where weaknesses in the portal's own automated verification logic allow an attacker to unlock or reset an account without human interaction.

A confirmed case where exploitation of the lockout mechanism (via any of the technique-specific siblings in this Type) directly resulted in a further confirmed security outcome — unauthorized account access, a successful denial-of-service with measurable business impact, or a confirmed fraudulent unlock leading to compromise.
An incident involving injection of credentials or authentication material into an application flow through an unintended technical mechanism, not yet matched to a more specific injection technique.

Malware installed on the victim's endpoint that hooks into the browser to intercept, modify, or inject content into an authenticated session in real time — capturing credentials as entered, or injecting fraudulent form fields/transactions into a legitimate, already-authenticated session.

Abuse of a browser's or password manager's automatic form-filling behavior — typically via hidden or off-screen form fields injected by a malicious or compromised page — to trick the autofill mechanism into revealing stored credentials to an attacker-controlled field.

Exploitation of a SQL injection vulnerability in an authentication mechanism, where crafted input into a login field manipulates the underlying database query to bypass authentication (e.g. always returning a valid user record) without knowing a valid credential.

Exploitation of an LDAP injection vulnerability in an authentication mechanism backed by a directory service (Active Directory, OpenLDAP), where crafted input manipulates the LDAP search filter to bypass authentication or return unintended directory objects.

Injection or replay of a stolen, predicted, or forged session token/cookie into a request to impersonate an already-authenticated user, bypassing the login step entirely rather than manipulating the credential-submission process itself.

c.n: Credential Injection via Malicious Browser Extension
c.d: A browser extension, installed by the user (maliciously disguised or later compromised via a supply-chain update), that uses its granted browser API permissions to intercept form input, read/modify page content, or exfiltrate credentials/session tokens.

c.n: API Parameter/Header Injection for Authentication Bypass
c.d: Manipulation of API request parameters, headers, or object identifiers (e.g. a trusted internal header, a role/permission parameter, an IDOR-style user-ID parameter) to bypass or subvert the authentication or authorization check on an API endpoint, without exploiting SQL/LDAP injection specifically.

c.n: Successful Credential Injection Attack with Confirmed Bypass
c.d: A confirmed case where a credential injection technique (via any of the technique-specific siblings in this Type) directly resulted in confirmed unauthorized authenticated access, as distinct from a blocked or unsuccessful attempt.

An incident involving a rogue or spoofed authentication system used to trick a human into authenticating against attacker-controlled infrastructure, not yet matched to a more specific leaf (e.g. evil-twin Wi-Fi, rogue DHCP/DNS, rogue IdP, rogue VPN gateway, captive portal, or a compromised legitimate system).

c.n: Rogue Wi-Fi Access Point (Evil Twin) Authentication Capture
c.d: An adversary stands up a rogue wireless access point using the same or a confusingly similar SSID as a legitimate network so that a victim's device connects to it, allowing the adversary to capture credentials entered on a spoofed captive/login page or to intercept authentication traffic.

c.n: Rogue DNS/DHCP Redirect to Fake Authentication Portal
c.d: An adversary manipulates DNS resolution or issues rogue DHCP responses on a network the victim already trusts, redirecting the victim's browser or client to an attacker-controlled fake authentication page.

An adversary responds to broadcast name-resolution requests (LLMNR/NBT-NS) or otherwise poses as a local authentication relay point, capturing or relaying credential material (e.g. NTLM hashes) offered by a victim's client during automatic authentication attempts.

An adversary stands up a fraudulent SAML or OAuth identity provider (or a forged federation/consent flow) that mimics a trusted IdP, tricking the victim into entering credentials or granting consent that the adversary then captures or exploits.

An adversary stands up a fake VPN or remote-access gateway login portal (or spoofs the legitimate one via DNS/typosquatting) so that a victim enters remote-access credentials, which the adversary then captures.

An adversary presents a fake captive portal on public wireless infrastructure that mimics a legitimate network's sign-in page, or clones the legitimate captive portal itself, in order to capture credentials the victim reflexively enters.

An adversary gains control of or modifies the organization's actual authentication infrastructure (e.g. by compromising the IdP server, injecting malicious code into a real login page, or modifying its authentication logic) so that legitimate users authenticating through the real system have their credentials captured or their sessions manipulated.

A rogue authentication system incident (of any of the sibling vector types) where it has been confirmed that the adversary obtained working credentials or authentication material and successfully used it to authenticate to a real system or take further unauthorized action, distinct from the capture attempt itself.

An incident involving the hijacking of an already-established, human-initiated authenticated session, not yet matched to a more specific leaf (e.g. network sniffing, session fixation, predictable tokens, malware-resident theft, cross-device, compromised proxy, physical device access, or confirmed successful outcome).

An adversary positioned on the network path (e.g. shared Wi-Fi, compromised switch port, on-path interception) captures a victim's session token or cookie in transit because the session was transmitted without adequate transport protection, then reuses it to impersonate the victim.

An adversary sets or supplies a known session identifier to the victim (e.g. via a crafted link or a vulnerable application that accepts pre-set session IDs) before the victim authenticates, then uses that same session identifier after authentication to impersonate the victim.

An adversary analyzes a sequence of issued session tokens or the application's token-generation algorithm, determines a predictable pattern, and computes or guesses a valid token for another user's session without ever intercepting or stealing an actual issued token.

c.n: Session Hijacking via Malware-Resident Token Theft
c.d: Malware running on a victim's endpoint (e.g. an infostealer or browser-targeting trojan) reads session tokens or cookies from browser storage/memory and exfiltrates them so the adversary can hijack the victim's active authenticated session.

An adversary transfers or replicates a victim's valid session token/cookie onto a different device (theirs) — for example via a trusted-device sync mechanism, a malicious browser-sync exploit, or manual token export — and continues the session from that device without the victim's involvement.

c.n: Session Hijacking via Compromised Reverse Proxy/Load Balancer
c.d: An adversary gains control of or implants malicious logic into a reverse proxy or load balancer that legitimately handles user traffic to an application, using that position to capture session tokens/cookies in transit or to inject/redirect sessions for multiple victims simultaneously.

c.n: Session Hijacking via Physical Device Access
c.d: An adversary with physical access to a victim's unlocked or improperly secured device directly uses an already-authenticated session (e.g. an open browser tab, unlocked mobile app, or extracted local session storage) to impersonate the victim, without needing to intercept network traffic or deploy malware.

c.n: Successful Session Hijacking with Confirmed Unauthorized Actions
c.d: A session-hijacking incident (of any of the sibling vector types) where it has been confirmed that the adversary not only obtained the session but actually used it to perform unauthorized actions (e.g. data access, financial transactions, further account changes), warranting escalation as a confirmed compromise rather than a hijacking attempt.
An incident involving replay of a captured authentication credential or artifact, not clearly matching a more specific leaf under Credential Replay.
An adversary captures a valid network-level authentication handshake exchange and resubmits or relays it to a service to complete authentication.

c.n: Replay Attack Against Missing/Weak Nonce Validation
c.d: An adversary resubmits a previously captured authentication request to an application that fails to enforce a unique, single-use nonce or timestamp check, allowing the request to be accepted again.

An adversary captures a previously issued, signed API authentication request (e.g. an OAuth token exchange, HMAC-signed call) and resubmits it to the same or a different endpoint to authenticate or act on behalf of the legitimate caller.
An adversary captures a valid Kerberos ticket (TGT or service ticket) and resubmits it to authenticate, logged as a discrete replay event rather than subsequent lateral-movement activity.

An adversary resubmits a captured or reconstructed biometric authentication artifact (e.g. a stored fingerprint template, recorded voiceprint, or replayed facial-recognition image/video) to authenticate as the legitimate user.
An adversary captures the output of a hardware authentication token (OTP or challenge-response) and resubmits it before it expires or before the legitimate user completes authentication.

An adversary positioned on-path between a user and an authentication service (e.g. via a rogue access point, proxy, or DNS manipulation) captures an authentication artifact in transit and replays it, independent of the specific artifact type captured.

c.n: Successful Credential Replay Attack with Confirmed Bypass
c.d: A confirmed outcome-based classification for any credential-replay attempt (regardless of artifact type or capture vector) where the adversary successfully authenticated or acted using the replayed artifact.

c.n: Insider Theft of Customer PII/Financial Records
c.d: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of customer PII or financial records for personal gain, sale, or harm to the organization.

c.n: Insider Theft of Proprietary Source Code or Trade Secrets
c.d: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of proprietary source code, algorithms, designs, or trade secrets for personal gain, use at a competitor, or harm to the organization.
A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of employee personnel files, compensation data, or other HR records.
A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized copying or removal of organizational data not clearly matching a more specific Data Theft leaf.

A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized destructive action against IT systems, applications, or infrastructure — deleting data, disabling services, or planting destructive logic — motivated by grievance, retaliation, or personal gain.

c.n: Insider Sabotage of Physical Equipment or Facilities
c.d: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized physical damage to organizational equipment, machinery, or facilities, motivated by grievance, retaliation, or personal gain.
A trusted insider's deliberate sabotage — of IT systems, data, or physical equipment — carried out in the period immediately surrounding their resignation, termination, or notice of termination.
A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized destructive or disruptive act not clearly matching a more specific Sabotage leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Credential Sharing (Malicious Insider Context)
c.d: A trusted insider's deliberate, unauthorized sharing of their own valid account credentials with another person, granting that person access they should not have.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Espionage (Malicious Insider Context)
c.d: A trusted insider's sustained, deliberate collection and exfiltration of sensitive organizational information over time, typically directed or sponsored by an external party (a competitor, foreign government, or organized group) rather than a single opportunistic theft.

c.n: Unclassified / General Accidental Data Exposure (Negligent Insider Context)
c.d: An employee's or contractor's unintentional exposure of sensitive organizational data — through misdirected communication, misconfiguration, or careless handling — with no malicious intent.
An employee's use of a third-party application, cloud service, or tool for organizational work without going through IT/security approval or procurement.

c.n: Data Handling Policy Violation (Storing Sensitive Data in Unauthorized Location)
c.d: An employee's placement of sensitive organizational data into a storage location — approved or unapproved tool — that is not authorized for that data's classification level.

c.n: Acceptable Use Policy Violation (Personal Use of Corporate Systems)
c.d: An employee's use of organizational systems, accounts, or resources for personal, non-work purposes in violation of the acceptable use policy.
An employee's violation of organizational security or IT policy not clearly matching a more specific Policy Violations leaf.
An organizational laptop or mobile device reported lost by its user, with no evidence suggesting deliberate theft.

c.n: Device Left Unattended in Public Location and Not Recovered
c.d: An organizational device left unattended by its user in a public place (a cafe, airport, public transit, etc.) and subsequently not recovered.

c.n: Unclassified / General Lost or Stolen Device
c.d: A lost or stolen organizational device incident not clearly matching a more specific Lost or Stolen Devices leaf.

c.n: Insider Credential Phished by External Attacker
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an insider's own valid credentials were obtained by an external attacker through a phishing email, SMS, voice call, or fraudulent login page, and are subsequently used to access systems as that insider. The insider did not knowingly participate; their account is the vector.

c.n: Insider Credential Compromised via Malware Keylogger
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which malware running on an insider's endpoint (keylogger, infostealer, clipboard/session-token grabber) captured that insider's valid credentials without their knowledge, and an external attacker subsequently used the captured credentials to access systems as that insider.

A confirmed or suspected insider credential compromise whose specific mechanism has not yet been established as phishing (ITID-13311) or malware/keylogger (ITID-13312), or that involves a mechanism genuinely distinct from both (e.g., credential reuse from a third-party breach, unattended-session hijacking). Used at initial triage and reclassified once the capture vector is confirmed.

c.n: Unclassified / General Blackmail or Coercion (Compromised Insider Context)
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an external party used blackmail, extortion, or coercive threats (e.g., threatening to expose compromising personal information, financial leverage, threats to the insider or their family) to compel an insider to grant access, exfiltrate data, or otherwise act against their employer's interests. The insider's actions are driven by duress rather than free will or personal profit motive.

c.n: Insider Manipulated via Long-Term Pretext Relationship Building
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an external attacker built a long-term pretext relationship with an insider (e.g., a fabricated romantic, professional, or friendship connection cultivated over weeks or months) in order to gradually gain trust and ultimately induce the insider to grant access, disclose information, or otherwise act against their employer's interests. The insider is manipulated but not under an explicit blackmail-style threat.

c.n: Insider Deceived into Unknowingly Facilitating Attacker Access
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an external attacker used a short, discrete deception (e.g., a fraudulent phone call impersonating IT support, a fabricated urgent request impersonating an executive, a fake vendor request) to induce an insider to unknowingly take an action — such as granting remote access, resetting a password, or forwarding information — that facilitated attacker access. The insider does not realize they are assisting an attacker and did not receive prior cultivation or grooming.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Engineering of Insider
c.d: A confirmed or suspected case of an insider being socially engineered by an external attacker into taking or facilitating an unauthorized action, where it has not yet been established whether the manipulation followed a long-term pretext relationship pattern (ITID-13331) or a single/short-duration deception pattern (ITID-13332). Used at initial triage and reclassified once the pattern is confirmed.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unauthorized Access (Insider Privilege Abuse Context)
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an insider, using access they were legitimately granted, deliberately views, accesses, or interacts with systems, applications, or data outside the scope of their job duties or any authorized task, for reasons of curiosity, personal interest, or personal benefit — without necessarily escalating privileges or hoarding data. The insider acts entirely of their own free will and is not being directed or manipulated by an external party.

c.n: Unclassified / General Privilege Escalation (Insider Privilege Abuse Context)
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an insider, acting of their own free will and without external compromise or direction, uses their legitimate access, technical knowledge, or administrative trust to grant themselves privileges, roles, or entitlements beyond what was authorized for their role — as distinct from simply misusing access already held. This includes self-approval of access requests, modifying entitlement systems, or exploiting an administrative role to expand one's own footprint.

c.n: Unclassified / General Data Hoarding (Insider Privilege Abuse Context)
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an insider, using access they legitimately hold and acting of their own free will, systematically collects, copies, downloads, or retains data in volumes or patterns beyond what their role or any authorized task requires — without necessarily exfiltrating it externally or acting in concert with another party. This includes local hoarding (personal drives, unauthorized local copies, personal cloud storage) as preparation for later use, departure, or simply out of possessiveness over 'their' work product.

c.n: Insider Providing Access Credentials to External Attacker for Payment
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an insider knowingly and willingly provides their valid access credentials (or facilitates provisioning of access) to an external attacker as part of a transactional, profit-motivated arrangement — a one-time payment or an ongoing paid relationship — with the insider's participation being voluntary rather than the product of coercion, deception, or manipulation.

c.n: Insider Actively Assisting External Attacker's Lateral Movement
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which an insider knowingly provides ongoing, hands-on technical assistance to an external attacker who has already obtained some foothold, actively helping the attacker navigate, escalate, or move laterally within internal systems — for example, by identifying valuable targets, explaining network architecture, disabling controls, or executing actions on the attacker's behalf from inside the trusted perimeter.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Collaboration with External Attacker
c.d: A confirmed or suspected case of an insider knowingly collaborating with an external attacker toward a shared malicious goal, where it has not yet been established whether the insider's role was primarily transactional/payment-driven credential provisioning (ITID-13511) or ongoing active technical assistance with lateral movement (ITID-13512), or where the collaboration takes a form distinct from both. Used at initial triage and reclassified once the role is confirmed.

c.n: Multiple Employees Colluding to Bypass Segregation-of-Duties Controls
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which two or more insiders knowingly coordinate their legitimate access and approval authorities to circumvent segregation-of-duties controls — for example, colluding across the requester/approver split in a financial or procurement workflow — in order to commit, conceal, or enable fraud or another form of process abuse that neither could achieve alone.

A confirmed or strongly suspected case in which two or more insiders knowingly coordinate their access, roles, or timing to collectively steal, collect, or exfiltrate data - for example, dividing responsibility for accessing different systems, covering for one another's absence, or combining separate partial datasets into a single stolen collection - toward a shared data-theft goal, without a primary external attacker driving the effort.

A confirmed or suspected case of two or more insiders knowingly conspiring together toward a shared malicious goal, where it has not yet been established whether the conspiracy is primarily structured around bypassing segregation-of-duties/financial controls (ITID-13521) or coordinated data theft/exfiltration (ITID-13522), or where the conspiracy takes a form distinct from both. Used at initial triage and reclassified once the structure is confirmed.

An unauthorized person follows an authorized person through a secured entry point, logged from a physical-access-control incident perspective, distinct from the pretext-technique taxonomy used for social-engineering-framed tailgating.
An adversary creates a functional duplicate of a legitimate employee's access badge — by skimming/cloning its credential data onto a blank card — and uses it to gain unauthorized entry.

c.n: Fabricated Fake Access Badge with Forged Credentials
c.d: An adversary manufactures a fake access badge — with a forged appearance, printed identity, and/or a fabricated (not cloned) credential — designed to visually or electronically pass as legitimate.

c.n: Stolen Blank Badge Stock Used to Create Unauthorized Badge
c.d: An adversary steals blank, unissued badge stock from the organization's own supply and encodes it with a forged or stolen credential to create a functional unauthorized badge.
Use of an unauthorized or fraudulent access badge, not clearly matching cloning, fabrication, or stolen blank stock.

c.n: Authorized Employee Propping Door Open for Unauthorized Entry
c.d: An authorized employee props open a secured door — for convenience, ventilation, or repeated back-and-forth trips — creating an unmonitored, unauthorized entry point.

c.n: Authorized Employee Lending Badge to Unauthorized Person
c.d: An authorized employee lends their personal access badge to another individual — a coworker, friend, or family member — allowing that person to enter using the employee's credential.

c.n: Access Granted to Restricted Area Beyond Job Requirement (Excessive Physical Privilege)
c.d: An employee's access-control profile grants entry to one or more restricted areas that are not required for their current job function, identified through an access review or audit.
Misuse of legitimately held physical access, not clearly matching door-propping, badge-lending, or excessive access-privilege provisioning.

c.n: Unclassified / General Device Theft (Physical Security Context)
c.d: Confirmed theft of an individual endpoint device (laptop, phone, tablet) from an employee, desk, or facility, where theft (not loss) is established but no larger pattern is yet identified.

c.n: Organized Theft Ring Targeting IT Equipment Warehouse
c.d: An organized group conducts a coordinated theft of IT equipment in bulk from a warehouse, staging area, or shipping/receiving dock, typically for resale.
An actor steals server, storage, or networking equipment from a data center, whether through unauthorized physical access or misuse of legitimate access.
Theft of organizational hardware, not clearly matching an organized theft ring targeting a warehouse/staging area or theft from a data center specifically.

c.n: Physical Theft of Confidential Paper Files/Records
c.d: An actor physically steals confidential paper files or records — personnel files, contracts, internal reports — from an office, filing cabinet, or storage area.

c.n: Theft of Printed Financial or Legal Documents from Office
c.d: An actor physically steals printed financial documents (statements, invoices, payroll records) or legal documents (contracts, litigation files) from an office.
Physical theft of documents, not clearly matching general confidential records or specifically financial/legal documents.

c.n: Physical Damage to Endpoint Device (Deliberate Destruction)
c.d: An adversary or insider deliberately physically destroys an endpoint device — laptop, desktop, mobile phone — through force, fire, water, or another destructive method, rather than removing or modifying it.

c.n: Unauthorized Physical Modification of Device Hardware
c.d: An adversary physically opens and modifies an endpoint device's hardware — installing an implant, keylogger, or altered component — without destroying the device, so it continues to appear and function normally.
Unauthorized physical tampering with an endpoint device, not clearly matching deliberate destruction or hardware modification.

c.n: Security Camera Physically Obstructed or Disabled
c.d: An adversary physically obstructs, redirects, covers, or disables a security camera at the camera itself — spray, tape, physical redirection, or power disconnection — to blind coverage of an area.

c.n: Motion Sensor/Alarm Sensor Tampered to Avoid Detection
c.d: An adversary physically tampers with a motion detector, alarm sensor, or contact sensor — masking, misaligning, or disconnecting it — to prevent an intrusion alarm from triggering.

c.n: CCTV Recording System Sabotaged or Feed Looped
c.d: An adversary sabotages the CCTV recording system, storage, or video feed — deleting footage, looping a static feed, or disabling the recorder — so that camera coverage exists but is not captured or preserved.

c.n: Unclassified / General Camera or Sensor Disablement
c.d: Unauthorized disablement or tampering with a security camera or sensor, not clearly matching camera obstruction, alarm-sensor tampering, or CCTV-recording sabotage.

c.n: Door Lock Mechanism Physically Bypassed or Picked
c.d: An adversary defeats a door's lock mechanism through mechanical means — lock picking, bumping, shimming, or force — without involving the electronic access-control system.

c.n: Door Access Control Wiring Tampered to Force Unlock
c.d: An adversary physically accesses and manipulates an electronic access-control door's wiring, controller, or strike-relay to force it into an unlocked state, bypassing the credential-check process entirely.

c.n: Fire Exit/Emergency Door Propped or Disabled for Unauthorized Entry
c.d: An adversary props open or disables the self-closing/alarm mechanism of a fire exit or emergency-only door to create an unauthorized, unmonitored entry point.
Unauthorized tampering with a door access mechanism, not clearly matching mechanical lock bypass, electronic access-control tampering, or fire-exit propping/disabling.

c.n: Paper Shredder Reconstruction (Piecing Together Shredded Documents)
c.d: An adversary who has obtained shredded paper documents attempts to reconstruct their content by manually or digitally piecing the fragments back together.

c.n: Manual Sorting of Mixed Waste to Locate Sensitive Materials
c.d: An adversary manually sorts through mixed general waste — not separated by material type — to locate any sensitive documents or materials that happen to be present.

c.n: Unclassified / General Information Recovery from Discarded Materials
c.d: Recovery of information from discarded materials, not clearly matching shredder reconstruction or manual mixed-waste sorting.

c.n: Data Recovery from Improperly Wiped Discarded Hard Drive
c.d: An adversary who has obtained a discarded hard drive performs forensic or standard data-recovery techniques to extract data that was not properly wiped prior to disposal.

c.n: Forensic Recovery from Discarded Mobile Device/SIM Card
c.d: An adversary who has obtained a discarded mobile device or SIM card performs forensic recovery techniques to extract contacts, messages, credentials, or other data.
Data recovery performed on a discarded device, not clearly matching hard-drive recovery or mobile-device/SIM recovery.

c.n: Unclassified / General On-Site Impersonation (Social Engineering Context)
c.d: An adversary physically presents as someone they are not to gain facility access, logged from a physical-security-breach incident perspective, distinct from the persona-technique taxonomy used for social-engineering-framed impersonation.

c.n: Fake Fire Drill/Evacuation Used as Access Pretext
c.d: An adversary triggers a false fire alarm or exploits a scheduled/genuine evacuation to gain access to a facility while normal occupants are evacuating and access controls are bypassed or unattended.

c.n: Fake Emergency Vehicle/Personnel Staged for Facility Access
c.d: An adversary stages a fake emergency vehicle (ambulance, fire truck) or a group presenting as emergency personnel at a facility's exterior to create a plausible pretext for facility access or staff cooperation.
A staged fake emergency used as an access pretext, not clearly matching a triggered fire drill/evacuation or a staged emergency vehicle/personnel presence.

c.n: Vandalism/Property Damage to Facility Exterior or Grounds
c.d: An external or unidentified actor causes property damage to a facility's exterior, signage, landscaping, or grounds, without targeting security hardware, life-safety systems, or on-site equipment specifically.

c.n: Sabotage of Physical Access Control/Security Hardware
c.d: An actor deliberately damages or disables physical access-control or security hardware — badge readers, turnstiles, security fencing, gates — to degrade the facility's security posture.

c.n: Sabotage of Fire Suppression/Life Safety Systems
c.d: An actor deliberately disables, discharges, or tampers with a fire suppression system, sprinkler system, fire alarm panel, or other life-safety system.

c.n: Arson or Incendiary Device Used Against Facility
c.d: An actor deliberately sets a fire or deploys an incendiary device against a facility, intending to cause damage, disruption, or harm.

An actor deliberately damages or disables on-site operational equipment or machinery (manufacturing lines, HVAC units, generators, general facility equipment) not classified as security hardware or a life-safety system.
Deliberate sabotage or damage to a facility, not clearly matching vandalism, security-hardware sabotage, life-safety system sabotage, arson, or equipment sabotage.

c.n: Electrical Power Line Cut or Disabled
c.d: An actor deliberately cuts, disconnects, or otherwise disables an electrical power line or supply feeding a facility, causing a power disruption.

c.n: Water Supply Line Cut or Contaminated
c.d: An actor deliberately cuts, disconnects, or contaminates a water supply line feeding a facility, causing a disruption or safety hazard.
An actor deliberately cuts, disconnects, or tampers with a gas or fuel supply line feeding a facility or backup generator, creating a disruption and a potential explosion/fire hazard.
Deliberate disruption of a facility utility, not clearly matching power, water, or gas/fuel line tampering.

c.n: Photographing Security Systems/Access Control Layout Without Authorization
c.d: The unauthorized photographing of security systems, access control hardware, or the physical security layout at a facility, performed to gather visual intelligence supporting a future physical intrusion or social-engineering pretext, rather than for espionage or business-intelligence purposes.

c.n: Drone-Based Aerial Photography of Restricted Facility
c.d: The unauthorized use of an unmanned aerial vehicle (drone) to capture aerial photography or video of a restricted facility's grounds, perimeter, rooftop, or parking areas as reconnaissance for a physical intrusion or to assess physical security coverage.
Unauthorized photography of a facility or its surroundings, taken as apparent physical security reconnaissance, that does not clearly match a more specific Unauthorized Photography leaf.

c.n: Facility Walk-Through/Casing to Identify Entry Points and Blind Spots
c.d: An adversary's in-person walk-through or casing of a facility's exterior or interior to identify unmonitored entry points, camera blind spots, unlocked doors, or other physical security gaps, performed as direct preparation for a later intrusion.

c.n: Observation of Security Patrol Patterns/Shift Changes
c.d: An adversary's observation of a facility's security guard patrol patterns, rounds, or shift-change timing, performed to identify predictable gaps in physical security coverage.

c.n: Testing Physical Security Response (Probing Alarms/Access Points)
c.d: An adversary's deliberate, low-level testing of a facility's physical security response — triggering a door alarm, testing a badge reader with an invalid credential, or similar — to observe and learn how security personnel or systems respond, as preparation for a later intrusion.
Physical reconnaissance of a facility, performed as apparent preparation for a later intrusion, that does not clearly match a more specific Physical Reconnaissance leaf.

c.n: Hidden Camera or Audio Recording Device Planted
c.d: The covert physical placement of a hidden camera or audio recording device within a facility or vehicle to capture video or audio without the knowledge or consent of the people present, for surveillance or intelligence-gathering purposes.

c.n: GPS Tracker Covertly Placed on Vehicle/Asset
c.d: The covert physical attachment of a GPS or other location-tracking device to a vehicle or physical asset, without the knowledge or consent of its owner or operator, to monitor movement patterns.

c.n: Unclassified / General Covert Surveillance Device Placement
c.d: The covert physical placement of a surveillance device — of a type not clearly a hidden camera/audio recorder or a GPS tracker — performed without the knowledge or consent of the affected individual(s).

Unauthorized replacement of website content with domestic political or election-related messaging, intended to associate the company's public web presence with a partisan position it did not authorize.

Unauthorized replacement of website content with propaganda messaging attributed to, or bearing the hallmarks of, a state-sponsored actor, used to advance a geopolitical narrative through the company's public web presence.
Unauthorized replacement of website content with anti-government or protest-themed messaging, reflecting general dissent rather than an election-specific or state-attributed narrative.
Website defacement with political content, not clearly matching the domestic/election, state-sponsored, or anti-government/protest leaves under this Type.
Unauthorized replacement of website content where a specific, previously identified hacktivist group claims credit for the act, typically via a signature, logo, or public claim of responsibility.

Unauthorized website content replacement occurring as part of a broader, coordinated campaign in which a hacktivist group or affiliated actors deface many organizations' websites within a short time window, typically using a common tool or shared vulnerability.

Unauthorized website content replacement carried out by an individual or small ad-hoc group specifically targeting the company for a stated grievance or cause, distinct from a mass campaign or an established hacktivist collective's branded operation.
Website defacement bearing hacktivist characteristics, not clearly matching the named-collective, mass-campaign, or single-target cause-based leaves under this Type.

Unauthorized replacement of website content with sexually explicit, graphically violent, or otherwise obscene material, intended to shock or offend visitors rather than convey a political message or claim credit.
Unauthorized replacement of website content with hate speech, slurs, or discriminatory material targeting a race, religion, gender, ethnicity, or other protected characteristic.
Unauthorized replacement of website content with a low-content vandalism tag, signature, or 'pwned by' message intended to demonstrate compromise capability rather than convey any specific message.
Website defacement with offensive content, not clearly matching the graphic/obscene, discriminatory, or vandalism/trophy leaves under this Type.

A defacement in which the company's website is altered to serve malware to a targeted population of visitors (customers, employees, or an industry community) who are known or expected to visit the site, as opposed to opportunistic mass infection.
A defacement in which the visibly altered page also loads an exploit kit that fingerprints visiting browsers/plugins and delivers a browser or plugin exploit to vulnerable visitors.
A defacement in which the altered page presents a fake browser/software update, codec, or plugin-install prompt, socially engineering visitors into voluntarily downloading and running malware.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malware Insertion via Defacement
c.d: A defacement combined with malware delivery, not clearly matching the watering-hole, exploit-kit, or fake-update-prompt leaves under this Type.
Unauthorized replacement of website content with a fake statement claiming the company suffered a data breach or security incident that did not occur, or misrepresenting the scope of a real one.
Unauthorized replacement of website content with a fake statement claiming the company is ceasing operations, filing for bankruptcy, or otherwise financially collapsing.
Unauthorized replacement of website content with a fake statement, resignation notice, confession, or quote falsely attributed to a named executive or employee.
Website defacement fabricating a company announcement, not clearly matching the breach, shutdown, or executive-statement leaves under this Type.

Unauthorized access to and control of the company's official corporate social media account (the primary brand-handle presence, not an executive's personal account), obtained through credential compromise or session hijacking.

Unauthorized access to and control of a named executive's personal or personal-branded social media account, where the account's association with the company creates a brand and reputational exposure distinct from the official corporate account.

c.n: Employee Personal Account Mistaken for Official Account
c.d: A scenario in which an employee's personal social media account (not an officially designated or brand-associated account) is compromised or misused, and the resulting content is mistaken by the public, media, or customers for an official company statement due to the employee's visible role or affiliation disclosure.

Unauthorized takeover of a platform-verified social media account belonging to the company or an executive, where the verification status causes audiences to treat any posted content as especially credible.

Unauthorized takeover of an inactive, legacy, or otherwise unmonitored company social media account (e.g., an old campaign or regional handle) that remains publicly visible and attributable to the brand.

Unauthorized access to a company social media account obtained through the compromise of one of multiple shared administrator credentials, agency logins, or management-tool integrations with standing access to the account.

c.n: Successful Account Takeover with Confirmed Unauthorized Defacement Posted
c.d: The escalation of any Social Media Account Takeover leaf to a confirmed state: the attacker not only gained account control but successfully posted unauthorized, brand-damaging content that was publicly visible before removal.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Media Account Takeover
c.d: Unauthorized takeover of a company-associated social media account, not clearly matching the official/corporate, executive, verified, dormant, or shared-access leaves under this Type.

A fake or misleading post published from an account that impersonates or parodies the company but is not itself the compromised official account, creating public confusion about the post's legitimacy.

c.n: Compromised Social Media Management Tool/API Integration Fake Post
c.d: Unauthorized content published to a company's real social media account(s) via a compromised third-party scheduling/management platform or API integration (e.g., a social media management SaaS tool), rather than direct compromise of the platform account credentials themselves.

A post published to a company social media account by an employee or contractor who had legitimate access to the account, but who posted the content without authorization, in violation of policy, or after their access should have been revoked.

Unauthorized modification, insertion, or reordering of content within a social media account's native scheduled-post queue, such that malicious content publishes automatically without requiring the attacker to be present at post time.

c.n: Fake Post via Compromised Third-Party Contest/Campaign Microsite Integration
c.d: Unauthorized social media content published as a result of the compromise of a separately-hosted contest, giveaway, or marketing-campaign microsite that holds an authorized integration or credential to post to company social accounts.

Unauthorized or fabricated content published to a company-associated social media channel where the deceptive core is an AI-generated deepfake (synthetic video, voice, or image) of a company representative, product, or event.

A fake or unauthorized post on a company-associated social media channel, not clearly matching the impersonator, third-party-tool, insider, scheduled-queue, microsite, or deepfake leaves under this Type.

c.n: Offensive Direct Message (DM) Blast from Compromised Account
c.d: A mass or automated blast of offensive, threatening, or otherwise inappropriate direct messages sent from a compromised company social media account to its followers, contacts, or a purchased/scraped contact list.
Offensive, threatening, or spam comments/replies posted publicly under other users' or the company's own content from a compromised or misused company social media account.
Offensive content published at high volume across posts, comments, or replies via automated scripts or bots operating through a compromised company social media account or connected integration.
Offensive, threatening, or inappropriate content broadcast in real time via a compromised company social media account's livestream or live video feature.

c.n: Offensive Content in Story/Ephemeral Post Format
c.d: Offensive, threatening, or inappropriate content posted to a company social media account's ephemeral story or status feature, where the content auto-expires after a short period, complicating detection and evidence capture.
Offensive content delivered via a company social media channel, not clearly matching the direct-message, public-comment, automated, livestream, or ephemeral-content leaves under this Type.
A post from a company social media account linking to a fraudulent cryptocurrency, token, or investment scheme, exploiting the account's trusted brand identity to lend the scam credibility.
A post from a company social media account linking directly to a malware payload or a fake download page, exploiting the account's trusted identity to drive follower infections.

A post from a company social media account linking to a fake login/credential-harvesting page, exploiting the account's trusted identity to drive followers to enter credentials on attacker-controlled infrastructure.

A post from a company social media account announcing a fake giveaway, sweepstake, or contest with a link that harvests personal data, payment details, or drives a follow-on scam, exploiting the account's trusted identity.
A post from a company social media account linking to a counterfeit or entirely fake e-commerce storefront, exploiting the account's trusted identity to sell fraudulent or nonexistent goods.

A post from a company social media account containing a URL-shortener-wrapped link whose ultimate destination and scam type are obfuscated at post time, requiring resolution before the underlying fraud (crypto, malware, phishing, giveaway, or storefront) can be identified.
A fraudulent link posted from a company-associated social media channel, not clearly matching the crypto, malware, phishing, giveaway, storefront, or shortener-obfuscated leaves under this Type.

c.n: Malicious Update via Compromised Official App Store Listing
c.d: Unauthorized publication of a malicious update to the company's mobile app through the compromise of its official developer account/listing on an authorized app store (e.g., Google Play, Apple App Store), such that the malicious version is distributed as if it were a legitimate release.

c.n: Malicious Update via Compromised CI/CD or Build Pipeline
c.d: Unauthorized injection of malicious code into the mobile app's build artifact via compromise of the CI/CD pipeline, build server, or code-signing process, such that the malicious code is baked into an otherwise normally-published update.

c.n: Malicious Update via Compromised Auto-Update/OTA Server
c.d: Unauthorized delivery of a malicious update via compromise of the company's own auto-update or OTA distribution infrastructure (used, for example, for enterprise-distributed or non-store-managed app updates), bypassing the official app store's review process entirely.

Distribution of a malicious, repackaged, or fake version of the company's mobile app via sideloading (direct APK/IPA distribution) or unofficial third-party app stores, while the company's own official app store listing and build pipeline remain uncompromised.
An unauthorized or malicious update to the company's mobile app, not clearly matching the app-store, CI/CD, OTA, or sideloading leaves under this Type.

An unauthorized push notification sent via the company's mobile app notification infrastructure, falsely claiming a security threat, account compromise, or required security action, exploiting the app's trusted push channel to alarm or manipulate users.

An unauthorized push notification sent via the company's mobile app notification infrastructure, falsely advertising a discount, sale, or promotional offer, typically to drive users to a fraudulent link or app.

An unauthorized push notification sent via the company's mobile app notification infrastructure, falsely claiming a system, policy, or account update requiring user action, distinct from a security-alert or promotional framing.

c.n: Fake Emergency/Urgent Action Required Push Notification
c.d: An unauthorized push notification sent via the company's mobile app notification infrastructure, using urgent or emergency framing (e.g., account suspension, imminent deadline, safety alert) to pressure users into immediate, unconsidered action.

An unauthorized push notification sent via the company's mobile app notification infrastructure, not clearly matching the security-alert, promotional, system-update, or urgent-action leaves under this Type.

Unauthorized modification of the mobile app's remote configuration or feature-flag settings, causing the live app to behave, display, or expose features in an unintended and potentially damaging way without any code update.

Unauthorized modification of the backend CMS or content feed that supplies text, images, or articles displayed within the mobile app, causing unintended or brand-damaging content to appear in-app without a code release.
Unauthorized modification of product catalog listings or pricing data displayed within the mobile app, causing incorrect, fraudulent, or brand-damaging product/price information to be shown to users.

Injection of malicious, offensive, or fraudulent content into the mobile app via legitimate user-generated-content features (e.g., reviews, comments, profile fields, uploaded media), exploiting insufficient content moderation or input validation rather than any backend system compromise.
Unauthorized tampering with the mobile app's displayed content, not clearly matching the remote-config, CMS, catalog/pricing, or user-generated-content leaves under this Type.

The presence of malicious functionality within the company's official mobile app that originates from a third-party SDK or library dependency, either because the SDK vendor was compromised or because the SDK itself was malicious from the outset, resulting in the malware shipping inside an otherwise legitimate company app.

An unofficial, repackaged copy of the company's mobile app in which an attacker has decompiled the legitimate app, embedded malicious code, and re-signed/redistributed it, typically outside the official app store, to deceive users into installing it in place of the genuine app.

c.n: Malicious Code Injected via Compromised Build/Signing Process
c.d: Malicious functionality embedded directly into the company's official mobile app codebase or binary through compromise of the internal build system or code-signing process, resulting in the malicious code shipping under the company's own legitimate signature.

Malicious functionality that is not present in the app binary at install time but is fetched and executed dynamically from an attacker-controlled or compromised remote server after the app is installed and running, evading app store static/dynamic review of the submitted binary.

c.n: Unclassified / General Embedded Malware in Mobile App
c.d: Malware embedded in or delivered through the company's mobile app, not clearly matching the third-party-SDK, trojanized-clone, build-compromise, or dynamic-payload leaves under this Type.
Unauthorized alteration of content on the corporate intranet portal or internal wiki, replacing or overlaying legitimate internal content with unauthorized material.
Unauthorized alteration of content or display on the HR/benefits self-service portal, distinct from the intranet/wiki by its sensitive-data context and its links to payroll/benefits actions.
Unauthorized alteration of the IT helpdesk or ticketing portal's content or display, distinct from other employee portals by the risk of undermining trust in IT support channels themselves.

c.n: Employee Portal Defacement via Compromised Insider Credentials
c.d: Defacement of any internal employee-facing portal performed after an attacker (or a malicious insider) authenticates using a compromised legitimate employee credential, rather than through a platform-level exploit.

c.n: Employee Portal Defacement via Compromised CMS/Admin Panel
c.d: Defacement of an internal employee-facing portal achieved by compromising the CMS or admin panel that controls its content, granting broad content-editing power beyond a single user account.
Defacement of an internal employee-facing portal, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (intranet/wiki, HR portal, helpdesk portal, compromised-credential, or compromised-CMS access vector).
Unauthorized alteration of content or display within the customer account dashboard, visible to authenticated customers viewing their own account.
Unauthorized alteration of content on the customer-facing support portal or help center, including knowledge-base articles and support-ticket landing pages.
Unauthorized alteration of content on the public-facing e-commerce or storefront portal, visible to any visitor without requiring authentication.

c.n: Customer Portal Defacement via Compromised Admin/CMS Access
c.d: Defacement of any customer-facing portal (dashboard, support, or storefront) achieved through compromise of the platform's administrative or CMS access, rather than a customer-facing application vulnerability alone.

c.n: Customer Portal Defacement Injecting Fraudulent Payment/Billing Content
c.d: Defacement of a customer-facing portal in which the injected content includes fraudulent payment instructions, fake billing notices, or altered payment forms intended to capture customer financial data or divert payments.
Defacement of a customer-facing portal, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (account dashboard, support/help center, storefront, compromised admin/CMS access, or fraudulent payment injection).
Unauthorized alteration of content on the company's vendor/supplier extranet portal, visible to external supply-chain partners.
Unauthorized alteration of content on the company's API developer portal, visible to external developers and integration partners.
Unauthorized alteration of content on the company's reseller/channel-partner portal, visible to external sales and distribution partners.

c.n: Partner Platform Defacement via Compromised Federated/SSO Access
c.d: Defacement of a partner-facing platform (extranet, developer portal, or reseller portal) achieved after compromising a federated/SSO identity trust relationship, granting the attacker partner-level access without directly compromising the target platform's own credentials.
Defacement of a partner-facing platform, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (vendor extranet, developer portal, reseller portal, or compromised federated/SSO access).
Unauthorized alteration of the marketing or newsletter email template, causing subscribers to receive an email containing unauthorized content.
Unauthorized alteration of a transactional email template, causing customers to receive automated notices (order confirmations, receipts, account notices) containing unauthorized content.

Unauthorized alteration of the company-standard employee email signature block (logo, tagline, disclaimer, or embedded links), typically pushed centrally via email client policy or a signature-management tool.

c.n: Email Template Defacement via Compromised Marketing Platform
c.d: Defacement of a company email template achieved through compromise of the marketing automation platform or email service provider (ESP) account used to design and send campaigns, rather than through a mail-server/transport-level compromise.

c.n: Email Template Defacement via Compromised Mail Server/Transport Rule
c.d: Defacement of company email content achieved through compromise of the mail server infrastructure or the insertion of a malicious mail-transport rule that alters outbound message content in transit, rather than through the marketing/ESP application layer.

c.n: Unclassified / General Company Email Template Defacement
c.d: Defacement of a company email template, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (marketing/newsletter, transactional, signature block, compromised marketing platform, or compromised mail server/transport rule).

c.n: Malicious/Rogue Chatbot or Workflow Bot Tampering
c.d: Unauthorized deployment or manipulation of an automated chatbot or workflow bot within an internal messaging platform to post unauthorized content into channels.
Unauthorized posting or content manipulation within an internal messaging platform performed by an attacker who has compromised a channel or workspace administrator account.
Unauthorized posting or content manipulation within an internal messaging platform performed through a malicious or compromised third-party application/integration granted access to the workspace.
Unauthorized alteration of a pinned message or content posted into a designated company-wide announcement channel within the internal messaging platform.

c.n: Unclassified / General Internal Messaging Platform Tampering
