c.d: Unauthorized content manipulation within an internal messaging platform, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (rogue bot, compromised admin, malicious third-party app, or pinned/announcement channel).

c.n: Digital Billboard Defacement via Compromised Ad Network/CMS
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of content displayed on a digital billboard, achieved by compromising the ad network or CMS platform used to schedule and push that content, rather than through direct physical access to the billboard hardware.

c.n: Digital Billboard Defacement via Physical Console/Local Access
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of digital billboard content achieved by physically accessing the billboard's local control console, media player, or hardware interface on-site.

c.n: Digital Billboard Defacement via Compromised Remote Management Software
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of digital billboard content achieved by compromising the remote device-management/fleet-management software used to administer and push updates to networked billboard hardware.
Defacement of a company digital billboard, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (compromised ad-network/CMS, physical/local access, or compromised remote management software).
Unauthorized alteration of content displayed on lobby or reception-area digital signage.
Unauthorized alteration of content displayed on a meeting room or conference room screen.

c.n: Office Display Defacement via Compromised Signage CMS
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of office digital signage content achieved by compromising the signage CMS that centrally manages and pushes content to multiple displays across one or more locations.

c.n: Office Display Defacement via Rogue HDMI/Casting Device
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of office digital signage or meeting-room display content achieved by physically attaching a rogue HDMI input source or unauthorized wireless casting/streaming device.
Defacement of an office digital display, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (lobby/reception, meeting room, compromised signage CMS, or rogue HDMI/casting device).
Unauthorized alteration of the displayed content, interface, or configuration of a customer-facing self-service check-in or ordering kiosk.
Unauthorized alteration of the displayed content, interface, or configuration of a retail point-of-sale terminal used to process customer payments.

c.n: Kiosk Tampering via Physical USB/Peripheral Access
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of a kiosk or POS terminal's content or configuration achieved by physically connecting an unauthorized USB device or peripheral to the terminal.

c.n: Kiosk Tampering via Compromised Remote Management/Update Channel
c.d: Unauthorized alteration of a kiosk or POS terminal's content or configuration achieved by compromising the remote device-management platform or software-update mechanism used to administer the terminal fleet.

c.n: Unclassified / General Kiosk or POS Tampering
c.d: Unauthorized tampering with a self-service kiosk or POS terminal, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (check-in/ordering kiosk, retail POS, physical USB/peripheral access, or compromised remote management channel).

A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears on both the corporate website and one or more official social media accounts at or near the same time, indicating a linked or shared compromise.

A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears on both the corporate website and the company's mobile application at or near the same time, indicating a linked or shared compromise.

c.n: Simultaneous Social Media + Internal Platform Defacement
c.d: A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears on both an official social media account and an internal platform (e.g. intranet, employee portal, or internal messaging) at or near the same time, indicating a linked compromise spanning both external and internal surfaces.

c.n: Full-Spectrum Coordinated Defacement (Three or More Channels)
c.d: A coordinated defacement incident in which unauthorized content appears across three or more distinct company channels (any combination of website, social media, mobile app, internal platform, email, or physical displays) at or near the same time.

A coordinated defacement incident spanning multiple company channels, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (website+social media, website+mobile app, social media+internal platform, or three-or-more-channel full-spectrum attacks).

c.n: Multi-Subsidiary/Brand Defacement Within Same Parent Organization
c.d: A defacement incident affecting two or more subsidiary brands or business units under the same parent organization, typically via a shared platform, infrastructure, or vendor common to those entities.

A defacement incident affecting two or more of the company's brands (or the company alongside unrelated external organizations) resulting from a shared vulnerability in a common third-party vendor or platform used across those brands.

A defacement incident affecting multiple franchise or licensee locations operating under the company's brand, typically via a shared franchise system, template, or vendor common to the franchise network.
A defacement incident affecting multiple company brands or affiliated entities, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (multi-subsidiary, shared third-party vendor, or franchise/licensee network).
An extended defacement campaign characterized by the same channel being defaced again after having already been remediated/reverted, within a relatively short recurrence window.
An extended defacement campaign characterized by an attacker maintaining persistent, long-dwell-time access to a defacement-capable system, discovered well after initial compromise.
An extended defacement campaign characterized by multiple distinct stages of escalating scope, severity, or channel reach, carried out deliberately by the same actor or campaign over time.
An extended, multi-event defacement campaign, not clearly matching a more specific leaf (repeated re-defacement, long-dwell-time persistent access, or escalating multi-stage campaign).

A fraudulent website that clones or closely imitates a banking, credit union, payment processor, or other financial institution's real site to harvest login credentials, card data, or authorize fraudulent transactions from visitors.

A fraudulent website replicating our organization's actual single sign-on or corporate login page, designed to capture credentials from customers, partners, or the public who mistake it for our real portal.

A fraudulent site posing as a government, tax, or regulatory agency page that references or spoofs our brand (e.g., a fake 'verify your account with [agency] via [our company]' flow) to extract personal or financial data.
A fraudulent site cloning our streaming/subscription service's sign-in, billing-update, or renewal pages to capture customer payment card data or account credentials.
A fraudulent website impersonating our brand for phishing purposes, not yet matched to a more specific sector-based leaf (banking, SSO, government, or subscription).

A fraudulent website posing as an official or unofficial download source for our software, offering 'cracked' or pirated versions bundled with malware, targeting the public rather than our own workforce.
A fraudulent site or unofficial listing offering a browser extension/plugin that claims affiliation with our brand, used to deliver malware, adware, or data-harvesting code to end users.
A fraudulent Android/iOS application distributed via sideloading, a third-party app store, or a direct-download link, impersonating our brand's app to deliver malware or harvest data.

c.n: Malware Distribution Site Disguised as Media/Streaming Site
c.d: A fraudulent site posing as a media or content-streaming service under our brand, using fake 'watch now' or 'download player' prompts to deliver malware.
A fraudulent malware distribution site impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific delivery-mechanism leaf.
A fraudulent web page posing as our official software support/help desk, typically urging visitors to call a scam number or install remote-access tools under the guise of fixing a fabricated problem.

A fraudulent page posing as our internet/telecom service support, used to scam customers into fraudulent payments, remote access, or credential disclosure under the guise of resolving a connectivity issue.
A fraudulent support/help page (not a full login-portal clone) posing as our financial services support, designed to extract account information or drive fraudulent phone contact.

c.n: Fake Support Page Surfaced via Malicious Search Ad
c.d: A fake support page impersonating our brand where the primary discovery vector is a malicious paid search ad (malvertising) rather than organic search, phishing email, or social media.
A fraudulent support page impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific sector or delivery-mechanism leaf.
A fraudulent e-commerce site that copies our actual branding, logo, and product catalog to trick customers into purchasing counterfeit goods or paying for goods never delivered.
A fraudulent e-commerce site inventing a fake affiliation or partnership with our brand (rather than cloning our real site) to sell counterfeit or non-existent goods.

c.n: Fake Marketplace Listing/Storefront on Legitimate Platform
c.d: A fake product listing or seller storefront on a legitimate marketplace (e.g., a major online retail or auction platform) that misuses our brand name, logo, or product images to sell counterfeit or non-existent goods.

c.n: Scam E-commerce Site Discovered via Paid Search/Social Ad
c.d: A scam e-commerce site impersonating our brand that is primarily discovered and reported via a paid advertisement (search or social) rather than organic search or marketplace listing.
A fraudulent e-commerce site impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific mechanism/discovery-vector leaf.

A domain-registration-level finding: a lookalike domain differing from our real domain by a common typographical error (e.g., transposed, missing, or doubled letters), registered by a third party, regardless of whether it is yet hosting active content.
A domain-registration-level finding: a lookalike domain that embeds our full brand name alongside an added word (e.g., '-support', '-secure', '-login') or hyphenation, registered by a third party.
A domain-registration-level finding: our exact brand string registered under a different TLD or ccTLD than our official domain, by a third party.

c.n: Newly Registered Lookalike Domain Pre-Positioned for Future Campaign
c.d: A lookalike domain (of any typosquat/combosquat/TLD-swap variety) confirmed registered and dormant, assessed as likely pre-staged infrastructure for a future phishing or brand-impersonation campaign, warranting proactive monitoring ahead of weaponization.
A lookalike domain registration impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific typosquat/combosquat/TLD-swap/pre-positioned leaf.
A domain using visually similar Latin-alphabet character substitutions to closely resemble our real domain, without requiring Unicode/IDN encoding.

A domain using internationalized domain name (IDN) encoding with non-Latin Unicode characters (e.g., Cyrillic) that render visually identical or near-identical to our real domain in a browser address bar.
A domain combining characters from two or more different scripts (mixed-script) within a single label to visually approximate our real domain, exploiting inconsistent mixed-script detection.
A homograph domain impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific Latin-substitution/Unicode/mixed-script leaf.

c.n: Subdomain Abuse via Compromised Legitimate Domain
c.d: A phishing page impersonating our brand that is hosted on a subdomain of a legitimate, unrelated third-party domain that has been compromised, inheriting that domain's clean reputation.

c.n: Subdomain Abuse via Dangling DNS/Takeover of Orphaned Subdomain
c.d: A phishing page impersonating our brand hosted after an attacker claimed an orphaned cloud resource (e.g., a decommissioned CDN/hosting endpoint) still referenced by a stale DNS record — potentially one of our own abandoned subdomains, or a third party's.

c.n: Subdomain Abuse via Cloud/SaaS Free-Tier Subdomain
c.d: A phishing page impersonating our brand hosted on a free-tier subdomain provided by a legitimate cloud or SaaS platform (e.g., a free site-builder or storage subdomain), exploiting that platform's trusted top-level domain reputation.

A phishing URL impersonating our brand that places our brand name early in a long, deeply nested subdomain chain (e.g., 'ourbrand.login.secure.verify.attacker-domain.com') so that a quick visual scan of the URL appears to show our brand, obscuring the actual base domain.
Subdomain-based abuse impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific compromised-domain/dangling-DNS/cloud-abuse/nested-obfuscation leaf.

c.n: Counterfeit Product Packaging/Physical Goods Logo Misuse
c.d: Physical, non-digital counterfeiting where our logo or trademark is reproduced on packaging for counterfeit goods sold through physical or online retail channels.

c.n: Fraudulent Trust Seal/Security Certification Badge Misuse
c.d: A digital trust seal, security certification badge, or 'verified by' mark falsely displayed on a third-party site, implying an association with our brand or certification program that does not exist.

c.n: Unauthorized Logo Use in Third-Party Marketplace Product Listing
c.d: Unauthorized display of our logo/trademark within a marketplace product listing (e.g., in listing images or descriptions) to imply an affiliation or endorsement that does not exist, tracked distinctly from the underlying counterfeit-goods transaction risk.

c.n: Logo Misuse in Print/Physical Marketing Materials
c.d: Unauthorized use of our logo or trademark in physical marketing collateral — flyers, brochures, signage, physical mailers — implying a nonexistent affiliation, sponsorship, or endorsement.
Unauthorized use of our logo/trademark, not yet matched to a more specific physical-goods/trust-seal/marketplace/print-materials leaf.
A malicious paid advertisement on a social media platform using our brand assets (logo, name, imagery) to drive traffic to a phishing site, scam storefront, or malware download.
A malicious video advertisement shown before or during streaming/video content, using our brand assets to drive traffic to a fraudulent destination.
A malicious native/sponsored-content advertisement (formatted to resemble editorial content) using our brand assets to drive traffic to a fraudulent destination.

c.n: Fraudulent App Store Advertisement Promoting Fake App
c.d: A malicious advertisement (on any ad network) specifically promoting a fake mobile application impersonating our brand for download, connecting the advertising vector to the malware-distribution outcome.
A fraudulent advertisement impersonating our brand, not yet matched to a more specific social/video/native/app-promotion leaf.

c.n: Fake Customer Support Email Reply-Chain Impersonation
c.d: A fraudulent email response impersonating our official customer support, inserted into or fabricated to resemble an ongoing email reply-chain with a customer, used to extract payment or personal data.

c.n: Fake Live Chat Widget Impersonation (Embedded on Cloned/Fake Site)
c.d: A fraudulent live chat interface embedded on a fake/cloned site impersonating our brand, used to interactively social-engineer visitors in real time (e.g., walking them through a fraudulent payment or remote-access session).
A fraudulent SMS/text message impersonating our brand's customer support, used to direct recipients to a phishing link, request sensitive information, or request a callback to a fraudulent number.

A fraudulent response to a customer's public review or complaint, impersonating our brand's official social media/review-management account, used to redirect the customer to a fraudulent 'resolution' channel.
A fraudulent customer communication impersonating our brand's customer support, not yet matched to a more specific email/chat/SMS/review-response leaf.

c.n: BEC via Compromised Legitimate Executive Mailbox
c.d: An adversary gains control of a real executive's actual corporate mailbox and uses that genuine, authenticated identity to send fraudulent payment/data requests to external recipients such as customers, vendors, or partners.

c.n: BEC via Display-Name Spoofing (No Domain Compromise)
c.d: An adversary sets an email display name to match a real executive's name, sending from an unrelated (often free webmail) address, to defraud external recipients who are relying on the visible display name rather than the underlying address.
An adversary registers a lookalike domain of our organization and sends email as a named executive from that domain to defraud external recipients who do not scrutinize the domain closely.

c.n: BEC via Compromised Vendor/Third-Party Email Account
c.d: An adversary compromises the email account of one of our vendors or third parties, and uses the trusted relationship with our organization (impersonating our executives or referencing our real transactions) to defraud that vendor's other customers or our own shared counterparties.

A business email compromise incident leveraging our organization's brand or executive identity against an external party, not yet matched to a more specific mailbox-compromise/display-name/lookalike-domain/vendor-compromise leaf.

c.n: Fake Executive Profile on Professional Networking Platform
c.d: A fraudulent profile on a professional networking platform (e.g., LinkedIn) impersonating a named executive of our organization, used to build false credibility for connection requests, recruitment scams, or follow-on fraud.

c.n: Fake Executive Profile Used for Investor/Shareholder Manipulation
c.d: A fraudulent profile impersonating a named executive, used to post or privately send fabricated financial statements, forward-looking claims, or investment solicitations intended to manipulate investor or shareholder behavior.

c.n: Fake Executive Profile Announcing False Departure/Succession
c.d: A fraudulent profile or post impersonating a named executive, used to falsely announce a resignation, termination, or leadership succession, intended to cause reputational, operational, or market disruption.

c.n: Executive Impersonation Call Authorizing Urgent Wire Transfer
c.d: A voice call, potentially using AI voice-cloning/deepfake technology, impersonating a named executive of our organization to instruct finance staff or an external party to execute an urgent, unauthorized wire transfer.

c.n: Executive Impersonation Call to IT Helpdesk Requesting Password/Access Reset
c.d: A voice call impersonating a named executive of our organization, directed at our internal IT helpdesk, used to socially engineer a password reset, MFA reset, or access-elevation action.

c.n: Executive Impersonation Call to Board Member/Investor
c.d: A voice call impersonating a named executive of our organization, directed at a board member or investor, used to extract confidential information, solicit an urgent decision, or authorize a fraudulent action under apparent executive authority.
A voice call impersonating a named executive of our organization, not yet matched to a more specific wire-transfer/helpdesk/board-investor leaf.

c.n: Impersonation via Compromised Real Vendor Account/Domain
c.d: An adversary compromises the real account/domain of a vendor connected to our brand's business ecosystem and uses that genuine, trusted vendor identity to defraud our customers or partners in transactions that reference or rely on our relationship with that vendor.

c.n: Impersonation via Entirely Fabricated Vendor Identity
c.d: An adversary invents a wholly fictitious vendor entity, falsely claiming a supply or service relationship with our organization, to defraud our customers or partners who believe the arrangement is genuine.

c.n: Impersonation via Newly Onboarded/Unverified Vendor Relationship
c.d: An adversary exploits the window of ambiguity around a newly onboarded or not-yet-widely-verified vendor relationship with our organization, impersonating that new vendor to defraud our customers or partners before the relationship's legitimate details are well established or easily verifiable.
Vendor impersonation exploiting our organization's brand or business relationships, not yet matched to a more specific compromised-vendor/fabricated-vendor/new-relationship leaf.

An adversary impersonates one of our actual clients (via spoofed/lookalike email or a compromised client mailbox) to instruct our organization to redirect a payment, invoice, or refund to a fraudulent account.
An adversary impersonates one of our actual clients to request sensitive data, reports, or account information from our organization that would not normally be shared outside a verified request.

An adversary impersonates one of our actual clients to request a change to account settings — contact details, authorized users, delivery/service configuration — that could facilitate further fraud or unauthorized access.

An adversary impersonates one of our actual clients to submit a fraudulent contract renewal, purchase order, or procurement request, intended to extract payment, favorable terms, or sensitive commercial information under false pretenses.

An adversary impersonates one of our actual clients to submit a fabricated support escalation or complaint, used to pressure staff into an unwarranted concession (refund, credit, account change) or to extract sensitive account information under the guise of complaint resolution.
An incident of a real client being impersonated to target our organization, not yet matched to a more specific payment/data/account-change/contract/support-escalation leaf.

c.n: Impersonation of Outsourced/Managed IT Service Provider (MSP)
c.d: An adversary impersonates our organization's real, named outsourced or managed IT service provider (MSP) — via phone, email, or a fake portal — to socially engineer our own employees into granting access, resetting credentials, or installing remote-access tooling.

c.n: Impersonation of SaaS Vendor's Official Support Team
c.d: An adversary impersonates the official support team of a SaaS platform we actually use, contacting our staff to socially engineer credential resets, OAuth consent grants, or account access.

An adversary impersonates the official support team of a hardware/equipment manufacturer whose products we actually use, contacting our staff to socially engineer physical or remote access, or to deliver malware disguised as a firmware/driver update.
Impersonation of a real third-party support provider connected to our organization, not yet matched to a more specific MSP/SaaS-vendor/hardware-vendor leaf.

c.n: Customer Data Breach via Compromised Database
c.d: An incident in which customer personal or financial data is exfiltrated from a company-owned and -operated database through direct technical compromise (SQL injection, exploited vulnerability, stolen application credentials), and the exposure becomes known to customers, regulators, or the public.

c.n: Customer Data Exposure via Misconfigured Cloud Storage Bucket
c.d: An incident in which customer data stored in a cloud object-storage bucket (e.g., S3, Azure Blob, GCS) is left publicly accessible due to misconfiguration and is discovered by a researcher, journalist, or threat actor, triggering public disclosure.

c.n: Customer Data Exposure via Third-Party/Vendor Data Processor Breach
c.d: An incident in which a third-party vendor, contractor, or data processor entrusted with company customer data suffers its own breach, resulting in exposure of the company's customer data and requiring the company to manage disclosure despite not controlling the compromised system.

c.n: Customer Data Exposure via Insider Data Theft
c.d: An incident in which a malicious insider steals customer data and the theft results in public disclosure, regulatory notification, or reputational impact — distinct from the insider's motivation and internal handling, which is tracked elsewhere.

c.n: Customer Data Breach via Ransomware Group Data Exfiltration/Leak
c.d: An incident in which a ransomware group, having exfiltrated customer data as part of a double- or triple-extortion attack, publicly posts or threatens to post that data on a leak site, triggering brand, regulatory, and customer-notification consequences.

A confirmed or suspected exposure of customer data that has not yet been attributed to a specific vector (compromised database, cloud misconfiguration, vendor breach, insider theft, or ransomware leak).

An incident in which employee personal identifiable information or HR records (SSNs, addresses, benefits enrollment, performance data) are exfiltrated from a company-operated HR system through direct technical compromise, and the exposure becomes known internally or externally.

An incident in which payroll, salary, bonus, or equity compensation data is exposed or leaked, creating distinct risks around employee financial fraud, internal pay-equity fallout, and competitive intelligence exposure.

c.n: Employee Data Exposure via Third-Party HR/Benefits Platform Breach
c.d: An incident in which a third-party HR, payroll, or benefits administration platform used by the company suffers its own breach, exposing company employee data and requiring the company to manage disclosure despite not controlling the compromised system.

c.n: Employee Data Exposure via Insider Data Theft
c.d: An incident in which a malicious insider steals employee data and the theft results in public disclosure, regulatory notification, or reputational impact — distinct from the insider's motivation and internal handling, which is tracked elsewhere.

A confirmed or suspected exposure of employee data that has not yet been attributed to a specific vector (direct HR system compromise, payroll-specific exposure, third-party HR/benefits platform breach, or insider theft).

c.n: Source Code Leak via Misconfigured Public Code Repository
c.d: An incident in which company source code is discovered publicly accessible via a misconfigured public code repository (e.g., a private GitHub/GitLab repo accidentally made public, or code pushed to a public repo), and the exposure becomes known to researchers, competitors, or the public.

c.n: Source Code Leak via Insider Exfiltration
c.d: An incident in which a malicious insider deliberately exfiltrates company source code and it subsequently becomes publicly known, sold, or leaked — distinct from the insider's motivation and internal handling, which is tracked elsewhere.

c.n: Source Code Leak via Compromised Build/CI Pipeline
c.d: An incident in which an attacker compromises a build server, CI/CD pipeline, or associated artifact repository to exfiltrate proprietary source code, and the resulting leak or theft becomes publicly known.

c.n: Source Code Leak via Third-Party Contractor/Vendor Access
c.d: An incident in which a third-party contractor or vendor with legitimate access to company source code (for development, integration, or support purposes) leaks or loses control of that code, resulting in public disclosure.

A confirmed or suspected leak of proprietary source code that has not yet been attributed to a specific vector (public repository misconfiguration, insider exfiltration, pipeline compromise, or contractor/vendor access).
An incident in which material, non-public financial results (quarterly earnings, revenue figures, guidance) are disclosed to the media, market, or public before the company's official announcement.

An incident in which non-public information about a pending merger, acquisition, divestiture, or other material deal is disclosed to media, market participants, or the public ahead of the official announcement.

c.n: Financial Data Disclosure via Compromised Finance System
c.d: An incident in which an attacker gains unauthorized technical access to a finance system (ERP, financial reporting platform, treasury system) and exfiltrates confidential financial data that subsequently becomes known externally.

c.n: Financial Data Disclosure via Insider Trading-Motivated Leak
c.d: An incident in which an individual with legitimate access to material non-public financial information leaks or tips that information to a third party (or trades on it directly) for the purpose of enabling securities trading ahead of public disclosure.

A confirmed or suspected premature disclosure of confidential financial data that has not yet been attributed to a specific vector (routine earnings leak, deal-specific leak, system compromise, or trading-motivated leak).

An incident in which a trade secret, proprietary manufacturing process, or other protected business methodology is disclosed to competitors, media, or the public, undermining the company's competitive advantage.

An incident in which details of an invention that has not yet been filed for patent protection, or is in a pending/unpublished patent application state, are disclosed publicly — potentially jeopardizing patentability due to prior-art or public-disclosure rules.
An incident in which details of an unreleased product, feature, or forward-looking product roadmap are disclosed to media, competitors, or the public before the company's planned announcement.

c.n: R&D Data/Research Leak via Compromised System
c.d: An incident in which an attacker gains unauthorized technical access to a research and development system or repository and exfiltrates confidential R&D data, which subsequently becomes publicly known.

c.n: IP Leak via Departing Employee Theft
c.d: An incident in which an employee, in the process of leaving the company (resignation, termination, or move to a competitor), takes proprietary intellectual property — trade secrets, research data, product plans — and it subsequently becomes known externally or is used by a competitor.

A confirmed or suspected leak of intellectual property that has not yet been attributed to a specific vector (trade secret, patent-pending invention, product roadmap, R&D system compromise, or departing employee theft).

An incident in which confidential documents related to active or contemplated litigation — legal strategy memos, privileged correspondence, discovery materials — are disclosed to media, opposing counsel improperly, or the public.

An incident in which a confidential commercial contract, partnership agreement, or non-disclosure agreement is disclosed to media, competitors, or the public, revealing terms both parties intended to keep private.
An incident in which board meeting minutes, board deck materials, or other corporate governance documents are disclosed to media, shareholders outside proper channels, or the public.

An incident in which confidential documents related to an active or contemplated regulatory investigation (subpoenas, information requests, internal investigative findings, regulator correspondence) are disclosed to media or the public.

A confirmed or suspected leak of confidential legal documents that has not yet been attributed to a specific vector (litigation materials, contracts/NDAs, board governance documents, or regulatory investigation documents).

An incident in which a current or former employee submits a whistleblower report to the SEC or another financial regulator alleging securities-law violations, accounting fraud, or financial misconduct by the company.

An incident in which a current or former employee submits a whistleblower report to OSHA or another workplace-safety regulator alleging unsafe working conditions or safety-law violations by the company.
An incident in which a current or former employee submits a whistleblower report to an environmental regulator (e.g., EPA) alleging environmental-law violations or pollution by the company.

An incident in which a current or former employee submits a whistleblower report to a data-privacy regulator (e.g., a Data Protection Authority, FTC) alleging data-handling or privacy-law violations by the company.
A confirmed or suspected whistleblower disclosure to a regulator that has not yet been attributed to a specific regulatory domain (financial, safety, environmental, or privacy).

c.n: Leak to Media/Journalist Over Internal Policy Dispute
c.d: An incident in which a current or former employee, in disagreement with an internal company policy or decision, discloses internal information to a journalist or media outlet, resulting in public reporting.

c.n: Public Social Media Disclosure Over Internal Policy Dispute
c.d: An incident in which a current or former employee posts about an internal policy disagreement directly on public social media, bypassing both internal channels and traditional media.

c.n: Leak to Advocacy/Union Organization Over Internal Policy Dispute
c.d: An incident in which a current or former employee discloses internal policy dispute details to an external advocacy organization or labor union, which may then amplify the dispute publicly or use it in organizing/advocacy efforts.

c.n: Internal Hotline/Ethics Escalation Later Leaked Externally
c.d: An incident in which an employee's internal hotline or ethics-escalation report — initially handled through proper internal channels — is subsequently leaked externally (to media, social media, a regulator, or an advocacy group) by the reporting employee or another party, typically due to dissatisfaction with the internal resolution.

c.n: Unclassified / General Internal Policy Dispute Leak
c.d: A confirmed or suspected external leak of an internal policy dispute that has not yet been attributed to a specific channel (media, social media, advocacy/union, or escalated hotline report).

An incident in which company privileged or administrator account credentials are discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace or forum, triggering organizational response to the discovery itself, distinct from how the credentials were originally obtained.

c.n: Cloud/SaaS Tenant Credential Listing for Sale
c.d: An incident in which credentials granting access to a company cloud infrastructure tenant (AWS, Azure, GCP) or a critical SaaS platform are discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace, triggering organizational response to the discovery itself.

c.n: Financial/Banking Account Credential Listing for Sale
c.d: An incident in which credentials granting access to a company financial or banking account (treasury, corporate card administration, banking portal) are discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace, triggering organizational response to prevent financial fraud.
A confirmed or suspected dark-web listing of company credentials for sale that has not yet been attributed to a specific access category (privileged/admin, cloud/SaaS tenant, or financial/banking).

c.n: Stolen Customer Database Listing for Sale
c.d: An incident in which a database of stolen company customer records is discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace or breach forum, triggering organizational response to the listing's discovery and any resulting disclosure obligations.

c.n: Stolen Source Code/Intellectual Property Listing for Sale
c.d: An incident in which stolen company source code or other intellectual property is discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace or specialized forum, triggering organizational response to the listing's discovery.

c.n: Stolen Internal Document Cache Listing for Sale
c.d: An incident in which a cache of stolen internal company documents (legal files, board materials, general correspondence not otherwise categorized as customer, employee, or source-code data) is discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace.

c.n: Stolen Employee/HR Data Listing for Sale
c.d: An incident in which stolen company employee or HR data is discovered listed for sale on a dark web marketplace or breach forum, triggering organizational response to the listing's discovery and any resulting employee notification obligations.

c.n: Unclassified / General Proprietary Data for Sale
c.d: A confirmed or suspected dark-web listing of stolen company proprietary data for sale that has not yet been attributed to a specific data category (customer database, source code/IP, internal document cache, or employee/HR data).

An incident in which a ransomware group publishes a public countdown, deadline, or extortion announcement on its leak site or communication channel naming the company, intended to pressure payment through public visibility ahead of confirmed data publication.

An incident in which a hacktivist group publicly posts a claim of responsibility for an attack (defacement, DDoS, data theft, or other action) against the company, typically framed around an ideological, political, or social cause.

An incident in which a threat actor or unknown party publicly claims a data breach or compromise of the company that cannot be verified against internal evidence, or is confirmed to be false, exaggerated, or recycled from an unrelated prior incident.

An incident in which a threat actor posts a pre-sale teaser or auction announcement referencing stolen company data, without yet publishing the full listing or sample data, intended to build buyer interest or increase extortion pressure.

A confirmed or suspected public threat actor announcement referencing the company that has not yet been attributed to a specific category (ransomware countdown, hacktivist claim, unverified/exaggerated claim, or sale/auction teaser).

An incident in which a network of automated or semi-automated social media bot accounts coordinates to spread false or misleading claims about the company, its products, or its leadership, at a scale and pattern indicating inauthentic coordination rather than organic public sentiment.

An incident in which a nation-state or state-affiliated actor conducts a coordinated disinformation campaign against the company, typically tied to geopolitical tensions, sanctions, or the company's operations in a particular region.

An incident in which a competitor is found to be directly or indirectly sponsoring a coordinated misinformation campaign against the company, typically to damage market perception or influence a competitive deal/procurement decision.

An incident in which AI-generated synthetic media (deepfake video, cloned voice audio, or fabricated imagery) depicting a company executive or representing the company is used to spread false statements or claims, and is disseminated as if genuine.

A confirmed or suspected coordinated misinformation campaign against the company that has not yet been attributed to a specific driver (bot network, state sponsorship, competitor sponsorship, or AI-generated deepfake content).

c.n: Paid Bot/Click-Farm Amplification of Negative Story
c.d: An incident in which genuine (not fabricated) negative press coverage of the company is artificially amplified beyond its organic reach through paid bot networks or click-farm services, distorting the apparent scale of public reaction.

c.n: Coordinated Inauthentic Social Sharing of Negative Story
c.d: An incident in which a coordinated network of accounts, designed to appear as genuine individual users rather than obvious bots, shares and amplifies negative press coverage of the company in a synchronized pattern indicating central coordination.

c.n: Search Engine Result Manipulation to Surface Negative Press
c.d: An incident in which a party manipulates search engine ranking signals (SEO manipulation, negative SEO, review/link farms) to increase the visibility and ranking of negative press content about the company in search results.

An incident in which a coordinated group posts a large volume of negative reviews or ratings against the company on a review platform (app stores, Glassdoor, Google/Yelp, etc.) within a short period, disproportionate to genuine customer/employee sentiment, typically in reaction to a specific triggering event.

A confirmed or suspected artificial amplification of negative press about the company that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism (paid bot/click-farm, coordinated inauthentic sharing, search engine manipulation, or review bombing).

An incident in which an influencer is paid (directly or through an intermediary, potentially including a competitor or hostile actor) to post disinformation or unfairly negative content about the company without disclosing the paid/sponsored nature of the post, violating advertising-disclosure norms.

c.n: Influencer Account Compromise for Negative Content Posting
c.d: An incident in which an attacker gains unauthorized technical access to an influencer's social media account and uses it to post fabricated negative content about the company, without the influencer's knowledge or consent.

An incident in which a third party coerces or blackmails an influencer — using their own account, under their own knowing control — into posting fabricated or unfairly negative content about the company.

c.n: Deceptive Influencer Outreach (False Pretext for Negative Coverage)
c.d: An incident in which a third party deceives an influencer — through a false pretext, fabricated documents, or a misleading briefing — into believing false claims about the company are true, leading the influencer to unknowingly and in good faith produce negative coverage.

A confirmed or suspected instance of influencer-driven negative content about the company that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism (undisclosed paid sponsorship, account compromise, coercion, or deceptive pretext).

c.n: Ransom Note Left on Encrypted Systems Threatening Data Publication
c.d: An incident in which a ransomware group's ransom note — discovered on encrypted systems at the moment of attack — explicitly threatens to publish stolen data if payment demands are not met, distinct from any later direct extortion communication channel or confirmed data publication.

c.n: Direct Extortion Email/Portal Threatening Data Publication
c.d: An incident in which a threat actor establishes a direct communication channel (email address, dedicated negotiation portal/website) to negotiate payment under threat of publishing stolen data, distinct from the initial ransom note or confirmed publication itself.

c.n: Double-Extortion Threat with Sample Data Proof Attached
c.d: An incident in which a threat actor provides a sample of the stolen data (a small file set or screenshot cache) as proof of the theft, to substantiate a double-extortion threat and increase pressure to pay.

c.n: Triple-Extortion Threat (Data Exposure + DDoS + Notification Threat)
c.d: An incident in which a threat actor combines the standard data-publication extortion threat with an active or threatened distributed denial-of-service attack and a threat to directly notify the company's customers, partners, or regulators, compounding pressure across three simultaneous vectors.

c.n: Unclassified / General Ransomware Data Exposure Threat
c.d: A confirmed or suspected ransomware-linked threat to expose stolen data that has not yet been attributed to a specific stage (initial ransom note, direct negotiation communication, sample-proof provision, or triple-extortion escalation).

An incident in which a threat actor obtains company data through means other than a ransomware/encryption attack (e.g., exploiting a vulnerability, database compromise, or purchasing stolen data from another source) and directly demands payment to prevent its publication, without any encryption having occurred.

An incident in which a threat actor obtains an executive's or other individual's personal data (not general corporate data) and threatens to publish it, with the threat framed to pressure the company (e.g., reputational damage to the individual's public company role) rather than the company's systems or corporate data directly.

An incident in which a threat actor's primary extortion leverage is not the data publication itself but the threat to directly notify regulators or customers of a breach ahead of or instead of the company's own controlled disclosure process, aiming to maximize reputational and regulatory pressure.

c.n: Unclassified / General Blackmail with Leaked Data
c.d: A confirmed or suspected blackmail attempt using leaked or stolen company-related data that has not yet been attributed to a specific pattern (pure corporate blackmail, executive personal-data blackmail, or notification-timing-focused blackmail).

c.n: Public Social Media Threat Campaign Against Organization
c.d: An incident in which a threat actor conducts a sustained, public social media campaign making threats against the company (operational disruption, further attacks, reputational harm) intended to intimidate or extort, without necessarily holding stolen data as leverage.

An incident in which a threat actor directly contacts company customers or employees (via email, text, or phone) with threats intended to intimidate, extort, or damage the company's relationship with those individuals.

An incident in which a threat actor reaches out to journalists or media outlets directly, threatening to provide them with damaging information about the company unless demands are met, using media exposure itself as the extortion lever.

A confirmed or suspected public threat campaign against the company that has not yet been attributed to a specific channel (public social media, direct customer/employee communication, or press/media outreach).

c.n: Bot/Fake Account Network Negative Review Campaign
c.d: A deliberate campaign in which a network of automated or fabricated accounts (no real purchase/usage history) floods a review platform with negative reviews of the organization's product or service to depress its rating and visibility.

A campaign in which a paid human workforce (a click-farm or gig-labor pool) is directed to post negative reviews of the organization's product or service, typically via instructions distributed through a task-marketplace or messaging group.

c.n: Review Platform Manipulation via Compromised/Purchased Verified Accounts
c.d: A campaign in which previously legitimate, verified reviewer accounts — obtained through account takeover or purchased on black-market forums — are used to post negative reviews that appear more credible than obviously-fake accounts.

A coordinated negative-review incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific mechanism (bot network, paid click-farm, or compromised/purchased accounts) before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

c.n: Direct Competitor-Sponsored Fake Negative Review Campaign
c.d: A campaign in which an identifiable competitor organization (or its employees/agents acting on its direction) directly authors or commissions fake negative reviews of the organization's product or service.

A campaign in which a competitor hires an independent third-party service (a 'black hat' reputation-management or review-manipulation vendor) to execute a negative-review campaign, obscuring the competitor's direct involvement.
A suspected competitor-sponsored negative-review incident awaiting further investigation to determine sponsorship structure before reclassification to a specific sibling ITID.

c.n: Viral Social Media Post Driving Mass Negative Review Influx
c.d: A spike in negative reviews caused by a social media post (often a single viral complaint, video, or thread) that drives real users, not fabricated accounts, to leave negative reviews en masse — an organically-triggered pile-on rather than a manufactured campaign.

A campaign in which an influencer or content creator explicitly calls on their audience to go leave negative reviews of the organization's product or service, converting follower engagement into a directed review-bombing action.

A campaign or organic pattern in which negative reviews (real or fabricated) are screenshotted and re-shared across multiple social media platforms, amplifying reputational reach well beyond the original review site's audience.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Media Amplified Reviews
c.d: A social-media-amplified negative-review incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific amplification mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

c.n: Bot Network-Generated Fake Positive Reviews for Competitor
c.d: A campaign in which automated or fabricated accounts post fake positive reviews for a competing product/service, framed comparatively to disadvantage the organization's standing (e.g., reviews explicitly contrasting favorably against the organization).

c.n: Paid Reviewer Ring Boosting Competitor Ratings
c.d: A campaign in which a paid ring of human reviewers posts fake positive reviews for a competing product/service, often with comparative language disadvantaging the organization's standing.

c.n: Astroturfed Competitor Praise Campaign Referencing Organization Unfavorably
c.d: A campaign designed to look like organic, independent grassroots enthusiasm for a competitor's product/service, which includes unfavorable references to the organization, but which is in fact orchestrated (e.g., by a marketing team or PR firm) rather than genuinely organic.

c.n: Unclassified / General False Positive Reviews for Competitor
c.d: A suspected fake-positive-review-for-competitor incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

c.n: Positive Reviews of Fake Products or Services
Fake Positive Reviews Supporting Counterfeit Product Listing
c.d: A campaign in which fake positive reviews are posted to a counterfeit product listing impersonating or trading on the organization's brand, to make the fraudulent listing appear trustworthy to buyers.

c.n: Fake Positive Reviews Supporting Scam E-Commerce Storefront
c.d: A campaign in which fake positive reviews are posted on a standalone scam e-commerce storefront (a dedicated fraudulent website, not a marketplace listing) that impersonates the organization's brand to build purchaser trust before defrauding customers.

c.n: Fake Positive Reviews Supporting Fraudulent App Listing
c.d: A campaign in which fake positive reviews are posted on an app-store listing for a fraudulent application impersonating the organization's brand, to drive installs before delivering malware or defrauding users.

c.n: Unclassified / General Positive Reviews of Fake Product/Service
c.d: A suspected fake-positive-review incident supporting an as-yet-unclassified fake product/service offering, awaiting further investigation before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

The use of fraudulent (fake or bot-driven) upvotes/likes to artificially boost the visibility and perceived legitimacy of scam or fraudulent content — such as phishing posts, fake giveaways, or counterfeit promotions — that misuses the organization's brand.

c.n: Fraudulent Upvoting to Suppress Legitimate Negative Feedback
c.d: The use of fraudulent (fake or bot-driven) downvotes/reports against a legitimate negative review, or upvotes on unrelated content, to push genuine negative feedback out of visibility on a platform's ranking algorithm.

Fraudulent upvoting/engagement activity attributable to a specific, identifiable bot network whose infrastructure (account clusters, automation signatures) is reused across multiple targets, distinguishing it from a one-off or purpose-built engagement-boosting effort.
A suspected fraudulent-upvoting incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific mechanism and target before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

c.n: Misinformation Post Fabricating Product Safety/Recall Claim
c.d: A social media post or thread falsely claiming the organization's product has a safety defect, contamination issue, or an active/pending recall, when no such issue or recall exists.

c.n: Misinformation Post Fabricating Executive Scandal Claim
c.d: A social media post or thread falsely claiming an executive engaged in misconduct, fraud, or scandal that did not occur, or grossly misrepresenting an actual minor event as major misconduct.

c.n: Misinformation Post Fabricating Data Breach/Security Claim
c.d: A social media post or thread falsely claiming the organization suffered a data breach, ransomware attack, or security compromise that did not actually occur, or grossly exaggerating a minor/unrelated event as a major breach.
A suspected fabricated social media misinformation post about the organization awaiting further investigation to determine its subject matter before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.
A campaign publishing video content presenting paid actors, stock footage, or fabricated scenarios as genuine, unpaid customer testimonials about the organization's product or service.

A campaign publishing content presenting fabricated or paid actors as genuine employees, misrepresenting the organization's actual workplace culture, benefits, or conditions — either overly positive (astroturfed employer branding) or falsely negative (a discrediting attack).

A single fabricated or impersonated social media post styled to look like an influencer's organic testimonial about the organization's product, where the influencer either does not exist, did not actually make the post, or is being impersonated.
A suspected fake testimonial incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific format before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

A viral social media hashtag campaign explicitly organized to call on consumers to boycott the organization's products or services, whether triggered by a genuine grievance or a fabricated/exaggerated one.

A viral social media hashtag campaign that frames the organization as the subject of a scandal (e.g., '#[BrandName]Exposed' style framing), generating reputational damage through narrative association rather than an explicit boycott call-to-action.

c.n: Hashtag Hijacking of Legitimate Branded Hashtag
c.d: An attack in which the organization's own established, legitimate marketing hashtag is flooded with negative, critical, or mocking content by outside actors, subverting the hashtag's intended positive purpose.

c.n: Unclassified / General Viral Negative Hashtag Campaign
c.d: A suspected viral negative hashtag incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

Review-platform abuse in which large numbers of freshly-created, disposable accounts (no aging, no purchase history, minimal profile completion) are used to post reviews, prioritizing volume and speed over evading detection.

Review-platform abuse using accounts that have genuine age and prior activity history — either stolen via account takeover or purchased on black-market forums — making the resulting reviews harder to distinguish from genuine activity than freshly-created accounts.

c.n: Cross-Platform Spam Account Network Reused for Reviews
c.d: Review-platform manipulation carried out by an account network whose infrastructure (registration patterns, automation signatures) is observed being reused across multiple, distinct platforms (e.g., the same underlying network posting fake reviews, fake social engagement, and fake app ratings), indicating a commercial engagement-fraud-as-a-service operation.

c.n: Unclassified / General Spam Account Review Manipulation
c.d: A suspected spam-account review-manipulation incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific account mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

Exploitation of a review platform's internal review-sorting or ranking logic (such as 'most helpful' voting weight or recency weighting) to artificially surface favorable reviews or bury unfavorable ones, independent of the reviews' actual content authenticity.

c.n: Search Result Ranking Manipulation via Review Signal Gaming
c.d: Exploitation of an external search engine's ranking algorithm using review-related signals (e.g., review-schema markup abuse, fabricated star-rating rich snippets, or review-farm-linked SEO tactics) to distort search-result visibility or star-rating display for the organization's listings.

Exploitation of a platform's recommendation engine (e.g., 'customers also liked', personalized recommendation feeds) using manipulated review signals to suppress the organization's products from recommendation surfaces or to inject a competitor's products in their place.

c.n: Unclassified / General Review Platform Algorithm Exploit
c.d: A suspected review-platform algorithm exploit awaiting further investigation to determine its specific target mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

A campaign using traditional scripted/automated bots to post reviews at scale, relying on fixed or lightly-varied templated text rather than generative-AI text production or advanced anti-bot evasion.

c.n: AI-Generated Fake Review Text at Scale
c.d: A campaign using generative-AI language models to produce large volumes of unique, non-templated fake review text, deliberately evading the text-similarity detection that catches traditional scripted bot campaigns.

A review-posting bot network whose defining and most technically significant characteristic is its capability to defeat CAPTCHA and other anti-automation verification challenges on the review platform, regardless of whether the review text itself is templated or AI-generated.

c.n: Unclassified / General Paid Review Bot Campaign
c.d: A suspected paid review bot campaign awaiting further investigation to determine its specific mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

c.n: Undisclosed Paid Positive Review for Competitor Product
c.d: An influencer publishes a positive review or endorsement of a competitor's legitimate product/service without disclosing that they were paid to do so, in violation of advertising-disclosure regulations (e.g., FTC endorsement guidelines), potentially drawing customers away from the organization under false pretenses of organic endorsement.

c.n: Undisclosed Paid Positive Review for Counterfeit/Scam Product
c.d: An influencer publishes an undisclosed paid positive review or endorsement of a counterfeit or scam product/service (as opposed to a legitimate competitor), directly exposing their audience to fraud while also drawing customers away from the organization.

c.n: Sponsored Content Misrepresenting Product Test/Comparison Results
c.d: Sponsored influencer content presenting fabricated, cherry-picked, or methodologically-biased product test/comparison results that unfairly disadvantage the organization's product relative to the sponsoring competitor's, while the sponsorship or methodology bias is undisclosed.
A suspected sponsored-misinformation influencer incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific target/format before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

An influencer purchases or otherwise fraudulently inflates follower counts, likes, views, or comments to misrepresent their genuine audience size and engagement, which misleads marketing/partnership decisions and audiences evaluating the influencer's credibility.

An influencer falsely claims professional credentials, expertise, or qualifications (e.g., a fabricated medical, technical, or industry credential) they do not actually hold, to lend unearned authority to reviews or claims made about the organization's or a competitor's products.

c.n: Undisclosed Financial Conflict of Interest in Review
c.d: An influencer publishes a review or endorsement without disclosing a material financial conflict of interest beyond standard sponsorship — such as holding an equity stake in a competitor, a short position benefiting from the organization's stock decline, or a referral-fee arrangement not disclosed as such — that would reasonably affect audience trust in the review's objectivity.
A suspected influencer-fraud incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific fraud type before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

c.n: Multi-Influencer Coordinated Negative Campaign (Same Talking Points)
c.d: A campaign in which multiple, otherwise-unconnected influencers publish negative content about the organization using strikingly similar or identical talking points, phrases, or claims within a short window — evidence of a centrally-supplied briefing or script rather than independently-formed organic opinions.

c.n: Influencer Network Timed Simultaneous Posting Campaign
c.d: A campaign in which a coordinated network of influencers is directed to publish negative content about the organization at deliberately synchronized times (rather than sharing identical talking points), designed to maximize algorithmic trending/visibility through simultaneous posting volume.

c.n: Cross-Platform Influencer Amplification of Single Attack Narrative
c.d: A campaign in which a single originating influencer's negative content about the organization is deliberately re-posted, translated, clipped, or re-shared across multiple additional platforms by a coordinated network of secondary accounts, extending the narrative's reach well beyond the original influencer's own audience.
A suspected coordinated-influencer-attack incident awaiting further investigation to determine its specific coordination mechanism before reclassification to the appropriate sibling ITID.

A coordinated campaign in which multiple actors publish their own negative blog posts about the company within a compressed timeframe or with shared fabricated talking points, intended to simulate a groundswell of independent criticism.

c.n: Blog Comment Section Flooding with Negative Content
c.d: A coordinated effort to fill the comment sections of third-party blogs (relevant to the company's industry, products, or news coverage) with fabricated negative claims, designed to shape reader perception at the point of consumption.

c.n: Fake Guest Post/Sponsored Blog Negative Placement
c.d: An attacker arranges for negative or misleading content about the company to be published on a legitimate blog through a guest-post submission or paid sponsored-content placement, exploiting the host blog's credibility while concealing the placement's true source or intent.

A catch-all classification for coordinated negative blog-platform activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Blog Review Bombing, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

A coordinated campaign in which multiple video creators publish negative review or reaction videos about the company's products/services within a compressed timeframe or with shared fabricated talking points, simulating widespread independent criticism.

A single video, produced to mimic the style and conventions of investigative journalism (narration, 'evidence' graphics, anonymous sources), presenting fabricated or materially distorted claims about the company in order to lend them false credibility.

A coordinated effort to flood the comment sections of existing, otherwise-unrelated videos with negative or fabricated claims about the company, using multiple accounts to simulate widespread organic criticism at the point of viewer consumption.

A catch-all classification for coordinated video-platform activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Video Platform Campaigns, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

c.n: Coordinated Negative Thread/Post Campaign on Forum
c.d: A coordinated campaign in which multiple actors post negative threads or replies about the company across general-purpose discussion forums, using shared talking points to simulate broad organic criticism.

An actor or small group creates and operates multiple fake ('sockpuppet') accounts to post reinforcing negative content within an existing forum thread, manufacturing the appearance of independent, widespread agreement.

A campaign that specifically targets a niche online community, subreddit, or specialized forum whose membership overlaps heavily with the company's actual customers or industry stakeholders, exploiting the community's credibility and influence within that specific audience.

A catch-all classification for coordinated forum-based activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Forum-based Attacks, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

c.n: Impersonation of Known Journalist/Critic Posting Fake Review
c.d: An actor creates content (a review, statement, or social post) falsely attributed to a real, named journalist or critic who did not write it, exploiting that individual's established public credibility to lend false authority to negative claims about the company.

c.n: Impersonation of Verified Platform Reviewer Account
c.d: An actor takes over, spoofs, or closely mimics a verified or otherwise high-trust reviewer account on a specific review platform (e.g. a 'Top Reviewer'-badged account) to post a fabricated negative review, exploiting the platform's own trust signals.

c.n: Fabricated Review Falsely Attributed to Real Customer
c.d: An actor fabricates review content and falsely attributes it to a real, identifiable customer of the company, who did not actually write or authorize the statement, in order to lend the fabricated claim the credibility of a genuine customer voice.

c.n: Unclassified / General Impersonation of Legitimate Reviewer
c.d: A catch-all classification for impersonation of a legitimate reviewer targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Impersonation of Legitimate Reviewers, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

c.n: Fabricated Executive Quote Taken Out of Context
c.d: An actor takes a real, verifiable quote actually spoken or written by a company executive and deliberately removes surrounding context, edits, or truncates it so that the presented meaning materially differs from the original statement's intent.

c.n: Entirely Fabricated Quote Never Actually Said
c.d: An actor invents a statement in its entirety and attributes it to a company executive or spokesperson who never said or wrote anything resembling it, fabricating the quote from nothing rather than distorting an existing statement.

c.n: Misattributed Quote from Unrelated Third Party
c.d: An actor takes a real quote genuinely spoken or written by an unrelated third party (not the company or its executives) and falsely re-attributes it to the company or one of its executives, borrowing the emotional impact of a real statement while misdirecting its source.

A catch-all classification for misattributed-quote activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Misattributed Quotes, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

c.n: Fabricated Endorsement/Partnership Claim with Controversial Figure
c.d: An actor fabricates and circulates a claim (written or verbal, without accompanying doctored visual evidence) asserting that the company has partnered with, sponsored, endorsed, or been endorsed by a controversial public figure, when no such relationship exists.

An actor creates or alters visual media (a photo or video, including digitally composited or AI-generated imagery) to falsely depict the company, its branding, or its executives in association with a controversial figure, in order to make the fabricated association visually convincing.

c.n: Misleading Historical Connection Resurfaced Out of Context
c.d: An actor resurfaces a factually real but historical, minor, or since-resolved connection between the company and a controversial figure or entity, deliberately omitting timeline, resolution, or context so that it appears to be a current or more significant association than it actually is.

c.n: Unclassified / General False Association with Controversial Figure
c.d: A catch-all classification for false-association activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Association with Controversial Figures, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

c.n: Fake Recall Notice via Fabricated Regulatory Agency Communication
c.d: An actor fabricates a product recall notice and presents it as an official communication from a genuine regulatory agency (e.g. a consumer safety, food/drug, or transport authority), impersonating that agency's identity, formatting, or channels to make the fake recall appear legally and factually authoritative.

c.n: Fake Recall Notice Distributed via Spoofed Press Release Wire
c.d: An actor fabricates a product recall announcement and distributes it through a spoofed or compromised press-release wire/distribution channel, exploiting the perceived legitimacy of newswire distribution to make the fake recall appear to be officially released company or media news.

c.n: Fake Recall Notice via Fabricated Email to Customers
c.d: An actor fabricates a product recall notice and sends it directly to customers via email designed to impersonate the company's own communications, exploiting the appearance of a direct company-to-customer channel to make the fake recall appear authoritative and urgent.

A catch-all classification for fake recall announcement activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Fake Recall Announcements, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

c.n: Fabricated Mass Consumer Complaint Campaign (Regulatory/BBB Filing)
c.d: An actor orchestrates the filing of numerous fabricated consumer complaints with a regulatory body or consumer-protection organization (e.g. the Better Business Bureau, a consumer protection agency), intended to manufacture the appearance of widespread, officially-documented consumer grievance against the company.

c.n: Fake Complaint Posted to Consumer Advocacy Platform
c.d: An actor posts a fabricated or materially exaggerated complaint directly onto an open consumer advocacy or complaint-aggregation platform (e.g. a public complaints board or consumer-review site), exploiting the platform's public visibility and search-engine indexing to spread the false claim.

c.n: Coordinated Fake Complaint Flooding of Customer Service Channels
c.d: An actor coordinates a high volume of fabricated complaint submissions directly into the company's own customer service channels (phone lines, email, live chat, support tickets), intended to overwhelm operational capacity and/or manufacture internal metrics suggesting a widespread genuine issue.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fake Customer Complaint Campaign
c.d: A catch-all classification for fake customer complaint campaign activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Fake Customer Complaints, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

An actor fabricates and circulates a claim describing a specific workplace safety incident (an injury, unsafe condition, or safety-violation event) at a named company facility, when no such incident actually occurred as described.

An actor fabricates and circulates a claim asserting that a specific, actionable-sounding service outage, system failure, or product malfunction has occurred, when no such outage/failure is actually taking place, intended to trigger customer alarm or operational confusion.

An actor fabricates and circulates a claim describing a specific, actionable-sounding environmental incident (e.g. a spill, contamination, emissions violation) or public health incident (e.g. a contamination or illness outbreak) attributed to the company, when no such incident actually occurred as described.

A catch-all classification for coordinated fabricated incident-claim activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Coordinated Incident Claims, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

A campaign, assessed with reasonable confidence to be sponsored or directed by a nation-state actor, that fabricates and disseminates false narratives about the company specifically tailored to and distributed within a particular country or region, typically tied to the company's market presence, geopolitical tensions, or local regulatory interests in that region.

A local or regional competitor, operating without state sponsorship, fabricates and disseminates false or misleading narratives about the company specifically within a defined regional market, exploiting local market conditions, cultural context, or competitive positioning to damage the company's regional standing.

A campaign that fabricates or disseminates misleading narratives about the company specifically targeted at regional regulators, legislators, or political figures, intended to influence a pending regulatory decision, policy outcome, or political relationship affecting the company's operations in that region.

A catch-all classification for region-specific reputation campaign activity that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Region-Specific Campaigns, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

An actor fabricates or materially distorts a claim that the company, its products, marketing, or representatives displayed cultural insensitivity or gave offense within a specific cultural context, in order to provoke public backlash within that market or community.

An actor fabricates or materially distorts a claim that the company, its products, marketing, or representatives displayed religious insensitivity or gave offense to a specific faith community, in order to provoke public backlash within that community.

An actor misrepresents or fabricates claims about how the company conducts business in a specific local market (e.g. labor practices, supplier relationships, pricing, or local partnership arrangements), framing legitimate or misunderstood practices as exploitative, unethical, or non-compliant with local norms/law.

A catch-all classification for cultural misinformation activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Cultural Misinformation, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

An actor deliberately mistranslates a genuine, verifiable official company statement (a press release, public statement, or executive remarks) into another language in a way that materially changes its meaning, and circulates the mistranslated version within that language's market as though it were the company's actual position.

c.n: Fabricated Localized Version of Legitimate Content
c.d: An actor fabricates an entire localized piece of content (a webpage, advertisement, or announcement) styled to appear as the company's official content in a local language, when no such genuine content or statement actually exists, exploiting the target market's reliance on localized (rather than original-language) sources.

An actor identifies a genuine, unintentional machine-translation distortion of real company content (arising from automated translation of a webpage, app, or document) and deliberately amplifies or frames that distortion as intentional or representative, spreading it as misinformation within the affected language market.

A catch-all classification for translation-manipulation activity targeting the company's reputation that does not match a more specific sibling ITID under Translation Manipulation, pending clearer categorization or reclassification.

An encrypting ransomware infection in which the initial malware or dropper reached the victim environment through a phishing attachment or a malicious link (e.g., a weaponized document, macro, or hyperlink to a payload host).

c.n: Ransomware Delivered via Exploited Public-Facing Vulnerability
c.d: An encrypting ransomware infection in which the adversary gained initial access by exploiting an unpatched or misconfigured internet-facing service or application.

c.n: Ransomware Delivered via Compromised RDP/Remote Access
c.d: An encrypting ransomware infection in which the adversary gained access via compromised Remote Desktop Protocol or another remote-access service (e.g., stolen or brute-forced credentials, exposed RDP).

c.n: Ransomware Deployed via Compromised Software Supply Chain/Update
c.d: An encrypting ransomware infection in which the payload was distributed via a trusted third-party software update, build pipeline, or vendor package that had been compromised upstream.

c.n: Ransomware Deployed by Affiliate via Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS)
c.d: An encrypting ransomware infection deployed by an affiliate using a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) offering, where the payload, leak infrastructure, and negotiation tooling are provided by a separate operator group.
An encrypting ransomware infection not yet attributable to a specific delivery vector (phishing, exploited vulnerability, compromised remote access, supply chain) or business model (RaaS affiliate).
Ransomware that locks the user out of the desktop/screen (a full-screen ransom message overlay) on a consumer or standard endpoint, without encrypting underlying files.
Ransomware that modifies or overwrites the Master Boot Record (MBR) or system bootloader so the affected device cannot boot into its operating system, displaying a ransom demand instead.
Ransomware affecting a mobile device (smartphone/tablet) that locks the screen, sets an unauthorized device PIN/password, or otherwise denies normal device use pending payment.
Locker ransomware not yet attributable to a specific target platform (standard endpoint screen lock, MBR/bootloader, or mobile device).

c.n: Pre-Encryption Data Exfiltration via Ransomware Affiliate Toolkit
c.d: The data-exfiltration phase of a double extortion ransomware attack, performed using a known/standard affiliate toolkit (e.g., commodity exfiltration or file-transfer utilities associated with a ransomware program), occurring before file encryption.

c.n: Double Extortion Ransomware with Automated Exfiltration Staging
c.d: A double extortion ransomware incident in which the exfiltration-staging step is performed by automated tooling (e.g., a scripted or built-in exfiltration module in the ransomware toolkit) rather than manual, hands-on selection of data.

c.n: Double Extortion Ransomware Following Prolonged Dwell-Time Reconnaissance
c.d: A double extortion ransomware incident characterized by a prolonged dwell time in which the adversary conducted manual reconnaissance and data discovery within the environment before staging exfiltration and deploying the encryptor.

c.n: Unclassified / General Double Extortion Ransomware Incident
c.d: A double extortion ransomware incident (confirmed encryption plus confirmed or threatened data exfiltration) not yet attributable to a specific exfiltration method (standard toolkit, automated staging, or extended dwell-time reconnaissance).

A ransomware attack in which a human operator manually navigates the target environment, selects deployment targets, and times execution, rather than relying on a self-propagating or fully automated encryptor.

c.n: Targeted Ransomware Following Initial Access Broker Handoff
