c.d: A targeted ransomware attack in which the deploying group purchased or otherwise received already-established access to the victim environment from a separate initial access broker (IAB), rather than performing their own initial compromise.

c.n: Targeted Ransomware Deployment Timed to Business-Critical Event
c.d: A targeted ransomware attack in which the adversary deliberately timed encryptor deployment to coincide with a business-critical event (e.g., financial close, a major holiday/weekend, a merger announcement, or peak operational period) to maximize disruption and pressure to pay.

A targeted (human-directed, non-commodity) ransomware attack not yet attributable to a specific defining characteristic (human-operated deployment, initial-access-broker handoff, or deliberate business-critical timing).
A backdoor trojan implemented as a web shell — a script uploaded to or planted on a web server that provides the adversary an ongoing, browser- or HTTP-reachable command interface into the host.
A backdoor trojan implanted in device firmware (e.g., UEFI/BIOS) or as a bootkit that loads before the operating system, providing persistence that survives OS reinstallation.

A backdoor trojan introduced into an environment via an open-source package or dependency (e.g., from a public package registry) that had malicious backdoor functionality inserted, whether through a compromised maintainer account or a deliberately published malicious package.

c.n: Backdoor Installed via Compromised Software Update
c.d: A backdoor trojan installed via a legitimate commercial/proprietary software vendor's update or distribution mechanism that had been compromised upstream, distinct from an open-source package compromise.
A backdoor trojan not yet attributable to a specific mechanism or layer (web shell, firmware/bootkit, backdoored open-source package, or compromised vendor update).
A banking trojan running on a desktop endpoint that injects malicious content into banking web pages or captures form-field data as it is submitted, to steal login credentials or transaction details.

A mobile banking trojan that displays a fake overlay screen mimicking a legitimate banking app's login interface, capturing credentials entered by the user before passing (or not passing) them to the real app.

c.n: Banking Trojan with Real-Time Transaction Manipulation
c.d: A banking trojan that intercepts and silently alters transaction details (e.g., destination account number, amount) in real time during a legitimate, user-initiated banking session, so the displayed confirmation differs from what is actually submitted.
A banking trojan incident not yet attributable to a specific technique or platform (desktop web-injection/form-grabbing, mobile overlay, or real-time transaction manipulation).
An infostealer infection where the malware was bundled within cracked, pirated, or 'keygen' software downloaded by the user from an untrusted source.

An infostealer infection using a known Infostealer-as-a-Service (or broader Malware-as-a-Service) offering, where the malware, panel, and log-distribution infrastructure are operated as a subscription product used by many independent customers/affiliates.

An infostealer infection using a variant with notable anti-analysis or sandbox-evasion capability (e.g., detecting virtualized/analysis environments and altering behavior to avoid detection by automated security tooling).
An infostealer incident not yet attributable to a specific delivery vector or capability (bundled with pirated software, subscription MaaS model, or notable anti-analysis capability).

A Remote Access Trojan infection using a widely available, commodity/off-the-shelf RAT (a publicly sold or freely available RAT family used broadly across many unrelated campaigns), rather than a bespoke tool built for a specific target.
A Remote Access Trojan infection using a custom-developed tool built specifically for use against this target or a narrow set of targets, rather than a widely available commodity RAT.

c.n: RAT Delivered via Fake Remote Support Tool Installation
c.d: A Remote Access Trojan infection delivered by convincing the victim to install what they believe is a legitimate remote-support/IT-help tool (e.g., via a fraudulent tech-support call or fake IT notification), when it is actually a RAT or a legitimate remote-access tool repurposed for malicious control.

c.n: RAT Providing Full Desktop/Screen Control Access
c.d: A Remote Access Trojan infection where the malware's capability provides the adversary full, interactive desktop/screen-control access (equivalent to sitting at the keyboard), rather than limited command-execution or data-collection functions.

c.n: Unclassified / General Remote Access Trojan (RAT) Incident
c.d: A Remote Access Trojan incident not yet attributable to a specific origin or capability (commodity/off-the-shelf, custom-built, fake remote-support delivery, or confirmed full interactive desktop control).

c.n: Worm Propagating via Unpatched Network Service Vulnerability
c.d: A worm that gains code execution on new hosts by directly exploiting a vulnerability in a network-facing service (e.g., SMB, RDP, RPC, a web/application server) and then repeats the process from each newly infected host, spreading automatically across reachable network segments.

c.n: Worm Propagating via Weak/Default Network Share Credentials
c.d: A worm that copies itself to new hosts by brute-forcing, guessing, or reusing weak/default administrative or share credentials (e.g., SMB admin shares, default service accounts) to write and execute its payload on the target, then repeats from each newly infected host.

c.n: Worm Propagating via Email Auto-Forwarding/Address Book Harvesting
c.d: A worm that, once running on a host or mailbox, harvests the local address book or contact list and mass-mails copies of itself (as an attachment or link) to those contacts, often spoofing the sender to increase the likelihood recipients open it, propagating one mailbox-to-mailbox hop at a time.

A worm that propagates not across a traditional on-premises network but across cloud resources, accounts, or tenants, by abusing over-permissive IAM roles, shared storage/CI-CD resources, exposed cloud service credentials, or cross-tenant trust/federation relationships to replicate itself into additional cloud accounts or subscriptions.

A self-propagating worm confirmed to be spreading across the network but whose exact propagation vector (vulnerability exploitation, credential abuse, email harvesting, or cross-cloud/tenant abuse) is unknown, mixed, or does not fit the other defined leaves at the time of classification.

A worm that places an autorun configuration file and payload on a USB or other removable drive so that inserting the drive into a host with Autorun/Autoplay enabled triggers automatic execution of the worm, which then copies itself to any other removable media subsequently connected.

c.n: USB Worm Spreading via Hidden/Disguised Executable on Removable Media
c.d: A worm that copies itself onto removable media as a hidden or disguised executable (e.g., using a folder icon, double file extension, or file name mimicking a legitimate document) so that a user, browsing the drive, is tricked into manually double-clicking it, triggering execution and further propagation.

c.n: USB Worm Re-Infecting Newly Inserted Removable Drives
c.d: A worm that maintains persistence on an infected host (rather than only on the removable media itself) and monitors for USB/removable device insertion events, automatically writing a fresh copy of itself onto any newly connected drive, causing repeated re-infection cycles even after individual drives are cleaned.

A self-propagating worm confirmed to be spreading via removable media but whose exact mechanism (Autorun/Autoplay execution, disguised executable requiring manual click, or host-side re-infection persistence) is unknown, mixed, or does not fit the other defined leaves at the time of classification.

A worm that uses PowerShell scripts and/or Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute its payload and replicate itself to other hosts entirely through native OS scripting and remote-management interfaces, avoiding disk-resident binaries and thereby evading traditional signature-based antivirus.

A worm that achieves execution and propagation using trusted, natively signed OS utilities (e.g., certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, bitsadmin) to download, execute, or transfer its payload between hosts, deliberately avoiding both malicious standalone executables and the PowerShell/WMI mechanisms covered by a sibling ITID.

c.n: Fileless Worm Persisting via Registry/Scheduled Task Only
c.d: A worm that establishes and maintains its foothold purely through registry-stored payloads (e.g., encoded scripts or shellcode in registry values) and/or scheduled tasks that re-trigger execution, propagating between hosts while leaving no traditional executable file and no dependence on PowerShell/WMI-based lateral movement as the distinguishing mechanism.

A self-propagating worm confirmed to be operating fileless (no on-disk malicious executable) but whose exact mechanism (PowerShell/WMI, other LOLBins, or registry/scheduled-task-only persistence) is unknown, mixed, or does not fit the other defined leaves at the time of classification.

c.n: Keylogger Targeting Financial/Banking Site Input Fields Specifically
c.d: Malware that records keystrokes entered on recognized banking or financial-institution web pages, filtering out other input to focus collection on payment credentials.

c.n: Keylogger Configured for Exfiltration via Steganographic/Covert Channel
c.d: Keylogging malware whose captured data is exfiltrated using a covert-channel technique (for example, encoding it within otherwise-innocuous network traffic or files) to evade content-inspection controls.
Malware that records keystrokes on an infected device, not clearly matching a more specific Keyloggers leaf.
Spyware that periodically captures still screenshots of a device's display and exfiltrates them, without continuous recording.
Spyware that continuously records a device's screen activity as video and exfiltrates the recording.
Spyware that monitors an infected device's clipboard and exfiltrates copied content.
Spyware that monitors for a specific targeted application window (for example, a banking or email client) and captures screen content only while that window is active.
Spyware that captures a device's screen or clipboard content, not clearly matching a more specific Screen Scrapers leaf.

A consumer monitoring application installed on a device without the device owner's knowledge or consent by a partner, family member, or other individual with physical access, used to covertly track the owner's activity, location, or communications.

c.n: Employee Monitoring Software Misused Beyond Authorized Scope
c.d: An organization's own sanctioned employee-monitoring software used to collect data beyond what was disclosed to and consented to by employees, or beyond its documented authorized purpose.
Spyware installed on a device that covertly collects and exfiltrates geolocation data.
Spyware that covertly collects and exfiltrates a device's browsing history or usage habits.
Spyware that covertly tracks a device user's behavior, not clearly matching a more specific Behavioral Trackers leaf.

Adware that spawns persistent, un-closeable, or endlessly re-spawning pop-up/pop-under browser or system windows, typically to force ad impressions, drive scareware clicks, or coerce the user into installing further software.

c.n: Pop-up Adware Bundled with Freeware Installer
c.d: Adware components silently installed alongside a freeware application via an opt-out (pre-checked) bundling model in the installer, rather than through a separate malicious download.

c.n: Pop-up Adware Injecting Ads into Legitimate Websites
c.d: Adware (typically a system-level proxy, browser helper object, or man-in-the-browser component) that inserts, overlays, or replaces advertisements within the rendered pages of otherwise-legitimate websites.
An incident involving pop-up adware, not clearly matching the un-closeable, bundled-installer, or ad-injection patterns captured by the sibling leaves.
Adware/browser-hijacker malware that silently changes the browser's homepage, new-tab page, or default search provider to an attacker-monetized search or landing page.

c.n: Ad-Fraud Click Injection Malware (Silent Background Clicks)
c.d: Malware that silently loads advertisements and simulates clicks on them in a hidden browser instance or background process, generating ad revenue for the attacker without the user's knowledge or interaction.
Malware that changes a device's or router's DNS server configuration, or installs a system-level proxy, to redirect web and ad traffic through attacker-controlled infrastructure.
An incident involving ad-redirecting malware, not clearly matching the browser-hijack, click-injection, or DNS/proxy-hijack patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

c.n: Ad-Injecting Browser Extension (Legitimate Extension Turned Malicious via Update)
c.d: A browser extension that was legitimate at install time but was later updated (via the extension store's auto-update mechanism) to include ad-injection or other adware behavior, usually after its developer account was compromised or the extension was sold to a new owner.

c.n: Browser Extension Monetized via Undisclosed Affiliate Link Hijacking
c.d: A browser extension that silently rewrites e-commerce/affiliate links the user clicks (or inserts its own undisclosed affiliate tag) to redirect commission revenue to the extension operator, without the user's knowledge.

c.n: Browser Extension Bundled with Ad-Injection SDK
c.d: A browser extension that is malicious/adware from its initial publication, embedding a third-party ad-injection SDK that overlays or inserts advertisements into the pages the user visits.
An incident involving a malicious/adware browser extension, not clearly matching the supply-chain-compromise, affiliate-hijacking, or bundled-SDK patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

A fileless attack stage in which PowerShell is used as a downloader/loader to retrieve a subsequent payload (script or in-memory executable) from a remote location and execute it, with no malicious binary persisted to disk.

A PowerShell-based command-and-control beacon or implant that runs persistently (in memory or via a scheduled task/registry trigger re-invoking PowerShell) to maintain an ongoing channel for attacker commands.

A fileless attack stage in which PowerShell is used to deploy, decrypt-in-memory, or directly execute ransomware encryption logic on a host or across multiple hosts, without a standalone ransomware executable being written to disk beforehand.
An incident involving PowerShell-based fileless malware, not clearly matching the downloader, C2 beacon, or ransomware-deployment patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

Fileless persistence achieved by writing a command (often invoking a script interpreter) into a registry Run/RunOnce key or equivalent auto-start registry location, so the malicious logic re-executes at logon/startup without a standalone executable being the persistence artifact.

c.n: Registry-Stored Encoded Payload (Fileless Loader via Registry Value)
c.d: A fileless loader technique in which the malicious payload itself (e.g. Base64-encoded shellcode or a script) is stored as data in a registry value, and a separate small loader (often a Run key entry) reads and executes that value's content directly into memory.

A persistence technique in which an adversary modifies the registry CLSID/COM object registration for a commonly-invoked component so that legitimate application or system behavior inadvertently loads and executes attacker-controlled code in place of (or alongside) the legitimate COM object.
An incident involving registry-resident fileless malware, not clearly matching the Run-key persistence, payload-storage, or COM-hijacking patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

A memory-only execution technique in which a malicious DLL is manually mapped and loaded into a target process's memory (reflective DLL injection) so that it runs without being written to disk or registered through the normal Windows loader.

A memory-only execution technique (process hollowing or general process injection) in which a legitimate process is started in a suspended state (or targeted while running) and its memory/execution flow is replaced or redirected to execute attacker-supplied code, so the malicious activity appears to originate from a trusted process.

A resident command-and-control implant that operates entirely in process memory, with no corresponding executable or script artifact persisted to disk, maintaining an ongoing channel for attacker commands.
An incident involving memory-only fileless malware, not clearly matching the reflective-injection, process-hollowing, or resident-C2-implant patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

Malware that scans for and compromises internet-connected IoT/embedded devices (routers, cameras, DVRs, etc.), typically via default credentials or unpatched firmware vulnerabilities, to recruit them into a distributed botnet.

c.n: Botnet Recruiting via Compromised Web Servers/CMS
c.d: Malware that compromises internet-facing web servers or content management systems (via exploited plugins, weak credentials, or unpatched vulnerabilities) to install a bot agent, adding the server to a botnet with higher available bandwidth and uptime than typical consumer devices.

A botnet in which infected nodes communicate directly with each other in a peer-to-peer topology to relay commands and updates, rather than checking in with a single centralized C2 server, making takedown by seizing a single server ineffective.

Botnet infrastructure that maps a small set of C2 domains to a rapidly-changing pool of bot/proxy IP addresses via short-TTL DNS records, so that blocking or seizing any individual IP has minimal effect on the botnet's availability.
An incident involving distributed botnet infrastructure, not clearly matching the IoT-recruitment, web-server-recruitment, P2P, or fast-flux DNS patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

c.n: Botnet-Operated Mass Credential Harvesting Campaign Across Multiple Organizations
c.d: A botnet whose bot nodes are tasked by their operator to harvest credentials en masse (via phishing page hosting, form-grabbing malware, or fake login pages) across multiple, unrelated victim organizations, with the botnet infrastructure and campaign orchestration as the classification focus.

c.n: Botnet Nodes Used as Distributed Credential-Testing Infrastructure
c.d: A botnet whose nodes are tasked by their operator to serve as distributed source IPs for automated credential-testing (login attempts) against target services, with the botnet infrastructure itself — its scale, distribution, and evasion of IP-based rate limiting — as the classification focus.

An incident involving a credential-harvesting-related botnet, not clearly matching the mass-harvesting-campaign or distributed-credential-testing-infrastructure patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

A botnet composed of compromised residential (consumer ISP) devices whose operator sells outbound proxy access through the bot nodes as a commercial "residential proxy" service, letting paying customers route traffic through victims' home IP addresses.

c.n: Botnet Used to Relay/Anonymize Attacker Traffic
c.d: Botnet nodes that an attacker uses directly as relay hops to anonymize the source of their own attack traffic (e.g. C2 communications, scanning, or further intrusion attempts), obscuring the attacker's true origin.

c.n: Botnet Proxy Nodes Used for Ad Fraud Traffic Relay
c.d: Botnet nodes that relay outbound ad-network requests on behalf of a centralized ad-fraud operation, distributing simulated ad traffic across many distinct residential IPs to evade ad-network fraud detection based on IP concentration.
An incident involving proxy botnet infrastructure, not clearly matching the residential-proxy-service, attacker-relay, or ad-fraud-relay patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

c.n: Metamorphic Malware (Full Code Rewrite Each Generation)
c.d: Metamorphic malware that rewrites its own underlying code body — instruction sequences, control flow, and logic structure — each time it propagates or replicates, rather than merely re-encrypting a static payload, so that no two generations share a meaningfully similar binary signature.

c.n: Polymorphic Encryption Engine Malware (Same Logic, Changing Signature)
c.d: Malware in which the core malicious payload is functionally unchanged across samples, but is wrapped each time in a newly-generated encryption or packing layer (with a correspondingly mutated decryption stub), producing a different static file signature per sample while the underlying logic is identical.

Malware that modifies its own executing code in memory during a single run (e.g. rewriting instructions after execution, decrypting/re-encrypting sections on the fly) to defeat memory-scanning and step-through analysis, independent of any variation between separate distributed samples.
An incident involving code-altering polymorphic/metamorphic malware, not clearly matching the metamorphic, polymorphic-encryption, or self-modifying-code patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

A malicious script whose payload is obfuscated primarily through a single layer of standard encoding (such as Base64), decoded at runtime by the interpreter before execution, to evade simple string/pattern-matching detection.

A malicious script obfuscated through several nested layers of encoding, compression, and/or encryption, such that each layer must be decoded in sequence to reveal the next, significantly raising the effort required for static or automated analysis compared to single-layer encoding.

A malicious script that obfuscates its intent by encrypting embedded strings (function names, URLs, commands) resolved only at runtime, and/or by inserting large amounts of non-functional junk code to defeat readability-based static analysis and pattern matching.
An incident involving an obfuscated malicious script, not clearly matching the simple-encoding, multi-layer, or string-encryption/junk-code patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

c.n: Runtime-Generated Payload from Remote Server (Server-Side Polymorphism)
c.d: Malware delivery in which the final payload is dynamically generated on a remote/attacker-controlled server at the moment of each download request, so every retrieved instance is uniquely built and no static signature can match more than one download.

Malware that inspects its execution environment at runtime (checking for sandbox/VM artifacts, analysis tools, or debugger presence) and branches its behavior accordingly — running benign or dormant when analysis is detected, and executing the malicious payload only in what it assesses to be a genuine target environment.

c.n: Encrypted Payload Decrypted Only in Memory at Execution
c.d: Malware that stores its payload encrypted on disk or in a delivery artifact, decrypting it only into memory at the point of execution and never writing the decrypted plaintext payload back to disk, so static analysis of the at-rest artifact reveals no usable indicators.

An incident involving a dynamically-generated or environment-aware polymorphic payload, not clearly matching the server-side-generation, sandbox-evasion, or memory-only-decryption patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

A custom-built malware implant whose code, infrastructure, or tradecraft matches a previously attributed nation-state threat actor's toolset, allowing confident attribution to a known advanced persistent threat group.

c.n: Bespoke Malware Built for Single-Target Campaign
c.d: A malware implant custom-engineered for use against a single specific target organization, with no code, infrastructure, or TTP overlap to a previously attributed threat actor, indicating bespoke development rather than reuse of an established toolset.

c.n: Custom Malware Reusing Leaked/Stolen Source Code from Prior Breach
c.d: A malware implant developed by an actor using source code that was leaked publicly or stolen in a prior, unrelated security breach (e.g. a leaked commercial malware builder or a breached red-team tool), adapted and deployed as the actor's own custom tooling.
An incident involving custom APT malware, not clearly matching the nation-state-attributed, bespoke single-target, or leaked-source-derived patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

An advanced persistent threat operating technique in which the actor performs its objectives using only legitimate, pre-installed operating system tools and scripting engines (living off the land), deploying no custom implant binary at all, to avoid leaving any novel artifact for signature-based detection.

An advanced persistent threat implant embedded in a device's firmware or UEFI layer, executing prior to OS load and surviving operating system reinstallation, disk wipe, or replacement, requiring firmware-level remediation or hardware replacement to fully remove.

Advanced persistent threat tradecraft focused on deleting, altering, or disabling security logs and forensic artifacts (event logs, EDR telemetry, command history) to conceal the actor's activity and impede incident response and root-cause analysis.
An incident involving stealth-focused APT malware/tradecraft, not clearly matching the living-off-the-land, firmware-implant, or anti-forensic log-wiping patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

An advanced persistent threat intrusion structured as a chain of discrete stages, where an initial small dropper retrieves and executes progressively more capable payloads culminating in the final operational implant, with each stage validating the environment before advancing to reduce exposure of the full toolset.

c.n: Multi-Stage Malware with Staged C2 Infrastructure Handoff
c.d: A multi-stage advanced persistent threat operation in which command-and-control responsibility is deliberately transferred from one piece of infrastructure to another as the intrusion progresses (e.g. a disposable first-stage C2 handing off to a more protected, long-term C2 channel), compartmentalizing the operation so early-stage infrastructure exposure does not compromise the full campaign.

c.n: Long-Dwell APT Campaign with Distinct Reconnaissance/Escalation/Exfiltration Stages
c.d: A long-dwell advanced persistent threat campaign classified at the level of its overall operational lifecycle — encompassing distinct, temporally separated reconnaissance, privilege-escalation/lateral-movement, and data-exfiltration stages — where the classification concern is the campaign's extended duration and stage progression rather than any single dropper or C2-handoff mechanic.
An incident involving multi-stage APT malware, not clearly matching the dropper-chain, C2-handoff, or long-dwell-campaign-lifecycle patterns captured by the sibling leaves.

Successful use of a zero-day (no available patch or public advisory at time of use) vulnerability in the Windows kernel or kernel-mode drivers to gain code execution, privilege escalation, or defense evasion.
Successful use of a zero-day vulnerability in the Linux kernel or kernel modules to gain code execution, privilege escalation, or defense evasion.
Successful use of a zero-day vulnerability in macOS or iOS (kernel, XNU, or platform frameworks) to gain code execution, sandbox escape, or privilege escalation.
Successful use of a zero-day vulnerability in the Android OS (kernel, framework, or bundled components) to gain code execution, privilege escalation, or sandbox escape.
An incident involving exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched operating-system vulnerability, not clearly matching a more specific platform leaf.

c.n: Zero-Day in Widely-Used Enterprise Software (Supply-Chain Impact)
c.d: Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in enterprise software (e.g., file-transfer, collaboration, network-management platforms) that is broadly deployed such that a single vendor flaw creates supply-chain-scale exposure across many organizations.
Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in a web browser's rendering engine, JavaScript engine, or sandbox to achieve remote code execution or sandbox escape on an endpoint.

Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in an office/productivity application (word processor, spreadsheet, PDF reader) triggered by a specially crafted document opened by the victim.
Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in software developed and maintained internally by the organization (not a commercial or open-source third-party product).
An incident involving exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched application-level vulnerability, not clearly matching a more specific application-category leaf.

Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in ICS/SCADA hardware or software (PLCs, HMIs, engineering workstations, historian servers) to achieve unauthorized control or manipulation.
Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in a consumer or enterprise IoT device (cameras, sensors, smart building/office equipment) to achieve code execution or device takeover.

Exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched vulnerability in the firmware or management software of a network appliance (router, firewall, VPN gateway, load balancer) to achieve code execution or unauthorized administrative access.

c.n: Unclassified / General Embedded System Zero-Day Exploit
c.d: An incident involving exploitation of a previously unknown, unpatched embedded-system vulnerability, not clearly matching a more specific embedded-category leaf.

c.n: Zero-Day Exploit Chain Used in Targeted Nation-State Campaign
c.d: A confirmed or attributed nation-state (or nation-state-aligned) intrusion using two or more chained zero-day vulnerabilities to achieve initial access, privilege escalation, and/or sandbox escape against a specific, targeted victim.

c.n: Zero-Day Purchased from Commercial Exploit Broker/Vendor
c.d: Exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability where the exploit itself was acquired via purchase from a commercial exploit-development/brokerage vendor, rather than developed by the using actor.

c.n: Zero-Day Used in Mercenary Spyware Deployment
c.d: Exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability as part of a confirmed commercial mercenary spyware product (e.g., surveillance-ware sold to government or private clients) deployed against a specific individual or organization.

c.n: Unclassified / General Advanced Threat Zero-Day Exploit
c.d: An incident involving zero-day exploitation attributed to a sophisticated/advanced threat actor, not clearly matching a more specific advanced-threat-category leaf.

Remote exploitation of a publicly known RDP-related CVE (e.g., a remote code execution or authentication flaw in the RDP service) against a system for which a vendor patch was available but not applied.

c.n: RDP Protocol-Level Exploit Bypassing Network Level Authentication
c.d: Exploitation of a flaw in the RDP protocol or its implementation that allows an attacker to bypass Network Level Authentication (NLA) and reach the RDP session/logon stage without valid credentials.

Exploitation of a vulnerability in RDP gateway, connection-broker, or session-management software (the internet-facing intermediary that brokers RDP sessions) to gain unauthorized access or code execution.
An incident involving remote exploitation of RDP, not clearly matching a more specific RDP-exploit leaf.

c.n: Known-CVE VPN Gateway Vulnerability Exploitation (Unpatched Appliance)
c.d: Remote exploitation of a publicly known CVE in a VPN gateway/concentrator appliance for which a vendor patch was available but not applied.

Exploitation of a vulnerability that allows an attacker to bypass VPN authentication entirely (e.g., via a logic flaw, default-credential-adjacent flaw, or authentication-check omission) rather than exploiting memory-safety code execution.

Exploitation of a flaw in how a VPN gateway issues, validates, or manages session tokens (e.g., session fixation, predictable token generation, improper token invalidation) to hijack or reuse a session without ever possessing valid credentials.
An incident involving remote exploitation of VPN infrastructure, not clearly matching a more specific VPN-exploit leaf.

c.n: Known-CVE Web Server Software Vulnerability Exploitation (Unpatched)
c.d: Remote exploitation of a publicly known CVE in web server software (e.g., the HTTP server daemon or its modules) for which a vendor/project patch was available but not applied.

Use of an evasion or obfuscation technique to bypass web application firewall (WAF) filtering rules, allowing an otherwise-blocked exploitation attempt to reach the underlying vulnerable web server or application.

Exploitation of a web application flaw that allows an attacker to induce the server to make unintended requests to internal or otherwise-restricted resources (e.g., cloud metadata services, internal-only APIs) on the attacker's behalf.

Exploitation of a web application/server flaw that allows an attacker to manipulate file-path input (e.g., using ../ sequences or absolute paths) to read, write, or execute files outside the intended directory scope.
An incident involving remote exploitation of a web server, not clearly matching a more specific web-server-exploit leaf.
Local exploitation of a memory-safety or logic vulnerability in a privileged local service/daemon (running as SYSTEM/root) to escalate an unprivileged local session to elevated privileges.

Local privilege escalation on a Linux/Unix system achieved by abusing a binary with the SUID or SGID bit set that is misconfigured (e.g., an unnecessary SUID binary, or one with an exploitable code flaw) to execute code with the file owner's (often root) privileges.
Local privilege escalation on Windows achieved by exploiting a technique that circumvents the UAC elevation prompt, allowing a process to gain administrative privileges without user consent.
Local privilege escalation achieved by modifying or hijacking a scheduled task or service that runs with elevated privileges, causing attacker-controlled code to execute in that elevated context.
An incident involving local privilege escalation via exploit-code mechanisms, not clearly matching a more specific privilege-escalation leaf.

Local exploitation in which an attacker places a malicious DLL where a legitimate application will load it in place of (or alongside) the intended library, due to search-order weaknesses or an application's insecure loading behavior, achieving code execution in that application's context.

Local exploitation in which an attacker modifies a file-type association or default handler so that opening a file of that type (or triggering an event associated with it) executes attacker-controlled code.

c.n: Living-off-the-Land Binary (LOLBin) Abuse for Local Execution
c.d: Local exploitation in which an attacker abuses a legitimate, signed, pre-installed system binary's built-in functionality (e.g., script execution, download, or proxy-execution capability) to execute arbitrary code or commands while evading detection tools that trust signed binaries.
An incident involving local code execution via file/execution-mechanism exploitation, not clearly matching a more specific file-execution-exploit leaf.

c.n: Known-CVE Kernel Vulnerability Exploitation (Local Privilege Escalation)
c.d: Local exploitation of a publicly known kernel CVE (Windows, Linux, or other OS) for which a vendor/project patch was available but not applied, used to escalate an unprivileged local session to kernel-level or SYSTEM/root privileges.
Local exploitation of a kernel vulnerability specifically to break out of a sandbox or container isolation boundary, gaining code execution on the underlying host operating system.

Local exploitation of a hypervisor or virtualization-stack vulnerability to break out of a guest virtual machine's isolation boundary, gaining code execution on the host hypervisor or other co-located guest VMs.
An incident involving local kernel exploitation, not clearly matching a more specific kernel-exploit leaf.

c.n: Drive-By Download via Malicious/Compromised Ad Network (Malvertising)
c.d: A drive-by download in which the malicious exploit payload is served via an advertisement placed through a legitimate ad network — either a compromised legitimate advertiser account or a malicious ad purchased directly — so that visitors to unrelated, otherwise-trustworthy sites are exposed.

c.n: Drive-By Download via Compromised Legitimate Website (Non-Defacement Silent Injection)
c.d: A drive-by download in which an attacker has compromised a legitimate website's own infrastructure or content (not an ad network) and silently injected exploit code, so that ordinary visitors are exposed without any visible sign the site was altered.

c.n: Drive-By Download via Browser Zero-Day Exploit
c.d: A drive-by download whose exploit payload leverages a previously unknown, unpatched browser vulnerability, focusing on the delivery-mechanism angle of a browser zero-day already characterized under the Zero-day Exploits branch.
An incident involving drive-by download exploitation, not clearly matching a more specific drive-by-download leaf.

c.n: Browser Extension Abusing Overly Broad Permissions for Data Exfiltration
c.d: A browser extension, installed with legitimate-appearing permissions, that uses those permissions (e.g., broad host access, tab/history read access) beyond its stated purpose to collect and exfiltrate user browsing data, form input, or credentials.

c.n: Browser Extension Used as Remote Code Execution/C2 Channel
c.d: A browser extension that provides an attacker with a persistent remote-control channel — receiving commands from and sending results to an external server — effectively functioning as a lightweight C2 implant running inside the browser.

c.n: Browser Extension Exploiting Cross-Origin/Sandbox Bypass Vulnerability
c.d: Exploitation of a technical vulnerability in a browser extension's implementation (e.g., a content-script injection flaw or improper origin isolation) that allows the extension — or a malicious web page abusing the extension — to bypass the browser's same-origin or sandbox boundaries.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Browser Extension (Security Exploit)
c.d: An incident involving a malicious or vulnerable browser extension exploited for security-relevant impact, not clearly matching a more specific extension-exploit leaf.

Exploitation of a web application flaw that reflects unsanitized user input back into an immediate HTTP response, causing attacker-supplied script to execute in the victim's browser when they follow a crafted link or submit a crafted request.

Exploitation of a web application flaw that permanently stores unsanitized user input (e.g., in a comment, profile field, or message) which is later served to other users, causing attacker-supplied script to execute in every subsequent visitor's browser without requiring a crafted link.

Exploitation of a client-side JavaScript flaw in which unsanitized data (e.g., from the URL fragment, document.referrer, or local storage) is written into the DOM in an unsafe way entirely within the browser, without the payload ever being sent to or reflected by the server.

c.n: XSS Used for Session Token/Cookie Theft
c.d: Cross-site scripting exploitation (of any injection type — reflected, stored, or DOM-based) whose specific, confirmed outcome is the theft of a victim's session token or cookie, enabling session hijacking distinct from the general script-execution event itself.
An incident involving cross-site scripting exploitation, not clearly matching a more specific XSS-type leaf.

Exploitation of weaknesses in DNS response validation (e.g., predictable transaction IDs, lack of DNSSEC, race-condition response injection) to insert a forged record into a resolver's cache, causing subsequent lookups for a legitimate domain to resolve to an attacker-controlled IP.

Abuse of an authoritative DNS server that permits unrestricted AXFR/IXFR zone transfers to an unauthorized host, disclosing the full set of hostnames, internal IPs, and infrastructure naming conventions within a zone.

c.n: DNS Tunneling for Covert Data Exfiltration/C2
c.d: Abuse of DNS query/response fields (subdomain labels, TXT/NULL records) as a general-purpose covert channel, encoding arbitrary data or command traffic inside DNS lookups to bypass network egress controls that do not inspect DNS content.

Exploitation of DNS's response-size amplification characteristics — sending small spoofed-source queries to open recursive resolvers so that large responses are reflected onto a spoofed victim IP — to conduct a volumetric denial-of-service attack.
An incident involving exploitation of the DNS protocol, not clearly matching cache poisoning, zone transfer disclosure, tunneling, or amplification.

c.n: Known-CVE SMB Remote Code Execution Exploit (Wormable Vulnerability Class)
c.d: Exploitation of a documented CVE in the SMB protocol implementation (e.g., an EternalBlue-class buffer overflow) to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution, characteristic of vulnerabilities capable of worm-like self-propagation across a network.

Exploitation of SMB/NTLM authentication flow weaknesses to capture a victim's authentication attempt and relay it in real time to a different target, granting the attacker access as the victim without ever obtaining the plaintext credential.
Abuse of legacy SMB support for null or anonymous sessions to enumerate shares, usernames, groups, or system information from a target host without providing valid credentials.
An incident involving exploitation of the SMB protocol, not clearly matching known-CVE RCE, relay, or null-session enumeration.

Active manipulation of the TLS handshake (e.g., stripping cipher suite offers, blocking version-negotiation extensions) to coerce a client and server into negotiating a legacy, weaker TLS/SSL version than either would otherwise use, exposing the session to further exploitation.

Exploitation of an endpoint's existing (non-downgraded) TLS/SSL configuration that permits weak cipher suites (e.g., RC4, export-grade ciphers) or outdated protocol versions, allowing an attacker to decrypt or manipulate traffic without needing to force a handshake downgrade.

Exploitation of a bug or design flaw in certificate validation logic (e.g., improper hostname checking, chain-of-trust bypass, acceptance of self-signed or expired certificates) that allows an attacker to present a fraudulent certificate as trusted.

Exploitation of a specific implementation-level vulnerability in a TLS/SSL library (e.g., a Heartbleed-class out-of-bounds memory read) allowing disclosure of sensitive in-memory data such as private keys, session tokens, or credentials, rather than an attack on the protocol design or configuration.
An incident involving exploitation of TLS/SSL, not clearly matching downgrade, weak-cipher, certificate-validation, or implementation-bug leaves.

c.n: Malicious Document Exploiting Office Application Vulnerability (Non-Macro)
c.d: A weaponized document (e.g., Word/Excel/RTF) crafted to trigger a memory-corruption or parsing vulnerability in the host Office application itself, achieving code execution purely through the exploit payload rather than through scripting features.
A weaponized PDF document crafted to exploit a vulnerability in the parsing or JavaScript engine of a PDF reader application, achieving code execution when the file is opened.

c.n: Malicious Archive File (ZIP/RAR) Exploiting Extraction Vulnerability or Hiding Payload
c.d: A weaponized ZIP/RAR (or similar) archive that either exploits a vulnerability in the extraction utility itself, or abuses archive-format features (path traversal, nested/encrypted archives, malformed headers) to conceal a malicious payload from security scanning.

An email attachment engineered as a polyglot (valid as more than one file format) or disguised via extension/icon/MIME-type spoofing to evade file-type filtering and mislead the recipient about its true nature.
An incident involving a malicious email attachment exploiting a technical vulnerability or evasion mechanism, not clearly matching document, PDF, archive, or polyglot leaves.

c.n: Email Link Redirect Chain Evading URL/Sandbox Scanning
c.d: A link embedded in an email that routes through a sequence of intermediate redirects (legitimate URL shorteners, compromised benign sites, conditional redirect logic) before reaching the final malicious destination, designed so automated scanners following the first hop see only benign content.

c.n: Email Link Exploiting Zero-Click Browser Vulnerability
c.d: A malicious link that, once clicked, delivers an exploit targeting a browser or browser-plugin vulnerability, achieving code execution or compromise with no additional user action (no download confirmation, no macro enablement) required.

c.n: Email Link Abusing URL Rewriting/Safe-Link Bypass
c.d: Exploitation of an email security vendor's link-rewriting ('safe link') feature — which proxies clicks through the vendor's domain for time-of-click checking — to disguise a malicious final destination behind a trusted vendor domain, or to exploit a re-scan gap in that service.
An incident involving a malicious email link exploiting a technical vulnerability or evasion mechanism, not clearly matching redirect-chain, zero-click browser, or safe-link-bypass leaves.

c.n: Malicious VBA Macro with Auto-Execute Trigger
c.d: A VBA macro embedded in an Office document configured with an auto-execute trigger (e.g., AutoOpen, Document_Open, Workbook_Open) that runs malicious code as soon as the document is opened and macros are enabled, without requiring any additional interaction.

A malicious Office macro that acts primarily as a lightweight downloader, reaching out to attacker-controlled infrastructure to retrieve and execute a second-stage payload (e.g., a commodity loader or ransomware precursor) rather than embedding the final payload directly.

c.n: Macro Exploiting Living-off-the-Land Office Application Features (DDE/XLM 4.0 Macros)
c.d: Abuse of legitimate, non-VBA Office application features — such as Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) fields or Excel 4.0 (XLM) macros — as a living-off-the-land execution mechanism, avoiding VBA-specific macro detection controls entirely.
An incident involving a malicious embedded macro or macro-adjacent feature abuse, not clearly matching auto-execute, downloader, or legacy non-VBA feature leaves.

c.n: Commodity Exploit Kit Landing Page (Off-the-Shelf Kit)
c.d: A web page hosting a commercially traded or freely circulated commodity exploit kit (e.g., a known kit family with a recognizable landing-page structure) that automatically attempts a battery of known browser/plugin exploits against any visitor, without victim-specific targeting or fingerprinting sophistication.

c.n: Exploit Kit with Automated Vulnerability Fingerprinting/Payload Selection
c.d: An exploit kit landing page that first fingerprints the visiting browser, plugins, and OS to identify known vulnerabilities present in that specific environment, then dynamically serves only the matching exploit — increasing success rate and reducing detectable noise compared to a commodity kit firing all exploits at once.

c.n: Exploit Kit Distributed via Compromised Ad Network
c.d: An exploit kit delivered to victims via malicious advertisements (malvertising) served through a legitimate ad exchange or network — either a compromised ad slot on a trusted site, or a malicious ad that passed initial ad-network vetting — rather than via a compromised website or direct link.
An incident involving a web-based exploit kit, not clearly matching commodity landing page, automated fingerprinting, or malvertising distribution leaves.

c.n: Custom Exploit Chain Built for Single-Target Watering-Hole Campaign
c.d: A custom-built sequence of exploits, developed or assembled specifically for one target organization or victim population, deployed by compromising a website that the intended victims are known to frequent (a watering hole) rather than through broad, indiscriminate distribution.

c.n: Targeted Exploit Kit Fingerprinting Specific Victim Environment Before Deployment
c.d: An exploit kit built for a targeted campaign that performs deep, victim-specific environment fingerprinting (organizational network indicators, specific software builds, internal hostnames) and only deploys its payload when the fingerprint matches the intended victim, refusing to fire against any other visitor to reduce exposure and evade broad detection.
An incident involving a targeted, custom-built exploit kit, not clearly matching watering-hole delivery or fingerprint-gated deployment leaves.

A phishing attack built using a subscription-model 'Phishing-as-a-Service' (PhaaS) commercial product, where the attacker rents access to a maintained kit (with regular template/evasion updates) from an underground provider rather than owning or building the kit themselves.

c.n: Phishing Kit Sold with Bundled Hosting/Infrastructure
c.d: A phishing attack built using a kit purchased as a discrete package from an underground marketplace, sold together with pre-configured hosting infrastructure (bulletproof hosting, pre-registered lookalike domains), as a one-time transaction rather than an ongoing managed service.

A phishing attack built by reusing a phishing kit template that has been leaked, open-sourced, or is otherwise freely circulating (e.g., posted on public code-sharing sites or underground forums at no cost), self-hosted by the attacker with no ongoing vendor relationship or purchased bundle.
An incident involving a phishing/social engineering kit, not clearly matching subscription PhaaS, bundled-purchase, or leaked/free template leaves.

c.n: Known-CVE Consumer IoT Firmware Vulnerability Exploitation
c.d: Exploitation of a documented vulnerability (with an assigned CVE) in the firmware of a consumer-grade IoT device, achieving code execution, privilege escalation, or persistence on the device via a known, previously patched-or-patchable flaw.

Exploitation of a device's failure to cryptographically verify the authenticity or integrity of a firmware update before installing it, allowing an attacker to deliver a malicious or backdoored firmware image that the device accepts and flashes as if it were legitimate.
Exploitation of a device's lack of anti-rollback protection to force installation of an older firmware version that reintroduces a previously patched vulnerability, which the attacker then exploits.
An incident involving exploitation of IoT device firmware, not clearly matching known-CVE, unsigned-update, or downgrade-attack leaves.

Exploitation of a hardcoded, manufacturer-embedded credential (username/password or service account) that is undocumented, not exposed in user-facing configuration, and typically discovered via firmware reverse-engineering rather than default-settings documentation.

c.n: Never-Changed Default Admin Credential Exploitation (Consumer Device)
c.d: Exploitation of a consumer device's factory-default administrative credential (e.g., admin/admin, or a printed default password) that is documented in the device manual but was never changed by the end user or installer, granting an attacker straightforward administrative access.

c.n: Default Credential Exploitation via Internet-Wide Scanning (Mass Exploitation)
c.d: Exploitation of default credentials at scale via automated internet-wide scanning tools (e.g., Mirai-class botnet scanners) that systematically attempt known default credential lists against every reachable device on the target port/service, rather than a manual, single-device credential attempt.

c.n: Unclassified / General IoT Default Credential Exploit
c.d: An incident involving exploitation of a default or hardcoded IoT device credential, not clearly matching backdoor, unchanged-default, or mass-scanning leaves.

c.n: IP Camera/Baby Monitor Hijacking for Surveillance
c.d: Compromise of an IP camera, baby monitor, or similar connected imaging device that grants the attacker unauthorized live video/audio access, exploited specifically for surveillance or voyeuristic purposes rather than as a foothold for broader network access.

c.n: Smart Home Device Hijacking for Physical Disruption (Locks/Thermostats/Alarms)
c.d: Compromise of a smart home device (smart lock, thermostat, alarm system) granting the attacker unauthorized control over a physical function, exploited to cause physical disruption, unauthorized physical access, or a safety-relevant condition rather than for data theft or surveillance.

Compromise of a connected vehicle's telematics, infotainment, or connected control systems granting the attacker unauthorized remote access to vehicle functions, ranging from location tracking to, in severe cases, safety-relevant driving system interference.

Compromise of a connected medical device or health-monitoring wearable (e.g., an infusion pump, insulin pump, cardiac monitor, or personal health tracker) granting the attacker unauthorized access to device function or patient data, with potential direct impact on patient safety.
An incident involving unauthorized takeover of an IoT device, not clearly matching camera/surveillance, smart home, vehicle, or medical device leaves.

c.n: Cloud Management Console API Abused via Stolen Access Key
c.d: Exploitation of a stolen or leaked cloud API access key/secret to make authenticated calls against the cloud provider's management console API, granting the attacker control-plane actions (resource creation, configuration change, data access) as the compromised principal.

c.n: Cloud Metadata Service (IMDS) Exploited for Credential Theft (SSRF-to-Metadata)
c.d: Exploitation of an SSRF vulnerability in an application running on a cloud compute instance to force that application to make a request to the cloud provider's Instance Metadata Service (IMDS), retrieving the instance's temporary IAM/role credentials for use by the attacker.

c.n: Cloud API Rate-Limit/Throttling Bypass for Mass Resource Enumeration
c.d: Exploitation of a weakness or bypass in a cloud API's rate-limiting/throttling controls (e.g., distributing requests across many source identities or IPs) to enumerate resources, accounts, or configuration at a scale the rate limit was intended to prevent.
An incident involving exploitation of a cloud provider API, not clearly matching stolen-key abuse, SSRF-to-metadata, or rate-limit-bypass leaves.

c.n: Overly Permissive Cloud Security Group/Network ACL Exploited
c.d: Exploitation of a cloud security group, network ACL, or firewall rule configured more permissively than intended (e.g., open to 0.0.0.0/0 on a sensitive port), granting the attacker network-layer reachability to a resource that should have been restricted.

Exploitation of a cloud storage bucket, database, or other resource left in its default configuration (e.g., public read access, no encryption at rest, default access policy) rather than hardened per organizational policy, resulting in unauthorized data access.
An incident involving exploitation of a cloud misconfiguration, not clearly matching network security group/NACL or default resource configuration leaves.

c.n: Cloud IAM Role Assumption Chain Abuse (Privilege Escalation via Role-Chaining)
c.d: Exploitation of a chain of overly permissive IAM role-assumption ('trust') relationships, where an attacker starting from a low-privilege identity assumes a sequence of roles — each individually appearing reasonable — to arrive at a highly privileged role that the original identity should never have been able to reach.

c.n: Cloud Service Principal/Managed Identity Token Theft
c.d: Theft of a short-lived or long-lived authentication token issued to a cloud service principal, managed identity, or workload identity (as opposed to a human user account), typically extracted from a compromised host, container, or CI/CD pipeline where the identity's token is cached or accessible.
An incident involving exploitation of a cloud identity mechanism, not clearly matching IAM role-chaining privilege escalation or service principal/managed identity token theft leaves.

c.n: Unclassified / General Credential Stuffing (Unauthorized Access Context)
c.d: The automated, high-volume use of credential pairs harvested from unrelated prior breaches against this organization's login surfaces, exploiting password reuse across sites to gain unauthorized access.

c.n: Unclassified / General Brute Force Attack (Unauthorized Access Context)
c.d: The systematic, repeated attempt of password guesses (dictionary-based or exhaustive) against a specific account or authentication endpoint to gain unauthorized access, distinct from credential-stuffing's use of pre-breached credential pairs.

Unauthorized access to an account achieved using credentials that were harvested from the victim via a phishing attack, where this ITID records the resulting access event rather than the phishing delivery itself.

c.n: Persistent Access via Unrevoked OAuth Refresh Token
c.d: Unauthorized persistent access to a user's account or data maintained through an OAuth refresh token issued during an earlier compromise or malicious consent grant, which continues to mint new access tokens after the initiating credential compromise has been remediated.

c.n: OAuth Token Abuse for Silent Mailbox/Data Access (No Password Needed)
c.d: Unauthorized silent access to a mailbox, file store, or other data resource via a valid OAuth access/refresh token, without any password entry, MFA prompt, or interactive sign-in event visible to the victim.

c.n: Malicious OAuth App Granted Excessive Scope Abused Post-Consent
c.d: Unauthorized access resulting from a user granting OAuth consent to a malicious or overly permissive third-party application — often via a consent-phishing lure — after which the app abuses its granted scope beyond what the user reasonably expected.

c.n: OAuth Token Reuse Across Unauthorized Third-Party Integration
c.d: Unauthorized access occurring when an OAuth token issued for one sanctioned application or integration is reused, replayed, or shared to authenticate a different, unauthorized third-party integration or service.
Unauthorized access achieved through misuse of an OAuth token or grant that has not yet been further classified into persistence, silent access, malicious consent, or cross-integration reuse.

Unauthorized horizontal access in which a user or tenant in a multi-tenant system gains access to another, unrelated customer's or tenant's data or resources due to a failure of tenant-boundary enforcement.

c.n: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) Exploited for Peer-Account Access
c.d: Unauthorized horizontal access achieved by manipulating a direct object reference (such as a record ID, file path, or account number) in a request to retrieve or modify another user's data without proper authorization checks.

c.n: Session/Object ID Manipulation for Cross-Account Access
c.d: Unauthorized access to another user's account or context achieved by manipulating, predicting, or substituting a session identifier or session-bound object reference, rather than exploiting a data object reference directly.
Unauthorized access by one user to another peer user's or tenant's account, data, or context, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific horizontal privilege escalation sibling.

c.n: Application Role/Permission Check Bypass (Broken Access Control)
c.d: Unauthorized vertical access achieved by bypassing or exploiting a flaw in an application's role- or permission-checking logic, rather than by exploiting a missing check on a specific API endpoint or a bad default role assignment.

c.n: API Endpoint Missing Authorization Check Exploited for Admin Function Access
c.d: Unauthorized vertical access achieved by directly invoking an API endpoint that performs a privileged/administrative function but has no authorization check implemented, in contrast to a broader role-logic flaw.

c.n: Privilege Escalation via Insecure Default Role Assignment
c.d: Unauthorized vertical access obtained because an application or system's default role assignment for new or unconfigured accounts grants more privilege than intended, and an adversary (or insider) leverages that default rather than bypassing any check.
Unauthorized elevation from a lower-privileged to a higher-privileged role or capability, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific vertical privilege escalation sibling.

c.n: Unclassified / General Service Account Exploitation (Unauthorized Access Context)
c.d: Unauthorized privilege escalation achieved by compromising or abusing a non-human service account (application, automation, or system account) that holds broader or more persistent privileges than typical human accounts, and using it to perform actions beyond the intended scope.

c.n: Internal RDP Lateral Movement Using Stolen Local Admin Credentials
c.d: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary uses a compromised local administrator account and password (frequently identical across multiple endpoints) to establish RDP sessions to other machines within the environment.

c.n: RDP Lateral Movement via Compromised Domain Account
c.d: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary authenticates via RDP to additional hosts using a compromised domain user or domain admin account, leveraging Active Directory trust to reach systems the account is entitled to.

c.n: RDP Session Hijacking for Lateral Movement (Existing Session Takeover)
c.d: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary takes over an existing, already-authenticated RDP session (e.g., via session shadowing or disconnected-session reconnection abuse) instead of presenting credentials to establish a new session.
Unauthorized lateral movement via RDP achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific RDP Access sibling.

c.n: Lateral Movement via C$/ADMIN$ Hidden Share
c.d: Unauthorized lateral movement achieved by mounting or accessing a remote host's hidden administrative share (C$, ADMIN$, or similar) using valid or stolen credentials, typically to stage files, read data, or prepare for remote execution.

c.n: Remote Service Creation via Admin Share for Code Execution (PsExec-Style)
c.d: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary uses an administrative share (typically ADMIN$) to stage an executable and then remotely creates and starts a Windows service (or scheduled task) to execute code on the target host, mirroring classic PsExec-style tooling.

c.n: IPC$ Null Session Abuse for Reconnaissance/Lateral Movement
c.d: Unauthorized access in which an adversary connects to a target host's IPC$ share using an anonymous or null session (no valid credentials) to enumerate users, shares, policies, or other system information as a precursor to further lateral movement.
Unauthorized lateral movement via administrative SMB shares achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Admin Shares Abuse sibling.

c.n: Unclassified / General Pass-the-Hash Attack (Lateral Movement Context)
c.d: Unauthorized lateral movement in which an adversary authenticates to a remote system using a captured NTLM password hash directly, without ever knowing or cracking the underlying plaintext password.

Unauthorized device access in which a maliciously programmed USB device (e.g., a BadUSB-style flash drive or Rubber Ducky-style tool) emulates a Human Interface Device to automatically inject keystrokes and execute commands on the host the moment it is connected.

c.n: Unauthorized Data Exfiltration via USB Storage Device
c.d: Unauthorized access to and removal of data via a USB mass-storage device connected to a corporate endpoint, used to copy files off the network without going through sanctioned data-transfer channels.

c.n: USB-Connected Device Used to Bypass Endpoint Lock Screen
c.d: Unauthorized device access achieved by connecting a specialized USB device or tool to a locked endpoint to bypass its lock-screen authentication, gaining an unlocked, logged-in session without valid credentials.
Unauthorized device access via a USB-connected device achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific USB Exploitation sibling.

Unauthorized access to corporate data and systems arising from theft of a laptop or workstation lacking full-disk encryption, allowing the thief to read the disk contents or boot the device directly without credential-based protection.

c.n: Stolen Encrypted Device with Compromised/Weak Unlock Credential
c.d: Unauthorized access to a stolen laptop or workstation that had full-disk encryption enabled, achieved because the disk-unlock or account credential was weak, guessable, reused, or separately compromised, defeating the encryption's practical protection.

c.n: Stolen Mobile Device with Active Session/Token Access
c.d: Unauthorized access to corporate accounts and data arising from theft of a mobile device that was unlocked or in an active session at the time of theft, granting the thief immediate access to authenticated apps, tokens, and data without needing to defeat any lock or encryption.

c.n: Stolen Server/Network Equipment from Physical Facility
c.d: Unauthorized access to corporate systems and data resulting from the physical theft of server, storage, or network infrastructure equipment (e.g., a rack-mounted server, switch, or NAS device) removed from a facility such as a data center, server room, or branch office.
Unauthorized access resulting from theft of corporate hardware, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Stolen Hardware sibling.

Unauthorized or unmanaged access to corporate resources from a personally owned device that has not been enrolled in the organization's MDM/UEM platform, meaning no security baseline, compliance check, or remote-wipe capability applies to it.

c.n: Jailbroken/Rooted BYOD Device Bypassing Compliance Check
c.d: Unauthorized access risk arising from a personally owned, MDM-enrolled device that has been jailbroken (iOS) or rooted (Android) to remove operating-system security restrictions, thereby bypassing the compliance checks the MDM relies on to grant conditional access.

c.n: BYOD Device Compromised by Personal-Use Malware, Then Used for Corporate Access
c.d: Unauthorized access to corporate resources originating from a personally owned device that was infected with malware through the user's personal activity (personal apps, browsing, side-loaded software), with the infection subsequently enabling access to corporate accounts, data, or systems reachable from that device.

c.n: Personal Cloud Backup Sync Exposing Corporate Data from BYOD Device
c.d: Unauthorized exposure of corporate data occurring when a personally owned device's built-in or third-party personal cloud backup/sync service (e.g., iCloud, Google Photos/Drive, personal OneDrive) automatically captures and uploads corporate content — documents, screenshots, photos of whiteboards, or cached app data — to an account outside organizational control.
Unauthorized or unmanaged access to corporate resources from a personally owned device, achieved or exposed by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific BYOD Exploits sibling.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cookie Theft (Session Hijacking Context)
c.d: Unauthorized access to an authenticated web session achieved by stealing the victim's session cookie — via malware, cross-site scripting, unsecured network traffic, or exposed browser storage — and replaying it to impersonate the victim without needing their password or MFA.

Unauthorized access achieved by capturing and later resubmitting (replaying) a previously valid session token, authentication request, or transaction, without needing to actively steal a live session in the current incident — the token was already in the adversary's possession from an earlier capture.

Unauthorized access to an authenticated session achieved by an adversary positioned actively between the victim and the legitimate service (e.g., via a rogue Wi-Fi access point, ARP spoofing, or a reverse-proxy phishing kit) who intercepts and captures session tokens or authentication material in real time.

c.n: Default Admin Credential on Network Infrastructure Device (Switch/Router/Firewall)
c.d: Unauthorized access to network infrastructure devices (switches, routers, firewalls, wireless access points) achieved by authenticating with a factory-default administrative username and password that was never changed after deployment.

c.n: Default Admin Credential on Database/Application Server Software
c.d: Unauthorized access to a database, application server, or middleware platform achieved by authenticating with a factory-default administrative username and password that was never changed after installation.

c.n: Default Admin Credential Left Active After Initial Deployment (Never Configured)
c.d: Unauthorized access enabled because a system, device, or application's default administrative credential was never configured at all following deployment — the setup/configuration process itself was abandoned or incomplete, leaving the asset running indefinitely on factory defaults rather than a single overlooked hardening step on an otherwise-configured system.

c.n: Unclassified / General Default Admin Credential Exploitation
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved via a factory-default administrative credential, on an asset type or in circumstances not yet classified into a more specific Default Admin Credentials sibling.

c.n: Unclassified / General Password Reuse Exploitation (Unauthorized Access Context)
c.d: Unauthorized access gained because a victim reused the same password across this system and an unrelated service, such that a password obtained from a breach or compromise of that other, unrelated service was sufficient to authenticate here — the device/application-side access outcome, distinct from mass automated credential-stuffing campaigns.

c.n: Unclassified / General Common Password Exploit (Unauthorized Access Context)
c.d: Unauthorized access gained by successfully guessing a commonly used, low-entropy password (e.g., 'Password123', seasonal/company-name patterns) that was not obtained from a breach list or targeted brute-force campaign, but was simply predictable enough to guess directly.

c.n: Web Server Directory Listing Exposing Sensitive Files
c.d: Unauthorized access to sensitive files achieved when a web server has directory listing enabled, allowing anyone to browse the full contents of a directory (rather than only fetching a specific known file), exposing files never intended for public discovery.

c.n: Cloud Storage Bucket Directory Listing Enabled (Public Enumeration)
c.d: Unauthorized access to files achieved when a cloud storage bucket (e.g., S3, Azure Blob, GCS) is configured to allow public listing of its objects, enabling enumeration and download of its full contents by anyone who discovers the bucket, rather than requiring a specific known object key.

Unauthorized access to files achieved when an FTP server or network file share is configured to allow anonymous or overly broad browsing/listing of its directory contents, exposing files to anyone able to connect.

c.n: Unclassified / General Open Directory Listing Exposure
c.d: Unauthorized access to files enabled by an open directory listing, on a platform or in circumstances not yet classified into a more specific Open Directory Listings sibling.

c.n: Overly Permissive Cloud IAM Role/Policy Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by leveraging an overly broad cloud IAM role or policy — attached to a user, group, or service identity — that grants permissions far beyond what its function requires, allowing an adversary who compromises that identity to reach far more resources than the identity's actual job justifies.

c.n: Publicly Writable Cloud Storage Bucket/Object Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized access in which a cloud storage bucket or individual object is configured to allow public write (upload/modify/delete) access, enabling any unauthenticated party to add, alter, or remove content, in contrast to a bucket that merely permits public read/listing.

c.n: Overly Broad File Share/Network Drive Permissions Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized access to sensitive files achieved because a network file share or drive is configured with permissions broader than necessary (e.g., granting Everyone/Domain Users read or write access), allowing users without a legitimate need to view or modify content they should not be able to reach.

c.n: Database Instance with No Authentication Required (Publicly Accessible)
c.d: Unauthorized access to a database instance (e.g., MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Redis) that has been deployed with authentication disabled or not configured, and is network-accessible (often directly from the internet), allowing any party who discovers it to connect and read or modify its contents without credentials.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unrestricted Access Permission Exploit
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by exploiting an overly permissive access configuration, on a platform or in circumstances not yet classified into a more specific Unrestricted Access Permissions sibling.

c.n: Unauthenticated API Endpoint Exposing Sensitive Data
c.d: Unauthorized access to sensitive data or functionality achieved by directly calling an API endpoint that requires no authentication token, key, or session, exposing data or actions to any party who discovers the endpoint URL/path.

c.n: Internal/Debug API Endpoint Exposed to Public Internet
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by reaching an internal-only, debug, or administrative API endpoint from the public internet, where the endpoint's exposure is caused by a network, load-balancer, API gateway, or routing misconfiguration rather than an application-level authentication defect.

c.n: API Missing Rate Limiting Exploited for Mass Data Scraping
c.d: Unauthorized access to bulk data achieved by exploiting an API endpoint's absence of rate limiting or throttling, allowing an adversary to make an abnormally high volume of requests and scrape data at scale that individual, low-volume requests would not have exposed as a meaningful risk.
Unauthorized access via an exposed API, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Exposed APIs sibling.

c.n: IP Spoofing to Bypass IP-Allowlist Access Control
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by forging or manipulating the source IP address of network traffic to match an entry on a system's IP allowlist, defeating an access control that relies on the client's apparent network origin as its sole or primary gate.

c.n: IP Spoofing for Source Attribution Evasion
c.d: Unauthorized activity in which an adversary forges the source IP address of network traffic specifically to evade source attribution, investigation, or IP-based blocking, without necessarily needing to defeat an allowlist-based access control.

c.n: IP Spoofing Combined with Session/Trust Relationship Abuse
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by combining IP address spoofing with exploitation of an established session or network trust relationship — such as TCP session hijacking or exploiting a trusted host relationship (e.g., rlogin/rsh-style trust) — to actively assume another host's identity mid-communication rather than merely satisfying a static allowlist check.
Unauthorized activity involving forged source IP addresses, achieved or intended for a purpose not yet classified into a more specific IP Spoofing sibling.

c.n: MAC Spoofing to Bypass Network Access Control (NAC/802.1X)
c.d: Unauthorized network access achieved by cloning or forging the MAC address of a known-authorized device to bypass MAC-based network access control (NAC) or 802.1X authentication that relies (in whole or part) on the device's hardware address for admission.

c.n: MAC Spoofing to Impersonate an Authorized Device on Wi-Fi
c.d: Unauthorized wireless network access achieved by cloning or forging the MAC address of a device already authorized on a Wi-Fi network's MAC-filtering access control list, allowing an adversary's device to be admitted in its place or alongside it.

c.n: MAC Spoofing for DHCP/IP Reservation Hijacking
c.d: Unauthorized network access or disruption achieved by spoofing another device's MAC address specifically to claim its DHCP reservation or static IP assignment, allowing the adversary's device to receive an IP address, and any associated network privileges or routing treatment, intended for the legitimate device.
Unauthorized network activity involving a forged MAC address, achieved or intended for a purpose not yet classified into a more specific MAC Address Spoofing sibling.

Unauthorized access achieved by crafting a fraudulent SAML assertion or exploiting a flaw in SAML signature verification (e.g., XML signature wrapping, accepting unsigned assertions, or algorithm confusion) to convince a service provider that an unauthenticated party is a legitimately authenticated user.

c.n: Federation Trust Misconfiguration Exploited for Cross-Tenant Access
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by exploiting a misconfiguration in an identity federation trust relationship — such as an overly permissive trusted-issuer list, incorrect audience restriction, or a federation trust established with an unintended or compromised external tenant — allowing a party outside the intended trust boundary to authenticate as if from a trusted source.

Unauthorized access achieved by tampering with or exploiting weak validation of claims within an OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token or access token — such as role, group, or subject claims — causing the relying application to grant access or privilege inconsistent with the user's actual identity.

c.n: Golden SAML Attack (Forged Assertions Using Stolen Signing Key)
c.d: Unauthorized access achieved by stealing an identity provider's SAML token-signing private key/certificate (e.g., from AD FS) and using it to forge fully cryptographically valid SAML assertions impersonating any user — including highly privileged accounts — without any interaction with the actual identity provider at authentication time.
Unauthorized access exploiting identity federation (SAML/OIDC/other) mechanisms, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Identity Federation Exploitation sibling.

c.n: End-of-Life (EOL) Application with No Available Patch Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized application access achieved by exploiting a security vulnerability in software that has reached end-of-life (EOL) status, meaning the vendor no longer issues patches, leaving any known or newly discovered vulnerability permanently unremediated at the source.

c.n: Legacy Application Lacking Modern Authentication (No MFA/SSO Support) Exploited
