c.d: Unauthorized application access achieved because a legacy application, while still vendor-supported and patchable, only supports weak legacy authentication (e.g., static passwords with no MFA option, or no SSO/SAML integration), leaving it a comparatively weak link in an otherwise modern authentication environment.

c.n: Legacy Application Running on Unsupported Framework/Runtime Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized application access achieved by exploiting a vulnerability in the unsupported framework, programming language runtime, web server, or operating system underlying a legacy application, even where the application's own code may be actively maintained.
Unauthorized access exploiting a legacy application, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Exploiting Legacy Applications sibling.

c.n: SaaS Platform Misconfigured Sharing/Permission Setting Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized access to data hosted in a SaaS platform achieved by exploiting a user- or tenant-level sharing/permission misconfiguration — such as an overly broad 'anyone with the link' share, a public-facing folder, or an incorrectly scoped collaboration setting — rather than a flaw in the SaaS admin console or a malicious third-party integration.

c.n: SaaS Third-Party Marketplace App/Integration Exploited for Data Access
c.d: Unauthorized access to SaaS-hosted data achieved through a third-party marketplace application or integration that was installed/authorized within the SaaS platform and subsequently abused to read, modify, or exfiltrate data beyond its legitimate purpose.

Unauthorized access to a SaaS platform's data or functionality achieved by exploiting a tenant-wide administrative console misconfiguration — such as an overly permissive global security policy, a disabled security feature, or an incorrectly scoped administrative role — affecting the entire tenant rather than a single document or a specific third-party integration.
Unauthorized access to a SaaS platform's data or functionality, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific SaaS Application Exploitation sibling.

Unauthorized access to corporate data occurring because employees stored or shared it via a cloud storage or file-sharing service that was never sanctioned, reviewed, or secured by IT/security, placing the data outside all corporate access controls, monitoring, and DLP coverage.

c.n: Unsanctioned SaaS Tool Never Reviewed by Security Exploited
c.d: Unauthorized access to or exposure of corporate data occurring because a team or individual adopted a SaaS tool (e.g., a project management, communication, or productivity application) for business use without security review, leaving the tool's security configuration, data handling, and vendor risk entirely unassessed.

c.n: Personal Email/Messaging Account Used for Business Data, Then Compromised
c.d: Unauthorized access to corporate data occurring because an employee conducted business communication or stored business data using a personal email or messaging account outside corporate control, and that personal account was subsequently compromised, exposing the business data it contained.

Unauthorized access or data exposure arising from use of an unsanctioned technology outside IT/security's visibility, achieved by a mechanism not yet classified into a more specific Shadow IT Exploits sibling.

c.n: Exfiltration via Encrypted C2 Channel Disguised as Normal HTTPS Traffic
c.d: Exfiltration of data from a compromised device to an attacker-controlled server over an encrypted (typically TLS/HTTPS) command-and-control channel that mimics legitimate web traffic patterns, ports, and often legitimate-looking domains or CDN fronting to avoid standing out to network defenders.

c.n: Exfiltration via Encrypted Messaging App API (Telegram/Discord/Slack Webhook Abuse)
c.d: Data theft in which stolen data is sent from a compromised device to an attacker-controlled channel/bot hosted on a legitimate, widely-trusted SaaS messaging platform, using that platform's own API/webhook mechanism as both the transport and the destination.

c.n: Exfiltration via Custom Encrypted Tunneling Protocol
c.d: Exfiltration over a custom-built encrypted tunnel or protocol (proprietary encryption, non-standard port/framing, or an encrypted wrapper around another protocol) designed specifically to evade signature- and protocol-based network detection.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred over an encrypted network channel, where the specific mechanism (standard HTTPS C2, SaaS API abuse, or custom protocol) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

Exfiltration in which data is chunked and encoded into DNS TXT record queries or responses exchanged with an attacker-controlled authoritative DNS server, exploiting the fact that DNS is almost universally allowed to egress.

Exfiltration where data is broken into chunks and encoded directly into the subdomain portion of DNS queries (e.g., <encoded-chunk>.attacker-domain.com) resolved as standard A/AAAA lookups, using the query itself — rather than any response content — as the covert channel.

c.n: DNS Tunneling Using a Commodity Tunneling Tool
c.d: Exfiltration of data over DNS using an identifiable, publicly-available DNS tunneling utility (e.g., iodine, dnscat2, DNSCat, Heyoka) whose known protocol signature, handshake, or client fingerprint is directly attributable to that tool.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via DNS tunneling, where the specific technique (TXT record encoding, subdomain label encoding, or named commodity tool) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

Data theft in which files are transferred from a compromised device to an external FTP or SFTP server under the attacker's control, using standard file-transfer protocols rather than web or email channels.

c.n: Exfiltration Disguised as Legitimate Scheduled Backup FTP Transfer
c.d: Data theft in which the attacker times, names, or configures the FTP/SFTP transfer to mimic a legitimate scheduled backup job (matching normal backup windows, filenames, or destinations) specifically to avoid drawing scrutiny from staff or monitoring tuned to expect such traffic.

c.n: Exfiltration via Compromised Internal FTP Server as Staging Point
c.d: Exfiltration technique in which the adversary first stages stolen data on a compromised internal (on-premises) FTP server — using it as an internal collection/aggregation point — before a subsequent transfer moves the aggregated data out of the organization's network.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred over FTP/SFTP, where the specific pattern (direct external upload, backup disguise, or internal staging) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Exfiltration via Attacker-Controlled Cloud Storage Account (Dropbox/Google Drive/OneDrive)
c.d: Data theft in which files are uploaded from a compromised or malicious process to an external cloud storage service (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, MEGA, etc.) account that is owned and controlled by the attacker, rather than by the organization or a legitimate employee.

c.n: Exfiltration via Abuse of Sanctioned Corporate Cloud Storage (Insider Using Legitimate Account)
c.d: Data theft in which an authorized employee uses their valid, organization-sanctioned cloud storage account (e.g., corporate OneDrive/Google Workspace Drive) to upload, share externally, or download sensitive data beyond their legitimate business need, exploiting the fact that the account itself is trusted infrastructure.

c.n: Exfiltration via Cloud Sync Client Auto-Upload Abuse
c.d: Data loss in which files are moved to a folder monitored by an installed cloud-sync client (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive desktop app) — whether by malware, a script, or an insider dragging files in — causing them to be automatically and silently uploaded to the cloud without any explicit upload/share action being taken.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud Storage Upload Exfiltration
c.d: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via cloud storage upload, where the specific pattern (attacker-owned account, insider abuse of a sanctioned account, or sync-client auto-upload) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Insider Self-Forwarding Sensitive Data to Personal Email
c.d: An authorized user sends, forwards, or auto-forwards sensitive organizational data from their internal corporate email account to a personal (non-corporate) email address they control, using their own legitimate mailbox access.

c.n: Insider Emailing Data to an Uninvolved Internal Colleague for Later Retrieval
c.d: An authorized user emails sensitive organizational data to a co-worker's internal mailbox where that co-worker has no legitimate business need for the data, with the intent of retrieving or re-accessing it later — often as a way to move data to a mailbox less likely to be scrutinized, or ahead of the sender's own access being revoked.

c.n: Departing Employee Bulk-Emailing Data Before Exit
c.d: An authorized user, in the period shortly before a known resignation, termination, or role change, sends an unusually large volume or breadth of sensitive organizational data via email (to a personal account, a colleague, or otherwise) compared to their normal baseline activity.

c.n: Unclassified / General Internal Email Account Exfiltration
c.d: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via an insider's own internal email account, where the specific pattern (self-forwarding, internal-colleague laundering, or departure-driven bulk send) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Auto-Forwarding Rule Configured for Silent Data Exfiltration
c.d: Following compromise of a legitimate user's email account (via phishing, credential stuffing, etc.), the attacker configures a mailbox rule (client-side or server-side) that silently forwards or BCCs some or all incoming/outgoing mail to an attacker-controlled address, providing ongoing, low-effort exfiltration.

c.n: Attacker Manually Sending Stolen Data from Compromised Mailbox
c.d: Following compromise of a legitimate user's email account, the attacker manually searches the mailbox for valuable data (financial documents, credentials, sensitive attachments) and sends it directly to an external address they control, as a discrete, one-time action rather than an ongoing rule-based mechanism.

c.n: Compromised Mailbox Used to Exfiltrate via Draft Folder (Never-Sent Message Technique)
c.d: An attacker who has compromised a mailbox composes or saves stolen data as an unsent draft message, which another party with access to the same account (a co-conspirator, or the attacker returning later) reads directly from the Drafts folder, deliberately avoiding the Sent/Inbox trail that a normal send-and-receive exchange would create.

c.n: Unclassified / General Compromised Email Account Exfiltration
c.d: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a compromised email account, where the specific mechanism (auto-forwarding rule, manual send, or draft-folder technique) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Bulk Data Exfiltration via Single Large Attachment
c.d: Exfiltration in which a large volume of sensitive data is sent in one outbound email as a single large attachment (a database export, archive, or large document), typically large enough to be conspicuous by size alone.

c.n: Data Exfiltration via Multiple Split/Segmented Attachments (Evading Size-Based DLP)
c.d: Exfiltration in which a large data set is deliberately broken into multiple smaller attachments and/or sent across several separate emails, each individually small enough to fall below a size-based DLP or mail-gateway inspection threshold, defeating detection that relies purely on single-message size.

c.n: Data Exfiltration via Compressed/Password-Protected Archive Attachment
c.d: Exfiltration in which sensitive data is packaged into a compressed archive (ZIP, RAR, 7z) that is additionally password-protected or encrypted before being attached to an outbound email, specifically to prevent DLP or mail-gateway content-inspection engines from reading inside the archive to identify sensitive content.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a large email attachment, where the specific pattern (single large attachment, split/segmented attachments, or compressed/password-protected archive) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Insider Copying Data to Personal USB Drive
c.d: An authorized user connects a personally-owned USB storage device (drive, external HDD/SSD) to an organizational endpoint and copies sensitive data onto it, physically removing the data from organizational control without using any network-based channel.

c.n: Encrypted/Password-Protected USB Drive Used to Evade DLP Detection
c.d: An insider or attacker copies sensitive data onto a USB storage device that is hardware- or software-encrypted (or otherwise password-protected at the volume level), specifically preventing endpoint DLP or forensic tooling from inspecting the content of what was copied, whether in real time or after the fact.

c.n: USB Device Disguised as Ordinary Object for Covert Removal
c.d: An insider or attacker uses a USB storage device deliberately built or modified to physically resemble an innocuous object (a pen, watch, charging cable, or novelty item) specifically to evade visual inspection by physical security or casual observation during removal of stolen data from the premises.

c.n: Unclassified / General USB Device Data Transfer Exfiltration
c.d: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a USB storage device, where the specific pattern (standard device, encrypted/password-protected device, or physically disguised device) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Data Copied to Personal Mobile Device via Cable/Wireless Transfer
c.d: An insider connects a personal smartphone or tablet to an organizational endpoint (via USB cable, or a direct wireless protocol such as Bluetooth or AirDrop) and copies sensitive files directly onto the mobile device's local storage.

c.n: Screenshot/Photo of Screen Content Using Personal Mobile Device
c.d: An insider uses a personal smartphone or tablet's camera to photograph or video-record sensitive information displayed on a corporate screen, extracting data through a purely optical/analog channel that leaves no digital copy or network trace on organizational systems.

c.n: Mobile Device Used as Wi-Fi Hotspot to Bypass Network DLP Controls
c.d: An insider connects a corporate endpoint to a personal mobile device's Wi-Fi or Bluetooth hotspot (tethering over the device's own cellular data connection), routing outbound traffic — including exfiltrated data — outside the organization's monitored network path, defeating network-based DLP and egress monitoring.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a personal mobile device, where the specific pattern (direct file transfer, screen photography, or network-bypass hotspot use) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

A physical hardware device (inline network tap, port mirror device, or covert packet-capture implant) is installed on organizational network cabling or infrastructure — typically requiring physical facility access — to passively capture and later retrieve or transmit intercepted network traffic containing sensitive data.

c.n: Covert Wireless Exfiltration Implant (Rogue Access Point/Cellular Modem Planted On-Premises)
c.d: A physical wireless device — a rogue Wi-Fi access point, a cellular (3G/4G/5G) modem, or similar radio-based implant — is covertly installed on organizational premises, either connected to the internal network or independently powered, to create an exfiltration path that bypasses wired network monitoring and egress controls entirely.

c.n: Malicious Peripheral Device Implant (Rogue Raspberry Pi/O.MG Cable)
c.d: A malicious peripheral device — such as a small single-board computer (e.g., a disguised Raspberry Pi) connected to an internal port, or a keystroke-injection/exfiltration cable (e.g., an O.MG Cable) substituted for a legitimate charging or peripheral cable — is planted at a workstation to provide the attacker with covert local access, keystroke capture, or a network implant for data theft.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via a covertly planted physical hardware device, where the specific type (network tap, wireless implant, or malicious peripheral) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: SQL Injection Used to Bulk-Extract Database Records
c.d: An attacker exploits a SQL injection vulnerability in a web application's input handling to craft queries that extract large volumes of data directly from the backend database, bypassing the application's intended access controls and business logic entirely.

c.n: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Used to Exfiltrate Internal Data
c.d: An attacker exploits a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability to make the vulnerable server-side application issue requests to internal-only endpoints (internal APIs, cloud metadata services, internal admin panels), exfiltrating the response content back to the attacker through the application's own output.

c.n: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) Used for Bulk Record Scraping
c.d: An attacker exploits an authorization-logic flaw in which the application fails to verify that a requesting user is authorized to access a specific record, allowing systematic enumeration of predictable or sequential object identifiers (record IDs, account numbers) to scrape large volumes of other users' data through an otherwise legitimate-looking, authenticated application feature.

Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via exploitation of a web application vulnerability, where the specific vulnerability class (SQL injection, SSRF, or IDOR) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Bulk Export via Legitimate Reporting/BI Tool Feature
c.d: An authorized user leverages a sanctioned reporting or BI platform's native export/download functionality (CSV, PDF, or data-connector export) to pull a bulk data set out of the system for a purpose beyond their legitimate business need, using entirely legitimate tool functionality with no exploitation involved.

c.n: CRM/ERP Mass Record Export by Authorized User
c.d: An authorized user leverages a CRM (e.g., Salesforce) or ERP (e.g., SAP) system's built-in mass-export or reporting-export functionality to extract a large volume of customer, sales, financial, or operational records beyond their legitimate business need, using entirely legitimate tool functionality with no exploitation involved.

c.n: Database Admin Tool Used for Unauthorized Bulk Query/Export
c.d: An authorized user with legitimate database administration access (DBA, developer, or similar privileged role) uses a database administration tool (e.g., SQL client, phpMyAdmin, a cloud database console) to run bulk SELECT/export queries against production data, extracting a volume or scope of data beyond what their role's normal duties require.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Tool Usage for Exfiltration
c.d: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred through an authorized user's use of a legitimate internal tool, where the specific tool layer (reporting/BI, CRM/ERP, or database administration) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: API Called with Stolen/Reused API Key Beyond Authorized Scope
c.d: An attacker obtains a valid API key or authentication token (via leakage in source code/config, credential theft, or reuse from another breach) and uses it to call an organization's API and extract data beyond the key's intended authorization scope, volume, or rate, exploiting the fact that the key itself is technically valid.

c.n: Automated Script Scraping API Endpoint at Abnormal Volume/Frequency
c.d: An attacker or unauthorized party writes and runs an automated script or bot that calls a legitimate, otherwise-authorized API endpoint at a volume, frequency, or sustained rate well beyond normal human or legitimate integration usage patterns, systematically scraping data over time.

c.n: API Pagination Abuse to Enumerate and Extract Full Dataset
c.d: An attacker exploits an API's pagination mechanism (page tokens, offset/limit parameters, cursors) by programmatically iterating through every available page to reconstruct and extract the complete underlying dataset, exploiting the fact that pagination controls were designed for incremental browsing rather than as an access-control boundary.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unauthorized API Call Exfiltration
c.d: Data exfiltration confirmed or strongly suspected to have occurred via unauthorized or abusive API calls, where the specific mechanism (stolen/reused key, high-volume scraping, or pagination abuse) has not yet been determined at time of logging.

c.n: Bulk Copy of Sensitive Files from Internal File Share to External Location
c.d: A single identifiable event in which a user or process copies a materially large volume of files from an internal (on-prem or mapped network) file share to an external location such as removable media, a personal cloud account, or an external network path, distinguished from sibling ITIDs by its bulk-copy technical signature rather than by who performed it or why.

c.n: External Sharing Link Generated for Internal File Share Folder
c.d: An event in which a user generates an external (anonymous or broadly shared) link granting access to an internal file share folder or its contents, exposing sensitive data to parties outside the organization's access boundary.

c.n: Network File Share Mapped and Mass-Copied by Compromised/Insider Account
c.d: An event in which an attacker-controlled or insider-abused account maps a network file share it would not normally access at that volume, then mass-copies files, indicating the access itself (not merely the copy) is the anomaly.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unauthorized File Share Exfiltration
c.d: An unauthorized file share exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Unauthorized File Shares, pending further investigation.

c.n: External Sharing Link Created on SharePoint/Google Drive Document
c.d: An event in which a user generates an externally accessible sharing link on a document or folder within a cloud collaboration platform, exposing its contents outside the organization's managed boundary.

c.n: Guest/External User Added to Internal Teams/Slack Workspace for Data Access
c.d: An event in which a guest or external identity is invited into or added to an internal collaboration workspace, granting standing access to channels, files, and conversations beyond the organization's boundary.

c.n: Collaboration Platform Bulk Download/Sync of Shared Files
c.d: An event in which a user (internal or guest) bulk-downloads or syncs a large volume of files from a collaboration platform, moving data from the managed cloud environment to an unmanaged local endpoint or external storage.

c.n: Unclassified / General Misused Collaboration Platform Exfiltration
c.d: A misused collaboration platform exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID, pending further investigation.

c.n: BitTorrent/P2P File-Sharing Client Used to Exfiltrate Data
c.d: An event in which a user installs and uses a BitTorrent or similar P2P client to upload/seed sensitive organizational data, distributing it to external peers outside any single controllable destination.

c.n: Direct P2P File Transfer App (AirDrop/Nearby Share) Used to Bypass Network Monitoring
c.d: An event in which a user transfers sensitive files directly to another device using a proximity-based P2P protocol (AirDrop, Nearby Share, or similar), bypassing network-layer monitoring entirely since the transfer never traverses the corporate network.
A P2P transfer exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Peer-to-Peer Transfers, pending further investigation.

c.n: Bulk Accumulation of Files Unrelated to Current Job Function
c.d: A pattern of an employee or contractor accessing and/or locally storing a broad set of files spanning topics, departments, or systems unrelated to their current job function, without an accompanying exfiltration event yet observed.

c.n: Repeated Access and Local Copying of Sensitive Records Over Time
c.d: A pattern in which a user repeatedly accesses and locally copies a specific sensitive dataset (e.g., a customer list, source code repository, or financial record set) over an extended period, indicating deliberate, targeted staging rather than incidental browsing.

c.n: Data Hoarding Detected Shortly Before Resignation/Termination
c.d: A pattern of file accumulation, local copying, or access-volume increase by a user in the window immediately preceding or following their resignation notice or termination, where the timing itself is the primary risk-elevating signal.
A data hoarding event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Data Hoarding, pending further investigation.

c.n: Insider-Configured Auto-Forward Rule to Personal Email Address
c.d: An event in which a user creates a mail-flow rule on their own mailbox that automatically forwards messages (all mail or a filtered subset) to a personal email address, establishing a standing, low-visibility exfiltration channel.

c.n: Insider-Configured Auto-Forward Rule to External Competitor/New Employer Domain
c.d: An event in which a user creates a mailbox forwarding rule that routes mail to an email address on a domain identified as a competitor or the user's confirmed new employer, indicating likely intentional competitive data transfer.

c.n: Delayed-Activation Forwarding Rule Set Up Before Resignation
c.d: An event in which a user creates a mailbox forwarding rule configured to activate at a future date, after a triggering condition, or well before their resignation notice is given, so that the exfiltration channel is already established before heightened departure-window scrutiny begins.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Email Forwarding Rule Exfiltration
c.d: An insider email forwarding rule exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Email Forwarding Rules, pending further investigation.

c.n: Bulk Printing of Sensitive Documents Outside Normal Job Function
c.d: An event in which a user's print activity, measured by page/document count of sensitive material, significantly exceeds what their role would normally require, independent of when the printing occurred.

An event in which a user prints sensitive documents outside their normal working hours or established printing pattern, where the timing anomaly itself is the primary indicator, regardless of print volume.

c.n: Printed Documents Removed from Facility (Physical Exfiltration)
c.d: An event in which printed sensitive documents are confirmed to have left the facility with an employee or contractor, whether observed directly, inferred from badge-out correlation, or discovered after the fact.
A printout exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Printouts, pending further investigation.

c.n: Data Hidden in Image File (LSB Steganography)
c.d: An event in which sensitive data is encoded into an image file using least-significant-bit (LSB) or similar pixel-level steganographic techniques, then moved out through a channel where the modified image appears visually and structurally unremarkable.

An event in which sensitive data is encoded into an audio or video file's data stream using steganographic techniques, then exfiltrated through a channel where the modified media file appears to play/render normally.

An event in which sensitive data is encoded into a document's metadata fields (author, comments, custom properties) or hidden via whitespace/formatting-based encoding (e.g., trailing spaces, font-color-matched text), then exfiltrated as an apparently normal business document.
A steganographic exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Steganography, pending further investigation or carrier identification.

c.n: Data Encoded in Social Media Post/Image Caption
c.d: An event in which sensitive data is encoded (via text pattern, hashtag sequence, or embedded image steganography) into a publicly posted social media post or caption, allowing an external party to retrieve it without any direct connection to the victim organization's network.

c.n: Data Exfiltrated via Direct Message to Attacker-Controlled Account
c.d: An event in which a user sends sensitive data through a social media platform's direct/private messaging feature to an account outside the organization, using the platform's messaging infrastructure rather than public posting or email/IM.

c.n: Data Exfiltrated via Social Media Draft/Scheduled Post Never Published
c.d: An event in which a user encodes sensitive data into a social media draft or scheduled post and leaves it unpublished, using the platform account itself as a shared storage location (dead drop) accessible to a colluding party with access to the same account credentials.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Media Covert Channel Exfiltration
c.d: A social media covert channel exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Social Media Channels, pending further investigation.

c.n: Data Sent via Personal WhatsApp/Signal/Telegram Message
c.d: An event in which a user sends sensitive organizational data through a third-party instant messaging application (WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or similar) installed on a corporate or BYOD device, where end-to-end encryption prevents network-layer content inspection.

c.n: Data Sent via iMessage/RCS to Personal Device
c.d: An event in which a user transfers sensitive data using the device's native messaging protocol (Apple iMessage or Android RCS) to a personal device, relying on OS-level messaging infrastructure that is typically outside the visibility of enterprise mobile DLP tools.

c.n: Ephemeral/Disappearing Message App Used to Evade Retention/DLP
c.d: An event in which a user configures or uses a messaging app's disappearing/self-destructing message feature when transferring sensitive data, indicating deliberate intent to prevent later forensic recovery or retention-policy capture, regardless of the specific platform.

c.n: Unclassified / General Instant Messaging App Exfiltration
c.d: An instant messaging app exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Instant Messaging Apps, pending further investigation.

c.n: Exfiltration via APT-Operated Dedicated Staging Server
c.d: An event in which an advanced persistent threat actor exfiltrates data to a server or infrastructure element it owns and operates as a dedicated staging point, distinguished by attribution to attacker-controlled (not third-party or compromised) infrastructure.

c.n: Exfiltration Timed to Avoid Security Team Working Hours (Time-Zone-Aware)
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor times data exfiltration activity to coincide with periods of reduced security monitoring coverage — nights, weekends, or holidays specific to the victim organization's time zone — as a deliberate detection-evasion strategy.

c.n: Exfiltration Using Compromised Third-Party Infrastructure to Mask Origin
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor exfiltrates data via infrastructure it does not own but has compromised (a legitimate third-party server, cloud tenant, or trusted vendor system), using that legitimacy to evade destination-based network defenses.
An APT-driven exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under APT-Driven Exfiltration, pending further threat intelligence attribution.

c.n: Data Staged Internally Before Bulk Transfer Out
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor collects and consolidates data onto one or more internal staging hosts in preparation for bulk transfer, distinguished as the pre-exfiltration internal-collection stage rather than the outbound transfer itself.

c.n: Exfiltration Split Across Multiple Compromised Hosts to Avoid Volume Detection
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor exfiltrates data by dividing the transfer across several compromised hosts, each sending a sub-threshold volume, so that per-host monitoring fails to flag any individual host as anomalous while aggregate loss is substantial.

c.n: Exfiltration via Sequential Handoff Between Multiple C2 Channels
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor exfiltrates data using a sequence of different C2 channels or protocols in succession (e.g., DNS tunneling, then HTTPS, then a cloud storage API), rather than a single consistent channel, to avoid building a detectable single-protocol pattern.
A multi-stage exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Multi-Stage Exfiltration, pending further investigation.

c.n: Low-and-Slow Exfiltration Below DLP Volume Thresholds
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor exfiltrates data in small increments deliberately calibrated to remain under configured DLP or network monitoring volume thresholds, prioritizing threshold evasion as the primary technique over duration or scheduling.

c.n: Exfiltration Spread Across Extended Dwell Time to Avoid Baseline Deviation Detection
c.d: An event in which an advanced threat actor spreads data exfiltration across a long time horizon (weeks to months), calibrating the pace so that behavioral baselining tools never observe a statistically significant deviation from normal activity.

An event in which data exfiltration is carried out through a scheduled task, cron job, or automated script that periodically transfers small batches of data at consistent, predictable intervals, distinguishing this leaf by its automated-scheduling mechanism rather than volume-threshold or dwell-time evasion strategy.
An exfiltration-over-time event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Exfiltration Over Time, pending further investigation.

c.n: Bulk Download from Publicly Accessible Misconfigured Cloud Bucket
c.d: An event in which sensitive data is downloaded in bulk by a party who located a cloud storage bucket (e.g., S3, Azure Blob, GCS) left publicly accessible due to misconfiguration, distinguished from automated scanning campaigns by its single-target, manually-driven nature.

c.n: Automated Scanning-and-Harvesting of Misconfigured Cloud Storage at Scale
c.d: An event in which sensitive data is accessed or downloaded from a misconfigured cloud storage resource by an automated scanning/harvesting tool operating at internet scale, indicated by scanning patterns, generic tooling signatures, or correlation with mass-scanning campaigns rather than targeted reconnaissance of this organization specifically.

c.n: Exfiltration via Misconfigured Cloud Database Snapshot/Backup Export
c.d: An event in which sensitive data is exposed and exfiltrated via a cloud-hosted database snapshot, automated backup, or export file left with overly permissive access, exposing structured records (databases) rather than arbitrary file objects.

c.n: Unclassified / General Public Cloud Misconfiguration Exfiltration
c.d: A public cloud misconfiguration exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Public Cloud Misconfiguration, pending further investigation.

c.n: Direct Console Download of Cloud Storage Objects Using Compromised Credentials
c.d: An event in which an actor authenticates to a cloud provider's management console using compromised or stolen valid credentials and directly downloads storage objects, distinguished from Public Cloud Misconfiguration leaves by requiring valid authentication rather than exploiting a public-exposure gap.

c.n: Bulk Cloud Database Export/Dump via Admin Console Access
c.d: An event in which an actor with cloud database administrative console access performs a full or large-scale export/dump of a managed database instance, using legitimate admin functionality rather than object storage download or snapshot mechanisms.

c.n: Cloud VM Disk Snapshot Exported and Downloaded Externally
c.d: An event in which an actor creates a snapshot of a cloud virtual machine's disk volume, exports it, and downloads it outside the organization's cloud environment, exposing the complete file system and any data at rest on that VM.

c.n: Unclassified / General Direct Cloud Download Exfiltration
c.d: A direct cloud download exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Direct Downloads, pending further investigation.

c.n: Ephemeral Cloud VM Spun Up as Exfiltration Staging Point
c.d: An event in which an actor provisions a temporary, short-lived cloud VM instance and uses it as a staging point or relay for data exfiltration, taking advantage of the VM's ephemeral lifecycle to minimize the window available for forensic analysis.

c.n: Serverless Function Abused for Automated Data Exfiltration
c.d: An event in which an actor deploys or modifies a serverless function within the organization's cloud environment to automate the collection and transfer of sensitive data, exploiting serverless compute's typically lighter logging/monitoring footprint compared to traditional VMs.

c.n: Temporary Storage Bucket Created and Deleted After Exfiltration (Anti-Forensic)
c.d: An event in which an actor creates a cloud storage bucket, uses it briefly to stage or relay exfiltrated data, and deletes the bucket shortly afterward, using the create-use-delete lifecycle itself as a deliberate anti-forensic technique.
A temporary cloud instance exfiltration event that cannot yet be classified into a more specific sibling ITID under Temporary Instances, pending further investigation.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high-rate stream of UDP packets, often to random or fixed destination ports, with the sole aim of consuming available bandwidth and/or forcing the target (or its upstream links/devices) to spend CPU cycles generating ICMP port-unreachable replies until legitimate traffic can no longer get through.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high-rate stream of ICMP packets (typically Echo Request/'ping') directly at a target to consume link bandwidth and force the target or intermediate devices to spend CPU cycles processing and replying to each packet.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary simultaneously or sequentially combines two or more direct protocol floods (e.g. UDP, ICMP, TCP) against the same target to exceed the capacity or scope of mitigations tuned for any single protocol.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear volumetric flooding characteristics (bandwidth or packet-rate saturation) where the specific protocol or delivery mechanism has not yet been determined or does not cleanly fit an existing Volumetric Flooding leaf.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of TCP SYN packets with forged (spoofed) source IP addresses to a target, causing it to allocate connection state for each half-open connection until its backlog/SYN queue is exhausted and legitimate connections are refused.

A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet of compromised, internet-routable hosts each open TCP connections toward a target and either withhold the final ACK or abandon the handshake en masse, exhausting the target's half-open connection capacity through sheer distributed source volume rather than spoofing.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary spoofs the target's IP address as the source of SYN packets sent to numerous innocent third-party hosts; those hosts each reply with a SYN-ACK directed at the spoofed (target) address, flooding the target with unsolicited SYN-ACK traffic it never requested.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear SYN flooding characteristics (half-open connection exhaustion) where the specific delivery mechanism (spoofed single-source, distributed botnet, or reflection) has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed UDP queries (commonly the deprecated monlist command) to publicly reachable NTP servers, causing each to send a disproportionately large response to the spoofed victim address, amplifying attack bandwidth well beyond what the adversary directly generates.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed UDP requests to publicly reachable memcached servers, causing each to return a vastly larger cached-data response to the spoofed victim address, achieving amplification factors that can exceed tens of thousands to one.

c.n: DNS Amplification Attack (as a DDoS Technique)
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed DNS queries (often crafted to return large responses, e.g. ANY or TXT record lookups) to open/misconfigured DNS resolvers, causing each to send an amplified response to the spoofed victim address.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends small, spoofed queries to internet-exposed CLDAP (Connectionless LDAP, common on Active Directory domain controllers) or SSDP (Simple Service Discovery Protocol, common on consumer routers/IoT devices) services, causing each to send an amplified response to the spoofed victim address.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear reflection/amplification characteristics (unsolicited, disproportionately large inbound responses with no matching outbound query) where the specific reflector protocol has not yet been determined or does not fit an existing Amplification Attacks leaf.

c.n: Classic ICMP Smurf Attack (Broadcast Address Spoofing)
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends ICMP Echo Request packets to a network's broadcast address with the source address spoofed as the victim's IP, causing every host on that broadcast network to send an ICMP Echo Reply to the victim simultaneously, amplifying traffic in proportion to the number of responding hosts.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends spoofed UDP packets (typically to the echo or chargen ports) to a network's broadcast address, causing every responding host to send UDP traffic to the spoofed victim address, amplifying attack traffic in the same manner as Smurf but over UDP rather than ICMP.
A denial-of-service event exhibiting broadcast-network reflection characteristics where the specific protocol variant (ICMP Smurf or UDP Fraggle) has not yet been determined.

A low-and-slow denial-of-service attack in which an adversary opens many HTTP connections to a target web server and sends partial request headers at a deliberately slow rate (or none at all after the initial line), keeping each connection open just below the server's timeout threshold until the server's maximum concurrent connection limit is exhausted and it can no longer accept new legitimate requests.

A low-and-slow denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a complete HTTP POST header declaring a large Content-Length, then transmits the request body one byte (or a few bytes) at a time over an extended period, holding the server-side request-processing thread or connection open until resources are exhausted.

A low-and-slow denial-of-service attack in which an adversary issues normal, complete HTTP requests but advertises a tiny TCP receive window (or otherwise throttles read speed), forcing the server to hold the response buffer and connection open far longer than a normal client would, exhausting connection/memory resources as more such connections accumulate.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting slow-rate (low-bandwidth, connection-exhaustion) characteristics where the specific stalled phase of the HTTP transaction (headers, body, or response) has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of complete, well-formed HTTP GET requests targeting a specific resource-intensive endpoint (e.g. search, report generation, large media, or database-backed pages) to exhaust backend compute, database, or I/O capacity rather than network bandwidth.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of complete HTTP POST requests to a form, login, search, or other data-submission endpoint, forcing the backend to process, validate, and often persist each submission until compute, database, or storage capacity is exhausted.

c.n: Cache-Busting HTTP Flood (Randomized Query Strings Bypassing CDN Cache)
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary appends randomized query strings, headers, or cache-busting parameters to each HTTP request so that CDN or edge caching layers treat every request as unique, forcing each one through to the origin server and defeating the very caching that would otherwise absorb a normal flood.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear HTTP flood characteristics (high-rate, complete application-layer requests overwhelming a web/application tier) where the specific request method, target endpoint category, or cache-evasion technique has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary repeatedly triggers TLS renegotiation (client-initiated handshake renegotiation within an established session) against a target, exploiting the significant asymmetry between the trivial client-side cost and the far higher server-side cryptographic cost of each renegotiation to exhaust CPU capacity.

c.n: SSL/TLS Connection Flood Exhausting Server Compute
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary opens a high volume of new SSL/TLS connections, forcing the server to perform a full cryptographic handshake (key exchange, certificate processing) for each, exhausting CPU capacity given the relatively high cost of handshake operations compared to plaintext connection setup.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear TLS-layer exhaustion characteristics (disproportionate server-side cryptographic CPU load) where the specific mechanism (renegotiation abuse or handshake flood) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Authenticated API Endpoint Flooded to Exhaust Backend Resources
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary, holding valid session tokens, API keys, or credentials (legitimately issued, stolen, or self-registered), sends a high rate of authenticated API requests to exhaust backend compute, database, or third-party integration capacity, bypassing controls that assume authenticated traffic is inherently trustworthy.

c.n: Expensive/Complex Query Endpoint Repeatedly Called to Exhaust Compute (Algorithmic Complexity Attack)
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary identifies and repeatedly calls an API or query endpoint whose underlying implementation has poor algorithmic complexity (e.g. unbounded joins, recursive lookups, unindexed searches, regular-expression denial-of-service patterns) so that a modest request rate produces a disproportionately large backend compute cost, exhausting resources far faster than a naive request-volume flood would.

A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet of many distinct, geographically distributed hosts sends a high rate of API requests to a target, using sheer source diversity to defeat IP-based rate-limiting and exhaust backend capacity.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear API request flooding characteristics (backend exhaustion driven by excessive API call volume) where the specific actor type (authenticated identity, algorithmic-complexity exploitation, or distributed botnet) has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet composed primarily of compromised Internet-of-Things devices (routers, cameras, DVRs, and similar embedded devices) is directed via C2 to generate application-layer request floods (e.g. HTTP) against a target, exploiting the sheer scale and geographic distribution of recruited IoT devices.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary purchases or rents attack capacity from a commercial 'booter' or 'stresser' service — a platform that packages access to botnet or amplification infrastructure as a paid, self-service product — to launch an attack against a target with minimal technical effort or infrastructure of the adversary's own.

A denial-of-service attack in which a botnet's command-and-control infrastructure directs member bots to execute multiple distinct attack vectors (e.g. volumetric flood, SYN flood, and application-layer flood) concurrently or in rapid succession against the same target, coordinated as a single campaign to exceed the coverage of any single mitigation layer.
A denial-of-service event confirmed as botnet-driven where the specific botnet category (IoT, booter-mediated, or coordinated multi-vector) has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack distributed across a botnet of compromised, internet-connected hosts of mixed or general-purpose composition (not specifically IoT-dominant, cloud-hosted, or vector-specialized), coordinated via C2 to overwhelm a target's network or application capacity.

A denial-of-service attack distributed across a botnet composed predominantly of compromised Internet-of-Things devices (routers, cameras, DVRs, and similar embedded consumer/industrial devices), coordinated via C2 to overwhelm a target's network or application capacity, leveraging the scale and poor security posture typical of the IoT device population.

c.n: DDoS Launched from Rented Cloud Compute Instances
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary provisions virtual machines or compute instances from one or more legitimate cloud providers (using stolen payment credentials, free-tier abuse, or compromised cloud accounts) and uses that rented infrastructure directly to generate high-volume attack traffic against a target.

c.n: Serverless Function Abuse for Distributed Attack Traffic Generation
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary invokes serverless functions (e.g. Lambda-style FaaS offerings) at massive parallel scale across one or more cloud providers, using each short-lived function invocation as a distributed source of attack traffic against a target, exploiting the platforms' elastic auto-scaling and per-invocation IP diversity.

A denial-of-service-adjacent attack (commonly termed 'denial-of-wallet') in which an adversary sends traffic or triggers workload patterns specifically designed to cause a victim's cloud auto-scaling infrastructure to provision excessive additional compute, storage, bandwidth, or third-party API calls, inflating the victim's cloud billing to a damaging or unsustainable level, whether or not availability is meaningfully degraded.
A denial-of-service event confirmed as sourced from or targeting cloud infrastructure where the specific mechanism (rented compute, serverless abuse, or cost-exhaustion) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Combined Volumetric and Application-Layer Multi-Vector DDoS
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary combines network-layer volumetric techniques (e.g. UDP/ICMP floods, amplification) with application-layer techniques (e.g. HTTP floods, slow-rate attacks) against the same target within a single campaign, forcing defenders to engage both network-layer scrubbing and application-layer (WAF/bot mitigation) controls simultaneously.

c.n: DDoS Combined with Ransomware Extortion Demand (RDoS)
c.d: A denial-of-service attack, or the credible threat of one, launched or maintained alongside an extortion demand in which the adversary requires payment (typically cryptocurrency) to stop an ongoing attack or to prevent a threatened future attack, distinguishing it from purely technical DDoS incidents by the presence of a financial coercion element.

c.n: DDoS Used as Smokescreen for Concurrent Data Breach/Intrusion
c.d: A denial-of-service attack launched concurrently with, or immediately preceding, a separate intrusion or data-exfiltration effort, where the DDoS traffic is intended (or suspected) to serve as a smokescreen that consumes SOC attention, logging capacity, and incident-response resources while the primary breach activity proceeds with reduced scrutiny.
A denial-of-service event confirmed as combining DDoS with another element (a second attack layer, extortion, or a concurrent intrusion) where the specific combination has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary generates a high volume of DNS queries for randomly generated, non-existent subdomains of a target domain, forcing the target's authoritative servers (and any upstream recursive resolvers in the resolution path) to process each unique, uncacheable query and typically return NXDOMAIN responses, exhausting query-processing capacity.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of DNS queries to a recursive resolver, each crafted (through randomization, TTL manipulation assumptions, or query variation) to avoid a cache hit, forcing the resolver to perform full iterative resolution against authoritative servers for every query and exhausting the resolver's processing capacity.

c.n: Authoritative DNS Server Direct Query Flood
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of DNS queries directly to a target's authoritative name servers, exhausting query-processing capacity through sheer volume rather than through cache-defeating randomization or third-party reflection.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear DNS query flooding characteristics (query-processing capacity exhaustion) where the specific pattern (random-subdomain water torture, resolver cache-bypass, or direct authoritative flood) has not yet been determined.

c.n: BGP Route Hijack Causing Traffic Blackholing
c.d: A denial-of-service condition resulting from an adversary announcing unauthorized, more-specific, or otherwise preferred BGP routes for a target organization's IP address space, causing internet traffic destined for the target to be diverted to the adversary's network (or a non-existent path) and effectively blackholed, denying legitimate users the ability to reach the target's services.

c.n: BGP Route Leak Causing Traffic Misdirection/Overload
c.d: A denial-of-service condition resulting from a BGP route leak — the propagation of routes beyond their intended scope, typically due to a configuration error at a network operator (which may or may not be the target organization) — causing traffic destined for the target to be misdirected through an unintended, often under-provisioned path, resulting in congestion, packet loss, or complete unreachability.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary causes an established BGP session between the target's network and a peer/upstream to reset or repeatedly flap (drop and re-establish), for example via spoofed TCP RST injection against the BGP TCP session or by exhausting router resources handling the session, causing loss of routing information and consequent traffic disruption for the duration of each reset/reconvergence cycle.
A denial-of-service event confirmed as BGP-routing-related where the specific mechanism (unauthorized route hijack, route leak, or session disruption) has not yet been determined.

c.n: SIP INVITE Flood Attack (VoIP Call Setup Exhaustion)
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of SIP INVITE requests (the message that initiates a call setup) to a target VoIP server or session border controller, forcing it to allocate call-state resources for each attempted session until call-setup capacity is exhausted and legitimate calls can no longer be established.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high rate of SIP REGISTER requests (the message endpoints use to bind their location for incoming calls) to a target VoIP server, forcing it to process registration/authentication attempts for each request until registrar capacity is exhausted, disrupting the ability of legitimate endpoints to register and receive calls.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear SIP flooding characteristics (VoIP infrastructure capacity exhaustion) where the specific SIP method driving the flood (INVITE or REGISTER) has not yet been determined.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends deliberately malformed IP fragments with overlapping offset values (in the style of the historical Teardrop exploit) to a target host, exploiting flaws in fragment-reassembly logic that cause the target's network stack to crash, hang, or otherwise fail when attempting to reconstruct the invalid fragment set.

A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a high volume of legitimately structured IP fragments — often deliberately incomplete fragment sets (never sending the final fragment) — forcing the target to allocate and hold reassembly buffer memory for each incomplete set until timeout, exhausting available memory or CPU capacity as buffers accumulate faster than they can be released.

c.n: Oversized Fragmented Packet (Ping of Death-Style) Attack
c.d: A denial-of-service attack in which an adversary sends a sequence of IP fragments that, when reassembled by the target, produce a packet exceeding the maximum allowed IP packet size (65,535 bytes), exploiting buffer handling flaws in vulnerable network stacks to cause a crash, hang, or reboot.

A denial-of-service event exhibiting clear IP fragmentation-based characteristics where the specific mechanism (overlapping-offset logic flaw, reassembly buffer exhaustion, or oversized-packet exploitation) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) Exploiting Catastrophic Backtracking
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary submits specially crafted strings to an application endpoint that evaluates them against a vulnerable regular expression, forcing the regex engine into exponential/polynomial backtracking that consumes CPU on one or more worker threads/processes until the service becomes unresponsive.

c.n: Cryptomining Payload Consuming Host CPU Resources (Resource Hijacking)
c.d: Sustained CPU exhaustion on a host or fleet of hosts caused by an adversary-deployed cryptomining process (T1496 Resource Hijacking) consuming compute resources needed by the legitimate application or service, resulting in degraded performance or outage for the legitimate workload.

A resource-depletion attack in which crafted compressed content (zip bomb, nested archive, or compressed request body) is submitted to a service that automatically decompresses input, causing the decompression routine to consume excessive CPU cycles relative to the small size of the compressed payload.

A CPU-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against application or host CPU capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (regex backtracking, resource hijacking, compression bombs) pending further investigation.

c.n: Memory Leak Triggered via Repeated Malformed Requests
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary repeatedly submits malformed or edge-case requests that trigger a memory leak (objects, buffers, or connections not properly released) in the target application, causing memory consumption to grow until the process is killed by the OS or becomes unresponsive.

A resource-depletion attack in which a small, highly compressed payload (zip bomb, gzip bomb, or nested archive) is decompressed into memory in full before size validation, causing the decompression buffer to exhaust available RAM and crash or degrade the target process.

c.n: Application Cache Poisoning to Force Excessive Memory Allocation
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary exploits cache-key generation or cache-population logic (e.g., by varying request parameters, headers, or cookies) to force the application or caching layer to allocate and retain an unbounded number of distinct cache entries, exhausting available memory.

A memory-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against application or host memory capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (leak, decompression bomb, cache manipulation) pending further investigation.

c.n: Direct Database Connection Pool Exhaustion Attack
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary establishes a high number of database connections (directly or via an application path that opens one connection per request) and holds them open, exhausting the configured connection-pool limit and causing subsequent legitimate requests to fail or queue indefinitely.

A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary crafts input (search terms, filter parameters, sort fields) that forces the application to execute expensive database queries lacking appropriate indexes, consuming disproportionate database CPU and IO and degrading performance for all users of the shared database.

c.n: Database Lock Contention Attack (Deliberate Long-Running Transaction Flood)
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary opens transactions that acquire and hold locks on rows, tables, or other database objects for an extended period, causing legitimate transactions that need the same locks to queue, time out, or fail — degrading or halting the affected service.

A database-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against database capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (connection exhaustion, expensive queries, lock contention) pending further investigation.

c.n: Log File Flooding to Exhaust Disk Space
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary sends requests specifically crafted to generate a high volume of log entries (e.g., repeated authentication failures, malformed requests triggering verbose error logging) until the disk partition hosting logs is filled, causing the application or host to fail.

A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary repeatedly triggers an application code path that writes temporary files (e.g., file-processing, session, or cache-to-disk operations) without adequate cleanup, filling the disk partition and degrading or crashing the affected service.

c.n: Storage Quota Exhaustion via Repeated Large Uploads
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary (an authenticated user, abused free-tier account, or automated script) repeatedly uploads large but individually valid files to a service, exhausting a shared storage quota or the backing disk/volume capacity and degrading the service for other users.

c.n: Unclassified / General Disk I/O Saturation Attack
c.d: A disk-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against disk capacity or I/O throughput, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (log flooding, temp-file accumulation, storage-quota abuse) pending further investigation.

c.n: Multi-Tenant Cloud Service Provider Outage Caused by Targeted Attack
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which the organization's cloud-hosted services become unavailable or severely degraded because an adversary launched a targeted attack against shared infrastructure of the multi-tenant cloud provider itself (e.g., a control-plane component, shared networking fabric, or a co-tenant causing provider-wide contention), rather than against the organization's workloads directly.

c.n: Cloud Load Balancer/API Gateway Overload Attack
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an adversary directs a volumetric or application-layer attack specifically at the organization's cloud load balancer, API gateway, or ingress controller, exhausting its request-handling or connection capacity and preventing legitimate traffic from reaching backend services.

c.n: Cloud Identity/Authentication Service Disruption (Widespread Login Failure)
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an adversary's attack against a cloud identity provider or authentication service (e.g., SSO, OAuth token issuance, MFA validation) causes widespread login failure, blocking legitimate users from accessing applications that depend on it even though those applications themselves remain otherwise healthy.

A cloud-service-disruption incident confirmed as an attack against cloud-hosted infrastructure, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (provider-wide attack, gateway/load-balancer attack, identity-service attack) pending further investigation.

c.n: CDN Edge Node Resource Exhaustion Attack
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an adversary directs volumetric or connection-based traffic at CDN edge nodes/points-of-presence themselves, exhausting their local compute, connection, or bandwidth capacity and degrading content delivery even for cacheable content that would not normally reach the origin.

c.n: CDN Origin Server Overload via Cache-Miss Forcing
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an adversary crafts requests with randomized or unique query parameters, headers, or cache-busting values so that the CDN cannot serve them from cache, forcing every request to be forwarded to the origin server and exhausting origin capacity that the CDN was meant to shield.

c.n: CDN Bandwidth Cost Exhaustion Attack (Denial-of-Wallet via CDN Billing)
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary generates sustained, large-volume traffic against CDN-served content (e.g., repeatedly downloading large files or media) specifically to inflate the organization's usage-based CDN bandwidth billing, with financial cost as the primary impact rather than service unavailability.

A CDN-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against CDN-delivered infrastructure, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (edge-node capacity, cache-miss forcing, billing/denial-of-wallet abuse) pending further investigation.

c.n: Pre-Attack Extortion Email Threatening DDoS Unless Paid
c.d: The receipt of an extortion email or message threatening a future distributed denial-of-service attack unless a ransom (typically cryptocurrency) is paid by a stated deadline, sent before any actual attack traffic has been observed against the organization.

c.n: Ransom Demand Sent After Initial Demonstration Attack
c.d: An extortion communication demanding payment to prevent further DDoS attacks, sent after the threat actor has already launched a short demonstration attack against the target to prove capability, materially raising the credibility and urgency of the threat compared to a threat sent with no prior demonstration.

c.n: Anonymous Cryptocurrency Ransom Demand with Named Threat-Actor-Brand Impersonation
c.d: An extortion communication demanding payment to prevent a DDoS attack, in which the sender claims to be (or be affiliated with) a publicly known RDoS threat-actor brand, using that brand's reputation and cryptocurrency payment conventions to increase perceived credibility, regardless of whether the sender has any actual connection to the named group.

c.n: Unclassified / General RDoS Ransom Note Threat
c.d: A received RDoS extortion communication confirmed as a ransom threat, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (pre-attack threat, post-demonstration demand, brand-impersonation demand) pending further investigation.

A brief, intentionally limited denial-of-service attack (minutes rather than hours) launched by a threat actor to demonstrate genuine attack capability against the target's general infrastructure, intended to lend credibility to an accompanying or forthcoming ransom demand rather than to cause sustained business impact.

c.n: Demonstration Attack Targeting a Single Critical Service Before Full Campaign
c.d: A brief denial-of-service attack in which the threat actor deliberately selects and targets one specific business-critical service (e.g., the primary customer-facing application, payment gateway, or a named subsidiary) to demonstrate that they have identified and can disrupt exactly what matters most to the organization, maximizing psychological leverage ahead of a full extortion campaign.

A brief denial-of-service attack confirmed as an RDoS demonstration/proof-of-capability event, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (general-infrastructure burst, critical-service-targeted burst) pending further investigation.

c.n: Recurring Scheduled DDoS Attacks After Ransom Non-Payment
c.d: A pattern of repeated, scheduled denial-of-service attacks launched against the target at intervals (e.g., daily or weekly) following non-payment of an RDoS ransom demand, intended to sustain pressure and force payment through cumulative business disruption rather than a single decisive attack.

c.n: Escalating Attack Volume/Duration Following Missed Deadline
c.d: A pattern of denial-of-service attacks in which each successive attack following a missed ransom deadline is deliberately larger in volume, longer in duration, or more sophisticated in technique than the last, signaling an intentional escalation strategy designed to force payment by demonstrating growing capability and impact.

c.n: Multi-Target Persistent RDoS Campaign Across Victim's Infrastructure
c.d: A pattern of denial-of-service attacks in which a threat actor, following non-payment, broadens the campaign to strike multiple distinct services, subsidiaries, or business units within the same victim organization, demonstrating breadth of reach and multiplying simultaneous business impact to increase pressure to pay.

A sustained RDoS campaign confirmed as ongoing following non-payment, but not yet classified into a specific pattern (steady recurrence, escalating intensity, multi-target spread) pending further investigation.

c.n: Noisy-Neighbor VM Resource Exhaustion Attack (Co-Tenant Abuse)
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which a co-tenant on shared virtualized infrastructure (whether malicious or an unwitting victim of compromise) deliberately or through abuse consumes a disproportionate share of hypervisor-level CPU, memory, or I/O capacity, causing measurable performance degradation or outage for the organization's own virtual machines sharing that physical host.

c.n: VM Sprawl/Uncontrolled Instance Creation Exhausting Hypervisor Capacity
c.d: A resource-depletion incident in which an excessive, uncontrolled number of virtual machine instances is created within the organization's own virtualization/cloud environment (via compromised credentials, runaway automation, or unmanaged self-service provisioning) exhausting hypervisor host capacity or account-level instance quotas, degrading or blocking legitimate workload provisioning and operation.

c.n: Hypervisor Scheduler Overload via Malicious Guest Workload
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which a guest virtual machine under the adversary's control deliberately crafts its workload pattern to exploit weaknesses in the hypervisor's CPU/IO scheduling algorithm, gaining disproportionate scheduling priority and starving other co-located guest workloads of execution time beyond what raw resource consumption alone would explain.

A hypervisor-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against virtualization-layer capacity, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (co-tenant noisy-neighbor abuse, uncontrolled instance sprawl, scheduler exploitation) pending further investigation.

c.n: Serverless Function Invocation Flood Exhausting Concurrency Limits
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary triggers a high volume of concurrent invocations of a serverless function (e.g., AWS Lambda, Azure Functions), consuming the account's or function's configured concurrency limit and causing legitimate invocations to be throttled or rejected.

c.n: Denial-of-Wallet Attack via Excessive Serverless Function Billing
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary triggers a sustained high volume of serverless function invocations specifically to inflate the organization's usage-based billing (per-invocation and compute-duration charges), where the function itself may continue operating normally for legitimate users while the financial cost accumulates.

A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary deliberately structures invocation patterns (e.g., bursty traffic with unique parameters preventing instance reuse, or exploiting scale-to-zero behavior) to force the serverless platform to repeatedly cold-start new function instances rather than reuse warm ones, degrading response latency and consuming disproportionate initialization resources compared to steady-state invocation.

c.n: Unclassified / General Serverless Function Abuse (DoS Context)
c.d: A serverless-function-abuse incident confirmed as having a denial-of-service or resource-depletion character, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (concurrency exhaustion, denial-of-wallet billing abuse, cold-start exploitation) pending further investigation.

A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary exploits a publicly writable or abusable object-storage upload path to deposit a high volume of objects or a large total data volume into a bucket, exhausting the account's storage quota, driving up storage costs, or degrading bucket listing/access performance for legitimate operations.

c.n: Cloud Storage Billing/Cost Exhaustion via Egress Bandwidth Abuse
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary generates sustained, high-volume download/read traffic against objects in cloud storage specifically to inflate the organization's usage-based egress-bandwidth billing, with financial cost as the primary impact.

c.n: Cloud Database Storage Quota Exhaustion Attack
c.d: A resource-depletion attack in which an adversary exploits a data-write path (e.g., an abusable API creating database records, an unauthenticated write endpoint, or excessive legitimate-looking record creation) to grow a managed cloud database's storage consumption to its provisioned or account-level quota limit, causing write failures or forced (and potentially costly/disruptive) auto-scaling of storage capacity.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud Storage Exhaustion Attack
c.d: A cloud-storage-resource-exhaustion incident confirmed as an attack against cloud storage capacity or cost, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (object-storage bucket fill, egress-bandwidth billing abuse, managed database storage-quota exhaustion) pending further investigation.

c.n: Deliberate Deletion/Disabling of Critical Service Configuration
c.d: An intentional denial-of-service incident in which an employee, contractor, or other trusted insider with legitimate administrative access deliberately deletes, disables, or corrupts the configuration of a critical service (e.g., removing a load balancer rule, disabling a service, deleting a DNS record) with the intent to cause disruption.

An intentional denial-of-service incident in which an insider with legitimate access deliberately develops and executes a script, job, or automation specifically engineered to consume excessive CPU, memory, disk, or database resources on internal systems, with the intent to degrade or crash a service.

c.n: Departing Employee Sabotaging Systems Before Exit
c.d: An intentional denial-of-service incident in which an employee, in the period immediately before, during, or shortly after their resignation or termination, deliberately damages, disables, or disrupts systems or services using access retained from their employment, motivated by grievance or retaliation related to their departure.

A denial-of-service incident confirmed as caused by a malicious insider, but not yet classified into a specific pattern (configuration deletion, resource-exhaustion script, departure-linked sabotage) pending further investigation.

c.n: Accidental Firewall/Network ACL Misconfiguration Causing Outage
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an authorized administrator, performing a legitimate change, unintentionally misconfigures a firewall rule or network access control list in a way that blocks legitimate traffic to a service, causing an outage; the incident is a human-error operational event, not an adversary attack.

c.n: Accidental Deployment of Faulty Code/Configuration Change
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an authorized engineer deploys a code change or application configuration update that contains an unintentional defect, causing the affected service to crash, hang, or reject legitimate requests; the incident is a human-error operational event, not an adversary attack.

c.n: Accidental Resource Quota/Auto-Scaling Misconfiguration Causing Self-Inflicted Outage
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an authorized engineer misconfigures a resource quota, rate limit, or auto-scaling policy (e.g., setting a scaling ceiling too low, misconfiguring a threshold, or applying an overly restrictive quota) such that the service cannot scale to meet legitimate demand, causing a self-inflicted outage or severe degradation; the incident is a human-error operational event, not an adversary attack.

A denial-of-service incident confirmed as accidental (no malicious intent) and caused by human configuration error, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (network ACL, deployment defect, capacity/scaling misconfiguration) pending further investigation; a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.

c.n: Internal Script/Automation Runaway Loop Overloading Internal API
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an internally developed script, job, or automation — due to a logic defect (e.g., a missing exit condition, retry loop with no backoff) — enters a runaway state and issues an excessive volume of requests against an internal API, degrading or crashing the API for other internal consumers; the incident is a human-error/operational event, not an adversary attack.

c.n: Employee Bulk Operation Performed Without Rate Limiting Awareness
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an employee, using legitimate tools and access, manually initiates a bulk data operation (e.g., a large export, mass update, or batch report generation) against an internal or shared API without awareness of the request volume or rate impact, degrading the service for other consumers; the incident is a human-error/operational event, not an adversary attack.

c.n: Third-Party Integration Misconfigured by Internal Team Causing API Flood
c.d: A denial-of-service incident in which an internal team, while configuring or integrating a third-party tool or service (e.g., a webhook, sync job, monitoring agent, or SaaS connector), introduces a misconfiguration (e.g., an overly frequent polling interval, a webhook loop, or missing pagination) that causes the third-party system to generate an excessive volume of requests against internal APIs; the incident is a human-error/operational event, not an adversary attack.

c.n: Unclassified / General Internal API Abuse DoS
c.d: A denial-of-service incident confirmed as caused by accidental internal API abuse, but not yet classified into a specific mechanism (runaway automation, manual bulk operation, misconfigured third-party integration) pending further investigation; a human-error/operational incident, not an adversary technique.
