c.d: Theft of employee or customer tax filing data that is subsequently used by the threat actor to submit fraudulent tax refund claims in the victim's name.
Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of tax data resulting from a compromise of the tax preparation software, platform, or vendor system used to process company or employee tax filings.

c.n: W-2/1099 Data Breach via Phishing (Tax Season Targeted)
c.d: A phishing-driven breach in which an attacker impersonates an executive or authority figure to solicit bulk W-2 or 1099 employee tax documents from HR/payroll staff, typically timed to the tax filing season.

A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed tax information breaches where the specific mechanism (downstream refund fraud, platform compromise, or phishing-driven bulk disclosure) has not yet been determined.
Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of private key material for a company-operated hot (internet-connected) cryptocurrency wallet, exposing the means to move funds directly.

c.n: Exchange-Hosted Wallet Breach via Compromised Exchange Infrastructure
c.d: Unauthorized access to company cryptocurrency holdings resulting from a compromise of the exchange or custodial platform's own infrastructure, rather than direct theft of a company-held private key.

c.n: Wallet Drained via Malicious Smart Contract Approval
c.d: Loss of cryptocurrency or tokens from a company wallet after the wallet holder unknowingly granted a malicious smart contract approval (allowance) that was subsequently exercised by an attacker to drain funds.

c.n: Seed Phrase Phishing Leading to Wallet Breach
c.d: Compromise and drain of a cryptocurrency wallet after its seed phrase (mnemonic recovery phrase) was obtained through a phishing or social-engineering pretext, granting the attacker full wallet control.

A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed cryptocurrency wallet breaches where the specific mechanism (private key theft, exchange compromise, malicious contract approval, or seed phrase phishing) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Publicly Accessible Cloud Bucket Containing Internal Operational Documents
c.d: An incident in which internal operational documents (internal reports, process documentation, non-customer/non-employee operational data) are exposed due to a cloud storage bucket or container being configured to allow public/anonymous access.

c.n: Cloud Storage Exposure via Shared/Public Link Left Active
c.d: An incident in which a shared or public link to cloud-stored operational data, generated for legitimate temporary sharing, remains active and accessible long after its intended purpose, resulting in unauthorized access.

An incident in which a snapshot, image, or backup copy of a system or dataset stored in cloud infrastructure is configured to allow public or unauthorized access, exposing a point-in-time copy of operational data.

An intake classification for incidents involving unauthorized or public access to cloud-stored operational data where the specific mechanism (bucket misconfiguration, stale shared link, or exposed snapshot/backup) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Full Database Dump Exfiltrated via SQL Injection
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploits a SQL injection vulnerability in an application to extract a full or substantial dump of an underlying database's contents.

c.n: Database Backup File Exposed on Public Server
c.d: An incident in which a database backup file (a .sql, .bak, .dump, or similar export) is discovered accessible on a public-facing web server, misconfigured file share, or otherwise improperly secured location.

c.n: Database Dump Sold/Leaked via Insider Access
c.d: An incident in which an insider (employee, contractor, or other authorized user) with legitimate database access deliberately extracts and leaks or sells a database dump.

An intake classification for incidents involving theft or exposure of a database dump where the mechanism (SQL injection, exposed backup file, or insider extraction) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.
An incident in which internal team collaboration platform (Slack, Microsoft Teams, or similar) message history is exposed or exfiltrated, revealing internal discussions, decisions, or shared files.
An incident in which an internal email thread or chain is disclosed to an unauthorized external party, whether through mailbox compromise, misdirected forwarding, or deliberate leak.

An incident in which a recording or transcript of an internal meeting is disclosed to an unauthorized external party, whether through storage misconfiguration, compromised meeting-platform access, or deliberate leak.

An intake classification for incidents involving disclosure of internal communications where the medium or mechanism (collaboration platform, email, or meeting recording) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Unencrypted Backup Tape/Media Lost or Stolen
c.d: An incident in which physical backup media (tape, external hard drive, removable disk) containing organizational data is lost in transit, misplaced, or stolen, and was not adequately encrypted.

c.n: Backup Storage Server Breached via Weak Access Controls
c.d: An incident in which an adversary gains unauthorized access to a backup storage server or repository due to weak, default, or improperly managed access controls, and exfiltrates or exposes backed-up data.
An incident in which a third-party backup-as-a-service or managed backup provider experiences a breach that exposes organizational data it holds on the organization's behalf.

An intake classification for incidents involving exposure or theft of backup data where the mechanism (physical media loss, backup server compromise, or third-party provider breach) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Vendor Holding Customer Data Suffers Own Breach
c.d: An incident in which a third-party vendor holding organizational customer data on the organization's behalf experiences a breach originating entirely within the vendor's own environment, exposing that customer data.

c.n: Vendor Employee Insider Breach Affecting Client Data
c.d: An incident in which an employee or contractor of a third-party vendor deliberately misuses their access to expose, leak, or sell organizational data entrusted to the vendor.

c.n: Vendor Breach Discovered via Downstream Fraud/Credential Reuse
c.d: An incident in which a vendor breach is inferred or confirmed through observed downstream harm (fraudulent transactions, credential stuffing success, targeted phishing using vendor-sourced details) before or without formal notification from the vendor itself.

An intake classification for incidents involving a vendor-originated data breach where the mechanism or discovery path (vendor's own breach, vendor insider misuse, or downstream fraud correlation) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Shared API Integration Breach Exposing Both Organizations' Data
c.d: An incident in which a shared API integration between the organization and a partner is exploited or misconfigured in a way that exposes data flowing through or accessible via that integration, affecting both parties.

c.n: Partner's Compromised OAuth/Service Account Exposing Shared Data
c.d: An incident in which a partner organization's OAuth token, API key, or service account used to access a shared integration is compromised, and the resulting unauthorized access exposes shared data.

An intake classification for incidents involving a breach of shared data through a partner integration where the mechanism (API design flaw or compromised credential) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Data Breach via Compromised Software Dependency/Package
c.d: An incident in which a software dependency or package (e.g., a public package registry component) used by the organization's software is compromised, maliciously modified, or typosquatted, and results in exposure of organizational or customer data.

c.n: Data Breach via Compromised Software Update Mechanism
c.d: An incident in which the mechanism used to build, sign, or distribute software updates (CI/CD pipeline, build server, or update distribution channel) is compromised, resulting in malicious code being delivered to production systems and exposing data.

c.n: Data Breach via Backdoored Third-Party Library
c.d: An incident in which a third-party software library or component in active use contains a deliberately embedded backdoor, allowing an adversary sustained, ongoing unauthorized access or data exfiltration capability over time.

c.n: Unclassified / General Software Supply Chain Data Breach
c.d: An intake classification for incidents involving data exposure via a software supply chain compromise where the mechanism (compromised dependency, compromised build/update pipeline, or backdoored library) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Shipping/Tracking Data Breach Exposing Customer Delivery Information
c.d: An incident in which a shipping, tracking, or delivery management system (whether the organization's own or a logistics partner's) is compromised or misconfigured, exposing customer delivery information such as addresses, delivery windows, and order contents.

An incident in which an inventory management system (stock levels, warehouse records, supplier order data) is breached or exposed, revealing internal operational and supply chain data rather than customer-identifying information.

c.n: Unclassified / General Logistics and Inventory Data Breach
c.d: An intake classification for incidents involving exposure of logistics, shipping, tracking, or inventory data where the specific system or data type has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.

c.n: Insider Steals Data for Financial Gain (Sale to Competitor/Dark Web)
c.d: An insider with legitimate access deliberately exfiltrates company data with the intent to sell it to a competitor, broker, or on the dark web for personal financial gain.

c.n: Insider Steals Data for Revenge/Retaliation Following Grievance
c.d: An insider with legitimate access deliberately exfiltrates or discloses company data as an act of retaliation following a perceived grievance, such as termination, demotion, or a disciplinary action.

c.n: Insider Recruited/Coerced by External Threat Actor
c.d: An insider with legitimate access is recruited (via payment or ideological appeal) or coerced (via blackmail or threat) by an external threat actor to exfiltrate company data on that actor's behalf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Insider Data Breach
c.d: A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed malicious insider data breaches where the specific motive (financial gain, revenge/retaliation, or external recruitment/coercion) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Sensitive Data Accidentally Shared with Wrong Recipient/Distribution List
c.d: Sensitive company or customer data is unintentionally sent to an unintended recipient or distribution list due to human error, with no malicious intent by the sender.

c.n: Sensitive Data Accidentally Made Publicly Visible via Misapplied Sharing Setting
c.d: Sensitive company or customer data becomes accessible to unintended parties (public internet, all-company, or an overly broad group) due to a misapplied sharing, visibility, or permission setting on a file, repository, or cloud resource.

c.n: Sensitive Data Accidentally Uploaded to Unauthorized/Personal Platform
c.d: An employee unintentionally exposes sensitive company data by uploading, syncing, or storing it on a personal or unauthorized third-party platform (personal cloud storage, personal email, unsanctioned SaaS tool) outside company control.

A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed accidental (non-malicious) insider data breaches where the specific mechanism (misdirected recipient, misconfigured sharing, or unauthorized platform upload) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Unclassified / General Privileged Access Misuse (Insider-Driven Breach Context)
c.d: A privileged user (administrator, executive assistant, database administrator, etc.) accesses or discloses data beyond their legitimate business need, resulting in a data breach, where the specific motive or mechanism does not warrant a dedicated sibling leaf.

c.n: Multi-Year Persistent Access with Periodic Data Collection
c.d: An advanced persistent threat maintains covert access to company systems over a period of years, periodically returning to collect data in discrete episodes rather than continuously exfiltrating.

c.n: Automated Long-Term Data Harvesting Script Left Running Undetected
c.d: An advanced persistent threat deploys an automated script, tool, or malware that continuously collects and stages company data over an extended period without requiring ongoing manual operator interaction, remaining undetected until discovery.
A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed long-term APT data collection where the specific mechanism (periodic manual collection or automated harvesting) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Nation-State-Sponsored Corporate Espionage Targeting Trade Secrets
c.d: A sophisticated, sustained intrusion attributed (or reasonably suspected to be attributable) to a nation-state-sponsored threat actor, specifically targeting the company's trade secrets, proprietary research, or strategic intellectual property.

A sophisticated, sustained intrusion attributed (or reasonably suspected to be attributable) to a business competitor or an actor acting on a competitor's behalf, targeting proprietary business information for commercial advantage.
A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed targeted corporate espionage breaches where the sponsoring actor (nation-state or business competitor) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Combined Phishing and Exploit-Based Multi-Vector Breach
c.d: A sophisticated breach in which the threat actor combines phishing (for initial access or credential theft) with vulnerability exploitation (for privilege escalation, lateral movement, or an alternate access path) across the kill chain, rather than relying on a single vector.

c.n: Combined Insider and External Attacker Multi-Vector Breach
c.d: A sophisticated breach in which an external threat actor's intrusion is combined with the involvement of a company insider (witting or coerced), such that both an internal and external actor jointly enable the data breach.
A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed multi-vector APT-style data breaches where the composition of vectors (technical-only versus insider-facilitated) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Data Breach Discovered Only via Third-Party Notification
c.d: A data breach that went undetected by internal security monitoring for its entire duration and was only discovered because a third party (customer, partner, law enforcement, researcher, or the threat actor itself) notified the company.

c.n: Data Breach Discovered During Unrelated Security Audit/Assessment
c.d: A data breach that went undetected by real-time security monitoring and was instead uncovered as a byproduct of an unrelated internal security audit, penetration test, or compliance assessment.

c.n: Data Breach Discovered via Dark Web Monitoring After the Fact
c.d: A data breach that went undetected by internal security monitoring and was instead discovered when the company's dark web monitoring program identified company data being sold, dumped, or referenced on dark web forums or marketplaces.

A catch-all classification for suspected or confirmed undetected data breaches where the discovery channel (third-party notification, internal audit, or dark web monitoring) has not yet been determined or does not cleanly fit a sibling category.

c.n: Unclassified / General Data-for-Sale Listing (Dark Web Dump Context)
c.d: The identification of company or customer data being listed for sale (fixed-price or negotiated) on a dark web forum, marketplace, or broker channel, following a prior (possibly separately classified) data breach.

c.n: Unclassified / General Free Data Dump (Dark Web Dump Context)
c.d: The identification of company or customer data being publicly released at no cost on a dark web forum, paste site, or public dump repository, following a prior (possibly separately classified) data breach.

c.n: Unclassified / General Auctioned Data Listing (Dark Web Dump Context)
c.d: The identification of company or customer data being offered via a competitive auction (bidding process, reserve price, deadline) on a dark web forum or marketplace, following a prior (possibly separately classified) data breach.

c.n: Unclassified / General Credentials Reuse Package Listing (Dark Web Dump Context)
c.d: The identification of company employee or customer credential pairs bundled into a combo list or credential-reuse package and distributed (sold or freely shared) on the dark web, following a prior (possibly separately classified) credential theft.

c.n: Insider Planted by External Organization Prior to Hire
c.d: A form of insider espionage in which an individual applies for and obtains legitimate employment as a deliberate placement by a competitor, criminal group, or state actor, with the intent of using their resulting access to collect or exfiltrate information over time.

c.n: Existing Employee Recruited/Turned by External Handler
c.d: A form of insider espionage in which an existing employee, with no prior placement intent, is recruited, turned, or otherwise brought under the direction of an external handler during the course of their employment.

c.n: Insider Espionage Using Dead-Drop/Covert Communication with Handler
c.d: An insider espionage case distinguished by the specific communication method used to transfer information to a handler: a dead-drop, steganographic channel, or other covert communication mechanism designed to avoid detection, rather than direct or obvious contact.

A general or not-yet-classified case of insider espionage — an internal actor suspected of providing information to an external party — pending sufficient investigation to determine whether it was a pre-employment plant, an in-tenure recruitment, or uses covert tradecraft.

c.n: Competitor-Directed Corporate Espionage via Hired Third-Party Operative
c.d: A form of corporate espionage in which a competitor engages an external operative — a contractor, private investigator, or intermediary — to obtain proprietary or confidential information, rather than acting through its own personnel.

c.n: Competitor Espionage via Poached Employee Bringing Stolen IP
c.d: A form of corporate espionage in which an employee, in the course of leaving to join a competitor, copies or retains confidential or proprietary information for the new employer's benefit.
A general or not-yet-classified case of competitor-directed espionage pending determination of whether it was carried out via a hired third-party operative or a poached employee.

c.n: Human Intelligence (HUMINT) Collection via Social Engineering at Industry Events
c.d: Human-intelligence-style collection in which an adversary uses a false pretext — posing as a peer, journalist, recruiter, or attendee — at an industry event to elicit confidential or proprietary information from employees.

c.n: Signals Intelligence (SIGINT)-Style Interception of Corporate Communications
c.d: Signals-intelligence-style collection in which an adversary intercepts corporate voice, data, or network communications — through network-level interception, rogue wireless infrastructure, or radio/cellular interception — to obtain confidential information in transit.

c.n: Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) Aggregation for Targeted Espionage
c.d: Collection in which an adversary compiles and cross-references publicly available information — organizational, personal, technical, or financial — to construct a profile supporting a subsequent espionage operation.
A general or not-yet-classified case of covert intelligence collection pending determination of whether it was HUMINT, SIGINT-style interception, or OSINT aggregation.

Espionage targeting a corporate executive during business travel, exploiting the reduced physical and network security typical of hotels, transit, and foreign venues to tamper with devices or intercept communications.

c.n: Executive Personal Device Compromise for Corporate Intelligence Access
c.d: Espionage in which an adversary compromises an executive's personal phone, tablet, or home computer — typically less protected than corporate assets — as a pivot point to access corporate email, credentials, or strategic information.

c.n: Executive Communications Surveillance for Strategic Intelligence
c.d: Espionage focused on intercepting or collecting an executive's calls, email, calendar, or messaging content to obtain strategically valuable, time-sensitive information, distinct from device compromise for general access.

A general or not-yet-classified case of espionage targeting an executive pending determination of whether it involved travel-based targeting, personal-device compromise, or communications surveillance.

c.n: Nation-State APT Group Attributed Espionage Campaign
c.d: A sustained, technically sophisticated intrusion campaign attributed — through infrastructure, tooling, or intelligence-community reporting — to a specific state-sponsored APT group, aimed at long-term covert access and intelligence collection.

c.n: State-Sponsored Espionage via Contracted Cyber Mercenary Group
c.d: A cyber espionage campaign in which a state sponsor uses a commercial surveillance/exploitation vendor or contracted hacking group to conduct intrusion and collection activity on its behalf, providing the sponsor a layer of deniability.
A general or not-yet-attributed case of suspected nation-state sponsored cyber espionage, pending determination of whether it involves a known APT group or a contracted cyber-mercenary group.

c.n: Defense Contractor Classified Program Data Theft
c.d: Cyber or human espionage targeting a defense contractor's classified, controlled unclassified information (CUI), or export-controlled program data, sponsored by or benefiting a foreign state.
Cyber or human espionage targeting the technical design, specifications, or performance data of a military technology or weapons system, sponsored by or benefiting a foreign state.

c.n: Unclassified / General Military and Defense Espionage
c.d: A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected nation-state espionage against a defense contractor or defense-related asset, pending determination of scope.

c.n: State-Sponsored Theft of Manufacturing/Industrial Process Secrets
c.d: State-sponsored espionage targeting proprietary manufacturing processes, industrial formulas, or production methods, typically to accelerate a foreign state's domestic industrial capability.

c.n: Critical Infrastructure Operator Targeted for Industrial Espionage
c.d: State-sponsored espionage targeting an operator of critical infrastructure (energy, water, transportation, healthcare, financial systems, etc.) to collect intelligence on operations or to pre-position for potential future disruption.
A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected state-sponsored industrial espionage pending determination of whether the target is a manufacturing process or critical infrastructure operations.

Espionage targeting diplomatic communications infrastructure — embassy networks, foreign ministry correspondence, or diplomatic cable/messaging systems — to obtain foreign-policy or diplomatic intelligence.
Espionage aimed at obtaining an organization's or government's confidential trade negotiation strategy, positions, or fallback terms, typically to benefit a foreign state's negotiating position.

A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected state-sponsored diplomatic espionage pending determination of whether it targets diplomatic communications infrastructure or trade negotiation intelligence.

c.n: Unclassified / General Patent and R&D Theft (Espionage Context)
c.d: Theft of unfiled patent material, research findings, or R&D output carried out as part of a broader espionage operation, as distinct from opportunistic data-breach-driven theft of the same material.

c.n: Unclassified / General Source Code Theft (Espionage Context)
c.d: Theft of proprietary source code carried out as part of a broader espionage operation, as distinct from opportunistic data-breach-driven source code theft.
Theft of proprietary manufacturing process, formula, or production-method information carried out as part of a broader espionage operation by a competitor, contracted operative, or state sponsor.

c.n: Theft of Proprietary Machine Learning Model Weights/Architecture
c.d: Espionage-motivated exfiltration of a trained machine learning model's weights, architecture definition, or checkpoint artifacts, enabling a competitor or foreign actor to replicate or fine-tune the model without the underlying investment.

c.n: Theft of Training Dataset for Competitive AI Development
c.d: Espionage-motivated exfiltration of a curated, proprietary training dataset — including labeled data, feedback/reinforcement data, or a proprietary data pipeline's output — to accelerate a competitor's or foreign actor's own model development.

c.n: Model Extraction via API Query-Based Reverse Engineering
c.d: Espionage-motivated collection in which an adversary submits a large, systematically designed volume of queries to a model's public or partner-facing API in order to reverse-engineer its decision boundaries, extract approximate parameters, or replicate its functional behavior in a competing model.

c.n: Unclassified / General AI and Algorithm Theft
c.d: A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected theft of proprietary AI/ML assets, pending determination of whether it involves model weights, training data, or API-based model extraction.

c.n: Unclassified / General APT Cyber Espionage Operation
c.d: A multi-stage, persistent intrusion campaign exhibiting advanced-persistent-threat tradecraft — careful operational security, long dwell time, and deliberate, targeted collection — used to classify cyber espionage activity within this Tier-3 category independent of whether the sponsor has been formally attributed to a specific state (see ITID-5221x for attributed nation-state cases).

c.n: Unclassified / General Covert Data Exfiltration (Cyber Espionage Context)
c.d: The deliberate, low-noise exfiltration of collected data through covert channels — encrypted C2 tunnels, alternative protocols, or staged small-volume transfers — designed to evade data-loss-prevention and network-monitoring controls.

Espionage in which an adversary compromises a supplier, software vendor, or service provider trusted by the target organization, using that trust relationship as the initial access vector into the target's environment.

c.n: Unclassified / General Steganographic Data Theft (Cyber Espionage Context)
c.d: Exfiltration in which stolen data is embedded within seemingly innocuous carrier files (images, documents, media) using steganographic or other data-obfuscation techniques, specifically to evade content-inspection and DLP controls.

c.n: Unclassified / General Keylogger Development for Espionage
c.d: The development, customization, or acquisition of keylogging software or hardware intended for use in an espionage operation, classified at the development/tooling stage rather than the deployment/collection stage.

c.n: Pretext Phone Call for Organizational Structure Reconnaissance
c.d: Social-engineering reconnaissance in which an adversary places a phone call using a false pretext — vendor, recruiter, journalist, or internal-sounding caller — to elicit organizational structure, reporting lines, or process detail from an employee.

c.n: Fake Industry Survey/Interview for Intelligence Gathering
c.d: Social-engineering reconnaissance in which an adversary poses as a legitimate researcher, journalist, or industry analyst conducting a survey or interview, using the pretext to elicit strategic, technical, or organizational information from employees.

c.n: LinkedIn/Social Network Connection Farming for Target Mapping
c.d: Social-engineering reconnaissance in which an adversary creates or uses professional networking (e.g., LinkedIn-style) profiles to systematically connect with an organization's employees, building a map of personnel, roles, and relationships to support later targeting.
A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected social engineering reconnaissance pending determination of the specific method used (phone pretext, survey/interview, or connection farming).

c.n: Public Job Posting/Org Chart Mining for Reconnaissance
c.d: OSINT reconnaissance in which an adversary systematically collects and analyzes public job postings, employee titles, and organizational structure signals to infer reporting lines, technology stack, and likely high-value targets.

c.n: Social Media Profile Aggregation for Target Reconnaissance
c.d: OSINT reconnaissance in which an adversary systematically collects and cross-references employees' social media content — posts, photos, connections, location check-ins — to build a targeting profile.

c.n: Public Financial Filing/Patent Database Mining for Intelligence
c.d: OSINT reconnaissance in which an adversary systematically analyzes public financial filings, regulatory disclosures, and patent databases to infer strategic direction, R&D priorities, or financial position ahead of a targeted operation.

A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected OSINT-based reconnaissance pending determination of the specific source exploited (job postings/org chart, social media, or financial/patent filings).

Physical surveillance in which an adversary maintains a covert, sustained watch on a corporate facility or an executive's residence to observe patterns of activity, access routines, or presence, in support of a subsequent operation.

c.n: Covert Photography/Video Surveillance of Target Location
c.d: Physical surveillance distinguished by the deliberate covert capture of photographic or video evidence of a facility, individual, or location, as distinct from mere observational presence.

c.n: Vehicle/License Plate Tracking for Movement Pattern Analysis
c.d: Physical surveillance in which an adversary tracks a target's vehicle — through direct following, license-plate reader data, or a covertly installed tracking device — to build a profile of routine routes, schedules, and locations.
A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected physical surveillance pending determination of the specific method (stakeout, covert photography, or vehicle tracking).

Coercion of an employee into acting as an insider source through the threat of disclosing compromising personal information (kompromat) — financial, relational, or reputational — obtained or fabricated by the coercing party.

c.n: Coercion Through Threats to Family/Personal Safety
c.d: Coercion of an employee into providing insider access or information through explicit or implied threats of physical harm to the employee or their family members.

c.n: Coercion Leveraging Employee's Own Prior Illegal Act
c.d: Coercion of an employee into providing insider access or information through threats to expose an illegal act or serious misconduct the employee previously committed, whether or not related to their employment.

A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected employee coercion pending determination of the specific leverage used (compromising personal information, physical-safety threats, or a prior illegal act).

c.n: Direct Cash Payment for Data Access
c.d: Insider recruitment in which an employee is offered and accepts a direct cash payment from an external party in exchange for providing information or access, without the more elaborate structuring of a job offer or contract arrangement.

c.n: Bribery via Lucrative Job Offer/Consulting Contract
c.d: Insider recruitment in which an employee is offered a highly favorable future job or consulting arrangement with a competitor or sponsoring organization, structured to appear as a legitimate career opportunity, in exchange for information or access.

c.n: Bribery via Cryptocurrency Payment for Anonymity
c.d: Insider recruitment involving bribery payment made in cryptocurrency, distinguished from other bribery leaves by the deliberate use of a payment method chosen to evade financial-crime monitoring and complicate attribution.
A general or not-yet-classified case of suspected insider bribery pending determination of the specific payment method used.
Unauthorized disclosure of confidential information by an employee acting alone out of grievance following a denied promotion or raise, with no evidence of an external handler or payment.
Unauthorized disclosure of confidential information by an employee acting alone out of grievance following notice of layoff or termination, with no evidence of an external handler or payment.

c.n: Leak Following Perceived Ethical Violation by Employer
c.d: Unauthorized disclosure of confidential information by an employee who believes the disclosure exposes unethical, unsafe, or unlawful conduct by the organization, acting alone and without external payment or direction.
A general or not-yet-classified case of a suspected disgruntled-insider leak pending determination of the specific motivating grievance.

A long-term insider agent maintained in a dormant, low-activity state by a handler for an extended period — often years — using only their ordinary, valid account access to preserve cover, until a decision is made to activate them for a specific collection task.

c.n: Insider Agent Receiving Ongoing Handler Tasking Over Extended Period
c.d: A long-term insider agent who maintains an active, recurring relationship with an external handler over an extended period, receiving periodic tasking and providing information on an ongoing basis using their valid, ordinary access and, frequently, a covert communication channel.
A general or not-yet-classified case of a suspected long-term insider agent relationship, pending determination of whether it involves a dormant sleeper arrangement or ongoing recurring tasking.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud Data Harvesting (Espionage Context)
c.d: Espionage in which an adversary — an external intruder or a directed insider — systematically collects data from cloud storage or file-sharing platforms (object storage, cloud drives, shared workspaces) rather than from on-premises systems.

c.n: Unclassified / General SaaS Exploitation for Espionage
c.d: Espionage in which an adversary exploits the specific features of a SaaS application (e.g., collaboration suites, CRM, HR platforms) — search, export, sharing, or integration functionality — to collect intelligence at a scale or scope beyond simple file access.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud API Abuse (Espionage Context)
c.d: Espionage in which an adversary uses a cloud or SaaS platform's programmatic API — often via a stolen API key, OAuth token, or service-account credential — to automate large-scale or persistent data collection outside the normal user interface.

Espionage in which an adversary reaches the target organization's cloud or SaaS environment through a trusted cross-tenant relationship — a shared parent/partner tenant, a multi-tenant platform misconfiguration, or a compromised partner organization's access — rather than direct intrusion.

c.n: Credential and Identity Theft for Espionage
Unclassified / General Credential Harvesting for Espionage
c.d: Theft or harvesting of employee credentials — via phishing, brute force, or credential-stuffing — carried out in service of a broader espionage operation, as distinct from opportunistic, non-espionage-motivated credential theft.

c.n: Unclassified / General Session Hijacking for Intelligence Access
c.d: Theft and reuse of an active session token, cookie, or authentication artifact — bypassing the need for a username/password or even MFA — carried out in service of a broader espionage operation.

c.n: Unclassified / General MFA Bypass for Espionage
c.d: Circumvention of an account's multi-factor authentication protection — through prompt-bombing/MFA fatigue, SIM-swapping, or exploitation of a weak MFA fallback method — carried out in service of a broader espionage operation.

Impersonation of a legitimate employee, executive, or trusted third party — via synthetic media (deepfake video/audio), fabricated identification, or fraudulent credential presentation — carried out to gain access or extract information as part of a broader espionage operation.

c.n: Unclassified / General Hardware Implant (Physical Espionage Context)
c.d: Espionage carried out through a covertly installed hardware device — a hardware keylogger, network implant, or malicious peripheral — added to a system or network to intercept data, independent of any software-based compromise.

c.n: Unclassified / General Data Theft via Removable Media (Physical Espionage Context)
c.d: Espionage in which data is copied onto a removable storage device (USB drive, external hard drive, memory card) for physical removal from the premises, bypassing network-based DLP and egress monitoring entirely.

c.n: Unclassified / General Rogue Network Device (Physical Espionage Context)
c.d: Espionage carried out through a rogue network device — an unauthorized switch, access point, network tap, or single-board computer — physically connected to the corporate network to intercept traffic or provide a persistent covert access point.

c.n: Covert Physical Search of Unattended Workstation/Desk
c.d: Physical intrusion in which an adversary with unauthorized or pretextual access to a facility covertly searches an employee's unattended desk, workstation, or nearby storage for sensitive documents, credentials, or devices, without removing anything or causing obvious disturbance.

c.n: Covert Photography of Sensitive Physical Documents/Whiteboards
c.d: Physical intrusion in which an adversary with unauthorized or pretextual facility access covertly photographs sensitive documents, whiteboards, or displayed screens, leaving no physical trace of the visit.

c.n: After-Hours Office Access for Document/Device Theft
c.d: Physical intrusion into a corporate office outside normal business hours, when fewer witnesses are present, with the specific purpose of stealing physical documents, storage media, or devices.
A general or not-yet-classified case of a suspected corporate office breach pending determination of the specific activity (covert search, covert photography, or after-hours theft).

c.n: Unclassified / General Executive Impersonation Fraud (BEC Context)
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cases where an adversary poses as a CEO, CFO, or other senior executive (via a compromised, spoofed, or lookalike email account) to pressure an employee into making an urgent, unauthorized wire transfer or financial action, and the case has not been further subtyped.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor Invoice Fraud (BEC Context)
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cases where an adversary impersonates or compromises a known vendor/supplier's email to submit a fraudulent invoice or change banking details on a legitimate one, diverting payment to an attacker-controlled account, and the case has not been further subtyped.

c.n: Unclassified / General Payroll Diversion Fraud (BEC Context)
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cases where an adversary, impersonating an employee (often via a compromised or spoofed personal/corporate email), submits a fraudulent direct-deposit change request to HR/payroll, diverting the employee's next paycheck, and the case has not been further subtyped.

c.n: Unclassified / General Gift Card Scam (BEC Context)
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cases where an adversary, impersonating an executive or trusted colleague via spoofed or compromised email, convinces an employee to purchase retail gift cards and send the redemption codes, and the case has not been further subtyped.

c.n: Wire Transfer Fraud via Compromised Vendor Banking Details Change Email
c.d: Fraudulent redirection of an outgoing wire payment to a legitimate vendor, achieved by an adversary impersonating the vendor (typically via a spoofed or compromised email thread) to request an update to bank routing/account details in accounts payable systems immediately before a scheduled payment.

c.n: Wire Transfer Fraud via Real Estate/Escrow Transaction Interception
c.d: Fraudulent interception or redirection of a high-value, time-sensitive real estate or escrow wire transfer, typically achieved by compromising the email of a title company, real estate agent, escrow officer, or one of the transacting parties and sending falsified wire instructions to the buyer or another party at the closing.
An unclassified or general instance of fraudulent wire transfer redirection or interception that does not fit an existing, more specific Wire Transfer Fraud leaf.

Unauthorized purchase made using stolen credit/debit card information (card number, expiry, CVV) in an online, phone, or mail-order transaction where the physical card is never presented, typically sourced from a prior data breach, skimming operation, or phishing campaign.

Unauthorized in-person transaction made using a counterfeit or cloned physical payment card, created by copying magnetic-stripe or (less commonly) chip data obtained through skimming devices, POS malware at a third-party merchant, or other physical/point-of-sale compromise, and presented at a card terminal or ATM.

c.n: Account Takeover Leading to Unauthorized Card Charges
c.d: Unauthorized card charges made possible by an adversary gaining control of a cardholder's online banking, card-issuer, or digital-wallet account (via credential theft, brute force, or MFA-fatigue), then adding a payment method, changing account controls, or directly authorizing fraudulent transactions from within the compromised account.
An unclassified or general instance of fraudulent card activity that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Credit Card Fraud leaf.

Chemical or mechanical alteration ('washing') of a legitimate check's payee name and/or dollar amount after it has been written and often after it has been intercepted from mail or a physical drop point, enabling the altered check to be deposited by a party other than the intended payee or for a larger amount.

Deposit or negotiation of a check that was entirely fabricated (fake account/routing numbers, forged signature, counterfeit check stock) rather than altered from a legitimately issued instrument, typically drawn against the company's real account and routing numbers obtained from a previously handled genuine check.

c.n: Remote Deposit Capture (RDC) Duplicate Deposit Fraud
c.d: Fraudulent duplicate negotiation of a single genuine check achieved by depositing it via remote deposit capture (photographing/scanning the check through a banking app) and then also depositing or cashing the physical check a second time — at a different bank, branch, or via a second RDC submission — before the first deposit clears and the physical item is flagged as already negotiated.
An unclassified or general instance of check fraud affecting the company that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Check Fraud leaf.

Unauthorized execution of cryptocurrency-mining JavaScript within a user's web browser, triggered by visiting a compromised legitimate site or a malicious page (a 'drive-by' delivery), consuming device compute resources for the duration of the browser session without installing persistent malware.

c.n: Cryptojacking Malware Deployed on Compromised Cloud Compute Instances
c.d: Deployment of persistent cryptocurrency-mining software onto company-owned cloud compute instances (VMs, containers, serverless functions) by an adversary who obtained access via stolen cloud API keys/credentials, exposed management consoles, or misconfigured resources, generating unauthorized compute cost and potentially degrading legitimate workloads.

c.n: Cryptojacking Worm Propagating Across Internal Network
c.d: Cryptomining malware engineered to self-propagate across internal network hosts by exploiting remotely accessible service vulnerabilities or weak authentication (e.g., exposed RDP/SMB, unpatched remote services), infecting successive machines automatically without further attacker interaction and deploying a mining payload on each.
An unclassified or general instance of unauthorized cryptocurrency-mining activity on company resources that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Cryptojacking leaf.

c.n: Online Banking Account Takeover via Phished Credentials
c.d: Unauthorized access to and control of an online banking account, obtained by an adversary through phishing (credential-harvesting) of the account holder's login credentials, followed by unauthorized transfers, bill payments, or account-control changes made directly through the compromised online banking session.

Unauthorized access to and control of a brokerage or investment account, obtained through credential theft, brute force, or MFA-fatigue attacks, enabling the adversary to liquidate holdings, execute unauthorized trades (including pump-and-dump-style manipulation using the victim's capital), or redirect withdrawal proceeds to an attacker-controlled account.
An unclassified or general instance of financial account takeover that has not yet been attributed to a specific account type or mechanism covered by another Financial Account Takeover leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fake Vendor Fraud (Procurement Context)
c.d: Establishment of a fake or fictitious vendor record within the company's procurement or accounts-payable system — often by a colluding or malicious insider, or through inadequate vendor-vetting — used to generate and approve payments for goods or services that were never actually provided.

Overbilling by an otherwise legitimate, real vendor who submits invoices reflecting inflated quantities of goods delivered, hours worked, or units of service performed relative to what was actually provided, resulting in the company paying for work or materials it did not receive.

Submission of the same invoice — or an invoice with only superficial changes such as a slightly altered invoice number or date — more than once for payment, resulting in the company paying twice for a single delivered good or service.

c.n: Shell Vendor Created for Fictitious Billing
c.d: Establishment of a shell vendor entity — a business with no real operations, employees, or delivered goods/services — within the vendor master file for the sole purpose of submitting and collecting payment on fictitious invoices, typically perpetrated or enabled by an employee with vendor-management or approval authority.
An unclassified or general instance of vendor overbilling or invoice-padding fraud that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Overbilling and Padding leaf.

Submission of an employee expense report containing fabricated expenses (never actually incurred) or inflated amounts (exceeding the actual cost paid), supported by altered, fabricated, or mismatched receipts, to obtain reimbursement in excess of legitimate business costs.

Submission of a claim for reimbursement of the same expense (same receipt, transaction, or cost) more than once, whether via duplicate submission within the same expense system, across multiple systems (e.g., corporate card auto-reconciliation plus a manual claim), or by resubmitting a previously reimbursed item with minor cosmetic changes.

c.n: Personal Purchase Disguised as Business Expense
c.d: Submission of an expense claim for a purchase that was, in fact, personal in nature (with no legitimate business purpose), misrepresented through a false description, category, or context on the expense report to make it appear business-related and therefore reimbursable.
An unclassified or general instance of employee expense reimbursement fraud that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Employee Reimbursement Fraud leaf.

c.n: P-Card Used for Unauthorized Personal Purchases
c.d: Use of a company-issued procurement or purchasing card by an employee to buy goods or services for personal benefit, with no legitimate business justification, in violation of the card's authorized-use policy.

c.n: P-Card Transaction Split to Avoid Approval Threshold
c.d: Intentional division of what should be a single purchase into two or more separate P-card transactions, each kept below the dollar threshold that would otherwise require additional approval or a competitive-bid process, in order to circumvent that control.
An unclassified or general instance of procurement card (P-card) misuse that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Procurement Card Misuse leaf.

Intentional submission of a corporate tax return to a tax authority that misstates income, expenses, or other reportable figures — through underreporting revenue, fabricating expenses, or misrepresenting entity structure — with the purpose of illegally reducing the company's tax liability.

Claiming of a tax deduction, credit, or incentive on a corporate tax filing that the company does not legitimately qualify for, or overstating the amount of a legitimate deduction/credit, in order to unlawfully reduce tax liability.

Establishment or use of offshore accounts, shell entities, or corporate structures with the primary purpose of concealing income, assets, or beneficial ownership from tax authorities, thereby evading legitimately owed tax obligations.
An unclassified or general instance of fraudulent tax filing activity that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Fraudulent Tax Filings leaf.

c.n: Employer Withholding Payroll Taxes Without Remitting to Government
c.d: Deduction of required payroll taxes (income tax withholding, Social Security/Medicare or equivalent) from employee wages, followed by the company's failure to actually remit the withheld funds to the appropriate tax authority, instead retaining or diverting the funds for other purposes.

c.n: Employee Misclassification to Avoid Payroll Tax Obligations
c.d: Intentional misclassification of workers who function as employees (subject to direction and control consistent with employment) as independent contractors or another exempt category, in order to avoid payroll tax withholding, unemployment insurance contributions, and related employer tax obligations.
An unclassified or general instance of payroll tax fraud that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Payroll Tax Fraud leaf.

Deliberate manipulation of the timing or existence of recorded revenue — booking sales that have not actually occurred, or recognizing legitimate revenue prematurely (before the earnings process is complete) — in order to inflate reported revenue and overall financial performance for a period.

c.n: Expense Understatement to Inflate Reported Profit
c.d: Deliberate manipulation of reported expenses — through improper capitalization of costs that should be expensed, delayed recognition of known expenses, or outright omission of incurred costs — in order to understate total expenses and inflate reported profit for a period.

Deliberate structuring or omission of liabilities — through undisclosed special-purpose entities, unrecorded guarantees, or other off-balance-sheet arrangements — to keep genuine financial obligations out of the company's reported balance sheet and thereby present a misleadingly favorable financial position to investors, lenders, or regulators.
An unclassified or general instance of financial misreporting that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Misreporting Financials leaf.

c.n: Insider Trading Based on Material Non-Public Information
c.d: Purchase or sale of the company's (or a related company's) securities by an individual in possession of material, non-public information about that company, or the passing ('tipping') of such information to another person who then trades on it, in advance of the information becoming public.

Coordinated scheme in which false, misleading, or exaggerated statements about the company are used to artificially inflate its stock price ('pump'), after which the individuals orchestrating or aware of the scheme sell their holdings at the inflated price ('dump'), leaving other investors holding devalued shares once the price collapses.

c.n: Earnings Manipulation to Influence Stock Price Before Insider Sale
c.d: Deliberate manipulation of reported earnings or other key financial metrics — timed and calibrated specifically to favorably move the stock price — shortly before an insider executes a planned sale of company shares, combining financial-statement fraud with a securities-trading benefit.

c.n: Unclassified / General Securities and Stock Manipulation
c.d: An unclassified or general instance of securities or stock manipulation that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Securities and Stock Manipulation leaf.

c.n: Loan Application Using Falsified Income/Employment Documentation
c.d: Fraud in which an individual applies for a loan or line of credit under their genuine identity but submits fabricated pay stubs, tax documents, or employer verification to qualify for an amount or terms they would not otherwise receive.

Fraud in which an adversary uses a real victim's stolen personally identifiable information (name, SSN, date of birth) to apply for and obtain a loan or credit line without the victim's knowledge, distinct from a wholly fabricated synthetic identity.

Fraud in which a real person (the 'straw borrower'), often paid or coerced, knowingly applies for and obtains a loan using their own genuine, valid identity, while the funds and true benefit go to an undisclosed third party who would not have qualified or wished to be named on the loan.

An unclassified/general leaf for loan-application fraud that has not been further classified into falsified-documentation (ITID-53511), stolen-identity (ITID-53512), or straw-borrower (ITID-53513) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Synthetic Identity Built from Combined Real and Fabricated PII
c.d: Fraud in which an adversary constructs a new identity that does not correspond to any single real person by blending a genuine identifier (typically an SSN) with a fabricated name, date of birth, and address, then uses that composite identity to open financial accounts or apply for credit.

c.n: Synthetic Identity Used to Build Credit History Before Bust-Out Fraud
c.d: Fraud in which an already-established synthetic identity is used responsibly over months or years to build a legitimate-looking credit history and raise credit limits, before the perpetrator maxes out all available credit lines simultaneously ('busts out') with no intent to repay.

An unclassified/general leaf for synthetic identity fraud that has not been further classified into identity-creation (ITID-53521) or credit-building/bust-out (ITID-53522) stages at the time of intake.

Fraud in which an individual (often for a fee, arranged through a broker) is added as an authorized user on a stranger's long-standing, well-managed credit card account purely to inherit that account's positive payment history and inflate their own credit score, with no genuine financial relationship or authorization to use the card.

c.n: Credit Repair Scam Falsifying Credit Report Disputes
c.d: Fraud in which a credit-repair operator files disputes against accurate, legitimate negative tradelines (e.g., real late payments, real charge-offs) on a client's credit report, exploiting dispute-processing timelines or fabricated identity-theft claims to have the accurate negative information removed rather than legitimately corrected.

An unclassified/general leaf for credit score manipulation fraud that has not been further classified into tradeline/authorized-user (ITID-53531) or fraudulent dispute (ITID-53532) subtypes at the time of intake.

Fraud in which a mortgage applicant, sometimes with the assistance of a colluding loan officer or broker, submits fabricated or inflated income, employment, or asset documentation to qualify for a mortgage or a larger loan amount than their true financial position supports.

Fraud in which a property is purchased at a low price and quickly resold at an artificially inflated price supported by a collusive or fraudulent appraisal, with the difference funded by a mortgage lender who is misled about the property's true value.

Fraud in which an adversary forges signatures or fabricates documentation to record a fraudulent deed transfer, quitclaim, or title change on a property, allowing the property to be sold, refinanced, or encumbered without the true owner's knowledge or consent.

c.n: Unclassified / General Mortgage and Real Estate Fraud
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for mortgage and real estate fraud that has not been further classified into income/asset falsification (ITID-53541), property-flipping appraisal fraud (ITID-53542), or title/deed fraud (ITID-53543) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Trading (Insider Financial Fraud Context)
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cases in which an employee, executive, or other insider trades company (or a business partner's) securities while in possession of material, non-public information obtained through their position, or tips such information to others who trade on it.

Fraud in which an employee with access to incoming cash or check payments (e.g., a cashier, collections clerk, or front-office staff) pockets some or all of a receipt before it is recorded in the accounting system, so that no transaction trail is created for the diverted amount.

c.n: Fraudulent Disbursement via Fake Vendor Payment to Self-Controlled Account
c.d: Fraud in which an employee with accounts-payable access sets up a fictitious vendor, or alters payment routing on a legitimate vendor record, so that a disbursement intended for a real business expense is instead paid to an account the employee secretly controls.

c.n: Diversion of Company Funds to Personal Account via Authorized Access
c.d: Fraud in which an employee with authorized access to initiate or approve wire transfers, ACH payments, or account movements uses that access to move company funds directly into a personal or associate-controlled account, without the intermediate step of a fake vendor or invoice.

An unclassified/general leaf for embezzlement that has not been further classified into cash-skimming (ITID-53621), fictitious-vendor disbursement (ITID-53622), or direct treasury-access diversion (ITID-53623) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Unclassified / General Payroll Fraud by Employees
c.d: Fraud in which an employee, typically one with HR/payroll system access or in collusion with such a person, manipulates payroll data (hours, pay rate, deposit destination, or a fictitious/'ghost' employee record) to receive compensation beyond what they are legitimately owed.

c.n: Unclassified / General Financial Report Falsification (Insider Context)
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cases in which an employee or executive with access to financial reporting systems deliberately misstates, alters, or fabricates financial statements, ledgers, or supporting records to misrepresent the company's true financial position.

c.n: Mobile Payment Wallet (Apple Pay/Google Pay) Tokenization Fraud
c.d: Fraud in which an adversary who has obtained stolen payment card data (via phishing, skimming, or a data breach) enrolls that card into a mobile digital wallet (e.g., Apple Pay, Google Pay) under their own or an accomplice's device, exploiting weak card-verification steps during the tokenization/provisioning process to make fraudulent tap-to-pay or in-app purchases.

c.n: Digital Wallet Takeover via SIM Swap
c.d: Fraud in which an adversary convinces or bribes a mobile carrier (or exploits carrier support processes) to port a victim's phone number onto a SIM the adversary controls, then uses SMS-based authentication tied to that number to take over the victim's digital payment wallets, banking apps, or exchange accounts.

c.n: Stolen Cryptocurrency Wallet Used for Immediate Fund Transfer Out
c.d: Fraud in which an adversary who has already obtained control of a victim's cryptocurrency wallet (by any compromise vector) immediately transfers the wallet's holdings to an attacker-controlled address, prioritizing speed over concealment given cryptocurrency's irreversible transaction model.

An unclassified/general leaf for stolen payment wallet fraud that has not been further classified into mobile-wallet tokenization (ITID-53711), SIM-swap takeover (ITID-53712), or cryptocurrency wallet fund transfer-out (ITID-53713) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Fraudulent Transactions via Digital Payment Apps
Peer-to-Peer Payment App Scam (Venmo/Cash App/Zelle Overpayment Scam)
c.d: Fraud in which a scammer sends a victim (or has the victim believe they received) a payment via a peer-to-peer app such as Venmo, Cash App, or Zelle that exceeds an agreed amount, then requests the victim refund the difference — after which the original payment is reversed, revoked, or was never genuinely completed, leaving the victim out the refunded amount.

c.n: Fake Buyer/Seller Payment App Transaction Reversal Fraud
c.d: Fraud in which a buyer or seller in a peer-to-peer payment app transaction disputes or reverses a completed payment through the app's or an underlying bank's chargeback/reversal mechanism after already receiving the goods, service, or counter-payment, exploiting the reversal process itself as the fraud vector.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fraudulent Digital Payment App Transaction
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for fraudulent P2P/digital payment app transactions that have not been further classified into overpayment-scam (ITID-53721) or transaction-reversal-fraud (ITID-53722) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Liquidity Pool Drain Rug Pull (DeFi Token Scam)
c.d: Fraud in which the creators of a decentralized finance (DeFi) token or protocol, after attracting investor funds into a liquidity pool, withdraw ('drain') that liquidity for themselves, instantly and permanently collapsing the token's tradeable value and leaving investors unable to sell their holdings.

Fraud in which the creators of a non-fungible token (NFT) collection collect minting proceeds from buyers based on promised future utility, roadmap features, or community benefits, then abandon the project and disappear with the funds without delivering on those promises.

c.n: Unclassified / General Crypto Rug Pull Scam
c.d: An unclassified/general leaf for cryptocurrency rug pull scams that have not been further classified into liquidity-pool-drain (ITID-53731) or NFT-project (ITID-53732) subtypes at the time of intake.

Fraud in which the operators of a cryptocurrency exchange (which may have appeared legitimate for a period of operation) abruptly halt customer withdrawals, cease communication, and abscond with the funds held on customers' behalf, having typically never fully backed customer balances with real assets.

Fraud in which an employee of a cryptocurrency exchange uses their legitimate internal access (to customer accounts, hot-wallet infrastructure, or trading systems) to misappropriate customer or exchange funds, front-run customer trades, or otherwise unlawfully benefit from insider access to the platform.
An unclassified/general leaf for cryptocurrency exchange fraud that has not been further classified into exit-scam (ITID-53741) or insider-fraud (ITID-53742) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Unclassified / General CEO Fraud (Social Engineering Context)
c.d: An unclassified or general instance of executive-impersonation ('CEO fraud') social engineering used to pressure an employee into an urgent, unauthorized financial action — a wire transfer, gift card purchase, or similar — through a spoofed or compromised communication purporting to be from a senior executive.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor Payment Diversion (Social Engineering Context)
c.d: An unclassified or general instance of social engineering used to divert a legitimate vendor payment to an attacker-controlled account, through impersonation or manipulation of the payment-approval process, that does not fall cleanly under a more specific, dedicated leaf.

c.n: Fake Lawsuit/Legal Threat Demanding Immediate Payment
c.d: Social engineering scam in which the perpetrator falsely claims the target (the company or an employee) is subject to an active lawsuit, legal judgment, or imminent legal action, demanding immediate payment — often via wire transfer or gift card — to 'settle' or avoid the fabricated legal consequence.

Social engineering scam in which the perpetrator impersonates a tax authority (e.g., a national revenue service) and falsely claims the target owes back taxes or penalties, demanding immediate payment — often via wire transfer, gift card, or prepaid debit card — to avoid threatened enforcement action such as asset seizure or arrest.

Social engineering scam in which the perpetrator impersonates a regulatory body (e.g., a licensing board, data-protection authority, or industry regulator) and falsely claims the company owes a fine or penalty for a compliance violation, demanding immediate payment to avoid threatened enforcement action such as license revocation or public sanction.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fake Legal or Government Notice
c.d: An unclassified or general instance of a fake legal or government notice scam that has not yet been attributed to a specific impersonated authority type covered by another Fake Legal or Government Notices leaf.

Social engineering scam in which an adversary impersonates an employee (or the pension plan administrator) to submit a fraudulent request for a pension plan distribution, loan, or withdrawal, directing the payout to an attacker-controlled bank account rather than the legitimate participant's account.

c.n: Fake Benefits Enrollment Change Redirecting Payments
c.d: Social engineering scam in which an adversary submits a fraudulent benefits-enrollment or direct-deposit change (e.g., HSA/FSA reimbursement account, benefits-related payment routing) through the employee self-service or benefits-administration portal, redirecting ongoing payments to an attacker-controlled bank account.

c.n: Unclassified / General Pension and Benefits Fraud
c.d: An unclassified or general instance of pension or benefits fraud that has not yet been attributed to a specific mechanism covered by another Pension and Benefits Fraud leaf.

c.n: Layered Shell Company Network for Fund Obfuscation
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which an individual or organization establishes multiple interconnected shell companies, often across jurisdictions, and moves funds between them in a series of transactions with no genuine business purpose, solely to break the audit trail between the funds' illicit source and their eventual legitimate-looking destination.

c.n: Shell Company Used to Receive Fraudulent Proceeds from BEC
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which proceeds from a successful BEC wire-fraud attack are deposited into an account held by a shell company (often set up specifically for this purpose, or a 'money mule' business front) before being further layered, converted, or withdrawn, breaking the direct trail between the victim's fraudulent wire and the ultimate beneficiary.

An unclassified/general leaf for shell company money laundering that has not been further classified into a broader layered-network (ITID-53911) or BEC-proceeds-specific (ITID-53912) subtype at the time of intake.

c.n: Cash Deposit Structuring Below Reporting Threshold
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which an individual makes a series of cash deposits, each intentionally kept just under the regulatory reporting threshold (e.g., $10,000 in the US), across one or more accounts or institutions, specifically to avoid triggering a mandatory currency transaction report.

c.n: Smurfing via Multiple Accounts/Individuals to Split Large Transfer
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which an organizer recruits or directs multiple individuals ('smurfs') to each deposit, transfer, or carry a portion of a larger illicit sum through separate accounts or transactions, so that no single individual's activity appears large enough to trigger reporting or scrutiny, before the funds are consolidated for the organizer's benefit.

An unclassified/general leaf for structuring/smurfing money laundering activity that has not been further classified into single-depositor structuring (ITID-53921) or multi-individual smurfing (ITID-53922) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Over-Invoicing/Under-Invoicing Trade Transaction to Move Value
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which parties to an international trade transaction deliberately misstate the price of goods on an invoice — over-invoicing to move excess value to the exporter, or under-invoicing to move excess value to the importer — using the price discrepancy itself as the vehicle for transferring value across borders outside normal financial-transfer scrutiny.

c.n: Phantom Shipment Trade Laundering (No Actual Goods Moved)
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which parties generate a complete set of trade documentation (invoices, bills of lading, customs paperwork) for a shipment of goods that never actually exists or moves, using the fabricated 'phantom' trade transaction purely as a justification to move funds across borders through the trade-finance system.

An unclassified/general leaf for trade-based money laundering that has not been further classified into mispriced-invoicing (ITID-53931) or phantom-shipment (ITID-53932) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Crypto Mixer/Tumbler Used to Obscure Fund Origin
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which an individual routes cryptocurrency through a mixing or tumbling service — which pools and redistributes funds from many depositors to obscure the direct transactional link between sender and receiver — specifically to launder the origin of illicitly obtained cryptocurrency before cashing out or further using it.

c.n: Chain-Hopping Across Multiple Cryptocurrencies to Break Trace
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which an individual converts illicit cryptocurrency proceeds through a rapid sequence of different cryptocurrencies (e.g., Bitcoin to Monero to Ethereum to a stablecoin) via exchanges or swap services, exploiting the fact that no single blockchain's public ledger captures the full cross-chain trail, to defeat straightforward on-chain tracing.

c.n: Cryptocurrency Layering via Numerous Low-Value Transactions
c.d: Financial-crime activity in which an individual splits illicit cryptocurrency proceeds into a large number of low-value transactions distributed across many addresses over time, exploiting the fact that most transaction-monitoring and exchange risk-scoring thresholds are tuned to flag high-value movements, to move the aggregate sum without any single transaction triggering scrutiny.

An unclassified/general leaf for cryptocurrency money laundering that has not been further classified into mixer/tumbler (ITID-53941), chain-hopping (ITID-53942), or low-value-layering (ITID-53943) subtypes at the time of intake.

c.n: Cloud Provider Outage Due to Third-Party Infrastructure Failure (Non-Attack)
c.d: A disruption to company operations caused by an outage, degradation, or control-plane failure within a cloud provider's (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS infrastructure layer) own infrastructure, where no adversary action against the company or the provider is implicated.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud Service Disruption (Infrastructure Context)
c.d: A cloud service disruption affecting company operations that has not yet been classified as either a confirmed third-party infrastructure failure or another specific cloud-disruption cause.

c.n: Power Failure/Grid Outage Affecting Data Center
c.d: A disruption of company data-center-hosted critical systems caused by loss of incoming utility grid power to the facility, considered from the data-center infrastructure-outage angle rather than the facility power-continuity angle.

c.n: Cooling System Failure Causing Data Center Shutdown
c.d: A shutdown of company data-center-hosted critical systems triggered by failure of the data center's dedicated precision-cooling infrastructure, resulting in thermal protection shutdowns or forced load-shedding.

Physical damage to a company-operated or colocated data center facility itself — from fire, flooding, or a natural disaster — that destroys or renders unusable the building or the equipment housed within it.
A data center outage affecting company-hosted critical systems that has not yet been classified to a specific root cause within this group.

c.n: Undersea Cable Cut Affecting Regional Connectivity
c.d: A disruption to company connectivity or transit-dependent services caused by a physical cut or fault in an undersea fiber-optic cable carrying regional or intercontinental internet traffic.
A disruption to company connectivity caused by a routing, peering, or configuration failure at an internet service provider or backbone transit provider the company depends on.
An internet backbone disruption affecting company connectivity that has not yet been classified as a physical cable fault or a provider routing failure.

c.n: CDN Provider Configuration Error Causing Widespread Outage
c.d: A disruption to company web or API delivery caused by a CDN provider pushing an erroneous configuration (e.g., a bad edge rule, certificate, or routing change) across its network.

A disruption to company web or API delivery caused by failure of the CDN provider's own edge infrastructure (points of presence, hardware, or internal network), independent of any specific configuration change.
A CDN-related disruption affecting company web/API delivery that has not yet been classified as a provider configuration error or a provider infrastructure failure.

c.n: Domain-Wide Ransomware Deployment via Compromised Domain Controller/GPO
c.d: A ransomware attack in which the adversary compromises a domain controller or abuses Group Policy Objects to deploy encryption payloads across the entire domain-joined estate simultaneously, tracked at the enterprise-wide business-impact level.

c.n: Ransomware Simultaneously Deployed Across Multiple Business Units/Subsidiaries
c.d: A ransomware attack that achieves near-simultaneous impact across multiple, organizationally distinct business units or subsidiaries — whether through shared infrastructure, replicated access, or independent parallel compromises — tracked at the enterprise-wide business-impact level.
An enterprise-wide ransomware attack affecting company operations that has not yet been classified as domain/GPO-driven or multi-entity-driven.

c.n: Ransomware Attack on Industrial Control System (ICS/OT) Environment
c.d: A ransomware attack that encrypts or otherwise disrupts systems within an industrial control system or operational technology environment (e.g., SCADA, PLC-supporting Windows hosts, HMIs), tracked for its critical-infrastructure targeting angle.

c.n: Ransomware Attack on Healthcare/Hospital Critical Systems
c.d: A ransomware attack that encrypts or disrupts systems supporting direct patient care or clinical operations (e.g., EHR, PACS, clinical devices' supporting infrastructure), tracked for its critical-infrastructure targeting angle.
A ransomware attack that encrypts or disrupts systems supporting utility or energy generation/distribution operations, tracked for its critical-infrastructure targeting angle.

c.n: Unclassified / General Targeted Ransomware on Critical Infrastructure
c.d: A ransomware attack targeting a critical-infrastructure environment that has not yet been classified into the ICS/OT, healthcare, or utility sub-categories.

c.n: Ransomware Specifically Targeting and Encrypting Backup Repository
c.d: A ransomware attack in which the backup repository (backup server, backup storage target, or backup snapshots) is itself directly targeted and encrypted, aiming to deny recovery.

c.n: Backup Deletion/Corruption Prior to Primary System Encryption
c.d: An adversary's deliberate deletion, corruption, or disabling of backup jobs, snapshots, or repositories prior to deploying ransomware against primary systems, intended to remove the victim's recovery option before encryption begins.
A ransomware event involving impact to backups that has not yet been classified as direct backup encryption or precursor backup deletion/corruption.

c.n: Unclassified / General RDoS (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: An extortion attempt in which an adversary threatens or launches a denial-of-service attack against company infrastructure unless a ransom is paid, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact.

c.n: Unclassified / General BGP Hijacking Attempt (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: An attempt by an adversary to hijack or manipulate BGP routing to disrupt company connectivity or redirect company traffic, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than its routing-protocol mechanics.

c.n: Unclassified / General DNS Poisoning or Takedown (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: An attack in which company DNS resolution is poisoned, hijacked, or taken down, disrupting the ability of users or systems to reach company services, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than its DNS-attack mechanics.

c.n: Unclassified / General VoIP System Disruption (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: An attack or attack-driven disruption that degrades or takes down company VoIP telephony infrastructure, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact on voice communications.

c.n: Unclassified / General ISP-Level Disruption (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: A disruption to company connectivity caused by an attack against, or failure at, an internet service provider the company depends on, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud-Based Critical Infrastructure Disruption
c.d: A disruption to a company critical-infrastructure function that is hosted in the cloud, where the disruption mechanism does not fall neatly into the already-covered cloud-outage, ransomware, network, or DDoS categories, tracked here as an intake/cross-reference leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Insider Sabotage (Disruption Context)
c.d: Deliberate sabotage of company systems or services carried out by an individual with authorized access (employee, contractor, or trusted third party) intending to cause operational disruption.
A disruption to company systems or services caused by an authorized individual's unintentional misconfiguration, error, or omission, with no malicious intent involved.

c.n: Unclassified / General Privileged Account Abuse (Disruption Context)
c.d: The use of legitimately assigned privileged access by an authorized individual in a manner inconsistent with their role or authorization, creating a risk of or actually causing service disruption.

c.n: Deliberate Database Record Corruption/Deletion by Insider
