c.d: The deliberate, unauthorized modification or deletion of production database records by an insider using their legitimate access, intended to corrupt data integrity or cause operational disruption.

c.n: Insider Deploying Wiper-Style Script Against Critical Systems
c.d: An insider's deliberate deployment of a destructive script or tool designed to erase, corrupt, or render unusable data or system state across multiple critical systems at once.

c.n: Insider Corrupting Backup Data to Prevent Recovery
c.d: The deliberate, unauthorized corruption or deletion of backup data by an insider using their legitimate access, intended to prevent recovery from data loss or system disruption.
An insider-driven data-corruption event that has not yet been classified as targeted database manipulation, wiper-style destruction, or backup corruption.
An operational failure in which an attempt to roll back a failed software deployment does not restore service, resulting in an extended outage beyond the initial deployment failure.

c.n: Deployment Failure Due to Untested Configuration Change
c.d: An operational failure in which a configuration change that was not adequately tested prior to deployment causes a production service outage.
A failed software deployment causing production impact that has not yet been classified as a rollback failure or an untested-configuration-change failure.

c.n: Critical Patch Delayed Past Vendor-Recommended Timeline, Then Exploited
c.d: A confirmed compromise resulting from exploitation of a vulnerability for which a critical patch was available but had not yet been applied within the vendor-recommended timeframe.

c.n: End-of-Life System No Longer Receiving Patches, Then Exploited
c.d: A confirmed compromise resulting from exploitation of a vulnerability on a system that has reached vendor end-of-life status and no longer receives security patches.
A confirmed exploitation of an unpatched vulnerability that has not yet been classified as a delayed-patch scenario or an end-of-life scenario.

c.n: Unclassified / General Supply Chain Software Compromise (Disruption Context)
c.d: A disruption to company operations caused by a compromised third-party software component or update that the company depends on, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact.

c.n: CI/CD Pipeline Code Injection Causing Production Outage
c.d: The deliberate injection of malicious or unauthorized code into a company's CI/CD pipeline — via a compromised build tool, pipeline configuration, or dependency — that results in a production outage upon deployment.

c.n: Malicious Code Tampering Introduced via Compromised Developer Account
c.d: The introduction of malicious or unauthorized code into a company codebase or deployment through the use of a compromised developer's legitimate source-control or deployment credentials.

c.n: Unclassified / General Code Injection and Tampering
c.d: A code injection or tampering event affecting company software that has not yet been classified as pipeline-based or developer-account-based.

c.n: Deliberate Physical Destruction of Server/Network Equipment
c.d: The deliberate, physical destruction or damage of server, storage, or network equipment by a person with or without authorized facility access, intended to cause operational disruption.

c.n: Sabotage of Building Power/Cooling Systems to Cause IT Outage
c.d: The deliberate tampering with or sabotage of a building's power distribution or cooling infrastructure, by a person with or without authorized facility access, intended to cause an IT service outage.
The deliberate, physical cutting or damaging of fiber-optic or copper cable lines serving company facilities or connectivity, intended to disrupt operations.

c.n: Unclassified / General Physical Sabotage of IT Infrastructure
c.d: A physical sabotage event affecting IT infrastructure that has not yet been classified as hardware destruction, power/cooling sabotage, or cable cutting.

c.n: Fire Damage to Office/Branch IT Equipment
c.d: Damage to IT equipment at a company office or branch location caused by fire, where no deliberate sabotage or adversarial cause is implicated.
Damage to company IT-supporting facilities and equipment caused by flooding resulting from a natural disaster (storm, hurricane, river/coastal flooding), where no deliberate sabotage is implicated.
Structural or equipment damage to a company facility caused by an earthquake or other seismic event, where no deliberate sabotage is implicated.
An environmental disruption affecting a company facility that has not yet been classified as fire, flood, or earthquake damage.

c.n: Grid Power Outage with UPS/Generator Failure to Engage
c.d: A facility power outage in which loss of utility grid power is compounded by the failure of on-site backup power systems (UPS or generator) to engage, resulting in an uncontrolled loss of power to IT systems.

c.n: Battery Backup Depletion During Extended Outage
c.d: A facility power event in which on-site battery backup (UPS) successfully engages upon grid loss but is depleted before power is restored or a generator takes over, resulting in a delayed loss of power to IT systems.
A power outage or UPS-related event affecting company systems that has not yet been classified as a backup-power-transfer failure or a battery-depletion scenario.

c.n: HVAC Unit Failure Causing Server Overheating Shutdown
c.d: A shutdown of IT equipment triggered by unplanned failure of an HVAC unit cooling a server room, closet, or non-data-center IT space, resulting in a thermal-protection shutdown.

c.n: Cooling System Maintenance Failure Leading to Thermal Shutdown
c.d: A thermal-protection shutdown of IT equipment caused by a failure or gap in cooling system maintenance procedures — such as a maintenance activity performed incorrectly, or scheduled maintenance being skipped or overdue.
An HVAC or cooling-related thermal shutdown event affecting company IT equipment that has not yet been classified as a discrete unit failure or a maintenance-process gap.

c.n: Unclassified / General High-Volume DDoS Attack (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: A volumetric, network-layer DDoS attack that saturates company network capacity or upstream links, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than the underlying flood-technique mechanics.

c.n: Unclassified / General Application-Layer DDoS (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: An application-layer (Layer 7) DDoS attack that exhausts company web/API server resources through high volumes of seemingly legitimate requests, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than the underlying request-flood mechanics.

c.n: Unclassified / General IoT Botnet DDoS (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: A DDoS attack against company infrastructure generated by a botnet of compromised Internet of Things (IoT) devices, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than the botnet's own build-out mechanics.

c.n: Unclassified / General DNS and CDN Targeted DDoS (Critical System Disruption Context)
c.d: A DDoS attack specifically targeting company or provider DNS/CDN infrastructure, aiming to prevent resolution of or access to company domains, tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than the underlying attack-technique mechanics.

c.n: SaaS Vendor Outage Affecting Business-Critical Function
c.d: A disruption to a company business-critical function caused by an outage of a SaaS application the company depends on, where the outage originates within the vendor's own environment and no compromise is implicated.

c.n: SaaS Vendor Data Loss/Corruption Incident Affecting Customer
c.d: An incident in which a SaaS vendor experiences loss or corruption of company data hosted within its platform, where the cause originates within the vendor's own environment (e.g., a failed migration or backup failure) and no compromise is implicated.
A SaaS-vendor-related disruption affecting company operations that has not yet been classified as a straightforward availability outage or a data loss/corruption incident.

c.n: MSP Breach Used as Pivot Point into Multiple Downstream Clients
c.d: A confirmed breach of a company's managed service provider (MSP) in which the adversary uses the trusted relationship and access the MSP holds into multiple downstream client environments — including the company's — as a pivot point for further compromise.

c.n: Compromised MSP Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) Tool Used for Mass Deployment
c.d: A confirmed compromise of an MSP's remote monitoring and management (RMM) software, or of the MSP's control over it, used by an adversary to mass-deploy a malicious payload (e.g., ransomware) across the company's endpoints managed through that tool.
A confirmed or suspected MSP-related attack affecting company operations that has not yet been classified as a general trusted-relationship pivot or specific RMM tool abuse.

c.n: Supplier ERP/Order System Outage Disrupting Fulfillment
c.d: A disruption to company order fulfillment or supply-chain operations caused by an outage or degradation of a supplier's ERP, order-management, or logistics system, where no compromise of the company or the supplier is implicated.

c.n: Supplier Bankruptcy/Business Failure Causing Sudden Service Loss
c.d: A disruption to company operations caused by a supplier's sudden business failure, insolvency, or bankruptcy resulting in an abrupt loss of contracted service, independent of any technical system failure.
A supplier-related disruption affecting company operations that has not yet been classified as a technical system outage or a business-failure/bankruptcy event.

c.n: Unclassified / General Software Supply Chain Attack (Third-Party Disruption Context)
c.d: A disruption to company operations caused by a confirmed software supply chain attack — a deliberate compromise of a third-party software vendor's build, update, or distribution process — tracked here for its critical-system-disruption business impact rather than the detailed compromise mechanics.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor Cloud Storage Exposure (Supply Chain Context)
c.d: An incident in which data belonging to, or processed on behalf of, the organization is exposed through misconfigured or compromised cloud storage operated by a third-party vendor, and the exposure has not yet been further classified.

An incident in which credentials used by a third-party vendor to access, process, or store organizational data or systems have been compromised, and the full scope and downstream impact are not yet determined.

c.n: Unclassified / General Customer and Partner Data Leak (Supply Chain Context)
c.d: An incident in which customer or business-partner data entrusted to a third-party vendor for processing or storage has been disclosed without authorization, and the leak's root cause has not yet been classified.

c.n: Data Broker/People-Search Site Breach Exposing Aggregated Records
c.d: A breach or unauthorized disclosure at a data broker or people-search aggregator, exposing aggregated personal records that include the organization's customers, employees, or executives, distinct from breaches at bureaus performing regulated credit-reporting functions.

c.n: Credit Bureau/Reporting Agency Data Aggregator Breach
c.d: A breach or unauthorized disclosure at a credit bureau or other regulated consumer-reporting agency, exposing financial identity records (credit history, SSNs, account data) belonging to the organization's customers or employees, distinct from breaches at unregulated data brokers.
An incident at a third-party data aggregator affecting organization-linked records, where the aggregator's type (unregulated broker vs. regulated reporting agency) has not yet been confirmed.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor VPN or Remote Access Breach
c.d: An incident in which a vendor's VPN, remote-access gateway, or remote-support tooling has been compromised, creating a potential pathway into the organization's network, and full impact has not yet been assessed.

A confirmed intrusion into a supplier's IT environment, where the supplier has direct network or system connectivity to the organization and the specific compromise vector has not yet been classified into a more specific sibling leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud SaaS Vendor Compromise
c.d: An incident in which a cloud-based SaaS vendor used by the organization has been compromised at the platform or tenant level, and the specific impact to the organization's data or operations has not yet been classified.

c.n: Unclassified / General MSP Breach (Third-Party Network Compromise Context)
c.d: An incident in which an MSP providing IT or security services to the organization is compromised, viewed and classified through the lens of the trust relationship and network access the MSP holds into the organization's environment, rather than through the multi-client pivot/blast-radius lens.

c.n: Malicious Code Injected into Vendor's Distributed Software Package
c.d: The compromise of a software vendor's distribution artifact (installer, update package, container image, firmware bundle) such that malicious code reaches the organization through a channel it has already whitelisted, resulting in a critical, wide-blast-radius disruption once the tainted release is installed.

c.n: Malicious Code Injected via Compromised Developer Environment
c.d: The introduction of malicious code into a vendor's codebase via a compromised developer workstation, IDE, source-control credential, or local build environment, such that the code is committed and later shipped as part of a legitimate release, producing a critical downstream disruption for organizations that consume that release.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Code Injection (Supply Chain Context)
c.d: A catch-all classification for malicious code discovered to have entered a vendor's product through the supply chain, used during initial triage before the specific injection point (distributed package vs. developer environment) has been determined.

c.n: Typosquatted Malicious Package Published to Public Registry
c.d: The ingestion of a malicious package published under a name deceptively similar to a legitimate open-source library (typosquatting) into an organization's build or dependency chain, resulting in critical system disruption when the malicious code executes.

c.n: Legitimate Package Maintainer Account Compromised to Push Malicious Update
c.d: The takeover of a legitimate open-source package maintainer's account (or its publishing credentials) used to push a malicious version of an already-trusted library, which is then automatically ingested by downstream consumers via routine dependency updates.

c.n: Dependency Confusion Attack (Internal Package Name Hijacked on Public Registry)
c.d: A dependency confusion attack in which an attacker publishes a package on a public registry under the same name as an organization's internal/private package, exploiting build-tool resolution precedence so the malicious public package is installed instead of the legitimate internal one.
A catch-all classification for a compromised open-source library incident used during initial triage before the specific compromise pattern is determined.

c.n: Vendor API Integration Exploited to Access Multiple Downstream Customers
c.d: The exploitation of a vendor-provided API integration such that a single compromise event grants an attacker access across multiple downstream customer organizations that share the vendor's platform, resulting in critical, multi-tenant business disruption.

c.n: Vendor API Key/Secret Exposed in Public Code Repository
c.d: The exposure of a vendor API key or secret belonging to the organization in a publicly accessible code repository, leading to unauthorized use of that credential and resulting critical disruption to the organization's own vendor-integrated services.
A catch-all classification for a vendor API exploitation incident used during initial triage before the specific pattern is determined.

c.n: Unclassified / General CI/CD Pipeline Attack (Supply Chain Context)
c.d: The compromise of an organization's or vendor's CI/CD pipeline infrastructure (build orchestrator, pipeline configuration, artifact repository, deployment automation) enabling an attacker to inject malicious code, alter build artifacts, or manipulate deployment targets without going through an individual developer's environment, resulting in critical downstream disruption.

c.n: Hardware and IoT-Based Supply Chain Attacks
Nation-State-Mandated Firmware Backdoor in Manufactured Hardware
c.d: The discovery of a firmware-level backdoor embedded in vendor-manufactured hardware, attributed with credible evidence to a nation-state mandate, export-control leverage, or state-directed intelligence requirement, rather than a compromise introduced independently by the contract manufacturer.

c.n: Firmware Backdoor Introduced at Contract Manufacturer/OEM Level
c.d: The discovery of a firmware-level backdoor embedded in vendor hardware, introduced by a contract manufacturer or original equipment manufacturer (OEM) acting independently — for financial gain, negligence, or unauthorized third-party subcontracting — rather than under state mandate.

c.n: Unclassified / General Firmware Backdoor in Vendor Hardware
c.d: The discovery of a firmware-level backdoor in vendor-supplied hardware where the responsible party has not yet been attributed to either a nation-state mandate or an independent manufacturer action.

c.n: Counterfeit IoT Device Sold Through Legitimate Retail Channel
c.d: The discovery of a counterfeit IoT device — one falsely branded as a legitimate manufacturer's product — that entered the organization's environment through a legitimate retail or distribution channel, distinct from devices shipped pre-compromised by their actual manufacturer.

c.n: IoT Device Shipped with Pre-Installed Malicious Firmware
c.d: The discovery of malicious or unauthorized firmware pre-installed on a genuine IoT device at the point of manufacture or distribution, rather than a device that is itself counterfeit.

c.n: Unclassified / General Rogue IoT Device (Supply Chain Context)
c.d: The discovery of a rogue or suspicious IoT device in the organization's environment, in a supply-chain context, where whether the device is counterfeit or a genuine device with compromised firmware has not yet been determined.

c.n: Hardware Interdiction During Shipping (Implant Installed En Route)
c.d: The interdiction of hardware while in transit through the shipping/logistics chain, during which an adversary installs a malicious physical implant before the equipment reaches the organization, distinct from tampering that is merely indicated by packaging evidence without a confirmed implant.

c.n: Tampered Packaging/Seal Indicating Equipment Compromise Before Delivery
c.d: The discovery of tamper-evident packaging or security seals showing signs of interference on hardware prior to its delivery and acceptance, indicating possible compromise during transit that has not yet been confirmed through forensic hardware analysis.

c.n: Unclassified / General Tampered Equipment in Transit
c.d: An initial report of possible tampering with equipment during transit, prior to determination of whether the case involves a confirmed physical implant or only indicative packaging/seal evidence.

c.n: Vendor-Issued Security Recall of Compromised Hardware Batch
c.d: A defensive/remediation classification capturing the organization's coordinated response when a vendor issues a formal security recall for a batch of hardware found to be compromised, encompassing inventory identification, replacement, and disposal of affected units.

c.n: Emergency Firmware Remediation Patch Deployed by Vendor
c.d: A defensive/remediation classification capturing the organization's coordinated deployment of an emergency firmware patch issued by a vendor to remediate a discovered security defect, distinct from a full hardware recall requiring physical unit replacement.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor Device Recall and Remediation
c.d: A defensive/remediation classification capturing vendor-issued device recall or remediation activity that does not specifically fall under a full hardware batch recall or an emergency firmware patch, such as configuration-only fixes or mixed remediation programs.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Insider at a Vendor
c.d: An individual employed or contracted by a vendor who knowingly and intentionally misuses their authorized access to the organization's systems, data, or infrastructure to cause harm, exfiltrate data, or facilitate a critical disruption.

c.n: Unclassified / General Accidental Insider Breach (Vendor Context)
c.d: A vendor employee's or contractor's unintentional action, such as misconfiguration, accidental data disclosure, or mishandling, that causes a critical disruption or data exposure despite no intent to harm the organization.

c.n: Unclassified / General Supplier Employee Credential Reuse
c.d: The use of a supplier/vendor employee's password across multiple services, such that a credential breach unrelated to the organization (e.g., a third-party website leak) is reused by an attacker to gain unauthorized access to the organization's systems through the vendor's legitimate account.

The use of a vendor employee's or contractor's legitimately-granted privileged access to perform actions outside the scope of their contracted function, such as accessing data or systems not required for their role, regardless of whether clear malicious intent can be established.

c.n: Vendor Failed to Maintain Required Security Certification (SOC 2/ISO 27001)
c.d: A vendor's lapse or failure to renew a security certification (such as SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001) that was contractually required as a condition of the vendor relationship, constituting a compliance violation to be tracked and remediated through legal and vendor-management channels rather than as a technical security incident.

c.n: Vendor Failed to Implement Contractually Required Security Controls
c.d: A vendor's failure to implement one or more specific security controls that were explicitly required under the terms of its contract with the organization, discovered through audit, incident investigation, or vendor self-disclosure, and tracked as a contractual compliance violation.

c.n: Unclassified / General Non-Compliance with Security Standards
c.d: A catch-all classification for a vendor security-standards non-compliance finding used during initial triage before the specific pattern (certification lapse vs. specific control failure) is determined.

c.n: Third-Party Violation of Data Protection Laws
Vendor GDPR Violation Affecting Customer Data
c.d: A vendor's failure to comply with GDPR obligations (lawful basis for processing, data subject rights, breach notification timelines, data minimization, etc.) with respect to personal data the vendor processes on the organization's behalf, constituting a regulatory compliance violation.

A vendor's failure to comply with an applicable US state privacy law's obligations (consumer rights to know, delete, opt out of sale/sharing, etc.) with respect to personal information the vendor processes on the organization's behalf, constituting a regulatory compliance violation.

A vendor's transfer of personal data across international borders without a valid legal transfer mechanism (such as Standard Contractual Clauses, an adequacy decision, or binding corporate rules) as required by applicable data protection law, constituting a regulatory compliance violation.

c.n: Unclassified / General Third-Party Data Protection Law Violation
c.d: A catch-all classification for a vendor's data protection law violation used during initial triage before the specific regulation and violation pattern is determined.

c.n: Vendor Sharing Customer Data with Unauthorized Sub-Processor
c.d: A vendor's disclosure of the organization's customer data to a downstream sub-processor without the disclosure, consent, or contractual approval required by the data processing agreement, constituting an unauthorized data-sharing violation.

A vendor's use of the organization's customer data for its own commercial monetization (sale, advertising, analytics-for-profit, or similar) beyond the scope of consent obtained or contractually permitted, constituting an unauthorized data-sharing violation.
A catch-all classification for a vendor's unauthorized data-sharing violation used during initial triage before the specific pattern is determined.

c.n: Vendor Delayed Breach Notification Beyond Contractual/Legal Requirement
c.d: A vendor's disclosure of a security breach affecting the organization's data or systems that occurs later than required under the contractual notification clause or applicable breach-notification law, without evidence of deliberate concealment.

c.n: Vendor Concealed Known Breach from Customer
c.d: A vendor's deliberate withholding of knowledge of a security breach affecting the organization's data or systems, discovered independently of the vendor's own disclosure (e.g., via threat intelligence, a third party, or forensic investigation), constituting active concealment rather than a mere notification delay.

c.n: Unclassified / General Failure to Disclose Vendor Breach
c.d: A catch-all classification for a vendor's failure to disclose a breach used during initial triage before the specific pattern (delay vs. concealment) is determined.

c.n: Financial and Operational Impact from Vendor Breaches
Vendor's Own Internal Fraud Discovered, Affecting Contracted Services
c.d: The discovery of internal fraud (financial misstatement, embezzlement, billing fraud) at a vendor organization, where the fraud directly affects the quality, continuity, or integrity of contracted services delivered to the organization.

c.n: Vendor Bankruptcy Following Fraud Discovery Disrupting Organization
c.d: The organizational disruption resulting from a vendor entering bankruptcy or insolvency proceedings following the discovery of internal fraud, including loss of contracted services, data-access disputes during insolvency, and asset-recovery complications.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor Financial Fraud Incident
c.d: An initial report of financial fraud discovered at a vendor organization, where the ultimate impact on the organization (service disruption short of bankruptcy, or full vendor bankruptcy) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Vendor Ransomware Attack Disrupting Shared Service Delivery
c.d: A ransomware attack against a vendor's IT environment that disrupts or halts the vendor's ability to deliver a contracted service to the organization, where the primary impact is operational/service availability rather than confirmed data exposure.

c.n: Vendor Ransomware Attack Exposing Organization's Data Held by Vendor
c.d: A ransomware attack against a vendor's IT environment in which the organization's data, held or processed by the vendor, is confirmed or strongly suspected to have been exfiltrated (double-extortion) or otherwise exposed as part of the attack.
An initial report of a ransomware attack against a vendor, where it has not yet been determined whether organizational data was exposed or whether impact is limited to service disruption.

c.n: Service Downtime Due to Vendor Breach
Unclassified / General Service Downtime Due to Vendor Breach
c.d: Operational downtime or degraded service experienced by the organization as a direct consequence of a security breach at a vendor, where the primary tracked impact is business/service disruption rather than the breach mechanism itself.

c.n: Unclassified / General Supplier Logistics and Manufacturing Disruption
c.d: A disruption to the organization's supply of goods, components, or manufacturing output resulting from a security incident (cyberattack, ransomware, system compromise) at a supplier's logistics or manufacturing operation.

c.n: Nation-State Attack on Supply Chain Vendor
Unclassified / General Nation-State Attack on Supply Chain Vendor
c.d: A full-lifecycle nation-state attack against a supply-chain vendor, in which a state-sponsored actor targets the vendor's infrastructure, software, or personnel specifically to gain access to the organization, its sector, or its customers.

c.n: Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) in Vendor Networks
Unclassified / General APT in Vendor Networks
c.d: The discovery of a sustained, persistent APT presence already established within a vendor's network — long-term access, staged infrastructure, and ongoing collection — as opposed to the initial compromise or targeting event.

c.n: Supply Chain Manipulation by Foreign Entities
Unclassified / General Supply Chain Manipulation by Foreign Entities
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected effort by a foreign state or state-affiliated entity to manipulate the broader supply chain — through ownership influence, regulatory leverage, or coordinated multi-vendor targeting — to affect the integrity of products or services reaching the organization, distinct from a single-vendor intrusion or established APT presence.

c.n: Targeted Attacks on Critical Infrastructure Vendors
Unclassified / General Targeted Attack on Critical Infrastructure Vendor
c.d: A confirmed or strongly suspected nation-state or APT attack against a vendor supplying products or services to critical infrastructure sectors (energy, water, healthcare, financial services, etc.), where the targeting is motivated by the vendor's role in supporting critical infrastructure rather than general commercial espionage.

c.n: Vendor Security Assessment Skipped or Delayed Past Schedule
c.d: A failure by the third-party risk management (TPRM) program to conduct a vendor's security assessment within the schedule defined by its risk tier, resulting in a period where the organization is operating without current insight into that vendor's security posture.

c.n: Vendor Self-Attestation Accepted Without Independent Verification
c.d: A failure by the third-party risk management (TPRM) program to independently verify a vendor's self-attestation of its security controls (via audit, evidence review, or third-party certification confirmation), resulting in a risk assessment that may materially overstate the vendor's actual security posture.

c.n: Unclassified / General Inadequate Vendor Security Audit
c.d: A catch-all classification for an inadequate vendor security audit finding used during initial triage before the specific pattern (missed schedule vs. unverified attestation) is determined.

c.n: Unmonitored Vendor Access to Internal Systems
Vendor Access Not Logged or Reviewed
c.d: A vendor risk-management failure in which a vendor's access to internal systems is either not logged in a form usable for review, or is logged but never actually reviewed on any cadence, such that misuse or compromise of that access would go undetected.

c.n: Vendor Access Granted Without Time-Bound Expiration
c.d: A vendor risk-management failure in which access to internal systems is granted to a vendor without a defined expiration date or automatic revocation tied to the engagement's end date, resulting in stale, unnecessary access that persists after the business need has ended.
A catch-all classification for an unmonitored vendor access finding used during initial triage before the specific pattern (logging/review vs. lifecycle/expiration) is determined.

c.n: Single Point of Failure Vendor with No Contingency Plan
c.d: A vendor risk-management failure in which a critical business function depends entirely on a single vendor with no documented contingency plan, alternative provider, or exit strategy, such that an outage or compromise at that vendor would directly and unavoidably disrupt the organization's operations.

c.n: Critical Function Outsourced to Vendor with Known Security Gaps
c.d: A vendor risk-management failure in which a critical business function remains outsourced to a vendor with previously identified and documented security gaps, without adequate compensating controls or a remediation plan being enforced, representing a knowing acceptance of elevated risk.

c.n: Unclassified / General Over-Reliance on High-Risk Vendor
c.d: A catch-all classification for an over-reliance-on-a-high-risk-vendor finding used during initial triage before the specific pattern (no contingency plan vs. known security gap) is determined.

c.n: Failure to Enforce Vendor Security Policies
Vendor Contract Lacking Enforceable Security Requirements
c.d: A vendor risk-management failure in which the contract governing a vendor relationship lacks specific, measurable, and enforceable security requirements (such as control specifications, audit rights, notification timelines, or remedies for non-compliance), leaving the organization unable to contractually compel or enforce an adequate security posture.

c.n: Known Vendor Security Gap Not Remediated Despite Contractual Right to Audit
c.d: A vendor risk-management failure in which a known security gap at a vendor was identified through an audit or assessment, and the organization possessed a contractual right to compel remediation, but that right was not exercised and the gap remains unresolved.

c.n: Unclassified / General Failure to Enforce Vendor Security Policy
c.d: A catch-all classification for a failure-to-enforce-vendor-security-policy finding used during initial triage before the specific pattern (contract lacking terms vs. terms present but not enforced) is determined.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Software Update (Third-Party Exploitation Context)
c.d: An incident in which a software vendor's official update mechanism (auto-updater, patch channel, or manual download from the vendor's own distribution point) delivered code that had been tampered with or replaced by an adversary, without a clearly established mechanism (injected code, forged signature, or compromised cloud build pipeline) yet confirmed.

An incident in which an adversary inserted unauthorized code into a third-party software product's source, build artifact, or distributed package, such that legitimate customers running the vendor's software unknowingly execute attacker-controlled code.

c.n: Unclassified / General Compromised Software Signing Certificate
c.d: An incident in which an adversary obtained or subverted a legitimate vendor's code-signing certificate (or induced installation of a rogue root certificate) so that malicious code passes operating-system and endpoint trust checks as genuine vendor software.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud Software Supply Chain Attack
c.d: An incident in which an adversary compromised a third-party vendor's cloud-based software delivery infrastructure — build service, artifact registry, CDN, or SaaS-hosted release pipeline — to distribute tampered software to customers.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unpatched Third-Party Application Vulnerability
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a publicly known, patchable vulnerability in a currently supported third-party application because the organization had not yet deployed the available fix.

c.n: Unclassified / General Zero-Day Exploit in Vendor Software
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a previously unknown or undisclosed vulnerability in a third-party vendor's software, for which the vendor had not yet published a patch or mitigation at the time of exploitation.

c.n: Unclassified / General API Exploitation in Third-Party Services
c.d: An incident in which an adversary abused a design flaw, authentication weakness, or logic error in a third-party service's API to achieve unauthorized access, data exposure, or functionality abuse.

c.n: Unclassified / General Legacy Third-Party Software Exploit
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a vulnerability in a third-party application that is no longer supported or patched by its vendor, regardless of whether the vulnerability was previously known.

An incident in which an adversary introduced malicious code directly into an open-source library or package that the organization consumes as a dependency, distinct from impersonation-based attacks like typosquatting or dependency confusion.

An incident in which an adversary published a public package under the same name as the organization's internal/private package, exploiting package-manager resolution order so that the build system pulls the attacker's malicious public version instead of the intended internal one.

c.n: GPL/Copyleft License Violation Discovered in Distributed Product
c.d: A compliance finding, not a security incident, in which a product the organization has distributed to customers or the public is found to include GPL/copyleft-licensed open-source code without meeting the license's source-disclosure or attribution obligations.

c.n: Unlicensed/Unauthorized Open-Source Component Usage Discovered in Audit
c.d: A compliance finding, not a security incident, in which an internal software composition audit discovers open-source components in use whose license terms are unknown, unverifiable, or were never formally reviewed and approved prior to inclusion.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insecure Open-Source License Issue
c.d: A compliance finding, not a security incident, covering any open-source license risk in a distributed product that does not fit the more specific GPL/copyleft-violation (ITID-62331) or unlicensed-component (ITID-62332) leaves.

An incident in which an adversary gained unauthorized control of an open-source project's source repository, maintainer credentials, or package-registry publishing rights, creating the capability to push malicious releases even if no malicious code has yet been distributed.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Browser Extension (Third-Party Plugin Supply Chain Context)
c.d: An incident in which a browser extension installed by an organizational user was found to perform unauthorized or malicious actions, such as data exfiltration, credential theft, or unwanted code injection into browsed pages, pending further classification.

c.n: WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited for Website Compromise
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party CMS plugin — such as a WordPress plugin — to gain unauthorized access to or control over the underlying website or hosting environment.

c.n: Malicious CMS Plugin Update Pushed by Compromised Developer Account
c.d: An incident in which an adversary compromised a CMS plugin developer's publishing account and used it to release a tampered plugin update, affecting every site that auto-updated to the malicious version.

c.n: Abandoned/Unmaintained CMS Plugin with Unpatched Vulnerability
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a vulnerability in a CMS plugin that is no longer actively maintained or supported, such that no vendor patch is forthcoming regardless of vulnerability severity.
An incident involving compromise via a CMS plugin whose specific mechanism (unpatched vulnerability, malicious developer-account update, or vendor abandonment) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Malicious ERP System Add-On Exploited for Data Access
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a malicious or vulnerable add-on/extension within an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system to gain unauthorized access to financial, supply chain, or operational data.

c.n: Compromised CRM Marketplace App Exfiltrating Customer Records
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a malicious or vulnerable third-party marketplace application connected to a customer relationship management (CRM) platform to exfiltrate customer personal or account data.
An incident involving exploitation of a third-party plugin/add-on within an ERP or CRM platform where the specific platform type or exploitation mechanism has not yet been determined.

c.n: Backdoor Introduced via Third-Party Application Add-On/Extension
c.d: An incident in which an adversary embedded persistent unauthorized access (a backdoor) into a third-party desktop, mobile, or enterprise application through an installed add-on or extension mechanism.

c.n: Malicious Macro/Script Add-In for Productivity Application (Excel/Office Add-In)
c.d: An incident in which an adversary distributed a malicious macro, script, or add-in through a productivity application's official or unofficial extension mechanism (e.g., Office/Excel add-ins), leading to code execution on the recipient's system.

An incident involving a backdoor introduced via a third-party application add-on or extension whose specific delivery mechanism (general add-on versus productivity-suite macro/script) has not yet been determined.

An incident in which insecure configuration settings applied by the organization within a third-party SaaS application — such as overly permissive sharing defaults, disabled security controls, or exposed public endpoints — resulted in unauthorized access or data exposure.

c.n: Unclassified / General OAuth/SSO Abuse (Third-Party SaaS Context)
c.d: An incident in which an adversary abused OAuth authorization grants, refresh tokens, or single sign-on trust relationships to gain or maintain unauthorized access to a third-party SaaS application without directly compromising the user's primary password.

c.n: Unclassified / General Account Takeover in Third-Party Service
c.d: An incident in which an adversary obtained a legitimate user's direct login credentials for a third-party SaaS service (via phishing, credential stuffing, or password reuse) and used them to log in as that user.

c.n: Unclassified / General Third-Party API Exploitation in SaaS
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a design flaw, authorization weakness, or logic error in a third-party SaaS application's own API to access data or functionality beyond what the requesting party should be permitted.

c.n: Code Injection in Continuous Integration Pipelines
Unclassified / General CI Pipeline Code Injection
c.d: An incident in which an adversary injected malicious code, commands, or configuration into the organization's continuous integration (CI) pipeline, causing unauthorized code to execute during build, test, or packaging stages.

c.n: Supply Chain Attack via Code Repositories
Unclassified / General Supply Chain Attack via Code Repository
c.d: An incident in which an adversary gained unauthorized access to the organization's code repository hosting platform — through stolen credentials, exploited platform vulnerabilities, or misconfigured access controls — enabling tampering with source code prior to any CI pipeline stage.

c.n: Compromised Secrets Manager/Vault Exposing Credentials to Pipeline
c.d: An incident in which an adversary gained unauthorized access to a secrets manager or credential vault integrated with the organization's DevOps toolchain, exposing API keys, passwords, or certificates used across the pipeline.

c.n: Compromised Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) Template Injecting Malicious Resources
c.d: An incident in which an adversary modified an infrastructure-as-code template or configuration (e.g., Terraform, CloudFormation) to provision unauthorized cloud resources, backdoored network paths, or overly permissive access when the pipeline applies the change.

c.n: Compromised Artifact Repository (Internal Package Registry) Poisoning
c.d: An incident in which an adversary gained unauthorized write access to an internal artifact repository or package registry, replacing or injecting malicious versions of internally built software components consumed by downstream teams.
An incident involving compromise of a DevOps toolchain component whose specific type (secrets manager, IaC template, or artifact repository) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Malicious Public Container Image Pulled from Docker Hub
c.d: An incident in which a developer or automated pipeline pulled a malicious container image directly from a public container registry, introducing attacker-controlled code into a build or production environment.

c.n: Backdoored Base Image Used Across Multiple Internal Builds
c.d: An incident in which a container base image that had already been compromised (whether pulled maliciously or tampered with after ingestion) was used as the foundation for multiple internal application builds, propagating the backdoor across many downstream containers.

c.n: Container Image Registry Poisoning (Legitimate Tag Overwritten)
c.d: An incident in which an adversary gained sufficient registry access to overwrite an existing, previously trusted container image tag with a malicious version, causing downstream pulls of that tag to silently receive attacker-controlled content.
An incident involving a malicious container image whose specific mechanism (initial public-registry ingestion, internal base-image propagation, or registry tag overwrite) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Unauthorized Data Access via Third-Party Software
Third-Party App Over-Permissioned OAuth Scope Leaking Data
c.d: An incident in which a third-party application, granted OAuth authorization with an overly broad data-access scope, leaked or improperly exposed organizational data as a result of that excess permission rather than a direct attack.

c.n: Third-Party App Vulnerability Exposing Customer Data at Rest
c.d: An incident in which a security vulnerability in a third-party application — such as a misconfigured database, insecure storage bucket, or flawed access control — directly exposed customer data at rest.

c.n: Unclassified / General Data Leakage from Third-Party App
c.d: An incident involving data leakage from a third-party application whose specific mechanism (over-broad OAuth scope versus a direct data-at-rest vulnerability) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Unauthorized Cross-Tenant Access in Multi-Tenant Software
Unclassified / General Cross-Tenant Access (Third-Party Software Context)
c.d: An incident in which a flaw in a multi-tenant third-party software platform's tenant-isolation mechanism allowed the organization's data to be accessed by, or the organization to inadvertently access, another customer's tenant environment.

c.n: File Sharing Platform Vulnerability Exploited for Unauthorized Access
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party file sharing or collaboration platform to gain unauthorized access to files or folders beyond what any legitimate sharing configuration intended.

c.n: File Sharing Link Permission Bypass Vulnerability
c.d: An incident in which a flaw in a file sharing platform's link-permission logic allowed a party to access a shared file or folder beyond the access level, audience, or expiration the original sharer configured.

c.n: Unclassified / General Third-Party File Sharing Exploit
c.d: An incident involving unauthorized file access through a third-party file sharing platform whose specific mechanism (core platform vulnerability versus link-permission bypass) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Unclassified / General ERP/Financial Software Exploit (Data Access Context)
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a vulnerability or weakness in the core third-party ERP or financial software platform itself to gain unauthorized access to financial records, payroll data, or other sensitive business data.

c.n: Third-Party Software Abuse for Initial Access
Legitimate Remote Access Software (TeamViewer/AnyDesk) Used by Attacker via Stolen Credential
c.d: An incident in which an adversary used stolen or phished credentials to operate a legitimate, already-installed remote access software tool as their initial access or persistence mechanism, blending malicious activity with expected administrative tooling behavior.

c.n: Remote Access Software Vulnerability Exploited for Unauthorized Access
c.d: An incident in which an adversary exploited a software vulnerability in a remote access or RMM tool to gain unauthorized access, bypassing the need for valid credentials.

c.n: Unclassified / General Remote Access Software Exploit
c.d: An incident involving unauthorized use of remote access software whose specific mechanism (stolen-credential abuse versus exploitation of the tool's own vulnerability) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Trojanized Legitimate Software Installer Distributed via Official Channel
c.d: An incident in which an adversary tampered with a legitimate software installer such that malicious code was bundled or embedded within it, and the tampered installer was then distributed via the vendor's official website or app store rather than an unofficial third-party source.

c.n: Malware Bundled with Legitimate Freeware/Utility Software
c.d: An incident in which a user downloaded legitimate freeware or utility software from an unofficial or third-party aggregator site that had bundled additional malicious code with the installer.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malware Distribution via Legitimate Software
c.d: An incident involving malware distributed alongside otherwise-legitimate software whose specific distribution channel (official vendor channel versus unofficial aggregator) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Fake Meeting Invite (Zoom/Teams) Link Used for Credential Phishing
c.d: An incident in which an adversary sent a fraudulent meeting invitation impersonating a legitimate video-conferencing tool (such as Zoom or Microsoft Teams) containing a link to a credential-harvesting page.

c.n: Fake Calendar/Scheduling Tool Invite Used as Phishing Vector
c.d: An incident in which an adversary sent a fraudulent calendar or scheduling-tool invitation (such as a fake Calendly or Outlook scheduling link) to deliver a phishing link or malicious payload to the recipient.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Engineering via Third-Party Tool
c.d: An incident involving social engineering conducted through impersonation of a third-party productivity or collaboration tool whose specific type (video-conferencing versus scheduling tool) has not yet been determined.
An incident in which an adversary exploited a vulnerability in the core third-party CRM platform itself to gain unauthorized initial access to the organization's environment or customer data.

c.n: Regulatory and Compliance Risks in Third-Party Software
Failure to Monitor Third-Party Software Security
Unclassified / General Failure to Monitor Third-Party Software Security
c.d: A governance finding, not a technical security incident, in which the organization is found to have failed to establish or maintain an ongoing security-monitoring process for a third-party software vendor, leaving vendor-side risk unassessed over time.

c.n: Unclassified / General Vendor Non-Compliance with Security Standards (Third-Party Software Context)
c.d: A governance finding, not a technical security incident, in which a specific third-party software vendor is found to be non-compliant with a contractually required or industry-standard security control or certification.

c.n: Third-Party Software with Hidden Telemetry or Spyware
Vendor Software Found to Contain Undisclosed Data Collection/Telemetry
c.d: An incident in which a third-party vendor's software is found to contain undisclosed telemetry or data-collection functionality that transmits organizational or customer data to the vendor or a third party without authorization or disclosure.

c.n: Vendor Software Found to Contain Covert Backdoor Access for Vendor's Own Use
c.d: An incident in which a third-party vendor's software is found to contain an undisclosed backdoor providing the vendor (or a party acting on the vendor's behalf) covert remote access to the organization's systems or data, independent of any legitimate support or maintenance access agreement.

c.n: Unclassified / General Hidden Telemetry or Spyware in Third-Party Software
c.d: An incident involving suspected hidden telemetry or spyware functionality in third-party vendor software whose specific mechanism (undisclosed data collection versus a deliberate covert remote-access backdoor) has not yet been determined.

c.n: Legal Risks from Third-Party Software Breaches
Class Action Litigation Following Vendor-Caused Data Breach
c.d: A legal risk finding, not a technical security incident, in which the organization becomes the subject of class action litigation as a downstream consequence of a data breach originating in a third-party software vendor's environment or product.

c.n: Regulatory Fine Imposed on Organization for Vendor's Security Failure
c.d: A legal/regulatory risk finding, not a technical security incident, in which a regulator imposes a fine or penalty on the organization for a security or privacy failure whose root cause traces to a third-party software vendor.

c.n: Unclassified / General Legal Risk from Third-Party Software Breach
c.d: A legal risk finding, not a technical security incident, involving legal exposure from a vendor-caused security failure whose specific form (civil litigation versus regulatory fine) has not yet been determined, or which takes a different legal form entirely (e.g., contractual dispute, indemnification claim).

c.n: Counterfeit Networking Equipment (Switches/Routers) in Supply Chain
c.d: The introduction of non-genuine networking equipment — devices manufactured or re-badged without OEM authorization — into procurement, deployment, or spares inventory, where the equipment is sold or represented as authentic vendor hardware.

c.n: Counterfeit Server/Component Hardware Sold as Genuine
c.d: The introduction of non-genuine server systems or internal components into procurement, deployment, or spares inventory, where the hardware is represented as authentic OEM product.
General or not-yet-classified reports of counterfeit hardware — end-user devices, peripherals, or other equipment types — introduced into procurement or inventory and represented as genuine.

c.n: Unclassified / General Hardware Backdoor (Physical Supply Chain Context)
c.d: A deliberate physical modification to a device's hardware (an added chip, altered circuit, or implanted component) intended to grant covert access or capability, introduced at some point in the physical supply chain (manufacturing, distribution, or in-transit tampering) rather than through firmware alone.

Evidence that a shipment's physical security (seals, packaging, chain-of-custody) was compromised in transit, indicating a window of opportunity for tampering, theft, or substitution, regardless of whether a specific hardware modification has yet been confirmed.

c.n: Power Analysis Attack Extracting Cryptographic Keys
c.d: An attack in which an adversary with physical or close proximity access to a device measures its power consumption during cryptographic operations to statistically infer secret key material, without needing to break the underlying algorithm.

An attack that abuses a CPU's speculative or out-of-order execution behavior (and its measurable timing/cache side effects) to read memory that should be inaccessible to the attacker, such as across process, VM, or privilege boundaries.

An attack in which an adversary with physical or close proximity access to a device captures and analyzes its electromagnetic emissions during operation to infer secret data, without requiring direct electrical contact with the device.
General or not-yet-classified reports of a hardware side-channel attack — such as timing analysis, acoustic cryptanalysis, or fault-injection — used to extract sensitive data from a physical device.
The physical theft of goods — an entire shipment, container, or portion of cargo — while in the custody of a carrier, at a transfer point, or in transit between supply chain nodes.

c.n: Fraudulent Shipment Diversion (Fake Delivery Address Redirect)
c.d: The rerouting of a legitimate shipment to an unauthorized delivery address through falsified delivery instructions, impersonation, or manipulation of shipping records, resulting in the goods being delivered into the adversary's control rather than the intended recipient's.
The use of a fabricated or impersonated freight-brokerage identity to insert an adversary into a legitimate shipping transaction, allowing them to take possession of cargo, redirect payment, or both.

c.n: Unclassified / General Supply Chain Theft and Fraud
c.d: General or not-yet-classified reports of theft or fraud affecting a shipment in the logistics/transportation chain.

c.n: Malicious Insider at a Logistics Provider

c.d: An employee of a carrier, warehouse, or logistics partner who uses their legitimate access or role to directly facilitate the physical theft of cargo — for example, by diverting a load, disabling security controls, or colluding with external thieves during handling.

c.n: Logistics Employee Providing Shipment Details to External Thieves
c.d: An employee of a carrier, warehouse, or logistics partner who discloses non-public shipment information (route, timing, contents, security details) to an external party, enabling that party to carry out a theft.

c.n: Unclassified / General Malicious Insider at a Logistics Provider
c.d: General or not-yet-classified reports of a logistics provider employee acting maliciously against the shipments or operations they have legitimate access to.

c.n: Deliberate Damage to Critical Hardware Shipment
c.d: An act of deliberate sabotage causing physical damage to a shipment of critical hardware, intended to render it unusable or delay its deployment, as opposed to theft or covert modification.

c.n: Contamination/Tampering of Perishable or Sensitive Goods in Transit
c.d: An act of deliberate contamination, adulteration, or tampering with perishable or sensitive goods (e.g., pharmaceuticals, chemicals, sensitive materials) during transport, intended to render the goods unsafe, unusable, or non-compliant.

c.n: Unclassified / General Destructive Sabotage of Critical Shipment
c.d: General or not-yet-classified reports of destructive sabotage against a shipment in the logistics chain.

c.n: Unauthorized Third-Shift Production Run at Contract Manufacturer (Overproduction Cloning)
c.d: The unauthorized manufacture of extra units of a legitimate device design by a contract manufacturer or OEM partner, beyond the quantity authorized by the design owner, typically sold covertly outside the authorized channel.

c.n: Device Design/IP Cloned and Sold as Counterfeit by Unauthorized Manufacturer
c.d: The unauthorized reproduction of a device's design, intellectual property, or trade dress by a manufacturer that has no legitimate authorization from the design owner, with the resulting devices sold as if they were genuine or equivalent.

c.n: Cloned Device with Duplicate Serial Number/IMEI Introduced into Supply Chain
c.d: A cloned or counterfeit device programmed with a serial number, IMEI, or other unique identifier copied from a genuine unit, enabling it to pass identity-based validation checks or to impersonate the genuine device on a network.
General or not-yet-classified reports of unauthorized device cloning encountered in manufacturing or the supply chain.

c.n: RFID, Barcode, and Asset Tag Spoofing
RFID Tag Cloning for Unauthorized Inventory Removal
c.d: The duplication of a legitimate RFID tag's identifier onto a cloned tag or device, used to make an unauthorized item removal appear as an authorized/tracked movement, or to bypass RFID-based exit alarms.

The deliberate replacement or alteration of a barcode label on a physical item so that it scans as a different, typically lower-value, item or price, enabling fraudulent purchase, shipment, or inventory records.

c.n: Asset Tag Spoofing to Evade Inventory Tracking
c.d: The deliberate falsification, duplication, or removal of an asset tag so that an item's presence, location, or status in the inventory-tracking system no longer reflects reality, enabling the item to go unaccounted-for.
General or not-yet-classified reports of tag-based inventory-tracking spoofing encountered in a warehouse or storage facility.

The act of an unauthorized individual gaining physical entry to a secure warehouse or storage facility by following closely behind an authorized person through a controlled access point, without presenting their own valid credential.

c.n: Compromised Access Badge Used for Unauthorized Warehouse Entry
c.d: The use of a lost, stolen, cloned, or otherwise compromised physical access badge/credential to gain unauthorized entry to a secure warehouse or storage facility.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unauthorized Storage Facility Access
c.d: General or not-yet-classified reports of unauthorized physical access to a warehouse or storage facility.

c.n: Inventory Record Falsification to Conceal Theft
c.d: The deliberate alteration of inventory records — counts, movement logs, or reconciliation entries — to make stolen or missing goods appear accounted for, concealing an underlying theft.

c.n: Inventory System Manipulation for Fraudulent Stock Write-Off
c.d: The deliberate manipulation of inventory system write-off, damage, or obsolescence processes to remove stock from the books as a pretext for diverting it, rather than concealing a theft that has already occurred.
General or not-yet-classified reports of inventory data manipulation encountered in a warehouse or storage facility.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Threat in Warehousing
c.d: Malicious or negligent action by a warehouse employee or contractor that abuses their legitimate physical or system access to harm inventory integrity, security, or operations, not otherwise captured by the more specific access, inventory, or tag-spoofing leaves.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cloud Environment Compromise (Critical Infrastructure Supply Chain Context)
c.d: Unauthorized access to or compromise of a cloud service environment supporting critical infrastructure, where the compromise originates from or is enabled by a physical supply chain weakness — such as compromised hardware supplied to the cloud provider, or credentials/access obtained through a physical intrusion or insider at a facility.

The compromise of a cellular base station or tower equipment through hardware introduced or altered somewhere in its supply chain, enabling covert access, interception, or disruption of the mobile network segment it serves.

c.n: Nation-State Compromise of Telecom Carrier Core Network Equipment
c.d: A nation-state or nation-state-affiliated actor's compromise of a telecommunications carrier's core network equipment (switching, routing, or signaling infrastructure) via the hardware supply chain, enabling large-scale surveillance, interception, or disruption capability.

The compromise of a submarine cable landing station's physical or hardware infrastructure, enabling covert access, interception, or disruption of the international telecommunications traffic passing through it.
General or not-yet-classified reports of compromised telecommunications equipment encountered in the critical infrastructure supply chain.

c.n: Nation-State and APT Supply Chain Attacks
Unclassified / General Nation-State Tampering with Critical Equipment
c.d: Deliberate tampering with critical infrastructure or mission-essential equipment attributed to a nation-state or nation-state-affiliated actor, occurring at any point in the physical supply chain, intended to establish long-term strategic access, disruption capability, or intelligence advantage.

c.n: Combined Cyber Intrusion and Physical Hardware Implant Attack
c.d: An attack in which an adversary combines remote cyber intrusion techniques with the physical installation of a hardware implant (an added component, device, or modification) on target infrastructure, using each vector to reinforce or enable the other.

c.n: Cyber Attack Triggering Physical Equipment Malfunction/Damage
c.d: An attack conducted entirely through remote or network-based means that manipulates a system's control logic or firmware to cause physical malfunction, damage, or destruction of the equipment it controls.
General or not-yet-classified reports of an attack combining cyber and physical elements against critical equipment in the supply chain.

c.n: Intellectual Property Theft via Supply Chain Exploits
Unclassified / General IP Theft via Supply Chain Exploit
c.d: The theft of proprietary intellectual property (designs, trade secrets, source material) by an adversary who gains access through a physical supply chain relationship — such as a contract manufacturer, component supplier, or logistics partner — rather than through a purely remote cyber intrusion.

c.n: Unclassified / General Large-Scale Supply Chain Manipulation
c.d: A coordinated, large-scale campaign by a nation-state or APT actor to manipulate multiple points in the physical supply chain (manufacturers, distributors, or logistics providers) simultaneously, intended to achieve broad strategic access or disruption capability across many downstream targets.

c.n: Regulatory and Compliance Risks in Physical Supply Chains
Unclassified / General Vendor Non-Compliance with Security Requirements (Physical Supply Chain Context)
c.d: A finding that a vendor, manufacturer, or logistics partner in the physical supply chain has failed to meet the security requirements specified in contract, policy, or applicable regulation, creating elevated risk exposure independent of whether an actual compromise has occurred.

c.n: Sub-Tier Supplier Unknown/Unmapped in Supply Chain Risk Assessment
c.d: A finding that a supplier below the organization's direct (Tier-1) vendor relationships — a sub-tier or fourth-party supplier — is materially involved in producing components or services the organization relies on, but was not identified, assessed, or risk-rated as part of the supply chain risk management program.

c.n: Lack of Chain-of-Custody Tracking for Critical Components
c.d: A finding that a critical component's chain-of-custody records — the documented history of its handling from manufacture through delivery — are incomplete, missing, or otherwise insufficient to verify the component's provenance and integrity.

c.n: Unclassified / General Supply Chain Visibility Failure
c.d: General or not-yet-classified reports of a gap in the organization's visibility into its physical supply chain.

A finding that a supplier or third-party manufacturer was granted an active role in the physical supply chain without completing the organization's required background, security, or risk vetting process.

c.n: Unauthorized Fourth-Party Subcontractor Used Without Disclosure
c.d: A finding that a properly vetted, authorized supplier has engaged a fourth-party subcontractor to perform work without disclosing this relationship to the organization, bypassing the requirement for the organization to assess and approve that subcontractor.

c.n: Unclassified / General Unverified Supplier or Manufacturer
c.d: General or not-yet-classified reports of a supplier or manufacturer operating in the physical supply chain without adequate verification.

c.n: Counterfeit or Unauthorized Components in Supply Chain
Unclassified / General Counterfeit or Unauthorized Component in Supply Chain
c.d: A finding, typically surfaced through supplier audit, procurement compliance review, or regulatory inspection, that a counterfeit or otherwise unauthorized (non-genuine, unapproved-source) component has entered the supply chain, considered here as a governance/vetting failure rather than an active-attack event.

c.n: Unclassified / General Executive Impersonation Attack (Trust Exploitation Context)
c.d: An adversary impersonates a trusted executive (real name, title, or authority) to manipulate a supplier, partner, or internal staff member into taking an action they would not otherwise take, where the operative mechanism is abuse of the trust placed in that executive's identity rather than a technical compromise of an account or system.

c.n: Spear Phishing Based on Trusted Relationships

c.d: A targeted phishing attempt that derives its credibility not from generic impersonation but from genuine knowledge of, or access to, an established trust relationship (a real vendor contact, a real internal colleague, a real project history) between the sender and the target.

c.n: Unclassified / General Fake Vendor/Supplier Scam (Trust Exploitation Context)
c.d: An adversary fabricates or impersonates a vendor/supplier identity (invoicing, onboarding, or account-update contact) with no genuine prior relationship, exploiting the general trust organizations extend to counterparties presenting as legitimate suppliers.

c.n: Unclassified / General Social Media Engineering of Employees
c.d: An adversary uses social media platforms to research, befriend, or otherwise manipulate an employee into disclosing information or taking an action that furthers a later trust-exploitation attack, distinct from a direct phishing or impersonation attempt.

c.n: Stolen Code-Signing Certificate Used to Sign Malware
c.d: An adversary obtains a legitimate organization's code-signing certificate (via theft, breach, or unauthorized issuance) and uses it to sign malicious code, exploiting the trust that operating systems, security tools, and users place in a valid digital signature.

c.n: Stolen TLS Certificate Private Key Used for MITM
c.d: An adversary obtains the private key associated with a legitimate organization's TLS certificate and uses it to stand up a spoofed, seemingly-valid endpoint or to decrypt/inject into intercepted traffic, exploiting the trust clients place in the certificate's validity.

c.n: Unclassified / General Stolen Certificate or Digital Signature
c.d: A generalized case of a stolen digital certificate or signing credential being misused to exploit trust, where the specific certificate type or usage does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Misuse of Trusted Third-Party Access
c.d: An adversary leverages access, credentials, or a connection that was legitimately extended to a trusted third party (vendor, contractor, managed service provider) to reach the organization's environment or data, exploiting the trust relationship itself rather than a separate technical vulnerability.

c.n: Cross-Domain Trust Relationship Abused for Privilege Escalation
c.d: An adversary exploits an established cross-domain trust configuration (e.g., federated identity, cross-forest Active Directory trust, cross-tenant application trust) to escalate privilege or move from a lower-trust domain into a higher-trust one.

c.n: Inherited Trust from Parent Company/Subsidiary Relationship Abused
c.d: An adversary exploits the implicit or configured trust extended between a parent company and its subsidiary (or between merged/acquired entities) to escalate privilege from the less-secure entity into the more-secure one, distinct from a purely technical cross-domain trust configuration.
A generalized case of privilege escalation achieved by abusing some form of established trust relationship, where the specific trust mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

c.n: Zero-Day in SAML/OIDC Authentication Protocol Implementation
c.d: An adversary exploits a zero-day flaw in a SAML or OIDC implementation (e.g., signature validation bypass, assertion replay, token confusion) to forge or manipulate authentication assertions, defeating the trust that relying parties place in the identity provider's signed tokens.

An adversary exploits a zero-day flaw in a Kerberos implementation (e.g., ticket validation bypass, encryption downgrade) to forge or misuse Kerberos tickets, defeating the trust the domain places in properly issued tickets.

c.n: Unclassified / General Zero-Day Exploit in Authentication Protocol
c.d: A generalized case of a previously unknown authentication-protocol vulnerability being exploited to defeat trust in an authentication assertion or ticket, where the specific protocol does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

An adversary technically compromises and exfiltrates or gains unauthorized use of a Certificate Authority's intermediate signing key, enabling them to mint certificates that inherit the CA's root of trust, exploiting the trust every relying party places in that CA's chain.

c.n: Rogue CA Certificate Issued via Social Engineering of CA Staff
c.d: An adversary manipulates Certificate Authority staff or its validation process (e.g., forged domain-control evidence, impersonated requester, deceived validation reviewer) into issuing a certificate for a domain or identity the adversary does not legitimately control, exploiting trust in the CA's human validation process.

c.n: CA Infrastructure Breached to Issue Unauthorized Certificates at Scale
c.d: An adversary breaches a Certificate Authority's broader infrastructure (issuance systems, databases, automation pipelines) beyond a single key or a single social-engineered validation, enabling issuance of unauthorized certificates across many domains or identities at scale.
A generalized case of a Certificate Authority compromise undermining certificate trust, where the specific mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

c.n: Corporate TLS Inspection Proxy Abused for Unauthorized Interception
c.d: An adversary (external attacker or malicious insider) abuses a legitimately deployed, organization-operated TLS inspection/interception proxy to decrypt and access traffic outside the proxy's authorized policy scope, exploiting the trust employees and systems place in the corporate network.

c.n: Rogue Certificate Installed on Endpoint to Enable TLS Interception
c.d: An adversary installs a rogue root or intermediate certificate into an endpoint's trust store (via social engineering, malware, or physical access) to enable transparent interception of that endpoint's TLS traffic, exploiting the trust the operating system places in its certificate store.

c.n: Unclassified / General MitM via TLS Interception
c.d: A generalized case of TLS interception undermining trust in encrypted communications, where the specific mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

c.n: Weakened Random Number Generator Backdoor in Cryptographic Library
c.d: A covert, technical weakening of the entropy or algorithm behind a cryptographic library's random number generator (e.g., a deliberately predictable or backdoored PRNG), undermining the trust users place in the library's stated cryptographic strength.

c.n: Key Escrow Backdoor Mandated in Encryption Product
c.d: An adversary (or an authorized party acting beyond legitimate scope) exploits an overtly built-in, policy-mandated key-escrow or backdoor mechanism in an encryption product to access data or communications the mechanism was ostensibly restricted to authorize, undermining trust in the product's confidentiality guarantees.

c.n: Unclassified / General Cryptographic Backdoor in Trusted Software
c.d: A generalized case of a cryptographic backdoor undermining trust in a product's encryption, where the specific mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

An adversary exploits a technical bypass in an operating system's or application's code-signing verification logic (rather than obtaining a valid or stolen certificate) to make malicious code appear as validly signed, exploiting the trust the verification mechanism is supposed to guarantee.

c.n: Fake/Lookalike Publisher Name Used to Spoof Trusted Signer
c.d: An adversary registers or presents a publisher/signer name that is visually or semantically similar to a legitimate, trusted vendor (e.g., a homoglyph or near-identical company name) to induce users or systems to trust signed code that is not actually from the vendor it appears to represent.

c.n: Unclassified / General Code Signing Mechanism Spoofing
c.d: A generalized case of code-signing mechanism spoofing undermining trust in signed code, where the specific technique does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Abuse of Trusted Business Partner
c.d: An adversary, or a compromised legitimate actor, exploits the trust extended to a formal business partner (joint venture, reseller, distributor, franchise) to gain access, information, or advantage beyond the scope of the legitimate partnership.

c.n: Supply Chain Fraud via Trust Exploitation
Unclassified / General Supply Chain Fraud via Trust Exploitation
c.d: An adversary defrauds the organization or a supply chain partner by exploiting the trust inherent in an established supply chain relationship (e.g., falsified shipment confirmations, fraudulent purchase order diversion, counterfeit goods passed off as genuine via a trusted channel).

c.n: Unclassified / General Exploiting Trust in Software Dependency
c.d: An adversary exploits the trust an organization places in a software dependency's maintainer identity, publishing account, or distribution channel (e.g., a compromised or socially engineered maintainer account pushing a malicious update) rather than exploiting a code-level vulnerability in the dependency itself.

c.n: Fake Webhook Payload Injected to Trigger Unauthorized Action (Fake Payment Confirmation)
c.d: An adversary crafts and delivers a forged webhook payload to a system that trusts webhook callbacks from a given source, inducing the receiving system to take an unauthorized action (e.g., marking a payment as confirmed, releasing goods, granting access) based on the forged event.

c.n: Webhook Endpoint Spoofed to Intercept Legitimate Trusted Callback
c.d: An adversary registers or configures a spoofed webhook endpoint (e.g., via a subdomain takeover, DNS manipulation, or configuration tampering) to receive callbacks intended for a legitimate trusted endpoint, intercepting the data or triggering downstream effects that depend on the callback reaching only the legitimate party.

c.n: Unclassified / General API and Webhook Manipulation
c.d: A generalized case of API or webhook manipulation undermining trust in an automated integration, where the specific mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.

c.n: Unclassified / General Rogue Employee in Trusted Position
c.d: A currently employed individual holding a position of significant organizational trust (executive, administrator, or otherwise privileged role) deliberately abuses that position for personal gain, sabotage, or on behalf of a third party, exploiting the trust inherent in their role.

c.n: Unclassified / General Insider Abuse of Privileged Access (Trust Exploitation Context)
c.d: An insider uses privileged access legitimately granted for their role to take actions beyond their intended authorization, exploiting the organizational trust that access was granted to be used only within its intended scope.

c.n: Segregation-of-Duties Bypass via Colluding Trusted Approvers
c.d: Two or more individuals who each legitimately hold a portion of an approval workflow's required authorization collude to jointly approve a transaction or action that segregation-of-duties controls were specifically designed to prevent any single individual from approving alone, exploiting the organizational trust placed in the segregation control's integrity.

c.n: Delegated Approval Authority Abused Beyond Intended Scope
c.d: An individual who has been delegated approval authority (e.g., to act on behalf of a manager while they are unavailable) uses that delegated authority to approve actions outside the scope, value threshold, or time window for which the delegation was intended, exploiting the trust placed in the delegation arrangement.
